paragraphs.text: THE WORKS OF ST PAULINUS OF NOLA, PART ONE: LETTERS.
1. Paulinus, servant of Christ Jesus, to Severus, his dearest brother according to our common faith: greetings in God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour.

How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth! My heart was, as it were, anointed with the honey of your words, and I plainly felt the truth of holy Scripture where it says: Good words fatten the bones. It does not mean, of course, the bones whose structure binds us together into a serviceable body, but those that hold the strength of the inner man, namely hope, faith and love. These are the bowels of mercy, the bones of patience and the limbs of every virtue. You have enriched these bones, limbs and inward parts with holy words of hope, faith and love. Through them you have taught that the hope of your faith is fixed on the Lord, that the faith of your hope stands firm in the Lord, and that the fullness of love abides in Christ, just as God's own love toward us abides. I was anxious and longing for news, yet I believed nothing else of you, or rather of God, who works out and perfects his power even in the weak. Then you told me of the increase of your patrimony in heaven, which you have achieved for your salvation by boiling away your present burdens. At the price of frail possessions you have purchased heaven and Christ, truly giving heed to the needy and the poor. You believed that the poor man is in Christ, and that in him, as Christ himself taught, Christ is clothed, fed and lent to.

Let this be an odour of death unto death to those who are perishing, to whom the flesh and the cross of the living God are foolishness or a stumbling block, because the flesh and blood they serve does not reveal to them that Christ Jesus is the Son of God. For us, however, may faith in the divine flesh and death become an odour of life unto life. And let not our feet be moved, dearest brother, from the ways of the Lord and from the track of the narrow road if at times the profane or foolish words of certain worldly people bark around us. Through the sacred writings we have been well enough instructed about them and about ourselves. Of them the blessed apostle tells us that we toil and are cursed for this, because we hope in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, especially of the faithful. With his own mouth in the Gospels he also foretold both the poison in the talk of the very people to whom you wish to give an account and what they deserve in punishment: Woe to those who cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble! It would be better for that man to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be thrown into the depths of the sea. But to us he says: Blessed are you when men curse you and say every evil against you and reproach my name as evil; rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven. Let us hold fast to these words of the Lord, my brother, and be strengthened in our faith, paying no attention to the reproaches or the hatred of unbelievers. They walk in darkness, because the sun of righteousness has not risen for them. The poison of asps is under their lips. It infects the mind and kills the soul if it is received by the ears and works its way into the heart. Their heart, says divine Scripture, is vain, and their throat is an open grave. Let us beware of their leaven, lest it corrupt the whole lump. For it is written: The wicked shall not dwell near you; and again: With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be overthrown; and: Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity. Stop up your ears, brother, and hedge them with thorns against their words. Those words are the thorns and arrows of the devil, who lurks hidden in their hearts and lies in ambush in secret, to seize Christ's poor man and hunt down the soul of a Christian. But, as it is written, their iniquity will come back upon their own heads, and they will fall into the pit they are digging.

But you, man of God, flee from these people. Do not labour to give an account to them as though they were wiser, since you know that the beginning of wisdom is in your keeping, for you fear the Lord. If they think what we are doing is foolish, rejoice in a good conscience, because you are doing the work of God and the command of Christ. Remember that God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and that the foolishness of God is wiser than men. To wish to clear oneself before such people is as good as being ready to deny Christ himself. He in turn will be ashamed to acknowledge before the Father those of his own who are ashamed of his name before this world.

You write that you are labouring to give an account of what I have done and what you have done. What will you do, then, if you fail to persuade men who argue with you about the work of God not to build themselves up but to destroy you? At once you will blush and grow pale, like the advocate of the weaker cause. Shaken from your footing, you will stagger on the way of the Lord and slip back from heaven to earth if you tear down what you have built. It matters a great deal who these people are to whom an account must be given. If someone comes eager to learn and admits his ignorance, scatter the seed of faith on him and unfold the divine command. If he receives the word, you have won a brother for the Church and a sheep for Christ. But he may not be a pure shoot from good seed. He may be harmful grass, sown among the wheat in the night by the enemy of the heavenly householder, an unhappy crop to be separated from the good grain at harvest, destined not for the barns but for the furnaces, material to burn as fodder for the eternal fire, growing meanwhile for its own burning. If so, flee from him and drive him from your conversation and your sight, so that if he cannot be healed by your faith, he may not wound you with his unbelief.

He may be your brother, a friend more closely joined to you than your right hand and dearer than your eye. Yet if he is a stranger and an enemy in Christ, let him be to you as an outsider and a tax collector. Whoever does not cleave to you in the body of Christ, let him be cut off from your body like a useless right hand. Let him be plucked out like an offending eye that darkens your whole body with its blemish or blindness. For it is better that one member should perish for the safety of the whole body than that the whole body, as the Lord says, should go into Gehenna for love of one diseased member. Nor should we fear offending such people. Indeed, we should even desire it, since from their reproaches and curses is born that reward which God has promised will be great in heaven. The disciple, he says, is not above his teacher, nor the servant above his master; and if they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more those of his household? If they have loved the Lord and God whom we follow, they will love us too; if they have persecuted him, they will persecute us too. What do we want with the favour of the world, which is hatred of Christ? If you were of the world, he says, the world would love its own.

You, then, who seek to give an account to men, and to unbelievers at that, consider what you are longing for. It is surely the favour of men, that is, of the world, and you cannot please the world unless you choose to displease Christ. For, he says, if I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ. Let us therefore displease these people, and rejoice that we displease those whom God also displeases. As you know, it is not our work they attack, but the work in us of the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, of almighty God. Him whom they scorn in their own actions they hate in our works. Too late they will say: Lord, when did we see you naked and not clothe you? hungry and not feed you? sick and not visit you? And then they will hear: Depart into the eternal fire which God has prepared for your father and his angels. For what they do not do for the needy they refuse to Christ, who, though he was rich, became poor, so that by his poverty he might make us rich.

Meanwhile let them enjoy their pleasures, honours and riches, if indeed these are really theirs. They prefer to possess them here, where we cease to be, rather than there, where we go on being. Let them keep their wisdom and their happiness for themselves, and leave us our poverty, as they think it, and our foolishness. They confess our God in name but deny him in deed, having the appearance of godliness but denying its power. Yet let them, if they like, claim prudence for themselves and reproach us with folly on the strength of the words of that very God. For the Lord says: The children of this world are wiser than the children of light. But he added: in their generation. Let them be more prudent, so long as they are not children of light. Let them be wise for one generation, so long as in that regeneration of ours they are found senseless. Let them be blessed now, or rather fortunate, drifting through every prosperity while the world flatters them. Let them be clothed in soft garments and live in the houses of kings, so long as they are not in trouble like other men and are not scourged like other men. Let them be rich in the world, since they are poor before God. Of them it is written: The rich have been in want and gone hungry; just as of us it is added at once: But those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing.

Would that we were counted worthy, my brother, to be cursed, branded, crushed and even killed in the name of Jesus Christ, so long as Christ himself is not killed in us. Then at last we would walk upon the asp and the basilisk and trample the head of the ancient dragon. But as yet, and this is worse, we are made slack by a friendly world and take our ease in Christ. We love only to be praised in his name, and we refuse to be grieved and afflicted, though that is more profitable. Remember that the mustard seed, from whose seed we spring, grows hotter when it is crushed, and only then is roused to its full strength. In this, therefore, we ought to live up to our nature: crushed by hostile words, we should blaze up for the faith and burn the very people who try to break us as the least of men, that is, like a mustard seed, the smallest of all seeds. But if those outside demand of you an account of the holy work and dart their poisoned tongues from a viper's heart into yours, do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine. For what part has the believer with the unbeliever? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial?

But you, soldier of Christ, have been armed by the apostle with the helmet of salvation, the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the sword of truth and the power of the Holy Spirit. Stand firm in your heavenly armour, and quench the fiery darts of the enemy with the fountain of wisdom and the river of living water within you. Guard what has been entrusted to you, keep the faith, pursue righteousness, hold fast to the love of Christ, strive after patience, and train yourself in godliness, which is profitable for all things. Be sober, labour in all things, fight the good fight and finish the course, so that you may lay hold of that for which you have been laid hold of. Henceforth there will be laid up for you the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award on that day to those who love his coming. There are those who will not endure sound doctrine, lovers of pleasure rather than of God, always going from bad to worse, deceiving and deceived. They are men corrupt in mind and estranged from the truth, and for that very reason given over to the lusts of their hearts, into a snare and many desires, which plunge those shipwrecked from the faith into ruin and perdition. For they have preferred the creature to the Creator; that is, they hold the idols of the nations, gold and silver, dearer than God, saving their souls in this world and losing them in Christ. Depart from such people and avoid profane novelties of speech. Otherwise you may begin to grow sick over old wives' questions and vain or impious disputes about words, and be put in danger by false brothers or by lost and reprobate wise men. Then all who see it, while the devil mocks, would say: This man began to build and was not able to finish. Far be that from us, who have dared to undertake the work of perfection relying not on our own works or strength but on God's power and mercy. He who is almighty is able to perfect in us the work of his own perfection. What he has already deigned to found and raise with the first scaffolding he is able to build up to his own measurements and complete to the roof. For when even his apostles were dismayed at the magnitude of this work, he deigned to tell them that it was impossible with men but not with God, in whom nothing is impossible for those who believe.

But so that we may comfort one another with the words of the Lord and advance in good works, go out from your land and from your kindred. Imitate faithful Abraham in his blessed departure, so that you may be worthy of Abraham's bosom. Hurry to come to us, so that for our common profit you may receive and give what is lacking in faith. This is acceptable before God, since a brother who helps a brother will be exalted. At present we are staying, as I wrote before, in the city of Barcelona. After the letter you answered, on the Lord's day on which he deigned to be born in the flesh, I was suddenly seized by the force of the crowd, as he himself is witness, though I believe it was by his ordinance, and I was initiated into the priesthood. I confess I was unwilling. It was not from distaste for the position, for I call him to witness that I wished to begin my sacred service even with the name and office of a sacristan. It was rather that I was destined for something else, and my mind, as you know, was settled and fixed elsewhere, so I was alarmed at this new and unexpected decree of the divine will. Having bowed my neck to the yoke of Christ, I see that I am handling works beyond my merits and my understanding. I have now been received and admitted into the secret inner sanctuary of the most high God, I share in heavenly things, and, brought nearer to God, I move in the very spirit, body and splendour of Christ. The narrow confines of my mind as yet scarcely grasp the meaning of this sacred burden, and, conscious of my weakness, I tremble at the weight of my office. But he who gave wisdom to little ones and perfects praise for himself out of the mouths of infants and nursing babies is able to perfect his work in me as well and to adorn the office, making worthy of himself the man he called while unworthy. Know, however, that by the favour of the same Lord the terms of our common vow remain intact. For I was induced to be consecrated in the church of Barcelona on this condition: that I should not be bound to that church, being dedicated only to the priesthood of the Lord and not also to a place in the church.

Come, then, if you will, before Easter, which we would much prefer, so that you may celebrate the sacred festival together with me as your priest. But if, by God's favour, you wish to meet us just as we set out on our journey, set out after Easter in the name of Christ. Yet we trust in our Lord that he will inspire in you so ardent a longing for us that you will not bear to put off your coming beyond the Easter season. How long the journey is your devoted servant will also tell you. He reached us from Eauze, as he declared, on the eighth day. The way is so short and easy that it is not steep even at the Pyrenees, that dreadful rampart between Narbonensis and the Spanish provinces, more a name than a mountain ridge. But why should I go on about distance? If you long for us, the way is short; if you do not care, it is long.
2. Paulinus to his lord and dearest brother Amandus.

Your Love's letter reached us after some delay, but the longer we had waited for it, the more eagerly we welcomed it. Cold water is sweeter to the thirsty, and good news from a far country is more delightful; so too the sweetness of your words has fattened our bones and filled our hungry soul with good things. What worthy return can we make for such words? We are thin in talent, gross in heart, barren in speech and, as it is written, idle bellies. Yet though we are inferior in all things, love alone makes us your equals. For we vie with the love you have for us, with a love of equal mind. It is planted in our inmost being, fixed in our heart and blended with our very soul by the Spirit of the Lord, who makes those of one way of life dwell in one house and binds countless thousands of believers together in one heart, since the One fills all in all.

Now this Lord has been pleased to place his treasure in an earthen vessel. He called me by his grace, raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dunghill, to set him among the princes of his people and clothe him with salvation among the priests. So, as I run after the fragrance of his ointments, I have become a drop of that ointment which ran down upon Aaron's beard. Mindful of my deserts, I refused, or rather did not dare, to become one of his household and to bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel. But I, a worm and no man, was seized against my will, I confess, by sudden force and compelled by a throttling crowd. Though I wished that this cup might pass from me, I had to say to the Lord: Yet not my will but yours be done. This was all the more so because I read that the Lord had said of himself: The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve. Forestalled by the Lord, then, and laid hold of by him whom we have not yet laid hold of, we serve at God's altar and minister at the tables of salvation. In name and office we are already elders, but in understanding we are still little children, and in speech nursing babies.

You are my venerable lord, my brother and my lord in Christ. Pray to the Lord, who is rich in every good, that I may minister this ministry well, gain a good standing for myself, and know how I ought to conduct myself in the house of God and handle the mystery of godliness. Pray that we may abound in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness and in your love for us as well, so that you too may abound in this grace. Moreover, instruct us often yourself in your letters, supplying what we lack. You have been nourished on the words of faith and of the good doctrine which you have followed in the sacred writings since boyhood. So shape us by the rule of right guidance, and feed us with spiritual food, that is, with the word of God. He is the true and living bread, by whom one lives more truly than by bread, since he is the food of the righteous who live by faith. Do not be any less careful about my training because we are separated by the place of our churches, though not in body. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, who is the head of the Church; and since we are all one in the Church, we live as if in one house. Nor can we say that we are without you, since we are of one spirit and dwell in the One who is one. Therefore, keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, as one body and one spirit, let us labour together for one another as fellow members, so that we may grow toward the building up of that body whose head is Christ.

We have been made citizens instead of enemies, neighbours instead of strangers far off, shepherds instead of sheep, and we have been set on the foundation of the apostles and prophets. Therefore train and strengthen my hands in the skill of building. Teach me to join both walls to the stone that has become the head of the corner, and to build bodies and hearts cleansed by faith into a holy temple and a dwelling place of God. Teach me, with the apostle's weapons, mighty through God, to take captive every lofty thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God and bring every thought into obedience to Christ. Teach me to lay the axe of the gospel to the roots of the trees, to slay the sinners of the earth with the sword of the Spirit, that is, the word of God, and to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked one with the shield of the catholic faith. Then, having fought the fight, finished the course, kept the faith and fulfilled the ministry, I may await what the Lord, the righteous judge, will award on that day to all who love his coming. So, seeing and holding me in the spirit as your own and as one who remains with you, instruct, help, exhort and strengthen me. I was born to God in Christ from you and through you, and so I ought to be your special care. I shall be your reproach if I am unworthy, or your joy if I am known by good fruits to be a branch of your tree.
3. To Alypius, his deservedly honoured lord and most blessed father, from Paulinus and Therasia, sinners.

This is true charity, this is perfect love, and you have shown that you hold it toward our lowliness, my lord, truly holy, deservedly most blessed and much longed for. Through our man Julian, on his return from Carthage, we have received a letter that brought us so much of the light of your holiness that we seemed not to be getting to know your charity but to be recognizing it again. Clearly this charity flowed from him who predestined us for himself from the beginning of the world. In him we were made before we were born, since he made us and not we ourselves, he who made the things that are to be. Formed, then, by his foreknowledge and his work into a likeness of wills and a unity of faith, or a faith of unity, we have been bound together by a charity that ran ahead of acquaintance, so that through the Spirit's revealing we knew each other before we saw each other in the body. So we rejoice and glory in the Lord. One and the same everywhere on earth, he works his love in his own people by the Holy Spirit, whom he has poured out on all flesh, gladdening his city with the rushing of the river. Among its citizens he has deservedly set you as a leader, with the princes of his people, in an apostolic see. And he has willed that we too should be counted in your lot, we whom he raised up when we had been dashed down and lifted out of the dust in our poverty. But we rejoice still more in that gift of the Lord by which he has given us a dwelling in your heart, and has deigned to work us so deeply into your inmost affections that we may claim a special confidence in your charity. These kindnesses and gifts so rouse us that we cannot love you hesitantly or lightly.

For we have received an outstanding token of your love and care: the work in five books by our brother Augustine, a man holy and perfect in Christ the Lord. We so admire and revere it that we believe its words were dictated by God. So, trusting in your oneness of heart with us, which we cannot but revere, we have dared to write to him as well. We presume that through you we will be excused to him for our lack of skill and commended to his charity. We presume the same for all the saints whose kind greetings you deigned to bring us though they were absent. No doubt you will take care, with equal affection, that through your holiness they in turn are greeted with our respects, both the companions of your holiness among the clergy and those in the monasteries who imitate your faith and virtue. For although you live among the peoples and over a people, guiding the sheep of the Lord's pasture as a shepherd keeping anxious watch, yet by renouncing the world and rejecting flesh and blood you have made a desert for yourself, set apart from the many, called among the few.

As some small return, though it is unequal to everything you have given, I have obtained, as you asked, that history of all the ages by Eusebius, the venerable bishop of Constantinople. The delay in obeying you came about because I did not have this codex myself. Following your instructions, I found it at Rome with our truly most holy father Domnio, who certainly obliged me all the more readily in this favor because I told him it was to be passed on to you. You also kindly told me where you would be, so, as you advised, we have written to the venerable colleague of your crown, our father Aurelius. We asked that, if you are now staying at Hippo Regius, he kindly send you there our letter and the parchment copied at Carthage. We have also asked the holy men Comes and Evodius, whom we have come to know through your words, which bore witness to their charity, to see to the copying themselves. That way father Domnio would not be without his codex any longer, and the copy sent to you could stay with you without needing to be returned.

But I ask this of you in particular, since you have embraced me with great love when I neither deserved nor expected it. In return for this history of the ages, give me the whole history of your holiness. Tell me your family, and from what house you were called by so great a Lord. Tell me by what beginnings you were set apart from your mother's womb, and how you forswore the stock of flesh and blood and passed over to the mother who rejoices in her offspring of the children of God, and so were transferred into a royal and priestly race. You have already told me that you learned my humble name at Milan when you were being initiated there. I confess I am curious to learn more about this, so that I may know you in every respect. I would rejoice all the more if it was by our father Ambrose, whom I so revere, that you were invited to the faith or consecrated to the priesthood, for then we would both have the same author. I was baptized by Delphinus at Bordeaux and ordained by Lampius at Barcelona in Spain, under pressure from a people suddenly inflamed. Even so, I have always been nurtured in the faith by Ambrose's love, and now in my priestly ordination I am cherished by him. Indeed, he wished to claim me for his own clergy, so that, though I live elsewhere, I am counted as his presbyter.

But so that you may not be ignorant of anything about me, know that I am a sinner of very long standing. It is not long since I was brought out of darkness and the shadow of death to draw the breath of life, and not long since I put my hand to the plough and took up the Lord's cross. May your prayers help us to carry it to the end. This reward will be added to your merits if your intercession lightens our burdens. For a saint who helps one who labors (we dare not say a brother) will be exalted like a great city. You indeed are a city built on a mountain, or a lamp lit upon a lampstand, shining with sevenfold brightness; we lie hidden under the bushel of our sins. Visit us with your letters. Bring us out into the light in which you yourself move, conspicuous upon golden lampstands. Your words will be a light to our paths, and our head will be anointed with the oil of your lamp, and our faith will be kindled when we take from the breath of your mouth food for the mind and light for the soul.

May the peace and grace of God be with you, and may the crown of righteousness await you on that day, my lord father, deservedly most beloved, venerable and most longed for. Please greet for us, with much affection and respect, the blessed companions of your holiness and those who imitate you in the Lord, our brothers if they will allow it, both in the churches and in the monasteries at Carthage, Thagaste and Hippo Regius, in all your parishes, and in every place known to you throughout Africa where people serve the Lord in the catholic faith. If you receive holy Domnio's parchment itself, please have it copied and send it back to us. And I ask you also to write and tell me which hymn of mine you recognized. We have sent your holiness a single loaf as a token of unity, and the solidity of the Trinity is also contained in it. By kindly accepting this loaf you will make it a blessing.
4. To Augustine, their lord and brother, of one mind with them and venerable, from Paulinus and Therasia, sinners.

The love of Christ, which urges us on and binds us together through the unity of faith even when we are apart, has itself driven away my shyness and given me the confidence to write to you. Through your writings it has set you in my inmost heart. Those writings are rich in the resources of the schools and sweet with honey from heavenly combs, and I hold them as physicians and nurses of my soul. For the present I have them in the five books that we received as a gift from our blessed and venerable bishop Alypius, not for our own instruction alone but also for the benefit of the churches of many cities. These books, then, I now keep for reading. In them I delight, and from them I take food: not the food that perishes, but the food that produces the substance of eternal life through our faith, by which we are made one body in Christ Jesus our Lord. For our faith, which disregards things visible and yearns for things invisible, is strengthened through charity, which believes all things according to the truth of almighty God, by the writings and examples of the faithful. O truly salt of the earth, by which our hearts are seasoned so that they cannot lose their savor in the error of the world! O lamp worthily set upon the lampstand of the church! From a sevenfold wick fed with the oil of gladness you pour out light far and wide over the catholic cities. You scatter the darkness of the heretics, thick as it is, and by the brilliance of your illuminating speech you clear the light of truth from the confusion of the shadows.

You see, my brother of one mind, admirable in Christ the Lord and worthy of reverence, how intimately I have come to know you, with what amazement I admire you, and with how great a love I embrace you. Every day I enjoy conversing with your writings and feed on the breath of your mouth. I could rightly call your mouth a channel of living water and a vein of the eternal spring, because in you Christ has become a spring of water welling up to eternal life. My soul has thirsted for him in you, and my earth has longed to be drenched by the abundance of your river. With this Pentateuch of yours you have armed me well enough against the Manichees. If you have also prepared defenses against other enemies of the catholic faith, please do not refuse to bring the weapons of righteousness out of your armory and give them to me. Our enemy has a thousand arts of doing harm, and must be fought off with as many kinds of weapons as the snares he attacks with. For I am a sinner still laboring under a great burden, a veteran in the ranks of sinners but a raw recruit to the eternal King in a warfare that is not of the body. Wretch that I am, until now I admired the wisdom of the world, and through useless letters and a prudence God rejects I was foolish and dumb before God. After I had grown old among my enemies and become vain in my thoughts, I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, looking up to the precepts of the law and the gifts of grace. From there my help came from the Lord. He did not repay me according to my iniquities, but gave light to the blind, freed the fettered, and humbled the one wrongly raised up, in order to raise up the one humbled in godliness.

So I follow the great footprints of the righteous, though not yet with equal steps, to see whether by your prayers I can lay hold of that for which I have been laid hold of by God's mercies. Guide me, then, a little one crawling unsteadily, and teach me to walk in your steps. I do not want you to judge me by the age of my bodily birth rather than of my spiritual rebirth. My age according to the flesh is already that of the man whom the apostles healed at the Beautiful Gate by the power of the word. But in the birth of my soul I am still at the age of infancy, the infancy that was sacrificed by the wounds meant for Christ, that ran ahead of the Lamb's sacrifice with its own worthy blood and began the Lord's passion. Bring me up with your words, then, as an infant still being suckled on the word of God and of a spiritual age, eagerly seeking the breasts of faith, wisdom and charity. If you consider the office we share, you are my brother. If you consider the maturity of your mind and understanding, you are my father, even if you may be younger in years, because a grey-haired wisdom has advanced you, young as you are, to a maturity of merit, which is the honor of elders. So nurture and strengthen me in the sacred writings and in spiritual studies. I am, as I said, recent in time, and therefore, after long perils and many shipwrecks, still unpractised, barely emerging from the waves of the world. You already stand on solid shore: receive me into a safe haven, so that, if you think me worthy, we may sail together in the harbor of salvation. Meanwhile, as I struggle to escape the dangers of this life and the depths of sin, hold me up with your prayers as with a plank, so that I may escape naked from this world as from a shipwreck.

This is why I took care to lighten myself of baggage and strip off the clothes that weighed me down. At Christ's command and with his help, freed from every covering of the flesh and from care for tomorrow, I wanted to swim across this billowy sea of the present life, where our sins bark and howl between us and God and keep us apart. I do not boast that I have accomplished this. Even if I could boast, I would boast in the Lord, to whom it belongs to accomplish what lies within us to will. But my soul still longs to desire the judgments of the Lord. Consider how far from attaining God's will is one who still only desires to desire it! Yet as far as in me lies, I have loved the beauty of the holy house, and, as far as it was up to me, I had chosen to be cast down in the house of the Lord. But he who was pleased to set me apart from my mother's womb and to draw me from the friendship of flesh and blood to his grace was also pleased to raise me from the earth, destitute as I was of all good merit. He brought me up out of the pit of misery and the mire of dregs, to set me among the princes of his people and to place my portion in your lot. So I, joined with you in office, have been made equal to you, who surpass me in merit.

So it is not on my own presumption but by the Lord's good pleasure and ordinance that I claim a bond of brotherhood with you, and count myself worthy of so great an honor though I am unworthy of it. For I know for certain that, in keeping with your holiness (for your wisdom is truth), you do not set your mind on high things but stoop to the lowly. I therefore hope you will readily and heartily receive the love of our lowliness. In fact I trust you have already received it through Alypius, our most blessed bishop and our father, since he is kind enough to be so. Without doubt he has given you in himself an example of loving us before knowing us and beyond what we deserve. We were unknown to him and separated from him by a great distance of land or sea. Yet by the spirit of true love, which penetrates and spreads everywhere, he was able both to see us by loving us and to reach us by writing to us. In the gift of books I mentioned, he gave us the first proofs of his own affection and pledges of your love. He took great pains that we should know your holiness not only through his words but more fully through your own eloquence and faith, so that we could not love you only moderately. We believe he took just as much care that you in turn, following his example, should love us very much. We pray that the grace of God may remain with you forever, as it does now, brother in Christ the Lord, of one mind with us, venerable and most longed for. With the greatest affection of united brotherhood we greet your whole household and everyone who is your companion and follows your holiness in the Lord. We have sent your charity a single loaf as a sign of our oneness of heart, and we ask you to bless it by accepting it.
5. Paulinus to his brother Severus.

Did you really think you had to apologize, dearest brother, for not coming to us yourself as you had promised and as we expected? In truth you came to us with the better part of yourself, not the part that stayed behind. You remained at home in body alone, but you came to us in will, in spirit and in word. And you were not wholly absent even in body, since members of your body came to us in your servants, who are bound to you in holy service in the Lord. Therefore, brother truly holy, most deservedly beloved and one in mind with us in Christ, the crown of godliness is already laid up for you in heaven. The just judge will award it on that day to you and to all who, like you, love their neighbour in Christ, or Christ in their neighbour, with perfect charity. For by looking at the things of the flesh we can easily infer the things of the spirit. From the evident love you show to the brother whom you see, we infer that heavenly, faithful and perfect love with which you love God, whom you do not see. We prove this by the obedience of faith: by loving one another we prove, as you do, that we are disciples of that Master who loved his own to the end and laid down his life for his friends, by the same power by which he also took it up again.

Therefore, brother truly most holy and deservedly blessed, your place and reward in the land of the living will be above the queen of the South. She was a sinner, still belonging to the nations not yet visited, yet already going before those who were to be visited. She did not have the law of the letter, but she had the faith of the law engraved on the fleshly tablets of the heart by the spirit of counsel and godliness. For her own benefit, and eager for great and saving gain, she was stirred to come across the vast distances from the ends of the earth, and she longed to hear divine wisdom, so as to receive what she did not have and to drink in the light of knowledge that she lacked. Even then, as the queen who was to come from the Gentiles, she longed for her bridegroom. Robed in many colours and in a garment of gold, as her prophet describes her, she ran toward the fragrance of Christ, which spread far and wide, and she forgot both her people and her father's house. Barbarian by nation but not in spirit, a foreigner outwardly but inwardly a Jew, she longed to become a fellow citizen of the saints. For this reason the Judge himself, with his own lips, deems her worthy not only of the heavenly prize of the blessed resurrection but also of the apostles' power to judge the adulterous Jews. For in marvelling at Christ in Solomon, she had fulfilled the true devotion of the heavenly queen as a mystic image of the Church that was to come. So if a divine reward awaits her in the future, even though she largely received her reward here and in her own time when she won the hearing of heavenly wisdom she desired, what rewards will at last be paid to you? You longed for me with equal grace and with greater effort, since you had less hope of any present benefit to yourself. What, I ask, did you find in me to desire? What did you hope to take from me that you did not already have? What good could you gain from talking with an unlearned man? What profit would there be in seeing a sinner? What could the wise take from the foolish, the upright from the crooked, the blessed from the wretched, the strong from the weak, the man rich in the Lord from the poor?

Truly you do not seek your own interests but those of Christ. Your motive, both in planning your journey and in putting your servants to trouble, was neither your own merit nor any advantage from me, but only that charity which is the fullness of the gospel. Blessed are you, because I have nothing with which to repay you. You will be repaid at the resurrection of the just by him who declares that he is loved and received even in the least of his own. That is why he said this, making himself a debtor by his own words on behalf of any servant who bears his name, even a false or useless one: "Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet's reward." My own burden, of course, will not be lightened by this, even though I, a sinner, receive from a just man the honour due to the just. But the very justice of your opinion will be credited to you as a reward for your goodness, because by a holy error, yet with a true feeling of godliness, you honoured the good Lord even in a bad servant.

What then shall we wretches do? We will owe an account and a penalty for this too: that we accept honours we have not deserved and, though we are only hearers of the law, are praised by those who do it. The sluggishness of our damnable idleness will be thrown in our faces all the more, together with the hunger of barren souls and hands withered in good works. Through your words we hear praises that are true of worthy servants of Christ such as you, and therefore false of us, and we recognise how great a debt binds us when we compare your judgment with our deeds and do not find in ourselves what we hear said about us. For what can we boast of that is like yours? Even if all boasting must be in the Lord, since we have received nothing except as his gift, still in my case there were reasons. My more advanced age, and a position that had been honoured from my earliest years, could have made me more serious. A weaker body and wasted flesh could have crushed the pursuit of pleasure. A mortal life often tried by toil and hardship could have bred a hatred of what disturbs us, and the need for hope and the fear of uncertainty could have increased my devotion to religion. Finally, when I seemed to have found rest from slanders and travels, I was not occupied with public affairs and was far from the din of the forum. In welcome tranquillity and the privacy of my home I enjoyed country leisure and the worship of the Church. So, as my mind was gradually withdrawn from worldly turmoil and shaped to heavenly precepts, I struggled toward contempt of the world and the company of Christ all the more readily, as if by a road that bordered on this way of life.

You, dearest brother, were converted to the Lord by a greater miracle. You were younger in age and richer in praise. You were less weighed down by the burdens of an inheritance, though no poorer in wealth. You were still living in the very theatre of the world, that is, the bustle of the forum, and you held the palm for eloquence. Yet with a sudden onset you shook off the slavish yoke of sin and broke the deadly chains of flesh and blood. Neither the riches heaped up through marriage into a consular family, nor, after your marriage ended, the licence to sin and the freedom of a youth left unwed, could call you back from the narrow entrance of salvation and the steep road of virtue to that soft and broad way of the many. Blessed are you, who fled from the counsel of the ungodly, refused to stand in the way of sinners, and scorned to sit in the seat of pestilence, so that in lofty humility you might recline at the feet of the Crucified.

You, then, are a true doer of the law and the gospel, not a deaf hearer. You nailed your body and the world to the cross. You turned away from the delights of youth and the evil joys of this present life as from poisons and griefs, and you spurned the burdens of your inheritance like dung. Deservedly you have gained as your eternal mother a holy mother-in-law more generous than any parent, because you had put the heavenly Father before an earthly parent. Following the apostles' example, you left your father in the tossing boat, that is, in the uncertainty of this life, along with the nets of his property and the tangles of an inheritance, and you followed Christ. Your wealth of talent was no less than the riches of your household, yet you did not accept praise from men for it. Loftily disregarding vain glory, you preferred the preaching of fishermen to all the writings of Cicero and to your own. You took refuge in the silence of godliness to escape the tumult of iniquity. You chose to fall silent before mortals, so that you might speak of divine things with a pure mouth, and cleanse with the praises of Christ and the very mention of his holy name a tongue polluted by the snarling eloquence of the courts.

O true Israelite! With so faithful a mind you saw the God of Jacob. As though strengthened by wrestling with the Lord himself, you prevailed against the prince of this world and defeated the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places with the shield of faith and the weapons of righteousness. You chose to please Christ rather than men, and to be a fool in the eyes of men rather than of God. You preferred the scandal of the cross to all the eloquence and wisdom of this world. So what is folly to those who are perishing, you, now given a share in salvation, have recognised to be the power and wisdom of God, as is plain to all who are to be saved. Blessed are you, brother, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but the Father who is in heaven, through our Lord Jesus Christ. He overturned their wisdom and made it foolish, and he chose the weak and foolish things of the world in order to confound this world by the very things for which it scorns to know God. Remember us, then, all the more, since your richer merits give you greater power in prayer. Our lamp has already been lit in the light of Christ, yet we still lie hidden under the bushel of our sins. You are conspicuous for the light of your faith and grace as much as of your works, and you shine through the Lord's seven lampstands. We long to be drawn out by your hand and to have our head anointed with your oil, so that we may not burn dimly like a smouldering wick (though the merciful Lord does not quench even that), but may shine with the pure light of a faithful example that could even be held up to others. Yet by the grace of the Lord, which shines in the darkness, we are not obscure, thanks to the brightness of his name, even though, as you have heard, we live in retirement. For we keep silent, secluded in our upper room, since it is good for a man, as the prophet says, to sit alone and be silent. The Lord himself taught us to keep silent even in causes that cry out to be voiced. Like a lamb before the shearer he did not open his mouth, and yet he also said: "I have kept silent; shall I keep silent for ever?" So we wait in silence for the will and judgment of him who is able both to keep silent in us now and, when he wills, to plead for us.

Meanwhile, however, we have felt our sins harm us in this: we have not deserved to see you. We count it as a further addition to our ills that we have been the cause of trials for you. As you told us, you fell ill twice over, struck down every time you tried to come to us. But it is written that the Lord our God himself often tests us, to prove the love with which we love one another in his peace. So we place our hope in your faith rather than in our own. If the trial that came first has worked its proof in you, may it no longer be able to frustrate the longings of a charity that has thus been proven. For we know there is such readiness of spirit in you that we do not fear the flesh, which is always weak, will prevail and hinder our common desire. You will strengthen your flesh by faith and subject it to your mind, so that it is compelled to be able in Christ to do what it cannot do of itself. Only say to it: "Do not fight against the spirit; come to terms with your adversary on the way, and there will be peace for your bones," and: "When my heart has exulted in the living God, then my flesh too will rest in hope."

Hold fast, then, brother, to what you have, so that no one else takes your crown. And it is in keeping with this that you should not cease to will what you once willed, but hold to an unchanging resolve to come to us. Your devout efforts will be brought to the fruit of your desire by him in whose power and favour it lies that we prosper in what we devoutly will. For we know that for one who desires the good, all things turn out for good. And this was a most welcome sign of our harmony in all things: we too were sick when we received the letter telling us of your illness. So we proved in ourselves the apostle's saying that the members of one body suffer with one another, even in feeling. For we felt ourselves restored by the very fact that you had written of your recovery. Though we live in different lands, we experienced the unity of the Spirit working in us. Our separate bodies were joined by a silent bond, and they matched each other in their ailments and in their remedies.

So you too, brother one in mind with us and the better part of ourselves in Christ, put away any sadness your devoted heart may have felt at the news of our chastening. For the Lord has chastened us sorely, but he has not handed us over to death. Visited by the healing hand of the Almighty, we were being nursed from our present sickness toward the hope of health, and we softened each other's scourging with mutual consolation. Being joined in suffering gave us great and sweet comfort, since the very fact that the same blows had struck us both seemed to have come about by the will of the Lord, without whose command not even a sparrow falls to the ground. So too our recovery had begun to advance together in both of us. Perhaps each breathed again through the other's relief, or perhaps the Lord, who works unity and binds all his own in one undivided Spirit, would not allow even our fleshly nature to differ.

Yet this was not the only cause that delayed our servants. Our Vigilantius too suffered from violent fevers in Campania, both before he reached us and after he arrived. Since he too was a fellow member, he shared our sickness and our suffering. But the catechumen, who was not yet a member of our body, did not feel our wounds. He stayed healthy and free of our ailments, because flesh that was still foreign could not feel the pain of a body not its own. So it was only when our Vigilantius was able to travel that I decided the letter should be sent. We admit that both had long been in a hurry. But one could not travel and was rashly hurrying before he had regained his strength, and the other could travel but would have been wrong to hurry on alone. Since we ourselves were not able to write, we held them both back: by our advice while they were willing, and by our silence when they were not.

So, as we wrote above, we have suffered our sickness together and have been restored by the prayers of the saints and of those dear to us, and, we believe, most of all by yours, as the Lord looked on us more mercifully. Yet our bodies are exhausted and we are still weak. The apostle teaches us to boast of such weakness, since, as he proclaims, weakness made him strong. The flesh wars against the spirit, but when it is broken by ill health its strength is broken too, and it cannot overcome the power of the spirit. We are weak in the flesh, then, for the advancement of the spirit, which exults at the loss of the flesh, rejoices at the distress of what is, as it were, an enemy substance, and grows strong as the tamed body weakens. But our charity is sound and strong, the great charity we have toward you through the Lord Jesus. In that charity we have sent you this letter for your comfort, just as we meanwhile hold on to yours, until we see you yourself, as you promised and as we never cease to hope from the Lord.

There are many things that should draw you to us and call you away from your homeland for a while. Above all there is the love of peace and the flight from jealousy, which is kindled most of all by the sight or nearness of a rival way of life. Indeed, our distance from the city puts out for us the fires lit by the jealous clergy at Rome, and all iniquity there shuts its mouth. With us absent, the flame of hatred grows cold and sluggish, as if its fuel had been taken away. It dares not burst into speech, though envy gnashes its teeth, for it is conscious of its own iniquity and blushes at itself, and it has nowhere at hand to light the torches of a spiteful mind. Yet the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, abounds in the hearts of very many, and all Campania reveres the work of God the Saviour in us. At Rome too, only a few are stirred by the bite of envy, even in the clergy itself, which is the only group we seem to scandalize. But thanks be to the Lord, who has allowed even me, his most wretched sinner, to say: "For they hated me without cause." As for my part, I am peaceable in mind even toward those who hate my peace. If anyone wishes to be contentious, that is not our custom. As for the very men who are said to hate us and to bar us from the fellowship of their holiness, scarcely a faint rumour of them slips through to us. Our ears are fenced with a hedge of thorns, and it is shut out like a cold breeze or the bothersome whine of an empty-headed gnat.

But our fellow servants, your servants, will be able to tell you more fully how little loss of the Lord's grace the proud aloofness of the pope of the city causes us. In the few days they were here, they saw how constant and how attentive were the services paid to us throughout our sickness by concerned brothers, monks, bishops, clergy, and often even laymen. I may boast of this to you, who are one in mind with me, though the boast is of the Lord's grace, since this too is his work and his gift: almost none of the bishops in all Campania thought it right not to visit us. Those who were kept away by illness or some necessity were present through clergy sent in their place and through letters. The African bishops too sent men to visit us at the beginning of summer. This being so, you see how eagerly you ought to hasten to me in my humble state. You would take away, for a little while, the occasion from those who are seeking an occasion, and you would journey away from your homeland for the increase of grace and charity, while, as a guest in the body, you are still away from Christ. For the Truth himself testifies that no prophet is accepted in his own country.

I confess that, though nothing could be more welcome to me than your presence, my longing for it has burned more fiercely since you promised that many spiritual brothers would come with you. Will that time come, I ask, will that day ever dawn, when I welcome you, my brother, coming with a band of God's elect, into the embrace of our common patron, my lord Felix? I now ask that this be obtained through his prayers, and then we may rejoice together in the Lord, in his presence, that it has been obtained. I will embrace you all together and each in turn, and as we sing together I will rightly say: "This is the day the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it," for "it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together in unity." Then I will settle you not only as a lodger in the monastery of the martyr next door but also as a tenant farmer in his garden, though rent-free. For you have already received your denarius from the householder, besides the coins that the same Lord generously gave to the innkeeper for your wounds. So you were healed with the oil of mercy and the wine of grace, and with your body made whole you might be hired to better purpose for the Lord's vineyard.

I already seem to see my little garden better tended by the Lord's labourers who arrive and work with you. It is not hard to judge how easily the lighter work of cultivation will be finished by those whom Christ chose for his vineyard, whom he would not allow to stand idle, useless to God, in the vain marketplace of this world. Already in my mind and thoughts I picture the joys we will share at home after the holy kiss. Intoxicated by the spirit of charity, we will mix a sober gladness in chaste cups. We will celebrate the holy feast not with the leaven of malice but with the unleavened bread of sincerity, singing psalms to the Lord with hymns and spiritual songs, singing to God with our tongues and our hearts, and doing whatever we do, in word or deed, in the name of Jesus Christ, giving thanks to the Father through him. He makes those of one way of life dwell in one house, and he will, I hope, make us dwell together in himself. He made the two one, and when he was lifted up he drew all things to himself. When he was humbled he made peace for all things, reconciling the world to God. When he has filled our mouth with joy through the presence of you who are one in mind with us, we will say: "The Lord has done great things for us." And in the abundance of our gladness we will bless you from the house of the Lord, for you are blessed by the Lord, you who have come in the name of the Lord. May you receive the cup of salvation and eat the bread of the blessed in the kingdom of God. For before the Lord Jesus you are our fulfilment and our joy.

Dare, then, to break away, relying not on your own resources and strength but trusting in Christ and leaning on him, because his rod and his staff comfort, sustain and guide us. He bears our sorrows and took on our infirmities. He gives strength to the weary and steadies feeble knees. He himself will make your way spotless and free of stumbling. He will gird you with strength and make your feet like the feet of a deer, so that you may exult like a giant running his course. The weakness of the fearful flesh cannot hinder you, since you walk not by the flesh but by the spirit. For when we serve Christ we use the service of the body, but still more the command of the mind. So the flesh, obeying orders, follows our will as Christ directs it. The body draws firmness from the strength of the mind, and as a servant it shapes its obedience to its master's bearing. And so strength is made perfect in weakness, when the soul serves God with the consent of the tamed flesh and fulfils the duties of strength through the ministry of weakness.

Set out, then, and go forward and prosper, and the right hand of God will lead you wonderfully. His mercy and grace will go before you, and if you leave home weak, you will gain strength as you go. For those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles. If you have a heart that burns on the way, your youth will be renewed like the eagle's; you will run and not grow weary, you will walk and not faint. No staff, no bag, no purse will weigh you down, and no shoes or second tunic will hinder you. Your feet will be freed from fleshly bonds, as is fitting for standing on holy ground, and your loins girded with a belt that carries no heavy money. You will run your way in haste, as the Lord's Passover and the work of Christ must be done in the time that has grown short. The God of our salvation will make your journey prosperous. Every valley will be filled for you and every hill brought low, and the rough places of iniquity will become level roads, so that you never strike your foot on the way. For he has commanded his angels to guard you in all your ways. The Lord himself, your protection, will surround you with the shield of his peace. He will shine before you in the light of his face and spread over you the shade of his wings, so that the sun will not burn you by day nor the moon by night. In every place he will guard and bless your going out and your coming in, so that everywhere you may find a son of peace and your peace may rest upon every host.

But if, as you set out, you should weep at the thought of being torn away from people dear to you or from places you know well, your passing sorrow will be turned into everlasting joy. "Going," it says, "they went and wept, sowing their seed; but coming they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves." So you too, even if you weep as you come, will rejoice as you return, and in joy you will reap what you sowed in tears. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God the Father and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with your whole house, a house not made with hands, for you are the living temple of God, built on the foundations of the apostles in Christ, who is God. My brother, one in mind with me, venerable, most beloved and most longed-for, I ask you to greet our holy parent, your mother and co-heir in Christ, with the reverence she deserves. My fellow servant in the Lord greets your brotherly self with the affection with which she reveres you. And please greet warmly for us all the holy brotherhood which we are sure lives with you. All who are with us in the Lord greet you: among them, from the Hebrews [?], Proforus, and Restitutus, who loves the Lord and, having come to know you in Christ, cherishes you and longs for you greatly.

In the heading of my letter I was afraid to imitate you, my brother, who surpass me in all things, because I thought it safer to write truthfully. So in future, servant of Christ called to freedom, take care not to write yourself down as the servant of a man, a brother, and a fellow servant lower than yourself. To offer to any human being, let alone a most wretched sinner, the honour that is owed to the one Lord, the one Master on earth, the one God, is the sin of flattery rather than an act of humility that justifies. Love from a pure heart and unfeigned faith is enough; whatever is more than that comes from evil. I beg you, brother, by the Lord, to look upon my presumption toward you with the spirit of revelation; otherwise I may well fear that I have offended you with so talkative a letter. But in the presence of love, which bears all things, the very thing that usually breeds distaste ought to increase goodwill, whereas where there is no love, nothing softens the tedium. For as I dictate, thinking of you and wholly absorbed in you, I talk on as if you were with me after a long separation, and I forget to bring the task in hand to an end.

We have sent you a Campanian loaf from our little cell as a blessing, trusting so much in your merits in the Lord that we believed it would reach you full of its grace. Though you are already filled with richer crumbs from the Lord's table, be pleased to make into a blessing this bread too, received from sinners in the Lord's name. And so that a loaf of fine wheat might not seem to go beyond the measure of our humility, we have also sent a boxwood dish as evidence of our riches. Accept it as a parting gift of spiritual devotion, and keep it as a model if you do not yet use silver of this kind. But if you have nielloed [?] ware, send it to us by means of the little vessels we have entrusted to the boys, our sons. For we love earthenware vessels, because they are akin to us through Adam, and we hold the Lord's treasure entrusted to us in such vessels.

Besides this I ask, since I am confident that I have the fullest claim on your heart, that, if it should be necessary for you to take the matter in hand because my freedmen, slaves and brothers are failing me, you would kindly arrange for the old wine which we believe we still have at Narbonne to be brought to us. Do not fear any loss, holy brother, even if you make us your debtors for money as well. For all our people have turned away from us and together have become ungodly, and a man's enemies are the members of his own household.
VI. To my lord Augustine, my holy brother, one in mind with us: Paulinus and Therasia, sinners.

Some time ago, my brother of one mind with me in Christ the Lord, I came to know you through your holy and devout labours, though you did not know it. I saw you though you were absent and embraced you with my whole mind, and I hastened to approach you by letter with familiar, brotherly words as well. I believe that my letter was carried to you by the hand and grace of the Lord. But the servant we sent before winter to greet you and others whom God loves just as dearly is still delayed, and we could no longer put off our duty or restrain our eager longing to hear from you. So we are now writing again, if our earlier letter was found worthy to reach you, or writing for the first time, if it did not have the good fortune to come into your hands.

But you, brother, are a spiritual man who judges all things, so do not measure our love for you only by the courtesy or the timing of letters. The Lord is our witness, who is one and the same and works his love in his own people everywhere. From the time we came to know you through your works against the Manichees, by the kindness of the venerable bishops Aurelius and Alypius, love for you was so deeply planted in us that we seemed not to be forming some new friendship but resuming an old affection. In short, though we now write as beginners in speech, we are not beginners in affection, and in the spirit, through the inner man, we seem to recognize you in our turn. Nor is it surprising that we are present to each other though absent, and know each other though unknown, since we are members of one body, have one head, are steeped in one grace, live on one bread, walk one road and dwell in the same house. With all that we are, and with all the hope and faith by which we stand in the present, we strive toward the future. Let us be one both in the spirit and in the body of the Lord, so that we do not become nothing by falling away from the One.

How little, then, does bodily absence deny us of each other! It denies us only the pleasure that feeds eyes looking for temporal things. Yet even bodily grace should not be called temporal in spiritual people, for the resurrection will grant them eternity even of their bodies. Unworthy as we are, we dare to presume this, trusting in the power of Christ and the goodness of God the Father. So may the grace of God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, grant us this gift too, that we may see your face in the flesh as well. It would not only bring great joy to our longing but would also increase the light in our minds, and your abundance would enrich our poverty. Indeed, you can give us this even while absent, especially now that our sons Romanus and Agilis are returning in the Lord's name with their work of charity completed. They are one in mind with us and very dear to us in the Lord, and we commend them to you as our other selves. We ask that they may enjoy your loving affection in a special way, for you know what lofty rewards the Most High promises to the brother who helps a brother. If you wish to repay me with any gift of the grace given to you, you may send it safely by them, for, please believe me, they are one heart and one soul with us in the Lord. May the grace of God remain with you forever, as it does now, my brother of one mind with me in Christ the Lord, venerable, most beloved and longed for. Greet for us all the saints in Christ, such as no doubt hold close to you. Commend us to all the saints, so that they may kindly pray for us together with you.
VII. To my lord Romanianus, my brother, rightly praised and honoured: Paulinus and Therasia.

The day before we sent this letter, our brothers came back from Africa. You saw how anxiously we were waiting for them. Through them we received from Africa the letters we had most longed for, from holy and very dear men: Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Profuturus and Severus, all of whom are now bishops. Rejoicing in such recent words from so many saints of this kind, we hastened to share our gladness with you, so that this very happy news might bring you too the joy you have been awaiting during your anxious stay abroad. If you have perhaps already learned the same things about these venerable and most loving men from other ships that have arrived, hear them again from us and rejoice once more with renewed gladness. But if this news reaches you first from us, rejoice that Christ has given us so much love in your homeland that we learn first, or among the first, whatever divine providence does there, for, as it is written, God is ever wonderful in his saints.

We are not writing this for you to rejoice only because Augustine has become a bishop, but because the churches of Africa have been found worthy of this care from God, that they should receive heavenly words from Augustine's mouth. To increase the grace of the Lord's gift, he was promoted in a new way: he was consecrated not to succeed the bishop in his chair but to join him in it. For Valerius is still alive, and Augustine is his fellow bishop of the church of Hippo. That blessed old man, whose pure mind was never tinged by any stain of spiteful envy, now receives from the Most High a fitting reward for the peace of his heart: the man he had simply hoped would succeed him in his priesthood he has been found worthy to have as his colleague. Could anyone have believed this before it happened? But of this work of the Almighty, too, the words of the Gospel may be said: "With men these things are hard, but with God all things are possible." So let us exult and rejoice in him who alone does wonders, who makes those of one mind dwell together in a house. For he has regarded our lowliness and visited his people for good. He raised up a horn in the house of his servant David, and now he has exalted the horn of his church in his chosen ones, so that, as he promises through the prophet, he may break the horns of sinners, that is, of the Donatists and the Manichees.

Through Augustine the Lord now thunders on this trumpet. If only its sound would strike the hearing of our son Licentius! But may he hear it with the ear by which Christ enters, from which the enemy cannot snatch away the seed of God. Then Augustine will truly feel himself a supreme priest of Christ, and know that he has been heard from on high, if the son he fathered for you as worthy in letters he also brings forth worthily for himself in Christ. Even now, please believe me, he has written to us with the most ardent concern about him. We trust in almighty Christ that Augustine's spiritual prayers will prevail over our young man's worldly desires. Believe me, he will be overcome even against his will. He will be overcome by the faith of a most loving parent, so that an evil victory does not win out, if he would rather win to his own ruin than be defeated for his salvation. So that this courtesy of brotherly kindness might not seem empty-handed, we have sent five loaves to you and to our son Licentius together. They come from the field rations of the Christian campaign, in whose ranks we serve each day for the provisions of frugality. We could not leave out of the blessing one whom we long to bind closely to ourselves by the same grace. Still, let us say a few words to him as well, so that he cannot deny that what was written to you about him was written for him too. As in the play, what Micio hears is said for Aeschinus. But why should I speak in other men's words, when we can say everything in our own? Borrowing other men's words is not usually the sign of a sound head, and we, by God's grace, are sound and safe in our head, for our head is Christ. In Christ may we have you safe for many years to come, and always happy with your whole household, as we desire, my lord and brother, most deservedly honoured and most longed for.
VIII. [Paulinus to Licentius, his dearest son.]

Hear, then, my son, the law of your father, that is, the faith of Augustine, and do not reject the counsels of your mother. Augustine's loving care rightly claims that name too where you are concerned. He carried you in his bosom when you were very small, and from infancy he fed you first on the milk of worldly wisdom. Now he longs to nurse you at spiritual breasts as well and to nourish you for the Lord. He sees that you are grown up in bodily age but still crying in a spiritual cradle, still an infant in the word of God, barely crawling in Christ with your first steps and tottering feet. May Augustine's teaching guide the unsteady little one, like a mother's hand and a nurse's arm! If you listen to him and follow him, my son (to entice you again with the words of Solomon), you will receive a crown of graces on your head. Then you will truly be that consul and pontiff, not as a figure seen in a dream but as one formed by Truth itself, for Christ will fill the empty images of a false work with the solid results of his own working. Licentius will truly be a pontiff and truly a consul if you cling to Augustine's footsteps and to the teachings of the prophets and apostles. Stay with him without parting along the paths of God, as blessed Elisha clung to the holy Elijah and the young Timothy to the illustrious apostle. Then you will learn with a perfect heart to deserve the priesthood, and with a teacher's voice to take counsel for the salvation of the peoples.

Enough warnings and exhortation. I think, my Licentius, that a few words and little effort can stir you toward Christ. From boyhood the spirit and voice of the venerable Augustine have set you aflame with zeal for truth and wisdom, and Christ is truly both of these, the supreme good of all that is good. If Augustine has achieved too little with you for your own sake, what can I accomplish, who come so far behind him and am poor in all his riches? But I trust in the power of his gifts and in the kindness of your nature, and so I hope that more and greater things have already been accomplished in you than remain to be accomplished. That is why I have dared to open my mouth, for a twofold purpose: to be like that man in the love I owe, through my concern for you, and to be counted among those who love your salvation, at least by declaring my affection. For I know that the real work, the prize for bringing you to perfection, is reserved above all for Augustine.

I fear, my son, that I may have offended your ears with the harshness of rash words, and through your ears wounded your mind too with weariness of me. But I remembered your letter, from which I learned that you are at home with musical measures. In my youth, at your age, I myself was not averse to that pursuit. So, remembering your letter, I found a remedy to soothe your mind if I had in any way chafed it: to call you to the Lord, the craftsman of harmony in all its forms, with the melody of a song. I beg you to listen and not to spurn the cause of your salvation in my words. Gladly accept my loving care and a father's heart, even in words that deserve little regard, for the name of Christ, which is above every name, is set within them and makes them worthy of such reverence that a believer cannot despise them.
Come, then, break off delay and the world's clinging chains,
And do not fear the mild yoke of a gentle Lord.
The world before us is beautiful, yes, but a marvel only to wandering
Minds; the wise soul is not dazzled by such things.
Now Rome, that tempter to evil, entices you with all her varied shapes,
Rome, alas, powerful enough to overturn even the strong.
But I pray, my son, that father Augustine may always
Stand before you against all the city's allurements.
If amid all the dangers of this fragile life
You look to him and hold him in your heart, you will be safe.
Yet I will warn you of this, repeating it again and again:
Flee the slippery paths of harsh imperial service.
Office is a flattering name, an evil slavery, with a sickly end;
What you now delight to want, you will soon regret having wanted.
It is a delight to climb the heights; to come down from them makes one tremble.
If you stumble, you will fall the harder from the top of the citadel.
Do false goods please you now? Does ambition sweep you off on every breeze,
And hollow fame carry you in her fold of glass?
But when the ruinous belt of office, bought at a great price, has girded you,
And fruitless toil has worn you down,
Too late and to no purpose you will blame your empty hopes
And long to break the chains you are now tying.
Then you will remember, in vain, and grieve
That you despised father Augustine's truthful warnings.
So if you are wise and dutiful, boy, listen,
And take to heart the words of fathers and the counsel of old men.
"Why do you pull your wild neck back from the yoke? My burden is light,
My yoke is sweet": this is the loving voice of Christ. Trust God,
Put your head under the yoke, give your mouth to the soft halter,
And bend your shoulders low beneath the light load.
You can do this now, while you are free, while no chains hold you back,
No cares of a marriage bed, no high office.
This is true freedom: to serve Christ, and in him
To be above all. Not to human masters,
Not to vices, not to proud kings is a man enslaved,
Only the man who has given himself to Christ as Lord.
Do not think that nobility free which you now
See carried aloft through the awestruck city,
Which you see thinks itself so very free
That it scorns to bend its neck to God.
That wretched noble is the slave of many mortals, even of slaves,
And buys slave-girls only for them to lord it over him.
Those who have put up with eunuchs and great palaces know,
And so does every wretch who willingly puts up with Rome,
How dearly, in sweat and lost dignity,
The military cloak is bought there, and here the rank of office.
Yet even the powerful man, who has bought the right
To stand above all, does not manage to serve no one.
Though he has boasted through the whole city that he is a master,
He is a slave to demons if he worships idols.
For shame! Is it for these that you linger in the city, Licentius,
And scorn the kingdom of Christ to please them?
Do you call them lords and greet them with bowed neck,
Men you see are slaves of wood and stone?
They worship silver and gold as if they were divine;
Whatever the disease of avarice loves is their religion.
Let whoever does not love Augustine love such men, I pray,
And let whoever likes to court them not worship Christ.
This is why God himself says that no one can serve
Two masters, since an undivided mind is what pleases God.
One faith, one God, and Christ, the only Son of the Father;
The one Lord is not served by a divided service.
As great as the distance between heaven and earth, so great
Is the gap between the affairs and empires of Caesar and of Christ.
Rise from the earth, and now, while the spirit still rules these limbs,
Pierce the heavens with your mind; the flesh's delay is no hindrance.
Die even now to bodily deeds, and with a clear mind
Ponder in advance the good things of the heavenly life.
You are spirit, though held in a body, if now
With a devout mind you conquer and destroy the work of the flesh.
These lines, dear boy, I have written to you,
Driven by faithful love; if you receive them, God will receive you.
Believe that Augustine is now doubled for you in me;
Take two fathers with a single devotion.
If we are scorned, you are torn away to the greater grief of two;
If we are heard, you will be a sweet pledge to two.
The glad care of two fathers has toiled over you,
And it will be a great honour for you to have gladdened two.
But when I join myself with Augustine, I do not claim
To equal him in merit; I compare myself only in love for you.
For what could I pour on you, trickling from my poor stream?
Even without me you are washed by a twin river:
Your brother Alypius and your teacher Augustine,
The one sharing your blood, the other the sower of your mind.
With such a brother and such a teacher to make you strong, Licentius,
Do you hesitate to follow the stars on such wings?
Whatever you do (and let the world not hope to have you as its friend),
You will not be handed over to the earth, for your soul is owed to Christ.
Though you now dream of marriage chambers and high honours,
One day you will be restored to your Lord.
