I believe that two righteous men will overcome one sinner,
And a brother's prayers will drive away your stains.
So come back. One with a father's voice, the other as a brother by blood,
Both of them priests, they bid you return.
They draw you back to what is yours, for now you are seeking what belongs to others;
These realms that keep their hold on you are far more truly yours.
Seek them again, long for them; do not waste your time on outward things.
If you refuse what is yours, will anyone give you what belongs to another?
You will not be your own; sent far away through foreign lands,
You will live, alas, as an exile from the feelings of your own heart.
It is enough for an anxious father to have sung this to his son,
Wishing and fearing for you what I wish and fear for myself.
If you receive this page, one day it will bring you life;
If you reject it, this same page will be a witness against you.
May Christ keep you safe for me, dearest son,
And make you his own servant forever.
Live, I pray, but live for God; for to live for the world
Is the work of death, and to live for God is life indeed.
IX. Paulinus to Amandus, holy, truly of one mind with him, and most deservedly beloved.

As far as I can tell, what I whisper in your ear you proclaim from the housetop. You love me too much and are too pleased with your foolish brother, so you do not hesitate to slip into the ears even of our holy and venerable common father the rashness of my folly, by which I am bolder in my words toward you than toward him. For how could he think me fit to be asked for something in writing worthy of his spirit, unless you had persuaded him, judging by affection rather than by reason, that my mouth too had been opened by the Lord among the mouths of the dumb and of infants, from whom the Almighty perfects praise? So he bids me produce for him a discourse seasoned with spiritual salt, that is, with his own; for he remembers that he sprinkled me with the salt of his word. Nor does he cease to do so, for all his letters are spiritual seasoning to me. He himself is the salt of the earth, bringing back the lively savor of the apostles' teaching. But I fear that with my insipid heart I have failed to take in his salt, and that my mind does not perceive what it is seasoned with, so as to taste the sweetness of the Lord, if the savor of Delphinus could fade in it and its strength grow dull.

Who has roused me, the man who says, “There is a lion in the roads, and murderers in the streets”? We are not stirred to provide for our life and to useful labor by the zeal of the mystic bee or the example of the industrious ant. Instead we sleep a little, we slumber a little, we fold our hands on our breast a little, and meanwhile poverty comes upon us like a good runner. And he who was rich and became poor, so that by his poverty he might enrich us who are truly needy, seeing us persisting in our neediness, rightly cried out: “What profit is there in my blood, while I go down to corruption?” But would that, even as we say these things, we might be roused by the very verdict of our conscience and the complaint of our own words, so that, late as it is, we might be able to say: “Now I have begun; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” But we are lazy bellies, and so our soul cleaves to the ground, although you long ago said to it: “Rise from the dead, that you may reach Christ.” It was through the intervention of your faith that you placed this Lord, by the sacrament of grace, in the little boat of our heart. But since he has fallen asleep in us through the sleep of our sloth, you must wake him, so that he may arise to awaken our soul, command silence to the turbulent gusts of earthly thoughts, and calm the waves of our senses with the peace of his word. Then a chaste calm will come over our heart, and with the Spirit of truth as helmsman and the Word of God as oarsman we shall be steered to the haven we desire.

For what is our hope but the Lord Jesus, who is able to save us from faintness of spirit and from the storm, and to grant your prayers that our flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath, that is, in idleness from spiritual business and in barrenness of good works? For the sabbath is idle, and winter is bare of growing things. So let us keep the sabbath by abstaining, not in carnal but in spiritual observance, from all servile work, which is the life of sin (whoever is given over to it is truly a slave and does not remain in the house). Let it be not the sabbath which the soul of the Lord cannot bear, but the one in which God finds rest, he who rests in the humble heart of his trembling servants. If we keep such a sabbath, the winter storm will not overwhelm our flight, nor hold back our feet, sluggish as if with cold, from the freedom to escape. Rejoicing in hope and fervent in spirit, with our hands not cramped by the frost of avarice but opened to give the relief of mercy, may that stealthy coming of the last hour find us covered and clothed in the saving garments of faithful works, so that we may stand before the face of his cold. He wishes us now to be made ready in fear of his command, so that on the day of wrath he may find us fit to be acquitted.

Support us now, then, and pray that we may lay hold of that for which we have been laid hold of, and that, stretching forward to the prize of the heavenly calling, we may forget what lies behind. Having put the hand of my mind to the plough of the cross, may I not look back at the furrows already made but look ahead to those still to be made, until we reach the mountains to which we have lifted up our eyes, so that from there help may come to us from the Lord, who is wonderful in his saints. They are the mountains of God, and to them we shall be carried up by the good working of a faithful soul. For if we walk worthily in the way of truth, which is undefiled, then the Lord himself, who is the way and the truth, will make our feet like the feet of harts and set us upon the heights. For “the high mountains,” it says, “are for the harts, and the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs.” Let us with the swiftness of harts flee over iniquity from Nimrod the hunter, who, as scripture shows, was a hunter against the Lord, and with Christ working alongside us let us climb by holy deeds the heights of the virtues, through the teachings of the prophets and apostles, who are the mountains of God, those fertile mountains. If we do, then, looking down as if from a towering crag on the empty shapes of the passing world, we shall sing with a voice of exultation: “I will exalt you, Lord, for you have lifted me up above those who rise against me, and my eye has looked down upon my enemies.” Formed by this height of the mountains to humility of heart, and with our limbs fortified on every side by wholesome disciplines as by spines, we shall become like hedgehogs, which, their small bodies armed with a rough covering, are protected by natural darts against the bites of hostile dogs or the hands of men. For those who are humbled by the fear of God and armed with the grace of humility itself, the rock is a refuge, that is, Christ, whose words are for us both hedges and darts against the devil. With them we hedge our ears against a wicked tongue and pierce the vices that oppose us in our heart. So through spiritual observance and upright faith we shall be hedgehogs and harts alike, if, like those smaller creatures, we hide ourselves, lowly and humble, in Christ as in the rock of refuge, and, fortified by the word and Spirit of truth, put up a bristling resistance both to the devil and to the allurements of this world.

We shall emulate those larger beasts, swift of foot and lofty of horn, if we have feet firm enough to stand in the way of the Lord, so that our footsteps are not moved from his path, and if we use those same feet to flee from sins and the deadly contagions of this world. We must carry the head of our salvation, which is the catholic faith, both adorned and armed with good works as with horns, so that we may fight off the hunters who are our enemies, or else, crowned with deeds pleasing to God, be above all your joy and crown. For we are your planting in Christ and your daily labor before Christ. We do not doubt that you pray daily for that blessed change wrought by the right hand of the Most High to be accomplished in us, so that we may truly say: “My heart and my flesh have failed; God of my heart, and God is my portion for ever.” For God will deign to be the God of our heart when our heart, which is carnal, has failed, torn down by spiritual building. Then we shall dare to call ourselves your portion in the land of the living, when we ourselves, renewed for the Lord in the understanding of our mind according to Christ, after the heavenly image, are able to say: “God of our heart, and God our portion for ever.”
X. PAULINUS TO DELPHINUS, MOST BLESSED AND IN A SPECIAL WAY OUR LORD, EVER OUR FATHER IN THE LORD CHRIST.

We have received the letter of your holy affection, in which you bid us add to the letters we write to you some discourse from the scriptures beyond mere courtesies, to reveal to you the treasure of our heart. But the order of piety requires, and the apostle our teacher teaches, that it is rather the parents who should lay up treasure for the children. And indeed you, made our father by the Lord and in the Lord, have always laid up good things for us and do not cease to do so. There is first that talent of saving grace which we received under your seal. It was not to be hidden in the earth or wrapped in a napkin but deposited with the moneychangers, so that it might be multiplied with rich interest, or distributed in due season to those who sell oil for the wise to buy and prepare their lamps for the bridegroom's coming. But besides this you are always laying up treasure for us in another way, when you ask that more from the treasures of the Lord be added to the grace given us through you. And would that we could take in as much as you can obtain for us to receive! Surely it is from this awareness of your petitions on our behalf, and from your confidence in them, that you ask of us, or rather demand back, that we say something spiritual to you, something worthy of your seed in us. You believe, in keeping with your faith, that you have obtained by prayer what you have prayed and still pray to be given us, and so you desire to grasp the effect of your solicitude and supplication from the offspring of our heart and mouth, through the evidence of our words; for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and the savor of the mind is tasted in speech.

Rightly, then, your holiness reclaims the debt owed on its deposit and expects its seed to sprout. But what am I to do, a barren field? With what crop shall I repay you, I who have produced thistles instead of wheat and thorns instead of grapes? And so, conscious of a bad harvest, or of an unfruitful tree, I offer in my letters only words of courtesy, so as at least to satisfy the duty of affection. Confounded with shame at my sloth, I hide a mind that has fallen away from your heart. For I know your excessive love for me, and I fear that I may sadden with disappointed expectation your spirit, which rejoices in its confident hope of me, and that you may be compelled to say or write to me: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, but you have turned into the bitterness of a strange vine. I waited for you to produce grapes, and you produced thorns.” And would that they were at least useful thorns, which make a hedge for pious ears against a wicked tongue and guard faith in a watchful heart like a crop in an enclosed field! But, as I perceive, you, like a rough bramble, have put forth useless and harmful thorns, which choke the word and turn it to affliction, while they still pierce hearts with carnal thoughts.

You ask, then, most devoted father, what more you can do for us that you have not done. You have planted us in the house of the Lord; around us, once planted, you have built the wall of the saving seal, to protect us from the attack of the wild boar and the grazing of the fierce wild ass; and you have dug a winepress, so that by a holy way of life we might pour out for you, as it were, a sweet vintage from your own vine. Yet there is still something you can do, in imitation of him who begged from the lord of the vineyard a reprieve for the barren fig tree and by his pledge postponed the cutting down that threatened the useless tree. So let your devoted care intercede for us too, and ask that the axe laid at the roots of the fruitless trees be held back, at least for a year of waiting by the indulgent Lord. Pledge to the householder your diligent concern for us, and promise your constant prayers like that apostolic basket of gospel dung, so that the soil of our heart may grow rich and the crop of your sowing be nourished, or the tree of your planting receive the sap of your fruitfulness. Then on the day of reckoning, when sower and reaper shall rejoice together, you will carry us too in your fatherly bosom among your sheaves and claim from him the fruit of your cultivation, when you offer to him who nourishes what the waterers have sown and makes fruitful the labors of the cultivators whatever in us he deigns not to order cut down for the fire but to reap for the barn.
XI. PAULINUS TO SEVERUS, HIS BROTHER OF ONE MIND.

In the Lord God Jesus Christ I feel, and in you above all I joyfully experience through the gift and word of God, that nothing compares with a faithful friend, and that a gracious tongue abounds in a good man. For the comfort of your love is to us like a medicine of life, and your words are like a honeycomb; as cold water to the thirsty, so to us is good news of you from a far country. This news fattens our bones with the token of your well-being and with the eloquence of your love. It gains a great increase of gladness and delight from being brought and delivered by your servants, who are our sons in the Lord, so that we possess not only your letters but, as it were, a part of your very side. What shall we render to our Lord, beyond all that he has rendered to us, for this grace too? You were already most dear to us earlier in worldly friendship, and now he has bound you to us in spiritual brotherhood as an inseparable companion and partner in his own affairs as well, which we count of incomparable value.

"Who is my mother," he says, "or who are my brothers?" Clearly not those born of the will of the flesh and the union of sleep, but those born of God through Christ, the wisdom of God. Abiding in himself, he makes all things new and gives power to become children of God and co-heirs of his kingdom. For this very reason he was conformed to the body of our lowliness, that he might conform us to the body of his glory, and that he might bring us, torn away not only from our land but also from our kindred, into his own lot and generation. By this gift he deigned to create us for himself and to join us in the bond of his love. He changed us from fleshly intimacy, in which even then, as we now understand, he had been preparing us for this covenant, into an eternal kinship of stronger affection. For this indeed is the love of Christ, which never fails, because it flows from God and abides in God, and by its own everlastingness makes everlasting every man in whom it abides. This love does not know how to be puffed up. It is free of guile, untroubled by envy, and zealous for God, not with pride of spirit but with the spirit of gentleness and the zeal of devotion. For our Lord, as he himself testified and as we experience, is sweet and gentle and lowly of heart.

You were born my brother from him, not only for present help but also for everlasting fellowship. So you surpass every affection that bodily kinship gives me by as much as the Parent who makes you my brother is greater than the parents of those whom flesh and blood alone link to me. For where now is my brotherhood of blood? Where is my old friendship? Where are my former companions? I have vanished in the sight of them all, "a stranger," as it is said, "to my brothers and an alien to my mother's sons." "My friends and those once near me now stood afar off"; and "like a torrent rushing down and like a passing wave," so they pass me by, and perhaps they are confounded over me and, as it is written, ashamed to come to me. Those who were near have become far from me, and those who were far have become near. "Instead of your fathers," it says, "sons have been born to you." So the Lord has made you for us in place of parents and brothers and friends. You are anxious with a parent's care, solicitous with a brother's love, and diligent with all the faithfulness of unfeigned friendship. Pouring out upon us all the affection of devotion, you visit us with constant letters and soothe us with the sweetest consolations.

Nor do you think it enough to visit us at every opportunity unless you also send your servants. You choose as letter-carriers not only household slaves but also your holy sons, whose offspring, blessed in the Lord, is your joy, so that through their eyes you may see us and through their mouths touch us. Their feet are beautiful to us, as the feet of those who bring good news. For they announce and bring us the things that make for peace concerning you, when they bring out the works of the Lord which you either work in the word of God or write in the spirit of the Word. What riches could furnish such precious gifts, what kinships such sweet consolations? Even if we put off reckoning what divine bounty promises for eternity, it is easy to see how much better than the things we gave up are those that are repaid even now in this world. For what loss, I ask, can an unkind parent, a neglectful brother or a forgetful friend inflict on me in the grace of devotion, when all the loves that belong to these names, pledges and bonds are richly repaid to me by you alone? I say nothing of the many, whether in our own world or even in an unknown one, who are like you both toward God and toward us, whose very great affection the grace of the Rewarder grants us in place of homeland, parents and inheritance. If we reckon up the good things we have received in you alone, we shall count all that was ours as repaid to us in you more abundantly and more preciously. "A brother does not redeem," it says; "a man will redeem." Likewise we may say: the world does not love us, but Christ loves us. Man neglects, but God cherishes. "A man's enemies are those of his own household," but again, a man's friends are those of God's household. We may have had brothers and friends and neighbours who were good and great, but in them the Lord was not pleased to provide for us. Instead he chose to give you to us as an inseparable brother and a most beloved neighbour, whom we rightly love as ourselves, because we have one heart and one soul with you in Christ.

So what we briefly said above about the love of many others who are equally spiritual was not at all fittingly or worthily said, for the grace we have in you cannot be matched in anyone else. Though they deign to love the Lord's grace in our lowliness just as much, this gift is special to us in you. We were predestined for one another in the love of Christ, and we were marked out for this also by a very close friendship in our former life, when we were still lovers of the things we now turn away from through Christ. Yet through the habit of that intimacy we grew into the bond by which we are now joined through God's intervention. By loving each other faithfully even on a faithless road, we learned to love spiritually as well. For each of us always loved the other so devotedly that no affection could be added to our love for one another except the love of Christ, which alone surpasses all sense and affection. All the greater are the thanks we owe to the good Lord. He deigned to look upon our lowliness, and having found us together in the field, he drew us out together like twins from the womb of the flesh and took us up together. For truly, as you wrote, we were two in the field; but by the goodness and omnipotence of God, I dare say, one of us was taken up in such a way that neither was left. For each of us was also two within himself, when the flesh in us rebelled and was at odds with the spirit, and our man had no peace, since the outer fought against the inner. But now, by the favour of him who made both one, we two are also one, because there is one spirit in the two, and there is no division between those whose body is one. But this, as I said, we share with all our brothers in Christ. One thing in you is peculiarly welcome to us and calls for our thanks: in your friendship we received the most blessed gift of God, that not even a change of path should part us from each other. That is a loss we have both experienced, as you recall, with many who were once very dear to us.

Truly, then, you are to us both parent and brother and neighbour. You fulfil in us the will of God and the fullness of the law, and you love us as yourself, our friend in the love of Christ and our brother in God's regeneration. Since you see and recognize this, why do you speak in a way that burdens us and is false about yourself, saying: "Two were in the field, and one was taken"? Let us not be ungrateful to God, who took up not one out of us, but one in us. We were two, but that was when we were paired with those brothers from whom this way of life has divided us. The same Scripture makes it clear enough that "one" is said not of a single body but also of the unanimity of many, since it presents these figures not as two men but as peoples, as the faith of the Gentiles and the remaining behind of the Jews show. For those two women grinding, of whom likewise one is taken, represent, I think, the synagogue and the church. In the whole scheme of sacred Scripture only these figures are treated: either the distinction, within the whole human race, between believing and unbelieving peoples, or the twofold substance created in the nature of every man. And therefore, my brother, since we have always clung to one another in one heart, as now we cling together in Christ, we were either taken up together or left together. But we were taken up not by our own merit but by the grace of God, whose gifts and calling are without repentance. Nor were we taken up by any privilege of works, but by the faith of good will, by which we were quickened together into his love, as the single course of our purpose and the single time of our conversion made plain. So we ought to glory and exult together in him who justifies the ungodly through faith and gives food to all flesh. This is not the food that perishes, but the food that is prepared for eternal sustenance, the kind that the soul busy in the things of God, or the catholic church, bakes. For it is the body of the true bread which came down from heaven and gives life-giving food to those who hunger for righteousness. It does not stuff the flesh but strengthens the heart of man. This bread is also a fountain: the more it is eaten, the more one hungers, and the more it is drunk, the more one thirsts. That we may eat this bread forever, let us grind good wheat in the mill of this world. That wheat is the work of faithful obedience, and love from a pure heart and unfeigned faith.

Since you are full of this grace and virtue, you grind good grain for God and present yourself as a feast for God in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. His food is whoever carries out his will and so is turned into the members of his very body, as he himself says that whoever joins himself to God becomes one spirit. This we attain if we bear the image of the heavenly with the same care and diligence with which we bore the image of the earthly. For by imitating the imitator of Christ we shall come to the imitation of God, to whom we are a good fragrance in Christ, if we present a living sacrifice in reasonable service. So let us offer him pure fine flour, sifted by the millstone of a clean heart from the inner recesses of our being. Let us set up a chaste altar in our breast and slay, in our vices, those animals the law commanded for sacrifice. We sacrifice the goat when we destroy sin, which carries the odour of death. We strike down the bull if we lay aside pride. We sacrifice the sheep if, not lukewarm in love but fervent in spirit, we cast out softness and sloth. We offer in ourselves the lamb also if we live without blemish, and the calf if we become children in malice, so that we reproduce the purity of the one by chastity and the foolishness of the other by simplicity. Such a sacrifice I see you present to God in the temple of your body, in the sanctuary of your heart, in the immolation of your flesh, in the oblation of your soul. You sacrifice the bull when, brought low in godly humility, you strike down your lofty neck with the fear of God. You sacrifice the kid when, as a follower of righteousness, you kill all the works of the left side. You cut the sheep's throat when, as a diligent worker and earnest student of God's will and law, you lay low in yourself inertia and sloth like a soft beast. With the shears of the heavenly word you cut away from yourself the encumbrances of this life like fleece, which is useful to the shearer but a burden to the one who wears it. With these shears Christ, who holds us gripped by the two testaments, strips us of worldly baggage as if of wool. He cuts it like fleece from our bodily vices, as from the sickly and soft bodies of sheep, and spins it out among the church's tasks of wool for the garment of his body, which he covers through the work of believers; for as we in turn put on Christ, we are put on by Christ. And he weaves it into the fringes of his robe.

This shepherd has already sheared you, I think, placed you on his threshing floor and drenched your fleece with heavenly dew. For grace is poured upon your lips and flows abundantly through your mouth like a stream from the fountains of Israel or [?] from paradise, as it is written. This teaches us that the Lord came down upon you like rain upon a fleece and gave you water from Jacob's well, since you too had come near to the Lord as one of the sons of Israel. If, then, you have been shorn, you see that you have received a twofold benefit. Lightened in the heat of the world, you crop the pastures of the Word, sprinkled with the dew of morning gladness, and you are not scorched by the heat of the noonday demon, because you rest under the shadow of the Lord's wings. Meanwhile a tunic is being made for you from your own wool to clothe you on that winter's day, so that you can stand before the face of its cold, if, when stripped of the body, you are not found naked of works. Then in turn Christ will offer himself to you as a sheep. He is the Lamb who was led to the slaughter for us and did not open his mouth before his shearer, but let his fleece, that is, the cast-off covering of his flesh, be stripped from him. For he laid down both his soul and his flesh for us and took them up again. He is priest and victim, lamb and shepherd; he was slain as shepherd for his sheep and as lamb for his shepherds. The Lord himself is the victim of all priests. Offering himself to the Father for the reconciliation of all, he was the victim of his own priesthood and the priest of his own victim. Now every new creature is a sacrifice to him, as the one Lord of all, and the victims themselves are priests. If we now offer ourselves to him to be shorn, in the silence of humility and patience with which he offered himself for us, he will take upon himself the burdens of our fleece. He will not disdain to carry the wool of his sheep, since he deigns to carry back to the fold on his shoulders the very sheep he has called back from straying.

He has no need of our goods, while we need all of his, and he is good to us only for our own good. So he takes what is ours, which is really his, and yet he does not want it to be his by right, so that he may credit it to us as though it were ours; for we have nothing that we have not received, and we ourselves could not even exist without his assent. So to us, who brought nothing into this world, he supplies the substance of temporal things like a fleece for shearing. He does this not so that the burden may hinder those whom he bids be born unencumbered, but to set before us material for virtue with which to earn merits. It also gives us the means to prove our faith and devotion toward God, our true Father and Lord, if we have dear or sweet things and, preferring God, give them up for a great reward. These things were not brought with us into this world and cannot be carried away from here with us. Yet if we obey his commands, his immense goodness so orders them that they are changed for the better and turned from temporal into eternal. Just as we did not bring them in, so by our nature and by the passing form of this world we cannot take them away. Yet through the work of almighty God we turn them to account by a blessed kind of trade, and we not only carry them out with us but even send them ahead of us, sown in the Lord's bosom.

Hence, I think, the rule that the lazy worker should not eat bread. This does not mean the bread of perishing food, but the bread by which one lives the true life. For each, as it is written, will eat of his own fruits and live by his own works, and so each person's own work is his bread. The true and living bread is Christ, and the lazy worker cannot eat him, because he is also our Passover. We are commanded to eat it in all haste, unencumbered and girded and firmly shod, without putting our staffs out of our hands, that is, never relaxing the works on which we lean. For the time is short, and, as the Apostle urges, it is better for us to be free of care because of the present necessity. So we must be found ready, and not be afraid to open when the Lord knocks, as if our sleep or negligence left us dreading what we deserve. That fear would do us no good. We should be dragged out all the same, to death after death, to pay the just penalties of negligence and impiety, if we are caught serving another master rather than our own, busy with the affairs of the world rather than of Christ, so that we do not open to the Lord when he knocks and are led unwilling to the Father. Therefore we are told beforehand to labour for this, that is, for the soul, and to pray at the opportune time, that is, the present. We are brought into this span of time precisely so that through this short and passing life we may seek the true life. The plain and field of this life is this world, or man himself, who is sent into this world. Of these two, one is taken up when, as we said above, the flesh is subjected to the spirit and the two are made one. For according to the Apostle there are two minds and two laws in each of us, and as these grind within us, they produce a flour that God either accepts or rejects.

But your eloquence, as fluent as it is chaste, testifies that you have overcome the law of the members and let the outer man decay. You prepare a pure dough, and you are being made unleavened bread for Christ. For you would not have been granted the power to tell the story of Martin had you not made your mouth worthy of sacred praises by a clean heart. Blessed, then, are you by the Lord, for you have recounted the history of so great a bishop and so manifest a confessor in language as worthy as your affection was just. Blessed too is he for his merits, for he deserved a historian worthy of his faith and life. He is consecrated to divine glory by his own merits and to human memory by your writings. These words of yours are also fleeces, and they cover the Lord Jesus with a most welcome covering. They surround his [?] with beautiful furnishings and adorn it with the flowers of your genius. That Lamb in turn will clothe you from his own fleece on the day of recompense, clothing your mortality with his immortality.

Only remember us and look back to us, not as one who looks behind him, but as one who remembers a friend. It is certain that, as the more skilful farmer, you have richer harvests, and as the swifter runner you fly ahead of my slowness toward the prize of the upward call. For I am weaker in mind than in body, and I follow you at a long distance, though I am separated from you only in space, not in road. I turn the same mill with a sick and unequal hand, your partner in the bakehouse but worse in my grain, because I grind tares mixed with wheat. That all of it may be turned into good grain, I need your prayers. By them I hope to escape both my riches and my poverty, since both are bad for me: I am poor in righteousness and rich in sin. For I should truly believe myself rich in good if I were already as poor as you think. On this point, however, let me take you to task a little over your own words, in which you disagree with yourself. Even if you did not proclaim virtues of my own in me, you still thought that others' virtues might be granted me by your words. How then is it consistent for you to profess that you admire poverty and also to confess that you dread it? You confess that you wish for this virtue but cannot attain it: to have food and clothing and be content with them, and to think of nothing beyond the day. If you believe that I have been granted it, why do you think the pressure of want will overcome me, so that I shall stop inviting you, when I cannot help longing for you? Or why do you show yourself so weak and so distrustful of Christ that you fear to come to such a friend as you describe, if you truly follow him who said, "Take up your cross and come, follow me"? How else do you think Christ is to be followed than by the law he taught and the pattern he set? When he came to his own, he still had no place among his own possessions to lay his head.

Imitate the imitator of Christ, so that you may die and yet live. Crucify yourself to the world and the world to yourself, dying daily through faith in the word and living in the word of faith. For man does not live by bread alone, and the Christian least of all, of whom it is properly written that he lives by faith. Did it say "by bread"? Why then do you fear hunger with me, if you have faith? Your bread is with you. If you are fed by the word of God, you will not long for food for the belly; for God will destroy both the one and the other while he builds himself up in us. That is, if we stand firm, founded in his love, and do not set our house on the sand of wavering distrust. Did we not both believe him and swear allegiance to him who said, "Do not think about tomorrow; each day has trouble enough of its own; seek first the kingdom and righteousness, and all these things will be added to you"? If you believe him, why do you fear hunger from the want of his brother? You know that this brother, secure in that word, has preferred poverty to riches. Or do you believe that the one who trusts the earth has more abundance than the one who trusts God, and that the one fed by his own care has more than the one fed by God's? What can that wretch have who does not have himself? For whoever hopes more from himself than from God does not have himself. And he is truly dead who fears that he will not live if he entrusts and commits himself wholly to God. I hope, then, that it was a jest of your good humour rather than a confession of weakness when you wrote that you believe I shall soon be so poor that I would no longer dare to invite you. I confess that I desire nothing more than the blessing of such freedom, since so inward a circumcision is full perfection. Yet if your faith in Christ is true, and your admiration for heavenly virtues in a man and your emulation of a man living in God are true, how could you not seek me all the more, the more perfect you heard I was? Unless, of course, you openly confessed that you do not believe in your heart what you profess with your mouth. You are a frequent visitor of the most blessed Martin, so you stand convicted of fleeing the sinner in me, not the poor man. You would certainly never have longed for Martin if you had been afraid of going hungry for bodily food.

For my part, since in the progress of spiritual work it is love above all, the fulfilment of the law, that must make progress, I will never cease to invite you, just as I never cease to long for you. Come to us, and if you can, fly to us. We have nothing but Christ, and see whether we have nothing when we have him who has all things. For we did not leave Ebromagus for the sake of a little garden, as you write; rather, we preferred that garden of paradise both to our inheritance and to our homeland, because the true home is rather there where the home is eternal, and the truer homeland is there where our original soil and first dwelling lie. For if you believe it, by the favour of Christ, for whose sake we possess all things in him even if we have nothing, the mud of the earth does not now hold us on this ground of thorns and toil, not even by a little clod of a garden. But would that no dust of sin clung to us in the same way! If you believe this good to be what you proclaim it to be, and believe me to be in it, as you write that you do, and yet you long for me less eagerly, then your offence is no longer against me, a sinner who is always and ever unworthy of your sight, but against the Lord himself, if you think that the food of mortal life will fail us at the very moment when God has begun to be our possession.
XII. PAULINUS TO AMANDUS, HOLY, DESERVEDLY VENERABLE AND MOST BELOVED.

I confess that I marvel at the holy kindness and patience of your love. I usually write you letters that are extremely talkative and more full of annoyance than of charm, yet you feel a longing for my words rather than weariness of them, since you provoke and rouse me to frequent and longer letters by the charm of your own writings. In them love, out of a pure heart and faith unfeigned, speaks sincere affection in the unleavened bread of truth, and in turn draws out my own affection from the depths of my mind. What, then, shall I do? Shall I obey you with an abundance of letters? But you have no need of my goods, and it is fairer that I be enriched by you, for the rich ought to give to the poor, so that there may be equality. Or should I rather look to my own advantage and set a guard over my mouth, so as to escape the danger of sin that comes from much speaking? But then again I fear that I may be found guilty of disobedience, and perhaps I would offend more seriously by failing you through not obeying than by fearing for myself through not writing.

May the Lord from the Lord, then, grant me the opening of my mouth to you, and set the lamp of his word before my feet, so that the night of my foolishness may be lit up like the day. May he loosen my tongue for a good word, he who also loosed the mouth of a donkey into human speech. For I too am one of those stones or beasts of burden that the donkey prefigured when it spoke on that occasion, signifying that the mute nature of Gentile hardness and dullness would speak once God had loosed their tongues. And if you will, let us draw out the fabric of this letter on this very grace of God, since all our discourse ought to be occupied with the commandments and praises of the Most High, and everything we say and everything we live ought to be paid back with unceasing thanksgiving to him by whose work and gift we speak and live. For it is he who made us, and not we ourselves. It is he, I say, the Lord, who made us, and who also remakes us; from the very beginning, through all that he has done and spoken in his saints, he has been working out the mysteries of our salvation, that is, of the restoration of humankind. For a holy generation in Seth at once restored righteous Abel; Seth reproduced in a likeness of face the father who had been formed in the image of God. From there the vein of righteousness flowed down through the rest from the first spring; and although the flood intervened, the seed of the destroyed universe stood firm in one man, one only, yet righteous, for already then the mystery of the one Redeemer was at work, so that reconciliation might come through one, since offense had come through many. But when righteousness again slipped back as the human race advanced, and nations and crimes grew together, then, so that human wickedness should not once more deserve the destruction of the race, again a man was chosen to be called the father of faith, from whom would spring both the promise of the kingdom and the seed of the eternal King. That seed, multiplied by the faith of the Gentiles, Christ fulfilled: he who was seen by the patriarchs, prefigured through the law, foretold through the prophets, himself came, to fulfill the law and the prophets, and to give by grace the healing that the law had been unable to bestow by works.

For by then sin had so pervaded the whole body, that is, the entire human race, that neither poultice nor bandage could help the weak and wounded; indeed, as the strength of the vices grew firm, the disease, stronger than any remedy, had shut out every cure that human help could offer. And so he came who is also to come, conformed to the body of our lowliness so that he might conform us to the body of his glory, since no one but the maker has power over his own work, and only the potter has rights over his clay. Thus the Lord of all, who had made all, deigned to come down to our condition and take us up into his own body, so as to remake us by the same skill or power by which he had made us. Yet he came not in the loftiness of the Lord, which he was, but in the form of a servant, which he was not. He who is the power of God and the Lord of hosts, the helper and protector of all, became like a man without help. He who was free among the dead died to set others free. He who justifies the ungodly through faith was counted among the wicked. That Lamb who takes away the sins of the world was led like a sheep to the slaughter. He who gives eternity suffered death.

But to perceive the reason for this great plan and gift is the light of him who enlightens us from the everlasting mountains. Lifting our eyes to them, let us see that we have been found again by the same paths by which we had perished: again by a tree, again by a virgin, but not again to be cast down by pride; on the contrary, we are to return by humility. For this is why the King of glory and the Lord of majesty emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and covered his invisible greatness with visible abasement: so that he might raise us, who through that old disease of wrongly conceived arrogance were lofty outside and crushed within, into the form of his own loftiness through the pattern of our humility in himself. For to this end the good Lord has worked and works daily, that we may attain the glory of being conformed to the divine, if we follow the example of our own conformity in Christ, recognizing that in the governance of the Most High a measure suited to our nature has been set, so that we may be carried above ourselves by his grace if we walk beside ourselves, mindful of what we are. To this measure we are fitted by that prophetic saying in Numbers which says: We will not turn aside to the right or to the left, but will go by the king's highway. This highway is Christ for us, the mediator between God and men, who holds us in balance between the divine and the human and leads us by the royal road to his kingdom, so that, humble in heart and lofty in deeds, we may be lifted from the left hand, that is, from sins, which drag us into death, and, called back by the law of humility from excess on the right hand, that is, from proud presumption, we may keep to the healthy middle way. So we shall neither bend our eyes to the earth and be compared to the beasts of burden, which have no understanding, nor search out things too high for us and become futile in our thoughts. Therefore, not minding high things but agreeing with the lowly, let us measure ourselves by the measure with which the Lord has measured us, so that we may be narrowed in ourselves and enlarged in the Lord, not like those wise men of this world whose wisdom the Lord rejected and destroyed and shut out through the foolishness of preaching. For they reasoned, it says, in order to hide snares; for clearly the whole art of the philosophers labors at this: to obscure the light of truth by asserting fictions, to entangle in the snares of empty disputes minds lured away from what is true, to deceive them by the trickery of cleverness and to lead them astray with the cosmetics of speech.

But since a light has risen in the darkness, the Lord, merciful and compassionate and just, those men have set their mouth against heaven in vain who, ignorant even of earthly things and of their own nature, search out the regions of the sky and seek God without God. So they have failed in their searching, and their wounds have become the arrows of little children, for the Lord, catching the wise in their own craftiness, has confounded them through the mouths of infants and sucklings, and has established his kingdom not in word but in power. Hence I too, the least of all the Lord's least ones, the slightest of the small and the most infant of infants, dare to burst into the voice of his praise, giving thanks to the Lord Most High because he has brought out for his little ones the mystery of exalted godliness that he kept stored in the treasuries of his wisdom, and has hidden it from the wise of the world, so that this world might not glory in the vanity of its wise men, through which, with darkness poured over it, it had failed to recognize the wisdom of God. But Jesus, our peace, who came to make both one and to set all things in equality, destroyed the strong and chose the weak, spurned the wise and took up the foolish, so that there might be equality, with no one claiming anything as his own, since every man, sharing in salvation and wisdom only by God's gift, must glory in the Lord. Therefore let us rejoice with trembling in the Lord our God, who is humble in heart and exalted in majesty, having the same mind in ourselves as was in Christ, who, as I said above, conferred on us the grace of salvation through the pattern of humility for this reason: that we, who had deserved to fall through a spirit of self-exaltation, might learn to rise again through a humble heart.

That the good Lord was crucified and rose again was done not only for the destruction of our death and the restoration of eternity, but also for the shaping of this present life, in which we acquire the merit by which possession of that life, blessed forever, is prepared. By what mystery and plan of godliness, then, was the Lord fixed to the cross? The apostle teaches us: so that, he says, he might break down the dividing wall, slay the enmities, strip bare the whole ambition of this world, and, taking captive the entire power of the enemy, triumph over captivity itself, taking up in his own flesh, he says, the likeness of sinful flesh. That is, not the likeness of flesh, for God is truth to all, and therefore the Word was truly and bodily made flesh, but the likeness of the sin of the flesh. Thus he who committed no sin, by his inviolable and impassible nature, nevertheless for our sake, as it is written, was made sin, that is, bore the sinner whom he took up in the form of a servant. For he became a curse for us, to free us from the curse of the law; by sin he condemned sin, that is, the stuff of sin that still lived in that flesh of Adam he emptied of power in the very flesh of Adam that he deigned to take up. And so, destroying the dividing wall, that is, sin, which separated us from God, he made both one, not only so that the faith of Jews and Gentiles might come together in Christ, but so that in each one of us who believe, our nature might be in harmony with itself, and the discord that once raged within us, when the fleshly soul fought against spiritual desire, might be dissolved in the peace of faith. For now that ancient war, in which the law of sin fought against the law of God, is abolished in Christ, since the spirit, serving God, governs by faith the soul made subject to it, and the flesh, as handmaid, accompanies in all obedience the soul that serves God.

Therefore by the Lord's passion and resurrection we are instructed not only in the hope of and faith in the resurrection, but also so that we may learn to die not only by the dissolution of the flesh but also by a voluntary withdrawal from this world, and by dying to this world through faith be made alive to God. For the life that is a friend to this world is the death of the soul. That is why the apostle tells us: Put to death your members that are on earth. He testifies that he himself dies daily, bruising his body, forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead. In this he teaches both humility and loftiness together, for the body cannot be subdued without a spirit of humility, nor can the soul rise to heavenly things except through the putting to death of the members. Yet even in humility itself we must keep a measure, so that we humble ourselves only in the fear of God, before the one Lord: for you shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve, and to serve him is freedom. For he who has subjected himself to God alone is subject to no one; but on the other hand, whoever wishes to be free from righteousness is a slave to all the lowest things, whether spirits or other creatures or his own vices and desires. There is, moreover, both a holy pride and a wicked humility. For that pride is justified which is proud toward this world, despises this age and makes use of all its great, sweet and beautiful things without attachment, intent on heavenly things and subject to divine commandments. On the other hand, that humility is condemned which is brought before men not from faith but from cowardice of mind, and cares more for human favor than for its own salvation: the handmaid of falsehood, the enemy of truth, a stranger to freedom, enslaved to iniquity, mixing water with wine, that is, weakening the pure wine of truth with the watery stuff of flattery. It is chiefly against this kind of humility, it seems to me, that the voice is directed which proclaims: Woe to those who call evil good and bitter sweet, and who proclaim the unjust righteous; men whom Truth also curses through Solomon, as you know.

The blessed psalmist, in a short psalm but with complete instruction, fittingly shapes us to the right balance in governing ourselves, when he puts forward the merit of humility in his prayers, saying: Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up; nor have I walked in great things, nor in wonders above me. And then he who had asked to be looked upon because of his humility of heart says: If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, as a child weaned upon its mother, so will you reward my soul. So he asks for a reward because he did not think humbly but exalted his soul. Will not the prophet's statement seem to contradict itself, unless we distinguish these things in our understanding as they were distinguished in his spirit and heart, so that they agreed with each other? For it was fittingly and humbly said in the fear of God by one who, as he himself testifies, offered to God as a sacrifice a troubled spirit and a humbled heart. Yet, while keeping his humility of heart, the same man exalted his soul by not thinking humbly, for he did not mind earthly things but kept his mind fixed on God, counting it the one good to cleave to God and to put his hope in God. Hence the apostle too, who teaches us humility, saying that we should strive to be imitators of Christ chiefly in this, Have this mind in you, he says, which was also in Christ, who did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, nevertheless also calls us to exalt the soul to things above and divine, when he says: Seek the things that are above, where Christ is at the right hand and in the glory of God the Father.

Holding, therefore, to this rule of both humility and exaltation, let us keep each of them in its proper order and measure, for each of them is sin when perverted, as I said above, but wins grace when rightly directed, as we are taught: in godliness both humbling our heart before God and exalting our soul to our Lord. Let us fear nothing but him, love nothing above him. Let us bow our necks only to his yoke, which is easy, and to his burden, which is light, so that, free from every yoke of the hostile power, we may be borne up to heavenly things. For this too is why the yoke of our Lord is easy and his burden light: because it lifts us above earthly and infernal things and raises us to the heights of the heavenly kingdom. For all lightness seeks the heights and is carried upward by the force of its fineness.

Contrary to this grace, the weights of sin press us down and drag us to the depths of hell. How heavy a burden they are the prophet testifies when he cries out with groaning: My iniquities have gone over my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me. But thanks be to the Lord Jesus our God, who is able to free us from the body of this death through the multitude of his mercies and the riches of his goodness, by which he overflows the abundance of our sins and saves those who hope in him. Before him, we believe, the watches of your prayers are kept for us as well. For we know that, serving as his soldier from boyhood, nourished on the sacred Scriptures and stained by no blot of earthly and fleshly conduct, you have found grace in the sight of the Most High, and can intercede for us who have been caught late from the forest of this world for the Lord's flock or chariot, since our iniquities are multiplied beyond the hairs of our head and we are unworthy that our names should be brought to the divine ears, lest perhaps your lips too become unclean when you name us, and your mouth must be touched with a burning coal. Yet you can say, with either the humility or the confidence of the ancient prophet: Lord, forgive them, or blot me out of your book. That man, a sharer in converse with God, neither careless of his own salvation nor insolent toward the Lord, dared to say this by the art of profound counsel: when the just Lord threatened the sinful people with the destruction they deserved, he set against it the offer of his own blotting out instead, secure, clearly, in the divine goodness and justice, so that the Lord's mercy would spare even the unjust, since his justice could not blot out the just man.

Bind the Lord Most High on our behalf too by this condition, so that, since he cannot remove you from his book, he may receive the unjust for the sake of his just one. For since he who is in us is greater than he who is in this world, righteousness is therefore stronger in defending sinners than iniquity is against the patronage of the saints. I would like, as far as I am able, to prolong my discourse still further, were it not that my paper is running out and the fear of tiring you compel me to set a limit to my words and bring the letter to an end. Pardon my boldness in everything, and reply to me, so that I may be consoled and instructed by your letter.

Now we commend Sanemarius, the bearer of this letter, especially to your fellow feeling, so that he may be settled by you as we have asked our holy bishop and father. For we have made him our fellow servant by granting him his freedom in the Lord; but he is to serve us in the house of the Lord, with duties assigned to him in memory of our parents, so that through religious service he may deserve to hold a secure freedom under your protection. Do approach our holy brother the priest Exsuperius as well, so that he may receive a small plot of land on the church's estate from which to earn his living. Further, I ask that you have my letter to our son Daducius, even though he is living in Gaul, sent on by the bishop without any delay by a faithful and energetic fellow servant. If perhaps the bishop does not want a cleric to be taken up with this, please send one of the men of Alingo with your own letters, to support ours; for you will learn from the letter I have written to him that the case is worthy of your intervention. Above all, speed in acting is needed, so that the most holy priest, venerable both in life and in age, who is enduring the violence I have described, may be freed as soon as possible from his exile in the houses of others.
XIII. PAULINUS TO PAMMACHIUS, MOST BELOVED BROTHER, DESERVEDLY PRAISEWORTHY AND MOST VENERABLE.

Until now I have kept the time for silence with fitting humility. Now, with the love I owe you, I recognize that the time for speaking has come, my venerable and most beloved brother in Christ the Lord. A letter from that holy man, our brother Olympius, who shares one mind with us both, recently brought me news of your grief, news as unexpected to me as it was unwelcome. Even setting aside the feelings of personal affection, the love of Christ our Lord and God would not allow you to go without my share in your sorrow and the service of my voice, for in him and through him we are joined like members of one body. Our Lord God himself, the teacher of both our life and our devotion, taught us through his heavenly chosen vessel to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep, to suffer with one another in turn and bear one another's burdens, so that by mutual consolation we might strengthen our common faith and cherish weary hearts. God set so high a value on this service that he promised that whoever performs it will be enlarged like a great city, declaring through the prophet that a brother who helps a brother will be exalted like a great city. He means that a brother's compassion brings a bulwark to the soul in its struggle and stands like a wall against the many blows that strike an afflicted mind.

Someone may judge it a fault rather than a kindness that I perform this duty of love so late. If so, please believe that I wrote the moment I learned the news. And do not think that I heard late because I neglected you. Both the remoteness of my home and my chosen way of life excuse me. Living there in seclusion and silence, I see only a few passers-by, and I do not care to ask news of the holy brethren except from those dear to me. Yet even in my silence I have always kept you in mind, and now that love seemed to demand it, I have unlocked the affection hidden in my heart and brought it out to you in this letter. By this letter I have set out toward your holy self, one in mind with me, by the only road open to me, since I could not keep my body and my soul within the same bounds. My flesh, weak as always, refused to travel any distance in winter, while my spirit, always the readier, flew off to you with fervent longing, so that I might embrace in mind the one I could not hold in body. So I have run to you, thirsting with longing, my brother in Christ, one in mind with me and venerable. If you look at me in turn with your mind, you will see and feel that I am wholly with you. If it is true that we see and hear chiefly with the mind, then I am certainly present to you by the better part of myself, since I have come to you in spirit. Unless we are present in spirit, we do not prove our presence even where we are there in body, for when the mind is absent, only an empty image of us remains. So I have offered this sealed gift of friendship and made it fit our faith, by visiting you through a spiritual approach. In return I ask this favor of you: that you too may see me with the inward eyes, as though I stood close by and spoke to you face to face, sighing with you in your anxiety over the necessity we all share, or congratulating you on the patience that comes from the hope of faith, and that in this way you may both receive me and behold me in these words. A man's speech is the mirror of his mind. God's own word confirms that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and the treasure of the heart is made public in speech. Therefore, in the truth in which we stand in Christ, receive my mind as this letter expresses it. I would not have you measure our friendship by time. It is not like worldly friendship, which is born more often of hope than of faith. It is that spiritual friendship which has God for its author and grows together through a hidden kinship of spirits. So it does not grow into love by long habit, nor does it hang on waiting for proof. As befits a daughter of truth, it is born at once firm and great, because it springs up through Christ and begins from fullness.

Embracing you with this love, I revere you as a member of Christ and love you as a member we share. How can those who have one faith not have one mind? How can those who have one God not have one soul? And so how could those who form one body in the framework of belief have different hearts in their way of bearing suffering? I speak the truth, I do not lie: as I think of the movements of your soul, I feel my own heart drawn by your sighs, and, since we are truly members of one another, pierced by the pain of your wound. Yet the thought of your wisdom and faith refreshes me no less than concern for your grief afflicts me. In fact I confess I hesitated whether to offer you words of sorrow, as my affection prompted, or words of congratulation, as your faith deserved. For I heard both of the calling of my holy sister to God and of the devoted piety you showed in Christ. This head of household who carries my letter has also told me of the wisdom and holiness of your true love for your wife. You did not escort her without weeping, as most people do not, but neither did you honor her with the vain show of empty processions, as those who lack our hope are accustomed to do. You followed her with saving remedies and living works, that is, with almsgiving. In due order you first paid her dear body its funeral rites, and then, drenched in loving tears and in the abundant dew of charity, you honored her funeral in a more devout way.

So I shall first praise this work of piety in you, for divine scripture shows that this too pleases God when it says: "Son, let your tears fall over the dead, and begin to lament as one who has suffered cruelly, and do not neglect his burial." Indeed our patriarchs are examples of this devotion too. The father of faith wept for his Sarah, the mother of our calling, certainly not because he doubted he would receive her back, but because he longed for her who had gone ahead. How could the father of faith, the first to hear the blessed promise, doubt the resurrection? Yet, mindful of his humanity, he did not scorn the care of the body because the soul was secure. He bought a field for a tomb and laid his dead in a costly resting place. In doing so he taught us what people ought to provide for themselves here. At God's word he had left the land of his kindred and acquired nothing else in all the expanses he wandered among foreign peoples, a stranger in every land; yet he bought a field for a tomb and nothing else, that is, a possession not temporal but eternal, land not for greed but for rest. Jacob too honored his beloved and long-awaited Rachel with a renowned tomb and a monument, both to pay a religious duty to his present grief and to bear witness to it for those who came after. And yet with a prophet's mind he marked that place with the monument of his wife's death, foreseeing that the law would be laid to rest by the birth announced in the gospel. In this mystery the patriarch's wife, who in many respects lived as an image of the Church, dies, I think, as a type of the Synagogue. She gave birth to a son of sorrow in the very place where the end of the law was to be born of a virgin; for Christ is the end of the law. Tobias teaches the holy and sanctified hope expressed in the care of burial. The Lord justified him with a special privilege for this very service, and the archangel's voice praised him, because he put the burial of a poor man before his own dinner. He neglected his belly because he cared for his soul, and preferred to go hungry in body rather than in spirit. In this he is an example to us too, that we should prefer to fast from the food of the flesh so as to bring fullness to the soul. Good, then, is the devout duty of burial. Good are the tears of love with which father Abraham carried out the mother of the promise. Good are the tears of filial devotion that righteous Joseph spent on his father. Good too are the tears of prayer with which David watered his bed every night. But why should I proclaim the weeping of holy mortals? Jesus too wept for his friend. He condescended to take on this suffering as well from our unhappiness, shedding tears for a dead man and mourning in human weakness the one he was about to raise by divine power. And yet in that one man the merciful and compassionate Lord lamented the whole condition of the human race at once, and with those tears in which he wept for our sins he also washed them away.

So your tears too, brother, are holy and devout, because they flowed from a like affection. They wept for the worthy partner of a chaste marriage bed, not from doubt of the resurrection but from loving longing. For a gracious wife raises up glory for her husband while she is with him, and so she also raises up longing when she is sent on ahead. But as she always was, so she will be forever a crown to her husband, and her lamp will not go out. For, as it is written, she stretched out her arms to useful work, she opened her mouth with wisdom, she did her husband good. She has crowned you with glory and honor, so that she may rejoice with you in the last days. For this reason she deserves weeping rather than mourning, and should be longed for steadfastly rather than lamented. The very thought of her merits imposes bitter grief on the one who survives her, because the death of a just person leaves regret behind. Yet it also gives rich consolation to the faithful, because immortality lies in the memory of the just. And do not let the fact that she died young, holy brother, drive a sharper sting of grief into you, since the divine word offers comfort for this very case: "For the just," it says, "if overtaken by death, will be at rest."

But lest you think she reached her death too soon, the same Wisdom proves to you in the words that follow that she was also old: "Old age," it says, "is venerable, not for its length, nor is it reckoned by the number of years. For understanding is gray hair for men, and a spotless life is old age." So let us rejoice at her righteous summons and her ripe end. Though she was still green in the flower of her years, she had grown gray in holiness of character and adorned a girl's age with the service of old age. So the very things that sharpen the wound in your mind can bring you greater comfort: though you no longer have so holy a woman, you did have her. To lose a mortal is something you share with everyone; to have deserved the best of women is something few share with you. So I am less surprised that she did not linger in this world and was called to Christ the sooner. Her soul was pleasing to God, and therefore, as it is written, he hastened to take her from the midst of wickedness, lest our wickedness should change our understanding. For, as it is written, the whole world lies in the power of the evil one, and evil talk often corrupts good morals, and whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it. In this fear a certain saint, dreading delay and anxious at a slow old age, prays God to make known to him his end and the number of his days. When the revelation of the Spirit by whom he prophesied showed him that his time had been prolonged, he groans and says: "Woe is me, that my sojourn is prolonged!" He declares that the cause of his groaning and fear is that he dwelt among the tents of Kedar, that is, in the darkness of this world. For Kedar in Hebrew means what in Latin is called darkness.

Indeed David himself, in losing two sons of differing merit, set forth the mystery of this truth. He had wept for his most beloved son while the child was sick, but did not weep for him once he was lost, being sure that the infant had been carried over into the blessedness of eternal peace. Yet the same David lamented the death of Absalom, who had been his enemy, because as a prophet who knew divine justice he despaired of rest for the wicked, and knew that the good of resurrection was not owed to a parricide. Yet the same man, as I said, had spent tears on his little one while he was sick. He exchanged his royal dress for black clothing, and, upheld by sackcloth, ashes and fasting, sent up his prayers to God. But once the end of life had released his son from sickness, he made the end of his mourning the same as the end the little boy had come to in his living, as though the matter for his cares had run out. So as the son was released in body, the father was released from grief. Laying aside at once his sad heart and his mourning clothes, he took food, put on his dress again, and anointed his head, filthy with dust, with oil. His servants were astonished at so unusual a way of fatherly devotion, in which a man who had mourned before his bereavement rejoiced once he was bereaved. When they asked him, he answered: "I shall go to him, but he will not return to me."

The prophet king has taught us well enough, I think, what concern we ought to take on after our loved ones are gone: we who follow should labor over our own journey rather than over the journey of those who have gone ahead and already arrived. It is devout to be saddened at being torn from our dear ones, but holy to rejoice in hope and faith in God's promises and to say to the struggling soul: "Why are you sad, and why do you trouble me? Shall not one who sleeps rise again?" Grateful joy is more acceptable to God than prolonged and, as it were, complaining sadness. David's example teaches us not to pour out useless tears. They are given to the dead to no purpose, bringing nothing to the one who has been received and weighing down the one who is left. That is why David wept while his son was alive and rejoiced when he died. While the child still breathed, David could win him a reprieve by prayers and tears. Once God had called the child away, David ought to rejoice, and so he did, for there can be no doubt that God's good pleasure is better than our wishes.

So let us pay the duties of devotion without harm to faith, and without harm to devotion let us put the joys of faith first. Granted, let devotion weep for a time, but faith must rejoice without ceasing. Let us long for our dead as ones sent ahead, but let us not despair of receiving them back. For our God is the God of the living, not of the dead, and the apostle says that the dead sleep in Christ, so that from the word sleep you may understand that death is temporary. Waking and rising follow naturally on sleep. Since this is so, let us in our love for our own carry the longing for their familiar company, but let us draw from our faith the comfort of confidence in the resurrection.

Most beloved brother, you have used these authorities of heavenly words and examples to justify the devotion of your tears. Use them as well to set a measure to those tears. For it is written: "For everything there is a time." Let the time for weeping have run its course; now is the time for rejoicing, because the Lord is near. Divine scripture, which allows us to let our tears fall as if grief were evaporating, also sets limits to them within a fixed time, when it says that the bitterness of mourning is to be borne for one day. O the riches of God's goodness! With what tender concern for us he guards against this very thing! He does not begrudge us our natural devotion, but knows our weakness and restrains all excess. He commands that tears be shed over the dead, but confines the bitterness of mourning to a single day. He lets the tears continue, since by them grief is relieved and the soul breathes again, but cuts short the bitterness, since it wears out our mind with immoderate and irrational torment, and our frailty cannot bear it for long. The goodness of God explains this more fully in its own words, for it adds: "And take comfort early because of sorrow. For from sorrow death comes quickly, and it will cover over virtue." Only that sorrow is salutary which is according to God. But the sorrow that is according to man, as the apostle says, that is, sorrow arising from the weakness of the flesh, works death. Though these passages have different authors, scripture speaks in harmony through both, by the one Spirit and Word of God's saints. For true death is the covering over of virtue. If Christ is the virtue of God and our life, you see that it is truly said that death comes quickly through this grief, which covers over virtue, so that the whole man is swallowed up, as the apostle says, by excessive sorrow, as if in some abyss of hell. But thanks be to God that my knowledge of your virtue and wisdom spares me this labor and this fear in your case. Their light shines too brightly in you to be covered by the darkness of sorrow. Rather, your virtue covers sorrow and swallows up death itself and the force of harmful grief. I do not grant you this with mere words, nor do I speak of your virtue by guesswork. Your works testify to it, and they compel me to speak of what I know for certain.

Now I shall turn to proclaiming your works, and pass from the holiness of your tears to your acts of devotion. You paid each part its due, pouring out tears for the body and pouring alms into the soul. Truly knowing the truth and a son of light, you wept where you knew there was death, and you worked where you believe there is life, paying empty things to what is empty and living things to what lives. So you gathered into the hall of the apostle the poor, the patrons of our souls, who beg for alms throughout Rome, a whole multitude of them. I feast my eyes on the beautiful spectacle of so great a work of yours. I seem to see all those devout swarms of the pitiable common people, those nurslings of God's goodness, streaming in such crowds deep into the vast basilica of glorious Peter, through that venerable entrance whose blue façade smiles from afar, until the whole space within the basilica, before the doors of the atrium, and before the steps of the open square is crowded. I see them gathered and arranged in good order at their places at table, and all filled with abundant food. Before my eyes passes the abundance of the gospel blessing and the image of those crowds whom Christ filled with five loaves and two fishes, he who is himself the true bread and the fish of living water. He did not create food for people in the usual way, but by a new kind of gift brought forth food already prepared. His hidden hand, at a divine prompting, served out visible meals and flowed with spiritual fruitfulness into bodily nourishment. With unspeakable fountains of bread and flesh, as a sign of hope for the nations still fasting, he filled in body and watered in spirit the peoples who hungered for faith. With an increase no one could detect he replaced what had been eaten, supplied what was still to be eaten, and brought out further fragments for the mouths of those who ate. As the food grew in the hands and mouths of those taking it, they felt rather than saw the abundance of their meal, for what was consumed came back for the next bite and fresh food came up under their teeth.

Following in your work the example of the Lord himself, you told the crowd to sit down on the ground; for so Jesus too, as we read, ordered them to recline on the ground. For the Lord himself was in you, as he still is, since no one does the works of Christ without Christ. By his gift and blessing you received abundant loaves in his name, as the disciples had received from him loaves blessed for distribution, and you portioned them out among the countless mouths of the poor. And they ate and were filled, and all took away what was left over of the loaves, each with his baskets full. But you gathered all the overflow of spiritual fragments: from the twelve baskets, the faith of the apostles; from the seven hampers, spiritual grace. Christ worked no less wonderfully in your loaves. At this banquet of yours he changed your earthly bread into heavenly food and prepared it to fill you for eternity. For you will rightly recline with the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at Christ's banquet, clothed in the wedding garment, because here Christ reclines with you in his poor, and in you the Son of Man has a place to lay his head.

It is a pleasure to linger still on the sight and praise of so great a work. For it is not man's works we praise, but God's works done through a man. As the sacred giver of the show, what a joyful spectacle, a full house, as they say, you presented to God and his holy angels! With what joy you lifted up the apostle himself when you had packed his whole basilica with dense throngs of the needy! They filled it where, under its lofty roof, the nave stretches broad and long between its coffered ceilings, and, gleaming from afar with the apostolic throne, catches the eyes of those who enter and gladdens their hearts. They filled it where, under the same mass of roofs, it spreads out its sides in twin colonnades on either hand. And they filled it where the shining atrium lies spread out in front as a vestibule. There a canopy crowned with solid bronze adorns and shades the fountain basin that pours out streams to serve our hands and mouths, and it surrounds the leaping waters with four columns, not without a mystical meaning. Such adornment befits the entrance of a church, so that what is performed within through the saving mystery may be signified by a visible work before the doors. For the one faith of the gospel supports the temple of our body too on a fourfold foundation. From that faith flows the grace by which we are reborn, and in it Christ, by whom we live, is revealed. So surely for us, within those four columns of life, there springs up the fountain of water leaping up to eternal life, which waters us from within and boils up in us, if only we can say, or deserve to feel, that we have a heart burning on the way, kindled as Christ walks along with us.

What a joyful spectacle, then, you offered to God, to the angels of peace and to all the spirits of the saints! First, in honouring the apostle, whose faith and memory you celebrated with such manifold devotion of your wealth: first you brought to God sacred offerings, chaste libations, together with a most acceptable commemoration of him; then, by the generosity that followed, you offered yourself to Christ as a most acceptable sacrifice, with a clean heart and a humbled spirit. In his tabernacles you sacrificed offerings of true rejoicing, refreshing and feeding those who would sacrifice to God an offering of praise with abundant blessing. How good was the uproar that filled our city then, when you poured out the depths of your mercy to refresh and clothe the poor, restoring the pale bodies of the hungry, moistening the parched throats of the thirsty, clothing the shivering limbs of the cold, and opening the mouths of all to bless God in harmony!
