But while you cherished needy bodies, your works returned to the better part of you by divine recompense, and so it was rather your own spirit that you fed full. You refreshed also the soul of your blessed wife, as the hand of Christ transferred to her whatever of yours was paid out to the poor, since in the twinkling of an eye fleshly food was changed and passed into heavenly food. However much money you, a cheerful giver and untiring distributor, had poured with heavy right hand into the cupped palms of those receiving it, just so much was at once carried by angels flying to and fro into the lap of the rejoicing Lord, and laid up for you to be reckoned as thirtyfold fruits and returns. Nor was it riches alone; the graces of blessings too were added to your rewards. For that shout and prayer of the poor, by which God was blessed through your gifts, was counted to you as righteousness. The voices of the needy find an easy road to God's ear, because, as it is written, the prayer of the poor pierces the clouds.

You, Rome, need not fear those threats leveled at you in the Apocalypse, if your senators always gave shows like this. Then that nobility of yours would truly be noble, one that the holy patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob would welcome into their fatherly bosoms, that the prophets, apostles and martyrs, that is, the senate of heaven, would acknowledge, that Christ would clothe in the royal robe of promised light after a toga defiled by no gore of unclean blood, and would enrol in the white book, that is, the book of everlasting life. Those riches would truly be rich which fed not the bloody savagery of the ancient dragon but the boundless goodness of God the Savior, if what is wickedly squandered on buying and feeding beasts or gladiators were given instead to one's own salvation, and if living were dearer to us than perishing. But with a perverse avarice and an equally perverse liberality we are stingy toward God, who acts on our behalf, and lavish toward the devil, who works against us. We count loss as gain and gain as loss; we do not care to redeem our life even at small cost, we who buy death instead of life at great expense. Happy would our condition be if we were as afraid of displeasing God, or as eager to please him, as we are with men; if we feared Christ's commandments as much as the hissing of the crowd; and if the praise that comes from God were bought at as high a price as this applause from the mob.

Blessed are you, who have not walked in such counsel nor sat in the seat of pestilence, but in the apostle's seat and in the assembly of the church, that is, in Christ's theater, are praised, with God himself as spectator, not by rioting tiers of seats but by tiers that bless; a giver of shows for the church, a seeker not of the arena nor of empty glory but of eternal praise. You do not buy gladiators or beasts; rather you do the things by which you may slay the true gladiators, that is, the princes of this darkness, and overcome the true beasts, that is, all the power of the devil, and with your foot pressed down unharmed may trample the lion and the dragon. Blessed are you, in whom the name of the Lord will be blessed, who have seed in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem, who may in turn receive you into the eternal tabernacles. For you will not fear the place of that rich man who, in Tartarus, that is, in the lower hell and the outer darkness, deservedly surrounded by fire, begged to be sprinkled even with the fingertip of the poor man he had despised in this life, and to whom father Abraham rightly replied: "Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are tormented."

That is why, I think, those rich men should shudder at this reversal of punishments and delights who here, abounding only for themselves and their vices, either brood over hidden wealth and have set aside no share for the poor, or, wickedly prodigal, are deservedly in want and will be punished with eternal want; who held themselves so cheap out of love of luxury that a single day's table is shown to have been more precious to them than the life of their whole time. Here, then, they will never share the heavenly goods of the poor, since the poor here never knew their earthly goods. And their tongues will burn the more fiercely who now either shrink from or mock the infirmities of the poor, deadly fastidious and witty, who pass by and leave their neighbors' sores for the dogs to lick; for by nature every human being is neighbor to every other. Tell me, are not these more truly to be called dogs, who have not even imitated the dogs in tending and soothing human beings, and who order their brothers, that is, those born of the same mother, nature, when they long to be fed even with the crumbs falling from their table, not only to be shut out behind barred doors but even to be driven off with savage blows? This is why, I believe, that rich man in the Gospel, though, as he cries, he was wretchedly tormented all over in that flame of the fiery abyss, asked for relief for his tongue alone: no doubt it burned more fiercely because, in his greed, he had often sinned with a proud mouth against Lazarus, who lay before his door abandoned to the dogs. For this reason we are warned elsewhere to set a guard on our mouth, as Wisdom teaches through Solomon, since death and life are in the power of the tongue; and elsewhere: "By your words," he says, "you will be justified, or by your words you will be condemned."

For you, then, my like-minded brother in Christ, who fear that punishment and share in that seat; whose mouth is full of blessing, whose riches are the breasts that nourish the poor, whose house is Christ's; who do not suffer a beggar to lie before your door while you feast, but on the contrary gladly bring him under your roof either to feast with you or even to be filled while you fast: for you there is a happy poverty in sins and a blessed wealth in virtues. You will rightly be numbered both among those poor to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs and among those rich whose possession is a strong city, for you are rich in the Spirit of God and poor in your own spirit. Such rich men, together with their poor, God loves, celebrates in the sacred writings, and ennobles with the authority of the everlasting pages.

For I want you to consider this very point: the names of those rich men whose crimes or punishments are recorded in the Scriptures are not given, because without doubt they were unworthy to be named by the divine word, since either the impiety of their lives blotted them out or their avarice erased them. That is why the Lord had foretold of them through the prophet: "Nor will I remember their names with my lips," that is, through the two testaments of immortal words, which are rightly called the lips of the divine mouth, because they cleave to one another and are opened by the one Word of God, and through them God kisses us with the kisses of his mouth. Divine justice would not have these lips defiled with the names of the wicked. So there is no name for that rich man whose vanity and avarice are recorded, to whom, as his life was already spent and he was thinking about the provisions of [?], it was said: "Fool, this night your soul is required of you; whose will the things be that you have prepared?" Nor is the name of this rich man in Tartarus made known, and since the poor man's name is given, we understand that it was not left out by chance. Of that rich man too who boasted that he had fulfilled the law, yet out of love for his riches turned away from the condition for attaining perfection, we read of his blindness but do not have his name. "For he had," it says, "many possessions," and so there followed that sentence which would almost have shut the kingdom of heaven to every rich man, had not God, as the only one who is good, reserved this gift to his own omnipotence: that he might enrich the rich with the will of the poor. These rich men, then, are hateful to God and blotted from memory, who have put perishable things before eternal ones and preferred to entrust their goods to the earth rather than to God, heaping up food for moths and plunder for thieves, and, as it is written, not knowing for whom they hoard, since they will not understand to whom they owe their treasures. They deserve not to know what heir they leave them to, since they do not know by what giver they possess them. "For what do you have, O man, that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it," and grow proud toward God of his own gifts? The names of such rich men, my brother, are not written in the Gospel, because they are not held in the book of life either.

Finally, so that you may know that it is not riches but people who are blameworthy or acceptable to God according to how they use them, read of the holy patriarchs Abraham and Job, who were made friends of God by means of their wealth. Indeed, in the very Gospel in which that rich man of Tartarus, the despiser of Lazarus, is passed over, we see the rich man Joseph of Arimathea named. For blessed is he who in a special way considered the needy and the poor, who honored the body of Christ with devoted service, who did not fear to petition the judge over the wrong done to the Lord's body, and who was rich in the Lord's burial through his devout expense on a costly shroud and a new tomb. With these names the holy page will enroll you, and you will be numbered in the lot of such rich men, whose wealth you match and whose spirit as well. For they did not hold what they had for themselves; no one called anything his own, and they thought nothing human foreign to them, like that multitude of the faithful in the beginning, who had one heart and one soul and held all things in common. And consider the reasoning: you will readily judge that it is a crime akin to parricide that the poor are despised at our whim, when we see them separated from us by no work of God. How can we shut out of our small dwellings those whom God has enclosed together with us in the one house of this world? How can we disdain to make sharers in the use of earthly possessions those whom, even against our will, we have as partners through the unity of our divine origin? By holding to this Abraham became the friend of God; by observing this Lot escaped from Sodom; by pursuing this Job triumphed over the devil.

Let us too open our homes to our brothers, either fearing the danger, after the example of the patriarchs just mentioned, lest perhaps in shutting out what seems a man we drive away an angel as well, or hoping to deserve angels as our guests while we welcome with ready kindness every stranger passing by. For father Abraham, in welcoming strangers, received also the Lord Christ with angels, and in his hospitable tent saw that day which the Savior in the Gospel points to in his own person. Wrong done to guests condemned the Sodomites, and Lot earned his deliverance chiefly by the devotion with which he put his guests before his daughters. He was not impious but perfectly devout. He did not hold his daughters cheap, he who earned his reward precisely for preferring the justice of charity, that is, the fear of God, to family affection; for it was surely at God's command and by his Spirit that he served in receiving guests. And so even then that mind fulfilled the perfection of faith of which we are told: "Everyone who leaves brothers and sisters, or mother, or sons or daughters, for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life." The perfection of this mind, or the mind of this perfection, already at the beginning of the world delivered righteous Lot from the burning of the Five Cities, and in return for his hospitable house he deserved to receive by God's gift a whole city as his house. For he who alone had been devout and chaste in an incestuous and impious city, surpassing natural affection itself in holiness, did not hesitate, so far as it lay with him, to redeem the chastity of his guests with the chastity of his daughters. Job, that silver tried in the Lord's fire, testifies that he was always eye to the blind and foot to the lame, and in the very contest of his trial he claims and receives the reward of these works. He is stripped of the wealth of his inheritance, not of his soul; but, invulnerable in heart, he does not sin even with his lips; bared of the striving for substance but armed with the strength of patience; bereaved of his children but not of the light of his heart, he embraces the children of his mind, that is, the works of righteousness, crying: "Naked I came out of my mother's womb, naked I must return to the earth. We brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything out." But because he had not lost his spiritual wealth, he received back his temporal riches too as the prize of his patience's triumph, and was enriched threefold, because he had been tested and purified sevenfold. For, as it is written, he had eaten the labors of his fruits by laboring in works of piety, and therefore he ate the fruits of his labors, receiving the rewards of his works even in this world.

Your lot is with these rich men, for you remember that the same God is the source of your riches; you are free from avarice because you are a servant of righteousness. You use unrighteous mammon righteously, and you are not the captive but truly the master of your money, because you are possessed by Christ, to whom captivity itself is captive. Glory, then, in the Lord, because it was not flesh and blood but he himself, Christ, who is the true light and the wisdom of God, who revealed to you the prudence of this foresight, by which you understand that in every needy and poor person Christ is fed, given drink, clothed and visited, in keeping with those whom, for this merit, as was said above, the Lord will deliver in the evil day.

May the Lord himself preserve you and give you life and make you blessed, and bring you help now upon your bed of grief; may he turn your devout mourning into holy joy for you. May he tear off the sackcloth of your sorrow and restore to you the joy of his salvation; with his guiding Spirit strengthening you, may he make your arms firm as a bow of bronze in prayers and almsgiving; may he make your feet like the deer's, so that you may be swift both to flee the devil and to overtake Christ, and may stand firm in the way of the Lord with your footsteps fixed by the double hoof of the two testaments, your feet rescued by the Lord's hand from stumbling and your eyes from weeping, so that together with your blessed wife you may please the Lord forever in the land of the living. For it will be done to you according to your faith, since the Lord, faithful in his words, will remember this sacrifice of yours forever, and your burnt offering will be made rich; and he will accept you yourself as a living sacrifice to him for a fragrant odor, he who will repay your loan on that day when the debtor, richer than his creditors, will return to each his deposit with multiplied interest. Nor is the day of repayment far off, for the fields are already white with the approaching harvest.

Meanwhile, promising yourself in joyful meditation the wealth you are to receive, you will comfort your soul far more richly by faith in what is to come than by any words of mine or anyone else's. For it is no small delight to believing souls to anticipate in sweet thought the good things promised to the faithful, and already to walk in paradise in spirit. If the farmer delights to gaze at the hope of the harvest in the standing grain while he awaits from the harvest the fruit of his labor, and the eagerness of his hopes bears the delay of the seasons more easily if it can feed his eyes while it waits for the outcome, how much greater delight can we take, sinners though we are, yet faithful little servants, whose account for the seed sown is entrusted not to the doubtful good faith of the earth but to the unchangeable truth of God, since we hope for what Truth itself has promised!

For we do not gather what is to come after this human life from human opinions, nor from the fabulous dreams of poets or the fancies of philosophers; we draw our faith in these things from the very fountain of truth. And who could know divine things better than God himself, who is privy to his own works and decrees? We shall not falsely claim that souls are transferred into other bodies, so as to become monsters after being human, nor that they will remain wholly without a body, nor that they perish in the body. Let those flatter themselves with the lies of poets who do not have the prophets of truth. Let those be blinded by the wandering opinions of philosophers who are not enlightened by the testimonies of the apostles, and let those console themselves with despair who have no hope, saying: "Our time is the passing of a shadow, and there is no return from our end, for it is sealed, and no one will come back"; blinded by the darkness of their wickedness and unbelief, they cannot say: "I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the light of the living." But we have no need of such poor remedies, for Truth itself, the Word of God who is God, has both pledged by his teaching and proved by his rising the resurrection of the flesh to eternal life. The Son of God himself, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing, himself testified: "I am the resurrection; whoever believes in me, though he die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die." And so as not to assert this by word alone, he confirmed it by example: he raised from the dead his own human nature, in which all humanity was taken up, and showed it to his disciples, establishing in himself the reality of the flesh when he said to Thomas: "Put your finger here and see my hands; and put out your hand and place it in my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have."

Having these testimonies, then, these proofs, this light of faith, on what pretext could we doubt the resurrection, which we have both heard from the Word of God and seen with the eyes of the apostles and touched with their hands? We are so bound and grafted to God through Christ that we hold in our earth God's pledge, the Holy Spirit whom he has given us, and have in God the pledge of ourselves, the flesh of Christ. For he spans that immense gulf by which mortal things are set apart from divine, by his own mediation, standing between and common to both, as if, so to speak, by a bridge, so that by his path earthly things may be joined to heavenly ones, when heavenly incorruption has suffused this corruptible nature of ours and, as it is written, immortality has swallowed up our mortality, and life, victorious in Christ and through Christ, has swallowed up death for us, defeated. As for attaining this, we may doubt not the truth of so great a good but our own capacity to deserve it. But let us do what Christ has commanded, so that we may obtain what Christ has promised. His truth is with us; let our faith not fail him. He is life for all, the way for all, the door for all. He shuts his kingdom to no one, and even allows it to be taken by force.

Press on where you are running, so as to lay hold of that by which you have been laid hold of; strive through the narrow way so as to reach the broad possession of the eternal inheritance. You already have in Christ a great pledge of yourself and a zealous advocate: your wife, who is preparing for you in heaven as much grace as you supply to her of wealth from earth. You honor her, as I said, not with vain mourning but heap her with living gifts, in which she now rejoices; and already she enjoys this work of yours in its fruit, while for you its reward is still in the seed.

Already she is honored by your merits, already she is fed by your bread and abounds in your wealth, clothed in a garment of gold, wrapped in many colors, in precious light. She has no need to be cooled by the finger of another's hand, since she herself is bathed in the dew of her own fingers, that is, in the works of your right hand. You did not enrich her as a bride with so ample a dowry as that with which you now make her rich in her rest. For what share of your gifts did she take then, when she enjoyed only what she could put on? Now, whatever you bestow, she will possess all of it at once, rich in spirit, with the delight of all the senses. Blessed is she who has so many advocates before Christ, and whose head is encircled by so manifold a crown of brilliant jewels, not woven of others' flowers but sparkling with lights of her own household. Truly precious to the Lord is that soul which takes its value from three pearls. For she is wife of faith, sister of virginity, daughter of perfection: Paula is her mother, Eustochium her sister, and you her husband.
XIV. Paulinus to Delphinus, his most blessed and venerable father, ever most longed-for by us.

We rejoiced at what Cardamas brought us in writing. The news of your recovery, like the oil of gladness, made our bones fat, so that, filled with joy, we said: The Lord has done great things for us. He visited us on the bed of your pain, so that, rising up at your recovery, we might sing a hymn to our Lord, because he had rescued our eyes from tears, putting off your crown but keeping you to help us. And so, with you lightening our burdens by your earnest prayers and going ahead of us on the road, we may run more lightly after the fragrance of the Lord's ointments. That fragrance breathes on us from your holiness, and though we do not reach it by our merit, we follow it with love, hoping that the unbreakable bond of your love will lead us on, so that under your guidance we may arrive where you will have arrived by your own effort. For your illnesses are not unto death but for the glory of God, so that they may bring perfection to your virtue and strength to our weakness. And many examples of the Lord's saints, starting with the patriarchs, already reassure us that we need not be troubled about you.

The fathers of the faith themselves had other labours in their lives. Yet even in that prophetic old age, when they were enlightened within and already foresaw the eternity of the world and the course of all the ages, their bodily eyes were dim, and in the weakness of the flesh they brought spiritual strength to perfection. In the same way blessed Job was tempted so that he might be proved, fought so that he might conquer, was humbled so that he might be exalted, and wept so that he might rejoice. And what of the Holy of Holies himself? Did he not conquer at the very moment he was judged, and by falling in death rise again into glory? The illnesses that the strong suffer spur the weak on to virtue. The strong man is made weak so that the weak may be strengthened, and by imitating the robust may learn to win the fight. That is also why the righteous man is chastised: so that the unrighteous may be corrected.

So the bodily weakness of the saints does good in two ways. Their own spiritual strength is exercised. And there is the man who prospers in his way, exults in the strength of unbroken health, and says, "I have sinned, and what has happened to me?" He will not dare to flatter himself on his bodily good fortune, and perhaps, held in check by fear of God's power, he may be set right. For when he sees that the avenging hand of the heavenly Lord is severe even to the righteous, he will rightly dread it for his own wicked deeds. If even you can scarcely escape the lash of chastisement, where shall we, the wicked and sinners, appear? We believe, moreover, that you have suffered heavier darts of bodily affliction than usual in these recent times, first tormented by burning fevers and now by a flux of the head, so that in the Lord's rest you may say in your blessedness: We went through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment. God in his mercy had looked kindly on our lowliness and spared us the pain of the gravest anxiety, since your letter told us in one breath both why we had been anxious about you and that we could be at ease. Gladdened by that mercy, we received in the same letter another gift of divine grace: the business we had been so concerned about, the house of the holy priest Basil, had been settled through your efforts just as we wished.

May all that blessing come upon your head and, woven over it, blossom to fill up your crown. For it was not only those who received the kindness who blessed the Lord because of you. Almost the whole of Capua, and the most renowned church of that city, rejoiced with the priest in his joy and gave praise to God. He had helped the poor man out of beggary and humbled the lofty hearts of the rich, so that they too may have hope of an eternal home in the city of habitation. For through the intervention of your words they were found worthy to be enlightened to a good understanding. By justly restoring a tiny dwelling they have prepared for themselves an eternal lodging in the heavenly tent of God's holy poor man, who will receive them in return.
XV. Paulinus to Amandus, his holy, deservedly venerable and most beloved brother.

We welcomed Cardamas with the joy of love and the blessing of sweetness, for he brought us every good thing. Your letter told us of your good health and gladdened our hearts. It was sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, and its sweetness sank into our inmost being like oil. Our humbled bones exulted, and with a voice of exultation we said to the Lord: We have received your mercy, O God, by which you have delivered the poor from the powerful and the lowly from the hand of one stronger than he. Reasons for rejoicing crowded into our minds from every side: we were receiving your letter; we found that you remembered us; we heard that you were safe, as we had prayed; we learned that my lord, our father, had been healed of a grave and long illness. We were gladdened about both of you alike. The same trial that wore him down in body had worn you down in heart, and so the same visitation that brought him divine help on his bed of pain also brought you the refreshment of relief on your couch of compassion. Even so, when we thought of his sufferings and of your state of mind, our love pricked us, because in that time of your trial we had perhaps been well and even merry. But thanks be to the Lord, who forgives the fault of ignorance and has not dealt with us as we deserved. He forestalled our sorrow with rejoicing, for he graciously arranged that we learned your illness had fled from the same messenger who also announced the return of health.

What shall I say of the deed of your holiness? By it you have added as much to our present joy as to your own store of eternal reward. I mean the affair of the holy priest Basil. You have turned his lament into joy and settled his old age in rich mercy. A voice of gladness and salvation has sounded in his tent. Rejoicing with his whole household, in harmony with the congratulations of the church, he never stops blessing the Lord. The Lord has regarded his lowliness and bound up his wounds. He has covered with shame those who rejoiced at his misfortunes, and has torn off his sackcloth of sorrow and girded him with the vigour of gladness.

Earlier we had asked that these brothers of ours be approached with a request. Now, on their behalf, we ask you in our shared spirit to love them beyond your usual affection. If they happen to come to Bordeaux, as they usually do, please thank them in person, and on behalf of our own hearts and feelings as well. Or if it is a long while before you can see them, kindly send them at the first opportunity the congratulations they are owed and the blessing their deed deserves. Then they will know and understand how acceptable a sacrifice they have offered to God by this obedience of their faith. They let themselves be moved and accepted our petition through your intervention, giving us present joy by their devotion but securing an eternal benefit for their own salvation. Admittedly they did only what they owed when they acknowledged what was just and ordered that what belonged to another be returned. Yet they deserve generous thanks for that very disposition of good will. They could have transgressed and did not transgress, and they chose to do what was fitting rather than what was permitted. And they kindly complied with us with a heart so unreserved and pure that their kindness could not be disputed. Even though the holy priest could not prove the house was his, they ordered it restored to him without difficulty, so that if he could not possess it by his own right, he might possess it as their gift. Nor have they lost the grace of so holy a generosity. That most holy man, for whom the Lord in keeping with his merit provided you as intercessors, gives thanks and proclaims it as though he had received a gift that was not owed to him. We have put off replying to these brothers of ours for the moment, though. Their own men travel from Campania quite often, so more convenient opportunities will not be lacking to send letters straight to them, wherever they are.

As for Cardamas himself, we confess that we owe you, who are one in heart with us, no small gratitude. We received him not only advanced in his ministry but also growing in spirit. He arrived during Lent, and we welcomed him with brotherly affection as a cleric. He did not shrink from the daily fasts, and as our evening guest he did not shudder at our poor little table. What is more remarkable, he was content with our cups. From this we understood that he had been reformed in your holy company, as indeed he has, and taught by the Apostle to be drunk no longer by the bucketful but on a little wine, which does not swell the belly but gladdens the heart, a drunkenness that leads to sobriety. In his spiritual surfeit he pours out a hymn to God, singing it not only with his voice but in the silence of his heart. He receives the Lord's will with faithful hearing, tells it in devout speech and carries it out with vigorous deeds. Blessed be the Lord who does wonders, who turns the rock into water: he has made Cardamas a cleric, as we saw, and sober, as we believed. But when the Easter feast brought back the days of lunches, he began to grumble to us around noon: "My throat is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to my jaws. My soul and my belly have failed, and from hunger and thirst my bones cling to my flesh." We answered him: "Son, endure in humility, and do not let the cravings of the belly take hold of you, for man does not live by bread alone but by every word of God." But like a deaf man he did not hear, and like the deaf adder he stopped his ears against us. It did him no good. At lunchtime he longed to fill his belly, and no one gave him so much as a husk, until the day drew toward evening and the hymn was said. Then, however sad he was at missing his lunch, supper made his peace with us. But I must not go on joking and seem to slight his gravity, which now delights more in drops from the cup than in rivers of drunkenness. So let me speak seriously about what he needs. He says that his wife is in poor health and therefore of no use to him. If that is so, I ask that he be given some young slave.
XVI. Paulinus to his brother Jovius, greetings.

Our sons Posthumianus and Theridius, who came from their homeland to Campania for my sake, are now returning home. I thought it would go against both duty and affection not to write to you, my kindred spirit, by them. I was guarding not only against seeming to neglect the courtesy we share through a carelessness unusual for me, but much more against seeming to think poorly of your attitude toward God. I am always quick to seize any chance of writing to you, and if I let you go ungreeted by men of religion, it might look as if you shrank from holy men. Yet you are clearly devoted to the Christian name, and out of love for me you even approve of the way of life I have chosen. So receive them gladly, and judge my letter by them rather than them by my letter. They were so scrupulous about this very thing that they made it a matter of conscience neither to revisit their homeland without calling on you nor to call on you without a letter from me. Letter-carriers of this kind also seemed to me well suited to a reply about that earlier letter of yours. You sent it in answer to the letter in which I had proclaimed the plain kindness of God's power over the elements and his care for us. You surely remember that I had learned from your own writing what I then answered with congratulations. So I urged you not to ascribe God's gift to chance. Nor should you suppose that it was luck rather than divine power that preserved the silver of that holy transaction amid winter storms and greedy sailors after its guardian was lost. For the ship was cast up on precisely that shore where a town familiar to us, and your own ancestral estate, received our property into its safest keeping.

But once again you have been more inclined to complain to me about the harm the storm did than to be grateful for God's mercy. Only the divine hand can protect human safety amid all the movements of the elements. Our actions too are governed by the power of the supreme Lord, who overturns or directs them according to our deserts. Yet you have made all of this subject to the empty names of fate and fortune, as though these were powers rivaling God. Do not imagine that you have shown God respect in this. On the contrary, you insulted him, as indeed you did, by refusing to let this be God's kindness. You argued that such things must be kept separate from divine power, because evils befit chance rather than God, and whatever often brings people danger or loss is undoubtedly evil. Among these evils, as I see, you place storms, which bring the devastation of fields on land or the misery of shipwreck at sea. But I can see that this view comes from those teachers who were proud of their own wisdom and disdained to seek the wisdom of God. They live as exiles from the borders of truth, champions of their own opinions. They sent their minds wandering through the great void and, as it is written and plainly proven, became futile in their thinking, and they invented God's works and counsels to suit their own fancies. No wonder sea and sky seem to them ruled and stirred by chance. Some of them argue that this world rolls on by random accidents, either because it has no ruler or because God idles and neglects it. Others hold that it was put together by no maker and so has neither beginning nor end. But bodily nature cannot have that, for this world consists of it and each of us is a portion of it, and every structure can be taken apart. Others, more foolishly still, claim that the world created itself, as if anything could be the cause of its own birth and be at once creator and creature, that is, craftsman and work. Yet these plainly differ in kind and condition as much as in name. For who does not see that this bodily world is governed by a bodiless power? The mind of the divine Spirit, by which the whole mass was made, is poured into the great body of the universe and mingled with it. By it the whole is moved to life, tempered for use, held firm in its condition and ordered to endure.

It is established, then, that whatever is seen or perceived needs help from outside itself in order to exist and endure. So there can be no doubt that it also needed something outside itself in order to be created. That being so, we must confess that all things arose from God, for only the profane can doubt that God made the world. It follows that the winds, and everything within the world that forms part of its mass and is, as it were, the inner organs of its body, must not be credited to the rule of anyone else. The powers of God's works, that is, the substances of all natures, are so much at odds with one another that they would not allow themselves to be ruled and held together by anything except that one nature and power, God. He is the one founder of all things, and by him alone could they be made and set in order. Unless they kept his laws, they would not keep their condition. It is far more foolish still to blame any nature and call it evil. If all things are from God and God is good, then surely everything God made is good. There may be things in the hidden depths of his decrees that lie beyond our senses and thoughts. Even if we cannot grasp or work out their reasons, it is safer for us to believe that those reasons are hidden than that there are none. We must not doubt that all God's dealings, even when we cannot see through them, are deliberate.

So if God, who founded the whole world, also governs it, where, or over what creature, will chance, fate or fortune rule? If they depend on the motions and arrangements of the stars, as some would have it, then the power you make a rival to God is drawn from little fires. These are smaller not only than God but than the world itself; indeed, they adorn only a third part of the world with the service of their light, which is a mere handmaid. Surely it belongs to divine power to stir up the elements, to rouse the violence of the winds when it sleeps or rein it in when roused, and to hand mortals over to the fury of storms or snatch them from it. Every creature obeys this power and is subject to the one creator of all. How, then, can divine force and power be given to things that lack not only the name of creator but even the form of a creature? They are empty names, belonging neither to spirits nor to bodies, devised for conducting and signifying affairs. 'Luck' is the word of someone in doubt, 'fate' merely something spoken, and 'chance' a term for things that fall out or befall. Yet through the habit of ancient error and their ignorance of God, people without reason shape these empty names into bodily forms in their foolish imaginations, as though that made them gods. Then, more foolishly than they invented them, they give them divine honor. So Hope, Nemesis, Love and even Madness are worshiped in images. Opportunity is consecrated with the back of her head bald, and that Fortune of yours is portrayed poorly balanced on a slippery globe. With no less falsehood the Fates are depicted spinning human lives from wool-baskets or weighing them in scales. Lest we blame this raving on the common people or admire philosophers too much, the tale is told even by Plato, raving too. He sets the spinning of Necessity in an old woman's lap and gives her three daughters, who sing in harmony as they turn the spindle and play among the threads. By this wool-work, if you please, he supposes that they bring about human affairs and weave out the span of time marked for each person. So far did the arrogance of empty eloquence abuse human ears that he did not blush to put the absurd ditty of an old wives' tale into the very writings in which he dared to discourse on the divine nature as though he had inside knowledge of it. In him we should look only at the charm of Attic style, not at the elegance of an empty tale. Things written merely to soothe the ears must not overturn the foundations of understanding.

Rather, as reason and truth teach, let us refer to God himself all his works, in which we exist and of which we are part. Let us refer to him also all his gifts, by which we are ruled and kept safe amid the uncertainties of this frail and fleeting life. Let us not, by our error, remove anything from his power, for like it or not, he is our creator and our God, as he is of all things. He is goodness and wisdom and the source of reason. He established nothing without reason, and he created all things as material for his goodness. So let us devote to him all that we are, eager to learn what pleases him and careful to do it. Then, seeing more clearly with a purified mind, we shall see the truth: that all that exists is from God. We shall also see what follows from it: that all God's works are supremely beautiful, and that nothing is evil which has a good author. He prepared everything in the world for our use and acts for our benefit. He built the fabric of this universe so that some things were created to serve, some to train us, and some to rule. So by reason we humans rule over bodily and animal natures. But so that we do not grow slack through the very freedom our power gives us, we are usefully trained by adversities. These may be the spirits of demons, difficulties in our affairs, or often the motions of the elements themselves, so that cares may stir us up and sharpen us to prudence and the fear of God. For security, which ought to make us more grateful to the eternal Lord, makes us neglect him. That is why the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, says that by a hidden counsel of God's love, and to the great profit of human salvation, obstacles are set in our path and prosperity turns to adversity: illnesses, losses, dangers. For tribulation produces the strength of patience, and patience brings forth the proof of faith and confers the reward of glory. Virtue certainly cannot win that reward unless it is victorious, and it will have no chance of victory unless it has first wrestled with some difficulty.

Your wisdom, both inborn and trained, could have learned this from the very books you read. I wish you would now rank them below sacred scripture in your devotion, as you already do in your judgment. Those books record that the virtues of men famous as generals or philosophers shone out to noble fame only through toil and danger. So I am greatly surprised that you chose to stay so clouded about the plain truth of God's gift. You assigned to chance that wonderful rescue of the storm-tossed ship and the protection of our property on land and sea, which God secured with evident signs, and so you threw away so great an opportunity to proclaim God. Lift your mind to the summit of wisdom and seek Christ himself, the very kindling of the true light, who enlightens faithful souls and glides through chaste hearts. You have shown that you think so too, though you offered an excuse. You said that you are still unequal to it and so cannot take in God, because you are beset by earthly business and cares and are kept, as if by intervening clouds, from lifting your gaze higher to heavenly things. I only wish you could plead this as truthfully as you can eloquently. The very richness of your eloquence and learning proves that what you lack for sacred letters is the will rather than the leisure or the ability. You did not, I think, amass such wealth of speech and heart while asleep or busy with other things. You breathe the flowers of all the poets, overflow with the rivers of all the orators, and are watered by the springs of philosophy. Rich in foreign literature too, you fill a Roman mouth with Attic honey [?]. Tell me, where are your taxes then, when you read Cicero and Demosthenes from end to end? Or when, sated and tired of more familiar reading, you go back over Xenophon, Plato, Cato and Varro, though you have read them all already? And there are many others besides whose names I perhaps do not even know, while you own their volumes. To be busy with these, you are exempt and free; to learn Christ, that is, the wisdom of God, you are burdened with taxes and busy. You have leisure to be a philosopher but no leisure to be a Christian. Rather, change your thinking, and turn your eloquence to a new purpose. You need not lay aside the philosophy of your mind, provided you season it with faith and religion. Join them together and use them more wisely, so that you may be God's philosopher and God's poet. Be wise not by searching into God but by imitating him, so that, learned in your life no less than in your tongue, you may do great things as much as you discuss them.

Be a Peripatetic toward God and a Pythagorean toward the world: walk with God, and keep silent toward the world. Be a preacher of the true wisdom in Christ, and fall silent at last toward vanity. Shun that harmful sweetness of empty literature as you would the Lotus-eaters, who with the sweetness of their berries made men forget their homeland. Avoid it as you would the songs of the Sirens, those chants of harmful allurement. It is often permissible to borrow things from empty fables, as from common proverbs, for use in true and serious discourse. So I will say that not only literature but every form of temporal things is a Lotus-eater or a Siren to us. The deadly sweetness of pleasures makes us forget our homeland when it blots out for us God, who is the common homeland of all. The enticements of desire act out the fable of the Sirens in a real disaster. What the Sirens are imagined to have been, the enticements of desire and the blandishments of vice truly are. They are seductive in appearance and poisonous to the taste; their use is counted as crime, and their price is death. We must flee them with more caution than even the cunning of Ulysses, sealing not only our ears but our eyes, and letting our mind fly past like a ship. Otherwise, enticed by deadly delight, we may be swept onto the rocks of sin and, stuck fast on the reef of death, suffer the shipwreck of our salvation.

Would that we might escape the heaving sea of this world even if we come out naked! In this life we drift in bodily frailty and on the slipperiness of possessions, as if in the untrustworthy frame of a ship that is falling apart. If only we remember to strip off our burdensome encumbrances like wet clothes so that we can swim clear. If only we remember to seize, like a plank of refuge, the saving faith by which, in the power of Christ, we rely on the standard of God's cross. Then from things that flow away we may gain a solid hope, and from the harmful material of our desires we may snatch something for innocence and salvation. That is, serving God and ruling our desires, we should limit our wants to the measure of necessity. Having the clothing we need, we should not seek superfluous finery, for we are reminded that we brought nothing into this world and can take nothing out of it. This truth is so powerful that even among the pagan philosophers, some of whom touched at least the outermost lines of truth with their loftier minds, there were those who felt they could have no leisure even to seek wisdom, let alone follow it. So some of them even threw the burden of their money into the sea, as if it were dung.

But as for you, divide things with God and repay the supreme Father with thanks, as though returning a kindness. Of everything he has given you, whether inborn or added from outside, he asks back from you only yourself. You may keep for yourself and your family everything you own, so long as you take care to confess that God is the giver of these things too. For we have nothing that we have not received, since, as I said, we came into this world naked. But dedicate the powers of your talent and all the riches of your mind and tongue to God. Offer him, as it is written, the sacrifice of praise with an eloquent mouth and a devoted heart. As soon as you turn your mind's gaze toward the heavenly sanctuary, truth will show you its face and will reveal you to yourself. For in coming to know divine truth we also come to know ourselves. Where do you think wretched mortals got so perverse a pride or sloth that, instead of worshiping God, they serve demons or the elements, which are subject to them? They venerate waters, fire, stars, trees and images, with a most impious insult to the divine majesty. Whether they worship demons or creatures in his name, they are honoring servants. For this they deserve to be blinded by such darkness that, because they refuse to understand the true God, they are struck with ignorance of themselves as well. From this darkness a person enlightened by faith is set free. Understanding the order and measure of his own kind, he recognizes that he is subject only to God, whose unity is acknowledged in an ineffable Trinity. He is equal to all other creatures that are rational, and superior to those that are bodily.

A person balanced in this middle place neither falls from his share in salvation nor from the dignity of his nature. He becomes aware of the truth, master of wisdom, servant of justice, free from error and lord over the vices. The soul that does not serve God is condemned to be a slave to those vices. Then, exiled from its proper state, such a soul is scattered along all the byways of its own thoughts or of other people's opinions. It wanders among the philosophers and pries among the soothsayers. It is devout toward superstition and profane toward religion, always hanging between hope and fear in wavering moods. So it is carried about by every wind of doctrine. Because it is empty of the fear of God, it lacks the beginning of wisdom, and its senses are, as it were, cut short. It does not know where to draw understanding of things from, or where to settle its judgment. It distracts itself in vain, roaming in thought through every region of heaven and earth. In the end it places all the force that drives the world in visible creatures and in the empty names of chance and fate, clinging to what is false and crooked as stubbornly as it is ignorant of what is true.

Your mind, however, has been kindled from heavenly seed and already breathes a divine ardor. Let it be directed, with faith leading the way, to Christ himself, the citadel of wisdom. In our studies too you have a better chance of possessing the eloquence of the philosophers, provided you stop loving a wisdom opposed to the true one. It is better for you to lay hold of divine things by seeking them than to keep seeking them by arguing. Leave those men behind. They are forever rolling in the darkness of ignorance, consumed in the quarrels of learned talkativeness, and enslaved to their own phantoms in mad wrangling. They are always seeking wisdom and never finding it, because they do not deserve to understand the God they refuse to believe. Let it be enough for you to have taken from them their fluency of tongue and ornament of speech, like spoils taken from an enemy's arms. Then, stripped of their errors and clothed in their eloquence, you may apply to things of real substance that gloss of eloquence by which empty wisdom deceives. Adorn not an empty body of fictions but the marrow-filled body of truth, and so compose what will not only please people's ears but also benefit their minds.
Letter 17. Paulinus to Severus.

We are worn out with inviting you and waiting for you, and we have no prayers or words left to add to those we have poured out so often, and in vain, in our entreaties and letters. Since words are the one thing you have left to our common friendship, now that the hope of seeing each other has been cut off, we repay words with words, and we long to be comforted at least by these consolations, though they bear no fruit. Yet you have begun to be sparing even in these, seeking us out now only when an occasion offers, and for almost two whole years you have kept us in suspense and tormented us with the daily expectation of seeing you. That summer which followed our servants' return to you we spent, until winter shut it off, believing that every day was dawning on your arrival. But since no messengers came to tell us of your delay, we consoled ourselves with the reflection that you had sent no one because you were going to come yourself, even if late. Meanwhile, as this summer too slipped away, with that hope or notion still beguiling us, we set out for Rome for the venerable day of the apostles' feast, promising ourselves that you would meet us there; it was a due expectation, but a festive one too. And although the delight of our confident hope was boiled away because you were not there, still we did not come away with nothing at all, for we received your letter through a man belonging to our dearest brother Sabinus. At first we were surprised at him, in his far from monastic boots and clothing, since his face too was as red as his cloak, with cheeks that were hardly spiritual. We realized he was not one of ours only when we learned through him that the courier's master, who was asking us for a letter in reply, was bound to you by close kinship. So now we embrace him, who was a friend before, with redoubled love.

There was no chance, however, to write back from the city. We saw it for barely ten days, and saw it without seeing it, spending the morning hours in the devotions for which we had come, at the holy shrines of the apostles and martyrs. Then, when we got back to our lodging, we were taken up with countless visitors, drawn some by friendship and some by religion, so that evening hardly broke up the gathering and set us free; and so, for lack of leisure, we had to put off this duty. Then, after we returned home, another delay arose: an illness fell upon our body and tried us severely for many days. But he who is our life and resurrection visited our lowliness for good, and though he chastened us sorely, he did not hand us over to death. For many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround those who hope in the Lord. And so we were beaten as sinners, and set free as those who hope in the mercy of him who heals the broken-hearted and binds up their wounds.

Now that we are recovering by the power and mercy of the Lord, we have written this by our dearest brother in the Lord Amachius, subdeacon of my lord and father Delphinus, because he was conveniently at hand; and since he said he was very well known to you, we thought him the most suitable person to entrust our letter to you. We greet you as much as we love you in the Lord and still long for you; for we cannot yet tear from our hearts the hope by which we confidently expect, by the Lord's gift, to see and embrace you in the dwelling and bosom of my lord Felix, our common patron, to whom I have so often attested your vows and recited your promises, as often as you remember giving me pledges. If we have deceived the martyr of truth, I do not think that I alone should be judged guilty of this fault, since I only promised what I believed. I beg you, my brother, one with me in heart and most dearly loved, see to it while there is time that you do not appear to have gone back on your word to so great a confessor, a saint of such powerful favor with Christ.

I do not know how you can plead weakness rather than laziness or partiality toward persons, since within a year you could have come to us and gone back again with the same effort with which you have for so many years made your pilgrimages through Gaul, often making repeated excursions within a single summer to visit Tours and places even more remote. I do not begrudge it; rather I praise your devotion in the Lord, whom you admire and honor in his saints [?]. Rightly, I admit, and deservedly is Martin visited often; but I say it is wrong and dangerous for Felix to be mocked with empty promises by the very man who honors Martin, or to be slighted by a careless disregard of the promise, as though it had been cancelled. With the same faith with which you hope for Christ's favor in honoring Martin, fear Christ's displeasure in offending Felix. Perhaps a stronger mind, a sturdier soul, or the powerful awareness of a perfect love in Christ gives you such confidence that you think this offense, by which you have wronged my lord Felix (God forbid!), will be washed away by setting against it the great merits of your faith and works. And indeed you promise yourself pardon from his own goodness, which he has most abundantly from Christ our God himself, whose Spirit he has, and you do so in faith. But I confess that I am either so timid through the fault of my weakness or so excessive in my love for you that I fear for you even where you are safe; and while I desire that the grace of Christ may abound for you in every saint, I would not want you to strike a stumbling stone in him above all, in whom the love of God is so distinguished and eminent. I know, of course, that according to the riches of God's goodness, compassion overflows in my lord Felix too; but I beg you, love and fear him all the more because he is so good and so forgiving. Such fear will bring you a great reward, making you more anxious precisely where you could be more secure: that is, the more readily God's dearest friend deigns to forgive, the more you should fear to offend him, because it is a greater impiety to wrong one who does not know how to take offense, and the Lord avenges more heavily one who does not seek vengeance. Weigh this matter, I beg you, with the affection of our mutual faith, and see whether you ought, being strong, to make excuses, or, being weak, to lose confidence. For our Lord is near us everywhere, who says, “In every place, while you are still speaking, behold, I am here,” and says, “All things are possible to one who believes.”
LETTER 18. TO VICTRICIUS, EVER MOST BLESSED AND VENERABLE FATHER, PAULINUS.

What we had long desired without success has suddenly come about by the Lord's gift when we no longer hoped for it: we have been given an opportunity to write to your venerable holiness through one of the household of the faith, and above all through a brother who is in the Lord yours and ours alike. For it happened that at Rome, on the most celebrated feast day of the apostles, we met our blessed brother the deacon Paschasius. Besides the grace of brotherly fellowship in the sacred ministry, we welcomed him with all the more reverence and affection because we learned that he belonged to the clergy of your holiness in both body and spirit. But we confess our use of force: though he was eager to return from the city to your holiness, and though we approved the pious haste of his most just desire, we nevertheless embraced him for love of you and brought him to Nola, so that by his entering it some breath of your spirit might bless the lodging of our lowliness, and so that we might enjoy for longer what was, as it were, a portion of your grace, seeing and holding him whom the modesty of his ways, his humility of heart, gentleness of spirit, faith in the truth, and speech seasoned in all things with salt proved to be both a disciple of your teaching and a companion of your way. So forgive our brother on our account, or us on his; for whether he is blamed for being slow or we for being presumptuous, the love of the Lord will excuse either fault before you, since it was by that love that he was compelled to yield to us and that we did not fear to seize him and keep him as though by our own right. We did this not from stubborn arrogance but with a pure heart and unfeigned faith, believing that what is yours is ours, and not doubting that you in turn would see it so, regarding him as not absent from you during the time you knew him to be with us. For though we are separated in body by the distance between our regions, we are joined in the Spirit of the Lord, in whom we live and abide, poured out everywhere, so that as members of one body we have one heart and one soul in the one God.

Therefore, considering in a spiritual mirror your mind toward us, and judging from the affection of our own heart that we are bound to you in turn, we have claimed for ourselves your spirit, one with ours, by keeping our brother; the Lord's grace, given you so abundantly, brought this very thing about, so that you are loved even in the members of your body and in the fringes of your garment. Yet we lost many days of his stay, while the Lord in his mercy corrected us and we were scourged with bodily illness for our spiritual amendment. But he who comforts the lowly and heals the broken-hearted comforted us by the presence of our blessed brother Paschasius; and while we were refreshed by it in spirit, we were also restored in body. For a good friend is medicine for the heart, and when two are rightly gathered into one, Christ stands between them.

Nor did he share our trouble and suffer with us only in our own illness; he was also worn down for a long time by the very grave sickness of our dearest son Ursus, whom he had had as the inseparable companion of his journey. In this we saw clearly his faith and his love in the Lord, full and complete. For as much as the one labored in body, so much was the other tormented in spirit. And so the Lord looked upon Ursus through Paschasius's humility, heaping up this further kindness: that one sick unto death should find safety out of danger through the faith and labor of Paschasius, in whom the Lord willed him to experience the power that his holy confessor Felix, most dearly loved, our patron in God, has with him. For he was born again by Paschasius's own hands, baptized on his sickbed, and has returned to health. The same Lord will grant it, he who by the prayers of the saint has given him back to our brother Paschasius, to our care along with his, and above all to your church, looking always, beyond doubt, upon you in your people wherever they may be: may he bring him into your presence unharmed and safe, free from sin and a servant of righteousness. We do not doubt that if he is found worthy to reach you, he too will make great growth in faith, matching Paschasius, with you as the teacher of both.

For your Tychicus, our dearest brother and faithful minister in the Lord, has made known to us, proclaiming not you so much as God in you, how many lights the Lord has kindled through you in regions once dark. He who brings clouds from the end of the earth brought you too from the farthest edge of the world into the light of his people, and turned bright lightning into abundant rain. As once the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee, saw a great light, those who sat in the region of the shadow of death, so now the land of the Morini at the farthest edge of the world, which the ocean pounds with its roaring barbarian waves, a people of remote nations, who sat in hiding along the sandy way of the sea beyond the Jordan, before the borders of the desert grew rich within it, rejoice in the light that has risen for them from the Lord through your holiness, and have laid aside their rough hearts as Christ entered. Where once barbarian invaders or native brigands haunted the empty forests and equally unsafe shores, now venerable and angelic choirs of saints throng cities, towns, islands and woods, with churches and monasteries full of people and harmonious in peace. Christ is at work among the peoples of all Gaul, as among nations everywhere; he goes round the whole world seeking those worthy of him, passes through the nations into holy souls, shows himself gladly in the ways of righteousness, and with all his providence goes out to meet those who love him. Yet in the most remote stretch of the Nervian coast, on which the faith of truth had before breathed only faintly, and where he chose you above all as a vessel of election, he shone forth first and more brightly in you, burned more warmly and appeared more closely; and he took you up as the one in whom he might hallow his name there, and through whose name his sound might go out even from the setting of the sun into all the earth.

So now we hear Rouen, once known only faintly by name even in the neighboring regions, spoken of with reverence in distant provinces too, and counted with divine praise among cities famous for their holy places. And not undeservedly, since the merit of your holiness has brought there the whole likeness of Jerusalem as it is remembered in the East, with the presence of the apostles as well. By the devotion of holy spirits and the working of divine deeds they make this city, a stranger to their shrines, equal to their own seats, for in you yourself they have found the most fitting lodging. It delights them, of course, as friends of God and princes of the people of the true Israel, that is, of the people that draws near to him, to dwell and work with you in that city where, with the holy angels, they are soothed day and night by the unbroken preaching of Christ the Lord; where through the most devout hearts of his faithful servants very many friendly virtues lay out for them a welcome rest and a homely lodging; where, through the daily harmony of those who sing psalms with understanding in many churches and secluded monasteries, they take delight in both the hearts and the voices of your most chaste sheep. And now unspotted virginity holds them in the temple of its consecrated body, making them guests of Christ, who rests in chaste hearts. With no less delight the purity of widows, unconquerable, serving night and day in holy works and devoted ministry, feeds them; and so does the hidden brotherhood of married couples who have submitted themselves to God, which by its constant prayers invites Christ, glad in his own works, to visit no longer a marriage bed but a brotherly couch, when, joined in turn with him and his saints in a union of chastity, it is mingled in spotless love with the spirits of its visitors. And now they are refreshed by the heart of mercy and find rest among the sons of piety and righteousness, loving you in all the sons of your teaching and loving Christ in you; and therefore they work the mighty deeds of God, that is, their own power in Christ, above all in your city, to testify that you are their partner.

Thanks and glory to him who does not neglect the works of his hands, who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and who, running through the whole world on the feet of the gospel, deigned to make you too a beautiful foot of his word, in which he might rejoice like a giant to run his course, and to shoe you with his own footstep in preparation for the gospel of his peace, so that through you too he might walk upon the asp and the basilisk and trample the lion and the dragon. And so that so bright a lamp should not lie hidden in darkness under the bushel of silence, he raised you to an apostolic see and set you there as on a lofty lampstand, so that you might give light to the whole house by enlightening many.

But by what paths did he bring you to the way of his truth? Training you through bodily duties for the spiritual tasks of his power, he made you first a soldier, whom he later chose as a bishop. He allowed you to serve Caesar as a soldier so that you might learn to serve God as a soldier, so that while you exercised your bodily strength in the toil of the camp you might strengthen yourself for spiritual battles, steeling your spirit for confession and hardening your body for suffering. That this was God's providential plan for you was shown afterward by your remarkable departure from military service and entrance into the faith. When you were first set on fire with the love of Christ, at the Lord's own arranging, you went out onto the parade ground, as a kind of public show of his work, on a day marked by a military assembly, girt with all the trappings of military defense which you had already rejected in your mind. While everyone admired the splendid dress and fearsome equipment you wore, you suddenly turned to the astonished army and, at the feet of the sacrilegious tribune, renouncing your military oath, you threw down the arms of blood in order to put on the arms of peace, scorning to be armed with iron since you were armed with Christ. At once, through the envy of the ancient serpent, the tribune was driven to fury; you were stretched out to be flogged and broken with huge clubs, yet you were not conquered, because you leaned on the wood of the cross. Soon the punishment of your body was doubled: you were laid on sharp fragments of potsherds, your limbs torn by terrible wounds. Then Christ supported you more gently, whose lap was your bed and whose right hand was your pillow. From there, your wounds not yet closed, your courage fired by their pain rather than broken, you sprang forth renewed and stronger to face a greater enemy, and when you were brought before the count you triumphed more gloriously over a more powerful foe. The devil's henchmen no longer dared to inflict the tortures you had overcome, and were planning a capital sentence, so that by the end of your bodily life they might at least stop being defeated; but our Lord, strong and mighty, unconquered in battle, confounded their hearts, however hardened, with conspicuous miracles. For the executioner who, on the road along which you followed your slayer as a holy victim, had mockingly and threateningly violated your neck by daring to touch it, feeling with his hand ahead of the sword as if to find the place for his stroke, at once lost his eyes and was struck blind. O ineffable goodness of Christ, how great a love it shows for its own! He who prayed that his crucifiers be forgiven did not let the wrong done to his confessor go unpunished; he who did not want his own passion avenged at once avenged the insult to his martyr. But even that anger is mercy. For one man was blinded so that many might be enlightened, and perhaps so that he himself, who had lost the eyes of the flesh, might receive the light of the mind. Then immediately came a greater proof: those who carried out the grim duty of guarding the condemned saw the chains, which they had bound tighter and pressed down to the bone, and which they had refused to loosen even a little when you asked for that small kindness, slip of their own accord from your freed hands before their very eyes, when you turned your prayer to Christ God. Not daring to bind again what God had loosed, they ran in fear to the count, confessing the truth of God on behalf of the confessors. The count heard this with reverence and believed it, and reported it to his emperor with the soldiers' testimony; and, so that his own sudden turn from fury to mercy might be counted among the wonders of God, he became a preacher of Christ in your case, where he had vowed to be a persecutor. I think that the Lord had filled him too with the Holy Spirit, as he once did Saul, because he loved you as his David; so that just as that king was once seized by the Spirit while setting out to persecute the prophets, so too that count, sprinkled with the grace of the Lord that overflowed from the abundance of your faith, who had come to punish a confessor, went away a confessor himself. For he believed, and those whom in his rage he had condemned in advance as guilty he sent away with praise as saints, and he who had wanted to punish the witnesses of the faith bore witness to the truth.

Why then should we wonder that you are so powerful in merits and so rich in graces, when your first lesson in the virtues of Christ was what for a few is the crowning of long labors? Should we still doubt whether you are perfect, you who began from perfection? Or whether you are to be crowned lawfully when your contest is run, since you began your race from the crown? Who will give us wings like a dove? Then we would fly to you and rest in the presence of your holiness, marveling at Christ the Lord and venerating him face to face in your mouth; we would wipe his feet with our hair in your feet and wash them with our tears, and kiss in those scars of yours what are, as it were, the imprinted marks of the Lord's passion. For the wounds of a friend are sweeter than the kisses of an enemy. Woe is me, a wretched sinner with unclean lips, who did not gain this fruit when it was in my hand.

For I believe you will be kind enough to remember that I once saw your holiness at Vienne with our blessed father Martin, to whom the Lord made you equal, though unequal in age. From that time, though I came to know you only briefly, I embraced you with great love and venerated your holiness as fully as I then could, and I commended to you forever myself and my own, who, though absent, saw you through me, since we are one, joined by Christ. And now I rejoice that I can at least boast of this, that I have seen your face in the flesh; but I mourn the carelessness of my misfortune, that in my ignorance I lost the chance of so great a good. At that time I was darkened not only by sins, which still weigh on me now, but also by the cares of this world, from which, by God's mercy, I am now free; and so I saw in you only the bishop, which was plain to view, and did not know how to see what lay within, more glorious still: a living martyr.

Remember us, I beg you, on that day when the hands of angels coming to meet you will bring you, escorted by a countless cohort of your merits, adorned with blessed ornaments, crowned alike with fillets and victory wreaths, both the snowy fillets of consecrated bishops and the bright purple of confessors; when the supreme refiner of his gold and silver will himself receive you as silver tried in the fire and gold proved in the furnace of this world, and the eternal King will set you as a precious pearl in his diadem; and when the just Judge will acknowledge that he owes you rewards not only for your own virtues, seeing around you countless flocks of saints of both sexes whom you beget for him daily by your teaching, a pattern of perfect virtue and faith for all. So too brother Paschasius shows, in whose graciousness and kindness we have gathered, as though reflected in a mirror, certain outlines of your virtues and graces. Truly you are blessed, parent of so many blessed ones, sower of so great a harvest, bringing forth for God a hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold from the fertility of your soil, and destined to receive a like measure from the various fruits of your offspring. The Most High has named you among the greatest in his kingdom, for he has granted you to make your deeds match your words, so that your life is your teaching and your teaching your life. So no disciple dares to excuse himself on the grounds that the command is too difficult, since he is first bound by the example of virtue.
XIX. Paulinus to Delphinus, most blessed and in a special sense my lord, ever our father in God, Christ.

Like a thirsty threshing floor we were waiting for the refreshment of your letter, and our soul, like earth without water, panted for your words with a thirsting heart. For nearly two years had already slipped by since you had sprinkled us, through our fellow servant Cardamas, with a few drops from your mouth, scanty but very sweet. Meanwhile we no longer hoped to be sprinkled with even a little drop of your speech: all summer we had been kept in suspense, waiting in vain for Uranus, who did not come, and so we thought all the more that the winter season too would have to be passed in your silence. And behold, the merciful and compassionate Lord, who gives food to the hungry and comforts the humble, and who is able to give us what we desire beyond what we hope, brought our Cardamas to us again by a sudden arrival. We had not hoped for this, though we had wished for it. And as soon as the voice of your greeting reached our ears through him, our heart leapt with joy, and all our bones said: Lord, who is like you? What is our lowliness, that you are mindful of it and visit it? You have blessed our land, Lord, and given us drink from the torrent of your delight. Our lips shall pour forth a hymn at evening, morning and noon. We will sing and make music to the Lord, who has given us good things. For he has sent good news from a far country, by which we learned that our sweetest and dearest father is safe, and received his words. So our heart was turned from the sadness of anxiety to the joy of security. Our anxious feelings changed for the better, and on that day, made a festival for us by your letter, we rejoiced in place of the days when the long duration of your silence had brought us low.

Let us therefore confess to the Lord his mercies and offer him a sacrifice of praise, because he has satisfied the empty soul. It was not empty of his grace, as we say by his favour, but starved of the fruit of our desire, since it had long hungered for the comfort of your letters, which, as I said, had been denied us for almost two years. May the Lord not count their transgression against them as sin, those whose iniquity has lied to itself and has wasted our soul with a long famine of the bread of your mouth. Let them stay where they wish, since they do not wish to be where they should have preferred to be. Let them do what they are permitted, since they do not do what is fitting. Just as the company of such people could have conferred no good on us, so it can take nothing away. Would that our sins too might do us no harm, being removed far from us along with such neighbours, through the multitude of the mercies of him who has not repaid us according to our sins! As a father has compassion on his son, so he has compassion on those who fear his name and hope in his mercy. We share in their number, since as wretched men we love his coming in the hope of his mercy, and as sinners we dread it in fear of his justice. But may he be appeased by your prayers for your sons and not enter into judgment with his wicked servants, among whom we are first, just as we are last among the good. We have even turned this very glory, by which we received you in Christ and from Christ as the father of our regeneration, into a heap of condemnation. For we, unprofitable servants and degenerate sons, show the Lord most high nothing worthy of you as our father. Even now we keep in a thorny heart the unhappy hardness of the natural wild olive. Yet long ago, by the goodness of the Lord, we were torn from the root of our kindred and seem to have been grafted into your tree, so that we might draw the sap of your richness into the marrow of our soul and, rooted by the spirit of gentleness in the way of peace, be known by our noble fruits as shoots of the good olive.

But as it is, made poor in our father's goods by the abundance of our vices, how shall we order our words on the day of recognition? We have not attained your virtues, and we show no likeness to your stock by which we might be recognized as yours. Who will rescue us from the wrath to come? Who will deliver us from ourselves, so that, cleansed of our own senses, we may be emptied by the purging of faith of all that provokes heaven's wrath? For we feel that the causes of eternal punishment are in us, since the roots of thorns and thistles live in our heart. The earlier growth of our old self, like the vine of Sodom, bore a grape of gall in the bitter fruits of the life of the flesh, and our mind, drunk on the poisons of malice, spewed out the venom of asps. But he who is mighty has done great things for us; he sent from heaven and delivered us; he sent his mercy through you, renewed the face of our land, and made us your planting for himself in his vineyard. Therefore, blessed and most venerable father, you must say to the Lord with unceasing care and constant prayer that he look down from heaven and visit these vines which your right hand has planted, so that, fixed in the true vine, we may live as branches to be pruned for fruit, not cut off for the fire. May he who is the vine and the life guide us in every rule of truth in his discipline, watering us from his upper rooms through your words, which are chaste and holy, as fiery as they are sweet. For your words are drops of that voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance, the rain that came down upon the fleece, that is, was poured into the Virgin in a silent descent.
