He it is in whose showers we rejoice, when he rises within us and distils on the reborn soul the first dew of the knowledge of him, so that he may heal all our infirmities. For the dew that comes from him is health to us, since he is the fountain of life, who sent his word and healed us. This Word of God is the one from whom the voluntary rain comes. It is voluntary because the Son humbled himself even to the death of the cross not by the compulsion of a subject but by the consent of one equal to God, obeying the Father as a duty of love, as he had said through the prophet: I will sacrifice to you voluntarily. For the same Lord, both priest and victim, offered himself for us, and by his own power both laid down his life and took it up again. And therefore this rain is voluntary, since it poured itself out of its own accord on the parched lands to turn the desert into rivers. How it was made weak, he teaches who says: For he was crucified out of weakness. And how it was strengthened and established, you find in the same passage, since, he says, he lives by the power of God.

Pray to this Lord until you prevail, that he not allow our fleeces, which he washed by your hands in the water of refreshment, to grow foul again, stained by our sins, and once more be dyed by the stains of vice and turned to scarlet. May he guard in us, through the vigils of your prayers, the gift of his grace, and not abandon the work of your hands in us until he ripens and perfects in us fruit and a crown for you. Then on that day, coming with rejoicing and carrying your sheaves in a full lap, you may say of us too, counted among your offspring and harvest: Behold I, Lord, and the children whom you have given me. But now fear of tiring you warns us, and not only that but fear of sin as well, which is not escaped in much speaking, to put a bridle on our mouth and shut the door of speech by ending the letter, late though that is. Let the close be a commendation of Cardamas. We congratulate him on being so renewed by the blessing of your hand that the gravity now taken on with the title of exorcist has won him reverence, where once he bore the ridiculous levity of an actor's name [?]. Yet we rejoiced all the more, and with wonder, that through his religious office he has changed even the habits of his former condition. As a constant sharer of our little table, he has so narrowed himself to the measure of our gullet that he did not shun either our humble vegetables or our cups. He can bear witness to this by the thinness of his body and the pallor of his face, unless perhaps on his way back he restores himself along the toilsome road by renewing his old familiarity with the cups he used to drink.
XX. Paulinus to Delphinus, most blessed and deservedly venerable father.

Keeping to the teaching of wisdom, we ought indeed to have put a yoke on our tongue and a balance on our words, so as to escape the double sin of our much speaking and of wearying you. But from the abundance of your love our mouth is opened wide to you, and we cannot lock the door of our mouth and hold back within the confines of a silent breast the affection that overflows from our heart. So we address your reverence in a second letter as well. The one in which we replied was long enough to weary you to the full, yet one letter to you is too little for us, since, as you recognize, we receive your conversation and return our own only at the longest intervals. For in this we give our soul some comfort, however slight. While we write to you in your affection, with our whole heart fixed on your face, we suddenly forget that you are absent, and as if lingering in conversation with you in person we draw out our words at greater length. In this way, though we will not quench the burning thirst of our longing, for that would not be good for us, we soften it by setting the image of your face and conversation before our inner eyes. For although our sojourn seems to be far removed from the places where you live, our spirit is not separated from the embrace of your love. For who, it says, will separate us from the love of Christ? If neither death nor life nor any other creature can, how much less can bodily absence, which cannot dissolve spiritual presence? The spirit is stronger than the flesh, and by so much is the union of souls more powerful than that of bodies, and the presence of the inner man better than that of outer men who are separated in mind, for such men are often joined in place to no purpose. For he is not a Jew, it says, who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, circumcised in spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not from men but from God. By this same law, then, by which the circumcision of the heart is truer than the cutting of the flesh, and a presence joined and held together in the spirit is firmer than one in the body, we are always with you and you with us. For though we are parted in face for a time, we remain ever knit together in heart, living in you, while you in turn dwell in our inmost being, so that we die together and live together. Since it belongs to the care and consolation of that same love that we be kept aware of each other's doings, so that we may worry less about one another in our absence when we are not left uncertain, we inform you, whose affection we know to be most anxious about all our doings, that by Christ's favour, as you pray, we are well. Our bodies are not indeed robust, but they are healthy in their frailty. We are poor in spirit, though in God's spirit, not our own: we lack his goodness and abound in our own wickedness.

Our Cardamas reminded us that you had asked us to report from here too how things stand with us in the Lord. As to that, let your reverence know that your holy brother Anastasius, pope of the City, is most loving toward us in our lowliness. As soon as he had the power to offer us his love, he hastened with most devoted affection not only to receive our love but to press his own upon us. Shortly after his ordination he sent letters about us to the bishops of Campania, full of religion, devotion and peace, so as both to declare his own affection and to give others an example of his kindness. Then, when we had come to Rome according to our solemn custom for the feast of the blessed apostles, he received us as warmly as he did honourably. Later, after some time had passed, he even deigned to invite us to his own anniversary, an honour he usually extends only to his fellow bishops. Nor was he offended by our excuse; he accepted the letter we had sent in place of our presence, and received us with a fatherly spirit even in our absence. Finally, if the Lord grants us leave to return to him at the customary time of the solemn feast, I hope to obtain from him a letter to your holiness, by which he may also begin to commend us to you.

Venerius too, the new bishop of Milan, until now your son and now your brother, had already written to us after his ordination. But since Cardamas reported that you had asked this too, we wrote to him through Cardamas himself, so that he might know the opportunity was at hand, if he wished to acknowledge the duty of devotion he owes, to write to your blessedness and commend his beginnings to your heart. For our part, we rejoice and glory in the Lord, because you work salvation for our house both visibly and invisibly, truly a good father and a saving patron. Invisibly you build us up by your prayers, asking that the kingdom of God may come to be within us. Visibly you work for us by building churches, so that you may give us a share with that man whose house was found worthy of a visit from Christ, because he had received the testimony of a devout people for building the synagogue, which now is the church. We confess to your venerable devotion that when we read the part of your letter in which you told us that a new daughter of the church of Alingo, born on your initiative, had now grown in the name of the Lord to the day of its dedication, our spirit so exulted in God our saviour that, as if we were present among the crowds at the dedication, we sang those words of prophetic joy from the psalms: Rejoice in God our helper; take up a psalm and bring the timbrel. Bring sacrifices and enter the courts of the Lord; worship the Lord in his holy court. Or that verse of the same prophet: Arise, Lord, into your resting place, you and the ark of your holiness. Let your priests be clothed with salvation, and let your saints exult. Let them appoint their day.

You were good enough to tell us that some of the party of him through whose envy death entered the world are gnashing their teeth and wasting away. We are not surprised, since in Jerusalem too, when the temple of God was being rebuilt, the Assyrians were envious and tried to hinder the rising building with frequent hostile raids. But since he who is in us is greater than he who is in this world, their desire will perish and ours will be confirmed, because we hope in the mercy of him who never puts to shame those who hope in him. Only let your holiness take care, as you do, that a house may also be built in ourselves, by Christ and in Christ. For unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain; and unless this house is founded on the rock, which is Christ, it will not be able to withstand the winds of spiritual wickedness and the torrents of worldly temptation.

Pray that the Lord Jesus may come into our heart as into his temple and shake out the scourge of his love, with which he chastises every son whom he receives, and drive out of the senses of our mind, as he drove the traders from the temple, all the commerce and contagion of iniquity. May he drive from us the oxen, the sellers of doves and the tables of the money-changers, so that, cleansed of all uncleanness and greed, we may hold fast to the chaste simplicity of faith and love. For the image of Christ is preserved where Caesar's coin is driven out; where there are no oxen, the mangers are clean; and where the dove is not sold, faith is kept uncorrupted. For unless we give ourselves up to God, we sell ourselves to the devil. That is why the old man, who bound himself over to the counsel of the serpent that urged him to evil, is said to have been sold under sin. And so, as one who had been sold, he needed a redeemer. The redeemer bought us at a great price, so that we should no longer belong either to the devil or to ourselves, and so that, changed from a brood of vipers into a royal and priestly race, we might become his own blood. Our souls had fallen away from the noble state of our first origin and been made worthless by persisting sin, but he made them precious by paying for them with his own blood, and in his generous love he granted that they should become co-heirs with him and sons of God. Let us exult and glory in him who became the refuge of the poor, so as to humble the eyes of the proud. Let us offer him both a temple and a sacrifice in ourselves, purging ourselves of the old leaven if we can, so that we may become unleavened, and Christ himself, who was sacrificed for us, may feast in us.

Let us remember that, set apart from the womb of our land and our kindred, we have become sons of Delphinus, so that we might become those fish that pass along the paths of the sea. Let us remember that you have become not only a father to us but also a Peter, because you cast the hook to draw me out of the deep and bitter waves of this world. So I became a catch of salvation, dying to the nature for which I used to live, so that I might live to the Lord to whom I had been dead. But if I am your fish, I must bear in my mouth a precious coin, on which shines not the image and inscription of Caesar but the living and life-giving image of the eternal King: the faith of truth, which has stamped the die of your teaching and the seal of your ring on the coin of my heart and the wax of my mind. For your teaching is silver tried in the fire, tested in the earth, purified seven times.

Through your prayers may the Lord grant that I may be a coin of your mint, a fish of your hook, a branch of your vine, a son of your chaste womb. For the sons of Delphinus will be counted among the sons of Aaron, but not with those who offered strange fire to the Lord and were burned up by divine fire, the very fire they had quenched in their own hearts. Let your sons have hearts that burn not with the wicked fires of greed and worldly allurements, but with that fire which the Lord came to kindle in us, of which he says: I came to cast fire on the earth, and what do I wish but that it be kindled already? So let not avarice, nor the lust of the eyes, nor the harmful love of temporal things burn in us with a pestilent fire, which is a fire strange to God. Rather, let our God himself, who is a consuming fire, recognize his own fire in us, so that we may say: The Lord is our light and our salvation; whom shall we fear? This fire gives light to hearts and consumes sins; it puts out the darkness by which we are put to death and kindles the light by which we are brought to life. If our lamps are always burning with this fire, we shall say with confidence: Even though I walk through the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Enlightened by this fire, and kindled by its heat to thirst for living water, in our longing for the Lord we shall truly say: As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light.
XXI. Paulinus to Amandus, his holy, deservedly venerable and most beloved brother.

In the sacred history of the Kingdoms we admire Asahel, the brother of Joab, who was winged of foot and light in running, so that he could compete with stags or roe deer in matching speed. We are no less amazed when we read of that giant among the Philistines who had grown beyond the measure of the human body and the size of human limbs. His hands, armed with six fingers each, and his feet, jointed with as many toes, made him stronger and swifter than other men. Yet against David, who fought by the hand of God and was always unconquered as the image of Christ, no hand or might of enemies prevailed, however great they were. By that hand the proud exaltation of the devil was cast down in the great men of the foreigners, and the saving form of God, all-powerful in humility, conquered in our little ones.

But let us run back to the head of the letter, which we began from the feet, so that we may praise the Lord's courier Cardamas with the examples of the swift men of old recorded in the divine law. And so there also comes to mind from the gospel that blessed swiftness of the young apostle. By it he outran Peter to the Lord's tomb, Peter being his equal in eagerness to run but slower under the weight of greater age. So he who alone had reclined on the Lord's breast was the first to look upon the resurrection of the body. From there he had drawn twin springs into the channel of his heart, and afterwards he poured them out over the world as herald of the revelation and of the gospel. That bodily nimbleness of his feet he later fulfilled with spiritual speed, running through the peoples of the whole world on the beautiful feet of the word.

His life too was prolonged beyond the times of all the apostles, and he is recorded as the last writer of the gospel. Thus, as the vessel of election says of him, he added a support like a pillar to the foundations of the Church, confirming the earlier writers of the gospel with harmonious authority. He was the last author in the date of his book but the first at the head of the mystery, for he alone of the four rivers flows down from the very highest spring of the divine head and thunders from a lofty cloud: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He surpasses Moses, who extended the bounds of knowledge by the keenness of his mind as far as the head of the world and the beginnings of visible creatures. The other evangelists began the gospel of the resurrection from the human birth of the Savior, or from the figurative sacrifice of the law, or from the prophetic proclamation of the forerunner, the Baptist. But John flew higher and pierced even the heavens. He did not halt among the angels but passed beyond the archangels too, and all the creatures above them, the virtues, principalities, dominions and thrones, and directed himself with lofty mind to the Creator himself. Beginning from that ineffable generation, he proclaimed the Son coeternal, consubstantial, co-omnipotent and co-creator with the Father, and in the Holy Spirit he discerned God with God, because in the Spirit the Trinity of the Godhead is made complete and the one Godhead of the Trinity is perceived. For the Spirit of God, like the Word of God, is God. Both abide in one head and flow from one source, the Father, but the Son by being born and the Spirit by proceeding, each distinguished rather than divided, with the distinctive property of each person preserved.

So blessed John, who lay on the Lord's breast, had drunk an understanding higher than that of all creatures from the very heart of Wisdom, the creator of all things. Inebriated by the Holy Spirit, who searches even the depths of God, he began his gospel from the inmost and infinite Beginning of all beginnings, and by this one stroke all the mouths of the devil that bark in the heretics are shut. Arius's tongue is the first to be cut out, but Sabellius's blasphemy is also made void, since the same sentence of our fisherman expresses both the unity of the Godhead in Father and Son and the distinction of persons. By the same passage Photinus, the mad teacher who held that Christ had only a human beginning, is hissed off the stage. Marcion, who separates the God of the law from the God of the gospel, is snuffed out. Manichaeus, who denies the true Creator and invents a false one, is crushed. He is confounded by the voice of the same supercelestial gospel that follows at once (I have called this gospel supercelestial because it begins from that origin which is above all the heavens and before all ages), for he hears it said of this Word of God, who is God: All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. The Gnostic glories in the name of a knowledge falsely so called and turns every notion of his perverse mind into airy phantoms, as if by a spiritual imagining of bodily things. The same author forces him to believe in Christ's flesh when he says of that same Word, who was God with God: And the Word became flesh. Yet he was not made flesh in such a way that he passed over from his own nature into ours, as certain other serpents are said to hiss. Rather, remaining in himself what he was, he began for our sake to be what he was not.

I am carried much too far, abusing the indulgence of our oneness of heart so freely that I fear neither to weary you with much talk nor to stray into foolishness in your company. For I know that, wise as you are, you gladly bear with your fool through that love which endures all things and never fails. Now, however, I will say to myself, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue, and I will come down briefly to Cardamas, that is, our Asahel. You have made his feet like the hart's and renewed his youth like the eagle's through the abundance of your love. With that love you received him out of regard for our lowliness and established him in the courts of the house of the Lord, so that he might be more fully free as a man once he had begun to be Christ's freedman. By this kindness you made him flourish again not only in spirit but also in body. And so he too is filled from your heart with the affection with which you love us. He brings your longings to us and consoles ours in turn, and as he travels almost regularly across the great distances between our regions, he keeps to hard ways because of the words of your lips. We believe indeed that he takes wings like a dove's from the very letters of your Holiness that he carries, and that he receives from your prayers the strength of feet that brings him to us. Yet we congratulate him on the very grace by which he has been placed in the service of so great a love. He serves in freedom, he runs about in his old age, and he would rather spend the rest of a well-earned retirement in the toil of travel than at home. For he refuses to tread the ways of the sluggards, which are strewn with thorns, lest he be turned to misery while the thorn of wretched anxiety pierces him out of the fruitless leisure of idleness. So he exults, untiring, to run his course, lest the poverty that follows the sluggard should come upon him like a good runner while he wears away his days in idle leisure. And when he comes to us, with what joy he floods and fills our soul with good news of your health! He makes our bones fat, and there is a voice of gladness in our tents, as with minds refreshed by the consolation we longed for we say: The Lord has been mindful of us and has blessed us.

Let us exult and rejoice in him who grants the wish of the one who prays and has given us the desire of our soul, for he has gone before us with blessings of sweetness. What blessing could be sweeter to us now, or what sweetness more delightful, than the fruit and consolation of love that your letters give us in the fullest measure? In them we embrace pledges of both your mouth and your heart, because your words are the offspring of your soul, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. That is why we love Cardamas when he arrives in your words and commend him in ours as he departs. He deserves that his old age should rest in abundant mercy, since it labors for the longings and duties of love. Moreover, there is something we admired in him even more than his swiftness in spite of his grey hairs. From the title of exorcist he has advanced to such frugality that he did not shrink from being our guest at table almost daily. And when he was sprinkled with rare and tiny cups that barely wet the edge of his lips, he made no complaint about the wrong done to his empty stomach or his dry throat. In short, Cardamas seemed to us so fine in every respect that we saw in him a cleric commendable to men and an exorcist terrible to demons. For the rest, brother, we commend to you both him and all our people and ourselves, so that through you we may be commended to the Lord by earnest prayers. May the freedom of all our people serve the eternal Lord, and may our servitude in Christ win the reward of eternal freedom.
22. Paulinus to Severus, his brother of one mind

The letters you had sent by that unspiritual monk of ours were intercepted and delivered by a truly spiritual letter-carrier, our son Sorianus. In him we saw that the Lord had conferred a double grace. First, he had longed for us with an affection instilled from your heart, and now he would not come to us without a word from you. Second, Marracinus would not bring us your letters a second time. By divine inspiration, I believe, he was either too bashful to see us or too lazy to extend his journey beyond the City, so he handed your letters at Rome to the brother I have mentioned. He was glad of the chance of the shortcut he had wished for, thinking that he had protected himself against your instructions. That way he would not be forced either to put on the monk in himself, as you had ordered, or to look upon one in me, as could not be avoided. So let him keep his soldier's cloak and his boots and his puffed cheeks. He was afraid to change the one and to let the other go down.

Let those come to visit us again who are our fellow servants and share our pallor. They are not proud in embroidered clothes but humble in rough haircloth. They are cloaked not in a cropped chlamys [?] but in coarse little capes, and girded not with a belt but with a rope. They do not wear their hair over the shameless forehead of a fashionably cut head. Instead, with a chaste lack of style, their hair is cut to the skin, unevenly half-shorn, and shaved in front to leave the forehead bare. Let them be unadorned with the adornment of modesty, decently unkempt and honorably contemptible. For they spurn even the natural beauty of the body for the sake of inner refinement and even disfigure themselves on purpose, becoming modestly unsightly in face while they are made, to their salvation, comely in mind. The faces, dress and smell of such men turn the stomachs of those for whom the odor of death is taken for the odor of life, to whom what is bitter is sweet, what is chaste is base, and what is holy is hostile. It is therefore just that we repay them in kind, so that their odor may be to us like the odor of death, lest we cease to be the fragrance of Christ. What right have they to be angry with us if, in turn, the odor of the life of those to whom our odor is unto death stinks to us? He shudders at my fasting; I cannot bear his drunkenness. He avoids the breath of a monk as he speaks; I flee the blast of a belching Thraso. If the dryness of our throats displeases them, the indigestion of their gullets displeases us too. If the dryness of frugality offends them, the gluttony of bellies offends us too. Let them see us, then, not drunk in the morning but fasting in the evening, not bloated with yesterday's wine but abstaining from today's. Let them see us not madly unsteady from the surfeit of lust but wholly wounded by honest vigils and soberly drunk, men made to stagger by thrift, not by gorging.

We rejoice to have received such a bearer of your letter, and I ask you to receive him as though he had come to me sent by you. For he too should be counted among those who have come to me in place of your Brotherhood, since the Lord handed your letters to him without your knowledge so that you might count him among them. I think, moreover, that you will also credit to him the benefit of this divine grace, since through him it was granted to you as well that your letters were not brought to us by a carrier who was not of your own body. Yet I want Sorianus to be praised with Marracinus's leave, so that you will not accuse me before him again. For I think I have praised him rather than blamed him by mentioning the very things in which a man who blushes to be or to seem a monk must glory. Indeed, you remember that in Virgil the Fury is praised with the things that are usually held against her. But see that you do not slander me for borrowing something from a poet who is no longer our study, as though I had broken my vow. I declare that I did this on the authority of your example. For I have your letter whose closing words are: Live happy, you whose fortune is accomplished. I also have the one in which, remembering a prologue of Plautus, you called your home your household Lar.
23. Paulinus to his brother Severus

Why are you trying to wring more love from us? The total has no room to grow. If the sea can overflow its barriers, and things that keep their natural fullness can grow over time, then our love for you can be heaped higher. But we have already filled it to its limit, since we love you as we love ourselves. So just as we cannot add a cubit to our stature, we cannot add to our love for you. Yet we set no limit to our longing. You think you satisfy us by your constant respect and affection, as you try to make up for your absence with so many letters. In fact you only whet love's appetite. The favour of your letters satisfies us less and less, because the very care and kindness of your words give us more reason to long for you yourself, brother so uniquely one in mind with us in Christ. For what can be done more devotedly toward God and neighbour than what you show to Christ in us? In him both of God's commandments are fulfilled, since he is God to us by the majesty of his own nature and became our neighbour by taking on ours. So as you advance in this, your love is made complete. May it be infinite in him who is perfect, since it finds its end in Christ, whose greatness has no end. But let our end be in him, so that through him we may live without end. For us Christ is both the beginning of all, since all things were made through him, and our own summit, since he is the head of the body whose members we are. The Lord is sweet and upright. He is sweet to me in you, and to me you are how great a multitude of his sweetness! For however great you are, in mind and in tongue, you are wholly a man of longing. To me you have the savour of Christ's sweetness, like a garden, like the scent of a full field, which you gathered as you ran in the fragrance of his ointments. For you are a field to him, and he in turn is a field to us, since in him we sow and from him we reap. But you are a field that does not bristle with thorns, is not dry with sand, and is not rough and bare with rocks, where the seed sown is choked, or left without root, or scorched. You are the field God blessed with the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth. That is why your tongue drips with the word of God and your fertile heart multiplies the seed it has received for God into a spiritual harvest. So the reaper may fill his hand from your fruits, and the one who gathers sheaves may fill his bosom. That is God himself, who is both sower and reaper of his word in us. He is also the hand, since he is the right hand of God, which we fill with good works. He is likewise that bosom of Abraham in which we rest as the reward of our works.

So this God, abounding toward us in your love, blesses, visits, feeds and enlightens us, not only by your letters but also by your couriers. By both he opens to us the good treasure of your heart, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and, as Scripture says, every creature gathers to its like. Therefore God has blessed you, because the innocent and upright have clung to you and you have not sat with the ungodly. You have hated iniquity and you love your soul. You threw it away in Christ, so that, lost to this life, it might be kept for eternal life, gaining itself by its own loss as it becomes cheap to itself through the love of Christ. Your soul is cheap to you and precious to God. With this in mind we smell its sweetness in the shrines [?] of your mouth, which breathe Christ, and we bless the Lord, God the Word of God. Just as he did in the man he took on, he passes through certain stages of bodily life in our minds: he is born, grows, gains strength and grows old. But we must pray that he does not stay a small, weak and poor child in us for long, or for ever. In you, though, we see his growth and recognize it. We say this to boast, since your good is our glory. In you he is great in goodness and small in malice, old in wisdom and strong in faith, poor in the spirit of devout humility and rich in love. In your earlier kindnesses to us in our lowliness, you had already outstripped others. As we have often testified, you were more devoted than all our friends, more faithful than our relatives and more attentive than our brothers. But now, by sending someone to visit us in this way, you have surpassed even yourself in kindness. It was enough for us to earn your letters through yearly journeys and to see the people you sent. In them we had not only a stand-in for your presence but an image of your faith. Yet it was not enough for you to keep the established custom with its usual exchange. Your great love made it seem too long to stay silent toward us through the delay of winter. Your heart grew hot within you, and as you meditated on devotion, a holy fire of good impatience blazed up. Nor was it enough to hurry your letters to us. You also had to heap up the favour of your words by choosing a carrier from among your holy companions.

Blessed is the man you chose and took on for this duty, by which you lend to God at interest. By the true confession of our conscience we are sinners. Yet, as you say, you mistakenly think us saints in your simplicity, and so you love us no longer with a human love but with the love of Christ. For this you will receive a prophet's reward, because for the name of Christ you receive with a prophet's honour even those who are not prophets. But we are owed no such favour for our part in this, in receiving brother Victor with deep affection and great joy as he came to us in the name of God and as your representative. We did only what we, unprofitable servants, ought to have done. The plain truth compelled us to welcome and revere a pure sheep in him. Not only his sheepskin revealed it, but also his spirit of meekness and the modesty of Christ that showed in his speech and in his silence. Truly we recognized in him the pattern of the saints, the blessed Martin and Clarus. Clarus, as we learned from you, followed that illustrious master at the closest distance. Victor, a son of peace, told us that he was the offspring of one of them by rebirth in baptism and had been the other's companion on the road. He is truly, as you wrote, a man of God: humble of heart but not humble in grace, a vessel of mercy and a dwelling of the Most High, whom the Most High receives and delights in as the peaceful lodging of a trembling soul. Besides the twofold blessings he brought from you, your letters and the cloaks, he added many more from the riches of his own mind. He was not only most welcome to us as a spiritual companion but also diligent in serving our bodily needs. I dare to confess something that weighs on me, since I want to keep back nothing of his good qualities from you. I know for certain that they are your joy, because the good of a member of your household is your portion.

So he served me. He served me, I say, and woe is me, wretch that I am, I allowed it. He who was no slave to sin served a sinner, and I, unworthy, was waited on by a servant of righteousness. But I hope for some relief from so great a weight in this: I did not claim the holy brother's service out of pride, but accepted it for fear of hurting his love and in the faith of receiving a blessing. For holy service in the name of God, and the love of one who serves in the spirit of freedom, was a blessing to me. That is why I accepted the good he offered freely, and for his own benefit too. I assumed that the more merit he gained from works of devotion, the more powerful he would be in praying for me. Surely by his prayers he will see to it that what he added to his own harvest through me does not add to my burdens. I confess that I loved the blessing in his service. I feared that if I refused it, it would go far from me, for I remembered what is written: "He did not want blessing, and it shall be far from him." So I gave myself wholly into his hands and to his tender heart. From a heart full of love he lent me a servant's hands, anointing my limbs and washing my feet. He was full of generous affection and snatched every menial task from me, so that he would hardly even let me pour water over his hands. It was from your book that I came to love the grace of such service, so that I might taste at least the smallest drop of Martin's sacred deeds. Every day he wanted not only to wash my feet but also to clean my shoes, if I had let him. He was greedy for mastery within, and so he was tireless in bodily service.

As for the washing of my feet, I confess that I gave in only once, following the example of the apostles. I had read that they offered their feet to be washed by the Lord when he served them. They would not have received a share in the inheritance unless they had submitted to being served. The good Lord and teacher of salvation granted them the merit of ruling through the ministry of serving. He gave an example of human humility to those for whom he was preparing a share in divine glory. That is why, once they saw the mystery of so great a gift and understood how great a good it was, those who had at first trembled to offer their feet as he prepared to serve them asked to be washed not only on their feet but wholly, up to the head. And I revered the Lord Jesus in brother Victor, since every faithful soul is from God and the humble of heart is the heart of Christ. I confess that I wanted a better fellow servant to touch me with oil or water as a remedy for my weakness. Nor was I disappointed in the help I had counted on. The oil seemed made medicinal by his devout hands, and the very gentleness of the anointing let it slip more softly into my marrow. The bones that had been humbled rejoiced. My soul blessed the Lord, and all that was within me blessed his holy name. This was an exercise in devotion more than in bodily training, and it also helped to revive my senses. As the good brother set my frail limbs in order with his shaping hand, he restored my bones and also raised up the vigour of my mind. Faith no doubt worked together with his hands, so that while the hand of one who loved me tended my weak flesh, the grace of a believer washed clean the soul that suffered with it. So the oil of health on the outside became for me the oil of gladness within.

Now hear about another service he did for our senses. He cared not only for our refreshment but also for our frugality, and he taught us to make do with plain food. He made porridge cooked with a drop of oil and plenty of water. But he seasoned it with such salt of grace and such sweetness of love that we did not miss cooks or sauces. Simplicity joined to love mixed into the pure water an oil of sweetness, and no troublesome flies spoiled it. Yet this spiritual cook was more skilled at feeding the inner man. To destroy the food of gluttony, he made our porridge not from fine wheat but from coarse meal or millet. He was preparing to train us in the appetite of monks, and so that he would not seem to treat us too delicately even in this, he crumbled beans into panic grass, so that we would sooner lay aside our senatorial fussiness. But in this blessing of sweetness we had delights for the soul. We rejoiced that our brother, spiritual even in bodily services, was feeding us with the food of prophets. In this mixed mash he copied those loaves of tribulation that the prophet Ezekiel was ordered to make for himself from various kinds of grain and meal. These stood for the confusion of the Jews, who forgot God and exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats hay. He was told to bake them on cow dung and, once they were baked under the foul ashes, to eat them by measure with the tears of captivity. In this way the people might foresee the punishment coming upon their faithlessness, which was signified in the prophet's own body. They might return to the Lord at least this way, if the wrath of the offended God called them back to repentance, not only announced in words but acted out in the bodies of the prophets.

So brother Victor wanted us to learn to humble the soul not only by fasting but also by food. Remembering our old sins and recognizing our present ones, we were to eat the bread of sorrow in sadness. He did spare us in part, mixing only beans with millet and panic grass, though perhaps that came more from forgetfulness than from restraint. The holy man would have been faithfully careful not to withhold from us anything in holy Scripture. To complete the whole recipe for the prophetic bread according to the word of God, he would also have mixed lentils, barley and vetch into the mash [?]. The heat of all these unlike grains would have boiled over the pot's lips, and the pot, splitting into cracks as though the cooking were at war with itself, would have crackled. Even so, he filled a roomy earthenware pot with the few grains he used and brought us dishes smoking with a heavy reek. He filled not only the space around our little table but the whole of our little cell with a smelly fog. And to multiply our blessing, he added another prophet's meal to our little supper, serving us Elisha's pot, into which flour was thrown. He cooked in it no poisonous herb but a seasoning of salvation, doing all he did in the name of the Lord. So we were safe and secure, and we did not cry out to him, "Man of God, there is death in the pot!" For now there is life in our pot, since the Lord Jesus, the Word of God, became flesh and dwelt among us. The earthen vessels of our bodies had slipped from his hands through the slipperiness of our own chosen wickedness and been broken by long sinning. He took them up into himself, so that he, the potter, might remake them for a better use. He himself was made from the clay of our body, like a vessel that was, as he says, lost, that is, in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that by sin he might condemn sin. That is why he says, "Moab is the pot of my hope": he took a body not only from Judah but also from Moab, that is, not only from a line of saints but also from a line of sinners. In the pot of our flesh, as it were, he cooked away its rawness and made his flesh our holy food for ever. For his flesh, as he himself says, is truly the food of life. It is also that pot in Jeremiah which burns away sins and consumes them with the fire of which he says, "I came to cast fire on the earth." Let us pray that this fire is kindled in us too. Then, in the pot of the Lord's body, that is, the Church, we may be cooked through. With our vices burned away and their dross removed, we may become silver tried by fire, tested in the earth, purified seven times. Then we may remain in the same Lord, the true vine, no longer as twigs fit for burning but as fruitful branches. And the same Lord may become our food, that sweet cluster of grapes which, hung on the carrying pole of the cross, both showed us the fruit of the promised land and let us taste it. Then we will no longer go after the worthless grasses of untilled ground, among which we risk picking even the deadly clusters of wild vines. This certainly happens to us when the soul, whose cultivation is the word of God, is overgrown with the thorns of worldly cares. Sighing over this life, short in its span and barren of good, we gather harmful sins among our pointless activities, like poisonous shoots among wild plants, and so we put death into the pot of our body or our heart. But thanks be to God, who has freed us from the body of this death through Christ Jesus our Lord. He mixes the power of his Spirit with our weakness. The word of God is poured into our hearts and transforms us, as if by a sprinkling of saving and living salt, so that the bitterness of our malice and the barrenness of our uselessness have been changed into sweetness and fruitfulness.

Let us return to brother Victor. Using our little supply of flour as he did, in the name of God, he made its jar overflow with blessing. So he gave us something also from the jar of blessed Elijah. Filled by the sacred word to a supply that never ran out, that jar let the heavenly prophet feed the blessed widow of Zarephath and her sons through three years of famine. In that widow, I think, Christ was already then feeding his Church through the prophet, with the bread not of grain but of the word. Of her he says, "Blessing I will bless her widow." This is the widow the Apostle speaks of, who is free to marry whom she will once her husband is dead. For when the law came to an end, and Christ is the end of the law, the Church passed over to the freedom of grace and, like the widow of the law, married Christ. Now the oil of grace and the flour of blessing in her jar have not run out during the famine of all the nations outside. Their wretched starvation, cut off from the food of life and from faith in the Trinity, was fittingly foreshadowed by that three-year famine of old. But to finish with this subject: in brother Victor's hands our flour felt the Lord's grace. What used to be barely enough for bread now has plenty left over for porridge as well. It fills the monastic brotherhood, hungry for the evening meal after fasting, in two ways, as leavened loaves or as loose meal.

Though my Victor tried to accustom our stomachs to stronger food, he was a brother we needed, and he also took thought for our weakness. Where our faith fell short in eating that porridge, he made up for it, and he completed the work of his hands with one helper to eat that dish for us. This is a man from the countryside whom we have taken in and are caring for at home. He is old in body and an infant in mind, for though already failing with age he has been reborn to grace and has blossomed from the oldness of the flesh into newness of life. Brother Victor's cooking fattened him on food that suited him on two counts: it was familiar to a countryman and suitable for a toothless one. This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him. He rescued him from darkness and the shadow of death. Now, sprinkled with hyssop and made clean, he feasts with a voice of joy and praise and cries out: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep. I will bless the Lord at all times, who gave me understanding, drew me out of the miry dregs and put a new song in my mouth. I was young and now I am old, but my days have not run out in emptiness, for he who is mighty has done great things for me. He has given me drink from the torrent of his delight, and my flesh has flourished again. He has sent me grain in abundance and filled the empty soul. Now my old age rests in rich mercy, until I sleep in peace and rest for length of days."

I come now to a greater service that brother Victor did for me. He kindly cut my hair with his own hands. Yet he wanted me to owe even this favour to you, saying that he was showing me his skill on your orders. So I asked him that you both would do with earnest prayers what he did with his skilled hand. When your prayers have won over the Lord, may our sins, which outnumber the hairs of our head and leave our soul unkempt, not just be trimmed halfway but cut down to the quick, as if shaved off with a razor. We have a razor that cuts to save and one that cuts to destroy. Our razor of healing and beauty is Christ God. He circumcises our heart, shaves off our vices, smooths the head of the soul and tends the face of the mind. He cleanses us and frees us, like that captive woman in the law, from the shaggy hair of wretched slavery. Then, as she was to pass into marriage with an Israelite husband, we who are to be joined to the Lord may be stripped of the sins of our flesh like barbarian locks. After that, with renewed senses, we may shine as with fresh new hair. And growing our life like a Nazirite's hair, we may consecrate it to God in chastity and frugality.

But we must beware of that hostile razor on the other side, which shaved the head of the human race when the first-made parents were deceived by harmful fraud. It must not climb up to our head, that is, to the faith by which Christ is made our head, and strip us of spiritual grace as if of that Nazirite hair. How great a good that hair remains for those who keep it, and what ruin follows when it is plucked from the careless, is shown by that hero in the book of Judges, consecrated by divine oracles. He was unconquerable while he kept his hair, a captive when it was cut off, and strong again when it grew back. If only he had been as wise in guarding against a woman as he was strong in strangling a lion! But he who had conquered by spiritual grace was conquered by carnal temptation, and though he had overcome the strong, he was overpowered by weakness. The same must happen to those who do not make their woman, that is, the flesh, subject to her husband, that is, the spirit, under God's laws. Like soft husbands with feeble minds, they give in to a wife who gives bad advice. They fall away from that teacher who, as soon as he knew Christ, won a great contest in his first days as a recruit and did not give in to flesh and blood.

So let us look at all that Samson suffered once his faithless wife had corrupted him. We sinners will suffer spiritually the same things he endured in the flesh, which were set down for our instruction. If we violate the grace of Christ, as his hair was cut, the enemy will mock us in the same way. He will take away our eyes, put us in prison and set us to turn millstones like asses. That is why the Lord warns us through the prophet not to let our necks, if we refuse the yoke of Christ, deserve the donkey's mill: "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding." For, as the same prophet says elsewhere, man does not understand his honour. That honour is the dignity of his nature, by which his reason rules over the other living things on earth. He was made rational so that he could understand and worship his Maker. But when he abuses so great a gift of the Creator to give free rein to his error, he is compared to the beasts and becomes like them. We see this plainly fulfilled in the king of Babylon. Stripped of human sense, he suffered with the heart of a beast the punishment for his impious stupidity and senseless pride. For when a man has fallen into error and slipped away from righteousness, he is justly abandoned, like Samson, by the strength of both wisdom and grace, and he is punished with blindness and the mill. Whoever has robbed himself of the light of reason and thrown himself down to the likeness of beasts as a slave of the body deserves the work of a beast of burden.

Consider the life of mortals of this sort, and the whole picture of a beast turning a mill will present itself to you. As the beast has the eyes of its body sewn shut with rags, so this man has the eyes of his mind sewn shut by the filth of his life. Through the wanderings of his senses, as if round the windings of the millstones, he trudges wretchedly at his toilsome post, useless for his own purposes and labouring for another's. He stands in the way of sinners, fettered by the chains of his own desires; he is his own prison, besieged by the darkness of his error and caked with the squalor of his conscience. Within himself he suffers the slave-house of the mill: like a millstone he turns the rock of his heart, hardened by obstinacy in wickedness, and makes flour for his enemies out of the corrupted grain of his soul. For as it is written that the sinner runs out of his own soul, so whoever works sin grinds the enemy's wheat at the mill of his own life, to feed the devil; and to the devil that soul becomes bread, while to itself it is famine. But if he becomes a spirit that does not always go away but at some point returns, he will be made whole again as grace blossoms anew, like hair growing back.

But to weave the whole of this letter out of hair, I am glad to give my discourse free rein and follow that strong man of the Lord to his end. For both in his blindness and in his death we shall marvel at the sacraments of the divine mystery sketched out beforehand. As for the statement in Scripture that he laid low more enemies in dying than he had struck down in the whole of his life before, I think it should be interpreted first and foremost of the power of the Lord's passion, by which the devil's house fell and the kingdom of death was dissolved. Christ always lived, as he lives now, and even before his coming in the flesh he was with the Lord the Father as God the Word, in the majesty of his nature. Nevertheless, when the ages had been set in their order, the power of death reigned in raging licence from Adam to Moses, and through the law, when sin was recognized but not avoided, it grew. This kingdom the King of kings and dispenser of times, the Son of God, divided and destroyed by his passion. He who was God was made under the law, to free those subjected to the law; he was made of a woman, but a woman in sex and a virgin in childbirth, so that the creator of both sexes might sanctify both, by taking up the Word and by being born of a woman. So by dying he destroyed death itself, dissolving, as it is written, the enmities in his flesh and making both one, that is, man and God, whom God and the man Christ Jesus joined together in himself. In him the substance of each nature laid aside its discord and acknowledged the eternal covenant of a grace that makes one. We had been stripped by the devil's robbery and lay wounded on the road, and our brother in the Levite and our brother in the priest had passed us by; the law had not redeemed us, either by sacrifices or by prophets. But that Samaritan did not pass by, who for our sake even bore the insult of that name. He did not pass by, because he was no hireling but the true and good shepherd, who had come to lay down his life for the sheep. Pitying his man, passed over by those who went before and left uncared for, he came near and took him up on his own beast, that is, the incarnation of the Word. With the oil of grace and the wine of his passion he healed him and entrusted him to the innkeeper, that perfect teacher of the Gentiles, at the wage of a denarius in the two Testaments. And from the countless fruits of this good he will repay the innkeeper with rich thanks and countless crowns for blessed virginity also, because Paul added this counsel to the commandment and spent beyond it from his own.

So this was not a brother, for by his condition he differed from servants as Lord, and by his nature from mortals as God. Yet he was also a man, of whom it is written: "He is a man, and who shall know him?" Nor is he our brother on that account. True, the divine kindness, out of the humility of his heart, granted this name to his servants, saying, "I will declare your name to my brothers"; yet our arrogance must not dare to call him brother. Not even the fact that he deigned to become man makes him one, since even in his very birth as a man he has nothing in common with us: apart from the way we are begotten, he was made flesh of the Holy Spirit, and was both conceived and born with his holy mother's virginity unviolated. And so, having become our body without any contagion of our body, he did not give God his own appeasement, because he himself was the propitiation; nor did he give the price of redemption for his own soul, but for ours, because the Saviour had no need of salvation. It was we, sold under sin, who needed the price of redemption, and so for us he became man, for us he took the form of a servant, for us he became the son of a handmaid. Though he is blessed and the sanctifier of the saints, he was nevertheless made for us both sin and curse, which he was not, so that he might free us from both, who were sin by our transgression and curse by our condemnation, nailing both to the cross in his own flesh. That, I think, is why it was said: "A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem." For those whom a brother, that is, a prophet or a lawgiver who was only a man, had not redeemed, this man redeemed who was also God. For, it says, God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. Only a man of this kind could prevail against the sentence of death and the sting of sin, so as to blot out the bond of death and humble the accuser. Yet he engaged him not in the majesty of his own nature but in the guise of ours, wresting nothing from him by violent domination but overcoming him by the law of justice. For when the woman had been deceived and the man cast down through the woman, the devil claimed all the offspring of the first man as sinners under the laws of death. He did so with a malicious desire to do harm, yet by the most equitable right of victory. His power was therefore to last until he killed a just man in whom he could point to nothing deserving death: not only because he was killed without fault, but also because he was born without lust. To lust the devil had subjected those he had captured, so that whatever was born of it he might keep as the fruit of his own tree, with a perverse desire to possess, indeed, yet by no unjust right of possession. Most justly, then, he is compelled to release those who believe in the one he most unjustly killed. So in dying in time they pay their debt, and in living forever they live in him who paid for them what he did not owe.

For this reason I think that he himself is for us that lion in whose mouth, when it was dead, we find the food of honey. For what is sweeter than the word of God? And what is stronger than God's right hand? Or in whose mouth, when dead, are the honeycomb and the bees, if not in his in whose word lies the good of our salvation and the gathering of the nations? Many have preferred to see in this lion a figure of the nations, because the people of the Gentiles who believed was formerly a body of savagery and now belongs to Christ. In that body the apostles, like bees, have stored up the honey of wisdom from the dew of heaven and the flowers of divine graces. And so food came out of the mouth of the eater, because the nations that were once savage toward God received the word of God and took it in with faithful hearts, and brought forth an utterance of salvation. Those, however, who prefer to see Christ in that same lion take Samson as a figure of the Jews: the Jew, that is, killed that lion as he killed Christ. They also ascribe to a mystical foreshadowing the fact that it was precisely when he was seeking a marriage that he carried out the longed-for slaughter of the mighty beast, because the marriage pledged between Christ and the Church could not be confirmed unless the lion of the tribe of Judah were slain. For the same Lord is the lion that has conquered and also the lion's whelp, who fell asleep of his own accord and was raised by himself, of whom it is written: "Who shall rouse him?" For of his own will he offered for us to the Father the sacrifice of his own body, and as the same high priest forever he took up his life again, as he himself testifies, by the same power by which he laid it down. He is the lion's whelp because he is the Son of God, and the same is the lion because he is equal to the Father. So, as it seems to me, this saying fits this lion more aptly: "Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came sweetness." It came, that is, from our Saviour, since he, whose speech is life, both chewed this food for us by teaching and brought it out by imparting it. Or, if you prefer another sense, food comes out of the eater in this way: this lion of the tribe of Judah, victorious for us, snatches us from the mouth of the hostile lion, and so he hunts in order to save, captures in order to release, breaks in order to make firm, chews in order to make whole, eating in us that by which we are corrupted. So let us long to become the prey of this lion, so that we may not be the prey of the enemy lion. Let us become God's food, so that we may not be the serpent's food. Let Christ eat us, so that the devil may not devour us. For when Christ eats, as I said, what consumes us is consumed in us. Christ is life, and we shall not be able to put off this mortal nature unless we are swallowed up, because Christ devours our death. But we cannot be Christ's food unless we do his will, so that in turn he too may become our food, in whom we live forever if we live by his commandments. So, then, sweetness comes out of the strong when the bitterness of our malice is changed through him into the sweetness of goodness, and we come forth as sweet food from his word. By eating us he consumed us, and so restored us from sin to life. He alone is strong, sweetly strong, who freed the poor man from the greedy mighty one. Through the mystery of his love he slew the savagery of my body in the death of his own body, and brought forth the food of life where the hunger of wretched death was parching. He changed for me offence into grace, sin into righteousness, weakness into strength, death into life, shame into glory, exile into a kingdom. We who used to hear, "You are earth, and to earth you shall go," now hear, "Your citizenship is in heaven."

So I think the image that is traced out again in Samson, whether when his hair has grown back or in his death, also fits every servant of Christ. Take a man who has been overtaken in some sin. Through wholesome penance he returns to the restoration of grace, as if his hair were growing again. He sets his arms like a bow of bronze, that is, faith of true hope and hope of unfeigned faith, and trains his hands for battle with works of piety, whose exercise is profitable for all things. Then, strong as it were with the muscles of a good conscience and firm faith, he will dare to attack and will be able to overturn the pillars of the enemies. These are the pillars of the hostile house on which it rests, the house in which the enemy feasts as though he had conquered us, mocking his captives, if he uses our members as the weapons of his wickedness. We bring this enemy down along with his house by the death of the flesh brought into subjection. With the flesh as his ally, the enemy is shut up inside us, within our very selves, and shakes our soul with civil war. He has gained power over us through the guilt of our own will; he has our own vices as his henchmen against us, and he attacks our inner man through the service of the outer.

But let us remember the covenant by which, buried with Christ through the grace of baptism, we swore our oath to the sacraments of the cross: that we would no longer act as though we were living in this world, and that we would live no longer ourselves, but Christ in us. When we are thereby restored to the honour of our head, the devil's house will fall and the whole cohort of enemies will die with the death of our sin. So from Samson's death I learn not only to die together with my enemies, that is, to kill sin along with my flesh by mortifying it, so that with my spirit surviving I may triumph as the victor of salvation and say to my soul, "Return to your rest, for the Lord has dealt kindly with me." I am also enlightened to good understanding by Samson's blindness, in which he was deprived only of his bodily eyes and did not lose his spiritual ones, so that by his example I may know which eyes I ought rather to have. For that man would not have called on the Lord to aid his strength unless he had kept the eyes of his mind unharmed. Their light is Christ, in whose light we shall see light. If that light burns always in the lamp of our body, then the works of darkness will perish and the prince of this world is cast out. He is not cast out of this world, of course, for, as it is written, he will be brought to nothing along with it in condemnation, sharing his end with those who are judged; but he is cast out of our hearts, and he is driven from them if we receive Christ.

Therefore, since those who belong to the devil's party imitate him, let us imitate the Lord Jesus. He called us into the lot of his inheritance and commanded us to take up his sweet yoke, so as to shake off from us that heavy yoke of the law and of death. Hair, too, is like a yoke of lightness; for, as divine Scripture teaches us, the hair of the saints is light and that of the ungodly heavy. The first is hair either of strength, as in Samson, or of sanctification, as in Samuel; the second is hair either of weight, as in Absalom, or of squalor, as in Nebuchadnezzar. This difference among men and their hair teaches us to judge deeds by hair. The Assyrian king was condemned to the wilderness and to savagery, and the grim matting of his uncut hair bristled into a lion's mane, so that even in bodily appearance he turned into a beast, since he was exiled not only from his kingdom but also from human reason. With his grim hair he resembled a lion, with his hooked claws a vulture, in his mind and his fodder an ox, so that he who had resembled many beasts in his character should not bear the likeness of only one in his punishment.

Yet when at last he came to know God, he was restored both to his reason and to his kingdom, and he too became for us an example of faith, so that we may fear to lose by sinning the kingdom that is within us, and remember to regain it by repenting. Absalom, though proud of both his handsome body and his head, could not say what Samson said: "If I am shaved, my strength will leave me." For however beautiful his hair, he did not have in it that strength, which belonged not to bodily hair but to spiritual grace, and this an ungodly man could not have. For Christ is the power and wisdom of God, and he did not enter a parricidal soul, because he does not dwell in a body subject to sins. Indeed, the need to cut it, which Scripture mentions, testifies that his hair was cut because of the mass of his iniquities. For so you read: "He used to cut the hair of his head because it weighed on him; and when it had been cut, he weighed the hair of his head, and it came to a hundred shekels by the king's weight." How could it be expressed more plainly that hairs are reckoned as deeds, when Scripture has marked in the head of the ungodly man no strength at all, but only a burden of hair? "He weighed," it says, "the hair of his head." For to the ungodly his iniquity is his glory. Not only does wicked action delight him, but also, as someone says, a reputation for wickedness. Hence you have this in the Psalms: "Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?" For the light of the ungodly is darkness, their honour a shadow, their eminence a passing away, their head the devil; and therefore their hair is a weight. That is why Scripture says the hair of that parricide was heavy by the king's weight, that is, by the devil's weight; for every ungodly man is the devil's kingdom. So too, it says, "those who are clothed in soft garments are in the houses of kings," that is, of the princes of this air and the leaders of spiritual wickedness. In their houses and kingdoms people live either hard in ungodliness or soft in wantonness; their riches are sin, their paths slippery, their end destruction, their glory in hell, their house in the tomb. The hairs of such people are crimes, and so they cannot be the hair by which the holy warrior snapped the enemies' ropes and new cords as if they were soft threads. They are rather the ones of which it is written: "The ropes of sinners have wound around me." For the soul is both entangled and weighed down by its sins. The prophet proves this fully when he says: "My iniquities have risen over my head; like a heavy burden they have weighed upon me."

You see how heavy the sinner's hair is. But the man whose hair is Christ exults, light and winged, saying: "God, who girds me with strength and has made my way spotless, who has made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me on the heights." For the yoke and the hair of Christ, as I said, are light, because in serving Christ we do good works, and on these as on wings we are carried aloft. That is why the apostle says to Christians even while they are still in the flesh: "But you are no longer in the flesh but in the spirit." For the flesh, made subject to a soul that is subject to God, passes into spirit, not by a change of substance but by a change of life. So I want both Samson's death and his blindness for myself, so that I may live and see for God. For perhaps, when his strength had been restored in his hair for the sake of the mystery to come, he did not desire to recover his eyes along with it, as he had lost them together, because that strength of heavenly grace, sound in its inner sight, had no need of bodily vision.

By this example, then, let us too strain our senses toward the Lord and blind our fleshly eyes by turning them away from worldly things. These are the eyes the prophet longed to be deprived of when he said: "Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity." And the Lord himself, preferring blindness to the eyes of the Jews, says: "If you were blind, you would have no sin." Let us remember with what ruin the eyes of the first couple were opened in paradise. They had them enlightened for God as long as they kept them closed to sin. For only then did they drink in the shame of their age of puberty, when through the crime of transgression they lost the chastity of a good conscience, with whose light they had been clothed. So it is a loss of the true light to use one's eyes in the service of darkness, and eyes fixed on earthly things are blinded to heavenly ones. But the soul is enlightened by that kind of blindness by which it looks down on the world in order to look upon God. Because, it says, "all that is in the world is the lust of the eyes," the apostle teaches that our sight should be veiled to this world and cleared of cloud for Christ, that is, for him who enlightens every man coming into this world, meaning the mind of every man who comes. So he urges us away from gazing at present things to looking up toward eternal ones, and says: "Do not seek the things that are in this world, for the form of this world is passing away"; and again: "Seek the things that are above, where Christ is at the right hand of the Father." For all things under the sun, as Ecclesiastes says, are vanity; it follows that above the sun is truth. So also those who stand in the truth, though they live within the world by their bodily dwelling, are nevertheless above the world by their heavenly way of life. With soaring spirit they climb up to the choirs of stars and the poles of the heavens and pass beyond them, and they live higher than the elements. They are not subject to the things and the uses of the elements, but with their life fixed in Christ they rise above the world, abiding in him who is God over all, blessed forever.

You see how the imitator of Christ carries us over from mortal things to God by his teaching and his example of virtue alike. He removes the veil from our heart, so that with unveiled face we may contemplate the glory of God, which is hidden from unbelievers by the veil of the law and uncovered for believers by the revelation of the gospel. So we no longer have any need of that fleshly hair. For "the old things," it says, "have passed away, and behold, now all things are new," since a light has risen in the darkness for the upright of heart, the Lord, merciful and compassionate and just. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. So long hair may have been an honour in the days when that spiritual veil of the law still had to be displayed in bodily appearance too. Now it is a burden, since the sun of eternal freedom has shone forth and Christ has become our head, to relieve us of the burden of bowed heads as well as of the yoke. That is why we now dare to cry out as free men with the voice of exultation and praise: "Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us." For now is the acceptable time, now is the day of salvation, since the truth is present no longer in the shadow of a cloud but in the light of its own body. And fittingly, for the time of grace and as a sign of freedom, the barber is at hand to relieve us of a longer covering of the head, so that our bodily form too may bear witness to the gift of spiritual grace, and the serenity of an uncovered brow may display the joy of inner freedom.

Apostolic authority has left long hair to women alone. For although the same faith removes the veil of the heart for them as for us, the grace of modesty still demands a covering for the head and a shade for the brow. That is why the perfect teacher of faith and discipline teaches that long hair is unbecoming to a man: the head of man, Christ, cannot be hidden, and he is also that city built on a mountain, in the Church, which is the body of Christ. So what is unseemly for a man is an adornment for a woman, who is head to no one. With the cultivation of modesty she adorns the man and, as though set at its foundation, supports the order of the body, which is woven together from God as the head of Christ, Christ as the head of man, and man as the head of woman. But through the fellowship of the body and the weaving together of its members, Christ makes her too a sharer in the supreme head, in whom we are neither male nor female. By all means let them have hair, with which, like the sinful woman in the gospel, they may wipe Christ's footsteps and be entwined about the feet of wisdom. So may they know nothing but to love wisdom, to embrace virtue, to kiss chastity, and, sprinkled with at least the last drops of the dew of the heavenly word, may they say: "For the dew that comes from you is healing to us." Let our women have as their hair the deeds of spiritual virtues: fasts, works of mercy, prayers. Such hair becomes a man as well. Let them be adorned by the grace of Christ, not by their hair; by the gem of chastity, not of stone; and let the ointment that is fragrant in them be that of good works, not of perfumes. Let them remember that they are daughters of that daughter of the King, all of whose glory is within. Let them understand why the apostle ordered them to be covered with a longer covering of the head: "because of the angels," he says, meaning those angels who are ready to seduce, whom the saints will judge. For these assail the weaker vessels more boldly, just as the serpent approached Eve and not Adam. That is also why women are forbidden to teach in church, lest with exalted spirit they dare to gaze upon the decrees of wisdom and, puffed up with knowledge, burst apart. Surely it serves to confound the wicked if they see a woman cover her understanding with silence under the appearance of ignorance, and confess the discipline of her mind by her modest dress. Then the serpent will not dare to approach her again to tempt her, since he despairs of capturing her.

It is not without reason that the apostle teaches that this must be done above all at the time when a woman prays or prophesies. For then she comes to conceive of the Spirit, and so it is then that she most arouses the envy of the tempter, when, aspiring to the perfect man, she passes beyond the bounds of her weakness. It is no wonder that the apostle thinks the same about prayer as about prophecy, since elsewhere he says that we pray by the Spirit: "For when we pray," he says, "we do not know how we ought to ask, but the Spirit himself teaches us." Since, then, a spiritual conception also takes place in prayer, the apostle wishes that no trick or snare of the enemy, as Scripture says, should confront a woman acting beyond the limits of her frail vessel. So he wants her dress to show that she has authority over her head, by which she is both ruled and defended. That very humility of heart gives her strength, by which she curbs the pride of knowledge with the rudder of discipline, and prefers to fear rather than to be high-minded, safer silent through the fear of faith than learned in speech. Yet she would cover her forehead with hair in vain unless she also veiled it with modesty.

Therefore let all of us together, every soul, strive to be adorned with those hairs which God counts, as he himself says: "Even the hairs of your head are all numbered." And whose hairs would he more readily deign to number than those of the one whose crowning head he himself is? Of him it is said: "His head is like gold of Cephas." By this name I think some purer and more tested gold is meant, like that gold of the land of Havilah. For this gold is the figure of the saints, who shine like lights in the head of the body and are gold refined by fire for God. For he tried them by the ordeals of suffering, melted down in the furnace of this world, and, as Scripture says, found them worthy of himself. On them he struck the sacred coinage of his own image, stamping the word of his truth on their hearts and tongues, and he made these same men his moneyers, so that they might mint for the Lord coins of proven worth after his likeness, and, once the figure of Caesar had been effaced from us, might stamp us with the living coin of the eternal King. Thus, inscribed with the Spirit of redemption, our necks now free of the yoke and our foreheads guarded by the title of salvation, we might sing: "The light of your countenance, O Lord, is sealed upon us."

Let us strive, then, with all our strength so to prepare ourselves that we may be worthy to be the hair and the gold of the divine Head, which for us, by the grace of God, is Christ. For from that Head springs the hair of which it is written: "His hair is like flocks of goats." And Christ's flocks are rightly signified by the name of those animals whose chief use lies in their milk, because everyone who believes Christ to be God embraces with the faith of devotion the whole fullness of the Trinity in him whom the Father anointed with the Holy Spirit. And so the very mother of all the living, the Church, the body of Christ, overflows with the sap of devotion, and her breasts are better than wine. In this I think it is signified that the freedom of grace in the milk of mercy is sweeter than the severity of the law in the wine of justice. "For the letter," he says, "kills"—there you see the neat wine of judgment; "but the Spirit gives life"—there you see the gift of the breasts and the work of milk. But let this be referred, as you prefer to understand it, to the seed by which the first milk of the newborn takes shape. Good, then, are the breasts which the good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, milked for those infants out of whose mouth he perfected praise for himself, to destroy the enemy of good and the defender of evil.

From the flocks of these goats came that "lord of the flock" who nursed the little ones of Christ, not yet ready for solid food, with tender nourishment, and said to them: "I gave you milk to drink, not meat; for you were not yet able, and even now you are not able." But when we have grown on the nourishment of this milk, our steps first made firm by conceiving faith, we shall grow up into the strength of youth; and with our endurance confirmed through faith and love, we shall lift up our hands to more vigorous action and live on the works of virtue as on stronger food. So we may become those locks of which it is written: "His locks are fir trees, black as a corax," that is, a raven. But this is a good raven: not the one that forgot to return to the ark, but the one that remembered to feed the prophet. To him are fittingly compared the locks that rival those fir trees of which it says: "Good and black fir trees, bringing the ships of Tarshish." So this corax is now a raven not of night but of light, and the hair made beautiful by its color is therefore the saints, a royal and priestly race, with whom he empurples the divine Head as with the purple of his glory; for youthful grace too clothes the flower of life above all in hair of this color.

We must not hide, however, that in the Scriptures this bird is sometimes found as a figure of sin and sometimes as an image of grace. It seems deadly when it is brought forward for the punishment of the wicked, since, as it is written, God sends evils through evil angels; or when it is said in vengeance for a curse: "The eye that mocks father and mother, let the ravens of the valleys pluck it out." Yet the same bird is praiseworthy when it feeds the prophet with bread in the morning and meat in the evening, or when the young ravens call upon the name of the Lord. Its color, too, is applied sometimes to the saints and sometimes to the wicked. For the bride of Christ says that she is dark and comely, and the Lord made darkness his hiding place; and again, on the other hand, the apostle warns us not to let darkness overtake us. Yet those black and good fir trees bringing the ships of Tarshish are shaped after the likeness of her who is both dark and comely.
