For the saints are her members: as they are flourishing palms and multiplying cedars, so they are also black and good fir trees, because in the Church, that is, on the mountain of God, they stand out with the lofty crowns of their merits, like fir trees on their mountains. And just as those trees are fit for building ships, so those princes of the people, hewn from the mountain of the law as from Lebanon, shaped the nations by the word of God and built from them the ark of the Lord, or the ship, that is, the Church, which was to sail through the floods of this world; and they taught her, joined into a frame of love bound tight by faith, to cut through the waves of this world without decay.

And now too, souls trained in the apostolic faith are black and good fir trees: black no longer, I think, from sin, but rather still darkened either by their dwelling in the body or by the battle dust, so to speak, of inner discipline, or by its dusty sweat; yet good because of their spiritual way of life even in the night of their bodies. So too they are ships that float upon the waves of the world, armed, as it is written, on the right and on the left with the faith of truth and the work of justice as with oars. They are steered by the word of God as by a rudder; they spread the folds of their minds to the breeze of the Holy Spirit and bind the sail of their hearts to the yard of the cross with the bonds of love as with ropes. Their mast is the rod from the root of Jesse, which governs the whole quadrireme of our body. If, as in that poetic fable, but in prophetic truth, we are bound to this mast, tied by willing knots, with ears stopped not with wax but with faith, and not the ears of the body but of the heart, then we sail safe and unharmed past the rocks of pleasure, like the crags of the Sirens, past the allurements of this world, varied in their ways of catching us but alike in doing harm. Let us be bound to this mast with the strongest rope, tied fast in hope, faith and love, believing in our hearts and confessing with our mouths the undivided Trinity, which is the threefold cord that is not broken. With this cord let our works also be woven, so that by it, as by the rope of our faith, the mast may be raised, the yard of love, and the sails of our life may billow; that we may be those fir trees which, bound together in great rafts, were brought from Tarshish for the building of the temple, or likewise ships that rival the one which once brought Solomon choice gold and the riches of Tyre. And our trading must be carried on with all the more zeal and gain, the more our eternal King Jesus surpasses that temporal Solomon. "For behold," he says, "something greater than Solomon is here," who will not shatter us with a violent wind among the ships of Tarshish if, by the good conduct of our life, we bring him profit, the most precious merchandise to God, so that he may receive from us his own price; for he himself is the pearl, and the whole business of this spiritual trade strives to acquire it. If our means suffice to buy it, we shall carry a cargo that does not weigh us down but lifts us up across this great and wide sea. And the Lord who sleeps in us because of our sluggishness—if we are worthy to carry him even asleep—we shall dare to wake, so that, rebuking the winds of hostile spirits or even of our own senses, he may save us from faintness of heart and from the storm, and may calm the seas for us as we make for his stillness; so that he may bring us like ships laden with his riches into the harbor of salvation, and joyfully set green garlands on our sterns, victorious over the waves.

Let us also be the right hand of him who is all right hand, having no left hand in our actions, so that we may be worthy to stand at the right hand of the Judge, or rather to be the very right hand of the Judge; and that on the day of recompense the Lord who rewards may count our works like the hairs of his own head, as he has already foretold in the gospel. These works are to be proclaimed at the judgment, when with divine blessing and royal bestowal he will reward the merits of spiritual virtues, that is, the most beautiful locks of his head. With such locks that woman, a type of the Church, wiped Christ's feet as she bathed them with ointment and tears. She pleased him not so much by the price of her gifts as by the devotion of her service. For the Lord loved in her not the ointment but the love by which, modestly shameless and devoutly bold, without fear of reproach or rebuff, she made her way uninvited into the Pharisee's house, a stranger to her, forcing her way with that violence by which the kingdom of heaven is seized. Hungering only for the heavenly word, she ran not to his riches but to the feet of Christ; there she washed and fed herself, and made those very feet her sanctuary, so to speak, and her altar. On them she poured her libation of tears, made her offering of ointment, and sacrificed her love. For a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; and by offering it to God she won not only forgiveness of her sins but also the glory of having her name proclaimed together with the gospel.

And because she prefigured the Church that was to be called from the Gentiles, she bore in herself all the signs of the saving mystery. She was anointed with the chrism of her own gift; she had the tears of repentance for her washing, the depths of her love for her sacrifice; she received beforehand with hands and mouth the living and life-giving Bread itself; and she tasted in advance with her eager kisses the blood of the cup before it became the cup of the blood. Blessed is she who tasted Christ in the flesh and received the body of Christ in his very body! Rightly was she preferred to the Pharisee, though he fed Christ; for while the Jew feasted she served fasting, hungry, as I said, not for food but for salvation. Blessed is she who was found worthy to be figured in this way too as a type of the Church, so that in the house and at the banquet of the Pharisee it was not the Pharisee himself but the sinful woman who was justified unto pardon. Her persistence counted for more. For the order of the mystery ordained from the ages required, according to that prophetic blessing of father Noah, that the dwelling of Japheth should pass into the tents of Shem: that is, that in the house of the law and the prophets it was rather the Church that should be justified, younger in age but greater by the law of grace. Hence, in the person of John, the law itself [?] declares: "He who comes after me has been set before me, because he was before me."

Now so that the Church might match her Head even in figure, she fittingly took the form of a sinful woman, because Christ too took the form of a sinner. But the Jew, who was to have neither head nor foundation in Christ, had anointed neither Christ's head nor his feet, both of which the woman of the gospel had bathed with precious ointments. Therefore the synagogue has from Christ neither the oil of grace nor the water of refreshment; for that Pharisee, who bore its type, both the water and the oil of love dried up, even beside the very fount of saving oil and water. Of this fount he had foretold through the prophet: "Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head," just as he could say to his Church: "You have anointed my head with oil." She had brought an ointment precious not only in its making but also in its vessel, fragrant with the blended grace and virtue of many herbs and flowers. Who but the Church could make such an ointment? From the various flowers and juices of heavenly graces she breathes out to God fragrant sweetnesses of many kinds from different nations, and by the Spirit of truth she exhales the prayers of the saints like spices burning in glowing bowls. So the Bridegroom himself, as she comes to him flowing with the scents of such flowers and the dews of such liquids, rejoices over her in the words with which he caresses her in the Song of Songs: "My dove," he says, "my perfect one, for my head is filled with dew"—the head of Christ is God, and his locks are the chosen saints, in whom the Father rejoices in Christ—"and my locks with the drops of the night." Dew, as we know, is not the moisture of rain but of refreshment, by which the grass parched by the day's heat is revived. The earth is sprinkled with the bright drops of this dew only on a clear night. Hence we are given to understand that those drops of the night, with which Wisdom rejoices that his head and locks are wet, are a figure of the saints, whom the apostle also describes as shining like stars, which likewise glitter on clear nights when the dews fall. And what night should be understood in the spiritual sense, if not the Lord's passion, which also lit up the day? Of it, I think, it is written: "And the night is my light in my delights." But you may also take this age as night: once bristling with the darkness of the Gentiles before their faith, it has been cleared, as of clouds, by their conversion. And now, in the light of the Church, as in the full mirror of the perfect moon, and in holy men, as in stars pure in a cloudless sky, the works of the faithful—by which each one gives life to his own soul and refreshes it from the thirst of its former drought—fall like dew, as we said, in this night of the world.

And so Christ rejoices that his head is filled with such dew, and though he is the one who lights up our nights, he is glad that his locks are drenched with the drops of our night, because his refreshment and restoration is that work of the faithful by which brothers are helped or the poor are comforted. That is why he spurned the voice of Judas, who, having taken the devil's spirit into his heart, begrudged the woman's ointment on Christ's feet. For by works of devotion and mercy Christ is anointed, is lent to, and is fed. But the traitor, before he betrayed the Lord, betrayed his own faithlessness. It was not care for the poor that moved him but care for his thefts and the spite of a faithless mind, so that, judging that ointment—precious though it was, yet utterly cheap compared with the Lord's blood—to be more precious than the saving body, he grew indignant at the woman in her devout extravagance. Yet the Lord himself testifies that she had done a good work for him, teaching that care for the needy is to be put second, but only to himself; and so he showed that Judas, with a perverse heart, had put mercy before faith, although faith is the kindling of works and he who gives the commands comes before his commands. Besides, in this too the son of perdition showed how cheaply he held Christ, saying that the ointment poured over Christ was wasted. And therefore he has no share in the price of Christ's blood, because he cannot have as Redeemer the one he chose to have as merchandise; and rightly is this dealer in death shut out from the trade of life, condemned by his own judgment, by which he sold for thirty gold pieces the one whom the woman anointed with three hundred, as he himself had valued it. But he was perverse in this, that holding the Lord himself cheap, he valued dearly that ointment which was being poured out in advance for his burial, which brings us salvation. Truly like the devil, ignorant of the grace of God in which he was to have no share, he valued highly, not from love but from envy, the price of that death by which he who bought us at a great price, and does not sell us, saves us freely. For he wishes to make us precious by the cheapness of his gift. And he is the more precious to us for this kindness, that he wishes to be valued cheaply, so that he may be bought by all. "For," it says, "he himself made the poor and the rich, and he cares equally for all." Hence he says: "Freely you have received grace; freely give." Rich in the free wealth of this grace, Peter, who had no money, enriched with health the crippled poor man who wanted nothing more than a beggar's alms.

So let us be empty of greed for gold, that we may abound in grace, and by becoming cheap to this world through voluntary poverty, let us become an ointment precious to the Lord. For we shall breathe forth to God the good fragrance of Christ if, carrying about the death of Christ in our body and showing forth his life in our spirit, we are fragrant with the scent of the Lord's passion and resurrection. And we pour ointment on the body of Christ if we devote our substance and our life to faith in his truth and obedience to his command. Then shall we, in his body, be ointments that fill the whole house with fragrance, if with perfect love we can at some time say: "But the world has been crucified to me"—to me who love not riches, not the honors of the world, not what is my own but what is Christ's, not what is seen but what is unseen. These will be locks for us, for strength and holy service, with which we may wipe Christ's feet and break the cords of sin, and rejoice in the spirit of freedom, saying: "You have broken my bonds; to you I will offer the sacrifice of praise."

But while there is room to run, while there is time to serve, let us grow hair of this kind, and let us imitate not only the love of that sinful woman in the gospel, so that by great love we may wash away great debts, but also her persistence, so that we may snatch salvation from the wrath that hangs over us. In season and out of season, seeking the bread of life, let us knock even at night at the door of the householder. "For in the nights," it says, "lift up your hands to the holy place." Wearing out, as we are commanded, the threshold of every man who is wise in Christ, let us seek the food of life everywhere, let us hunt for the word of God wherever it may be; let us hang on the lips of all the faithful, for the Spirit of God breathes in every believer. And surely even from the least servant of God some drop of heavenly wisdom must fall, to water the dryness of my heart and to overflow for me, as a wholesome drink, beyond the rivers of the wise of this world; for I would rather speak five words in the law than many thousands in a tongue, just as I would rather live one day in the courts of the Lord than thousands in the tents of sinners, since the Spirit breathes where he wills, and I hear his voice but do not know where it comes from. Wherever, then, I can, I will catch his breeze; from wherever I can, I will gather even his faintest breath. If I hear that the Just One has come even into the house of an unworthy man, even of a Pharisee, I will strive to snatch away the host's grace, to snatch, if I can, the kingdom of heaven. Wherever the name of Christ rings out for me, I will run there; into whosever inner house I learn that he [?] has entered, I too will hurry. When I find Wisdom, when I find Justice reclining in someone's inner rooms, I will run to Christ's feet, to be marked by even the last footprint of Wisdom. Nor will I scorn his feet; rather, I will pray that Christ may touch my head even with his feet. That woman touched the hem of his garment and was healed; others were healed even by the shadow of an apostle's body as it passed.

Let us spread out our hair before him, that is, let us lay down before him all the honors of our distinctions, and let us cast ourselves down from ourselves, so that we may be raised up by him who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly. Let us confess our sins with tears, so that that heavenly Justice may say of us too: "She has bathed my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair." Perhaps the reason he did not wash his own feet when he washed those of the disciples was so that we should wash them with our tears. No small merit has that soul of which Wisdom can say: "From the time she came in, she has not ceased to kiss my feet." What is this kiss but the eternal pledge of that love which covers a multitude of sins? These kisses the Church was already preparing for her Bridegroom when she sang: "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth." This privilege Catholic love alone rightly claims for herself, she who, the one and perfect bride of one husband, asks from the mouth of the Word himself the kisses of truth, so that she may not be defiled by the poison of heretical deceit, as by the kisses of a strange and unchaste mouth.

Let us, then, press chaste kisses on Christ's feet, so that we may be worthy to rise from the feet to the head, and, growing up toward the higher members of the body, may now dare from close by to ask for kisses of his face and mouth. And when, sipping the word of God with a pure heart, we have tasted how sweet the Lord is, then let our soul, set on fire in its inmost depths with love of Wisdom, be refreshed by that sweet burning, and, pierced by the fiery arrows of the Lord's love, by which every other delight of hostile pleasures is slain, let it say with a contrite heart: "For I am wounded with love." Blessed indeed is he who can anoint Christ's feet even with a kiss. Who will burn my mouth, wretch that I am, and cleanse my tongue with that heavenly coal, so that I may be worthy to touch even Christ's heel with the very edge of my lips, and with bowed head to wipe his holy soles—so that my head might rather be wiped by Christ's feet, and, while I lick those divine feet, I might cleanse my unclean lips by those chaste footprints?

So let us urge one another on, and say to each other as though in a contest: Come, let us worship and weep before the Lord who made us. Weeping before him we shall sow our joys; anointing his footprints we shall heal our wounds. Whatever we spend on Christ, we really bestow on ourselves. That woman, by pouring ointment over Christ, washed herself; by wiping his feet she cleansed her own sins; by loving him she loved herself. And so she was worthy to hear: Daughter, your faith has saved you. The man who was one of the sons of the kingdom was not worthy to hear this, and she was justified more by her service than he by his banquet. For the Pharisee had not believed, and she did believe. He said: If this man were a prophet, he would surely know what sort of woman this is who touches him. So he was not justified by the banquet to which he had invited Christ as a mere man. Perhaps he even held it to Christ's account, since for our sake Christ was poor, that he, a rich man, had thought so highly of a poor man as to take him in to his feast. But she would not have hoped for the forgiveness of her sins through such an outlay of service, expense and tears unless she had believed that God was in Christ. And so, though only at the farthest footprint of the Saviour, she found the head of her salvation.

Where will you boast now, wretched Jew? In your own house our sinful woman has gone ahead of you, entering into your labours. You feasted so as to be proud; she fasted so as to serve. The water you refused to pour from your jugs she supplied from her eyes. You did not wipe Christ's feet even with a towel; she wiped them with her hair. The feet you, unworthy man, would not even touch with your hands, she did not cease to caress with kisses. Surely it was rather you who owed this service to a guest received in your house, if you had kept the law of hospitality at least by the example of the fathers. But for you it is enough, to feed your pride, to boast of father Abraham. And so she went ahead of you, for by her faithful love she proved herself rather the daughter of your father. From him this very inhumanity shows you to be degenerate, since you disdained to wash the Lord's feet, when Abraham washed the feet of angels and the Lord himself washed the feet of his servants. Indeed, even then the father of faith washed the feet of Christ too, whom he saw with prophetic eyes as one of the three and worshipped. And so Christ himself rebukes you with his own mouth, in person: If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. And he added: He saw my day and rejoiced. But he also blessed those who had not seen, yet believed together with those who saw. From this it is plain that faith has been gained by us, while for you only the nature of unbelief remains.

So let them keep their arrogance to themselves, and their riches, their nobility and their own righteousness, those who glory in Abraham as their father by the body rather than by the spirit, uncircumcised in heart and Jews only in the flesh. For us Christ is enough, both for salvation and for glory, and him crucified. He raised us up from stones to be children of Abraham, while they, on the contrary, from being children of Abraham are hardening into the stones from which we came. For us Ephraim, the left-hand son blessed with the right hand, brings profit. Them he marked in Manasseh, who by the presumption of the elder had stood at his grandfather's right, when the left hand was moved across onto his head in the mystery of the cross. For the cross, a stumbling block to the Jews and the future glory of Christians, was to make him left instead of right and me right instead of left. As the Jews slip into our deserts and we move into their sown fields, they are by blindness what we were, and we are by grace what they were. But we shall not rejoice in our salvation in such a way as to exult in your ruin. For we have been taught by one who was a brother of your body but is the master of our spirit not to insult the broken branches, since we ourselves were grafted into the tree of your stock not by works but by the gifts of God's mercies. And the Lord of all, though he is the Father of Christians, that is, the God of the faithful, is able to graft you back into the native folds of your bark and replant you in your own soil. It is he who has filled our marrow with the sap of your richness through the gift of adoption, so that one root may sustain both, bearing fruit together for the Lord.

Meanwhile I prefer the riches of our poor sinful woman, in tears and love, to yours, in impiety and the letter; her fasting to your banquet. I would rather be bound to Christ's feet among her hair than recline with you among your dishes, beside Christ yet without Christ. If I have no ointment now for Christ's feet, I shall have no oil for my torches at his coming. And woe to me if my ointment is cheap. Precious ointment is needed, so that I may be worthy to be buried with him in his burial, for unless I die with him in his death, I shall not live in his resurrection. So let us love him whom it is our duty to love. Let us kiss him whom it is chastity to kiss. Let us be joined to him whom it is virginity to marry. Let us submit to him, beneath whom to lie is to stand above the world. Let us be cast down for his sake, for whom to fall is to rise again. Let us die with him in whom is life.

And how could we worthily repay this Lord, in whom even in death we live, and who in turn deigns to be to us whatever we, his lowly servants, have been to him? He so mingles himself with us and joins us to himself that what he receives he makes profitable to us, and what is given to us, that is, to his least ones, he counts as received by himself. So, drawing his own into his honour, he has shared almost everything with us, even his names. As he is called the power of God, so he deigns to be power for us too: for God is our refuge and strength. He is an inheritance: as we are his, so he is ours. For as you have in Moses: His people Jacob became the Lord's portion, so in the Psalms you have: The Lord is my portion. And as he says of himself: I am the light of this world, so he said to his own: You are the light of this world. I am, he says, the living bread; and we all are one bread. I am the true vine; and to you he says: I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly true. Christ is the mountain of God, the mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell, and his saints are mountains of God, fertile mountains, from which the Wonderful One gives us light from the everlasting mountains. Christ is the rock: for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. Even to his disciple he did not deny the grace of this name, saying to him: On this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

But why should we be surprised that he has granted his names to his servants, when he shares even his Father and his kingdom with them? For he gave those who receive him power to become children of God, and, as far as it lies with him, he said to all people: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. But we, through the guilt of our own wills, die like men and fall like one of the princes. For the devil was one of the princes of the angels before he fell, cast down, and became the devil; and to him it is said: How has Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning? Yet we are not condemned to everlasting destruction as he is. He was the author of sin, and he will be punished both for himself and for man, perishing by the same crime by which he brought ruin. But man did not deserve to be banished from paradise and to be earth for ever, because divine justice judged more leniently one who sinned through another's design than through his own. It is more criminal to deceive than to be deceived, and to devise a sin than to commit it. So the one who consented to the fraud was punished for a time and for his correction, but the inventor of death was destined for eternal punishment. The penalty of sin will never fail him, because he never stops sinning. So it was not an angel, not an envoy, as it is written, but the Lord himself who came to raise up the crushed, to free the fettered and to save what was lost. And to confound our deceiver by a deception, as it were, in return, the only-begotten Son of God deigned, through the mystery of his love, to take on the very nature of our frailty. So the devil would be conquered by means of the very nature he had deceived, and he who was always under God's power and laws would be made subject to man as well.

What, then, shall we render to him for all that he has rendered to us? He did render, but as a good Lord he rendered good for evil, though we had heaped evil on him in return for good. He blessed, and we cursed. He healed, and we blasphemed. He justified the ungodly, and was counted among the wicked. What, then, shall I give him back for my evils which he bore, and for his good things which he bestowed? What for the flesh he took on? What for the blows? What for the insults? What for the scourges? What shall I repay for the cross, the death, the burial? Suppose we return cross for cross and death for death: could we ever repay the fact that from him and through him and in him we have all things, and that we who have them exist at all? For he made us, and not we ourselves, and our soul is always in his hands. So let us return love for our debt, charity for his gift, gratitude for money. For woe to us if we do not love.

But when could I, poor and needy, hope to repay this Lord, when not even the apostles claim to have repaid him? Hear one of them admitting that he has not repaid, when he says: Who has given to him first, so that he should be repaid? But thanks be to him, who remits the interest on so great a loan and grants us a settlement of an immense debt, asking back from us only our love for him. By putting this first among his commandments, he showed how even we who are destitute could pay an unpayable debt. So let no one excuse himself on the grounds that paying is difficult, for no one can say that he has no heart. Not sacrifices, not costly gifts, not hard labours are demanded of us. We have within us the means to pay, for our love is something within our own power. Let us spend it on the Lord, and we have paid. So David, delivered from the hand of all his enemies, paid for the full security of his safety not with the riches of his kingdom but with those of his heart, saying: I will love you, Lord, my strength.

I add, further, that he who is our creditor will become our debtor if we pay him the price of his goodness, which he grants us though it is not owed, by loving him with the free payment of our hearts. And he is loved in ourselves too. For he himself said that this would be the sign of his disciples: if they loved one another with the love with which he loved us, that is, if we have one heart and one soul in Christ, and each of us does to his neighbour what he would wish done to himself. All the more, then, do we glory in the Lord in our love for you, which alone enables us to pay God, in some measure at least, even one of our great and countless debts. For in all other good things we confess that we are scarcely even beginners, and in only a few of them; but in our love for you alone we profess to be perfect.
24. Paulinus and Therasia, sinners, to their brother Severus.

I still have something more to say to you, even though you receive my letters into storerooms left unlocked and, as you yourself admit, do all you can to proclaim them from the housetops. But if you bring out this complaint, which we are now about to lodge with you against you, along with the other foolish things our talkativeness has produced, you will at the same time make public your own rashness. That rashness is what we are complaining about in this letter, and the end of the previous letter, with its word about love and perfection, prompted us to make it the beginning of this one. Our reason for remonstrating with you comes from the excessive affection of the oneness of heart between us: your great love draws you even into the sin of lying. Whether I consider what you say about yourself or what you say about us, heaping up our burdens with unjust praise and lightening yours with false reproaches, I would charge you with sinning against love out of love. For "love," it says, "is kind; love does no evil to a neighbor." That you show it to be kind toward us we know by experience, and indeed we glory in it. But take care that you do not seem to break its rule and do evil to your neighbors, piling the weight of undeserved praise onto their load of sins. And since you seem not to wish for us what you wish for yourself, if you really think it right to speak of us in a way you judge would do you no good if it were said of you, you will rightly hear: "If you love rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned." Unless perhaps you do this too by some deeper plan of devotion: by indulging us in words with good qualities that are not ours, you may prick us with the goad of shame. Then, reading what we ought to be, we may learn to be good and strive to show ourselves as your words describe us, and perhaps we may be made what we are not, while we blush not to be what we are said to be. Meanwhile, however, as long as our conscience does not recognize the truth of your words, our modesty spurns the flattery. Let this modesty, as I said, confront you within yourself. Why do you dare to award us the palm of perfection, as if we were victors with the contest already fought, because we seem to have laid aside every burden of earthly possession? And why, on the other hand, do you lament that you are still unhappy and stuck in the mire of hell's dregs, because, as you wrote, you seem not to have sold even one little estate? In fact you have removed it from your present ownership just as if it had been sold, so that you might stand doubly devoted to God with greater fruits of faith. By a different kind of trading but with the one gain of life, within the bounds of the same command, you are both a seller and a giver of estates, and so you are an owner without captivity of soul, since what you have kept back is possessed by the church, and you are its servant.

So weigh our circumstances and yours alike by the words of the Lord himself, so that you neither despair of yourself as still entangled nor congratulate us as already free. There are different kinds of gifts and measures of endowments, which one and the same God, their dispenser, works as in the members of his own body. He distinguishes the different members of his body with gifts as he pleases, yet out of the variety of members he builds one body for himself, so that in this way too the grace of the sacred body may be increased when manifold virtue is counted within one framework, and so that the queen may stand at his right hand in golden fringes, clothed in many colors. See now how much God has given you within her. He has granted you a share in the lot of those who lived perfect lives under the law, possessing things in such a way that they were not possessed by their possessions, and setting no love of property or of family above love of the Lord and his discipline, as Job, Abraham and Lot show. But you are also a sharer with those whom the fullness of the gospel brings to completion, since you have sold estates of greater wealth and allure.

So I trust that rest awaits you equally in the midst of the divine lots, so that you may sleep, as it is written, "among the clergy," that is, among the lots of the Lord, which are understood as the two Testaments; from them the Lord's inheritance and the fullness of the saints are made complete. I am ready, then, to turn the Lord's word against you the other way round and say to you: You see the speck of grace in your brother's eye and do not notice the great mass of the same good in your own. For, as I said, you have taken hold of both portions of the saints: you are no possessor in the estates you have kept, and you are perfect in those you have sold. And so even where you seem to be a possessor, you are perfect, because your mind has been freed from the chains of possessions. Mindful that the time has grown short, you fulfill that saying of the apostle, to have as though not having, because what you have, you have not for yourself but for those who have nothing. You are a guest in your own house, so that your house may be a guesthouse. You are a stranger in your homeland and a sojourner [?] in this world, so that you may be a dweller in paradise and a citizen of the ancient homeland. You do not fill your rooms with dining couches or cram them with heaps of furniture or money. Instead you fill them with strangers and the needy, and mark out a single corner for yourself. A fellow servant of your own household slaves, you do not claim the temporary lodging under your roof as its master, but stay on as a hired hand or a tenant, paying the Lord the rent, as it were, for a dwelling held at his pleasure, through the joint service of your body and soul.

But if the reward is to be enlarged or reduced according to the measure of the work, and a balance is to be struck between what has been done and what has not, the perfection of your mind will be fairly reckoned against the work of those who sold everything. For you have kept nothing for yourself either in legal title or, what matters more, in your heart, since you use the world as though not using it. Indeed, I rather think that this constancy and firmness of your heart should be judged a stronger faith. Among fires you are not burned, among snares you are not caught, you touch pitch and are not defiled. Those whom you think strong I consider should be judged weaker, because, not trusting their own weakness, they hurried to get rid of everything they were afraid of clinging to. You, then, are free among the dead. Though you hold earthly property, you are no longer earth, and you rise above the earth. You are not polluted by contact with carcasses, nor do you live in the tombs of the cast-out sleepers, because you have buried your life in heaven, having hidden it in Christ. As for us, let us not bear the envy that perfection attracts, but rather receive pardon for our weakness. For you cannot deny that it takes more courage to do without things that are still there than things given away, and to scorn what you have than not to have what you scorn.

Indeed, consider the very words of the Lord on which you base your claim that we are perfect, and you will see that you have taken the beginning for the end. "If you wish to be perfect," he says, "go and sell all you have and give to the poor." If he had ended the sentence there, I would be wrong to reproach you. I would even go further and ask you, as a soul close to mine through likeness of purpose, to congratulate me, because we would already be holding in our hands the palm of a finished contest, like that tenth drachma, I mean, which was lost in the first father of our flesh but was at last found within the house once the lamp of the saving word was lit. But you can see how weighty a saying remains, since the Lord of majesty himself adds: "and come, follow me." Consider rather that difficulty and measure it with an enlarged heart. Then you will understand that you have more reason to be anxious for us than to congratulate us. For our goods, or rather the burdens laid on us, fell away easily when we let go of our cloak. What we had not brought with us into this world and could not carry out with us we gave back as though it had been borrowed. We did not tear it away like skin from flesh, but laid it aside like a garment from the body.

Now we must pay to God what is truly ours: that is, we must present our heart, soul and bodies to the Lord as a living sacrifice, as it is written, and build ourselves into a holy temple for him upon the cornerstone himself, who gave us in his own person the pattern of our sanctification and said: "Be holy, for I am holy." What credit, then, is due to us if we have been faithful only in what belongs to another, unless we also serve from what is our own, that is, from the free choice of our will, loving God with our whole heart and, as it is written, with the whole inmost being of our soul? The prophet stirs us to this affection when he says: "I will sacrifice to you freely." For this is acceptable and pleasing before God, that our goodness be voluntary, and by it we may recover what is ours, namely the home of paradise and the eternal life for which we were created. If we recover it, cleansed of the possession of this earth into which we fell by condemnation, then truly, like people restored from exile to their homeland or brought back from a long journey abroad to the house where they were born, we shall be able to say: "The Lord is our portion in the land of the living."

So giving up or selling the temporal goods we hold in this world is not the running of the race but the entry into it; it is not the finishing post but the starting gate. An athlete does not win when he strips; he strips in order to begin the fight, and he will be crowned only when he has competed according to the rules. Likewise a swimmer who has to cross a river in his path takes off his clothes. Yet for all that preparation of undressing he will not swim across unless, with the effort of his whole body and the skilled movement of all his limbs, the kick of his feet, the oaring of his arms and the gliding of his side, he cuts through the force of the current and sees the labor of swimming through to the end.

Yet I see that the order of this campaign was rehearsed for us in the blessed patriarch Jacob too. I read that after crossing the torrent and sending ahead the burdens of his cares, that is, the encumbrances of his material wealth and his family, he remained alone at the place of his tent and wrestled with God; he prevailed and wrung a blessing from him, and received the name Israel, hallowed in heaven and on earth. Admittedly, this seems first and foremost to prefigure the mystery of salvation: in the figure of the Jews, that is, of the offspring of his body, Jacob prevailed over the Lord, just as that people prevailed in wringing the Lord's passion from Pilate. As it is written, they said, "Crucify him, crucify him," and "their voices," it says, "prevailed." Nevertheless, for the purpose of our present discussion the story may fairly be used insofar as it gives an image of the gospel command. By that example we may understand that we cannot be fit to grapple with God, and we certainly do grapple with him when we strive to fulfill his word and try to prevail in attaining divine virtues by imitating him. And so we cannot be fit to seize the way of life, to lay hold of God's word and to prevail into the kingdom of heaven, which since the days of John has suffered violence from those who snatch at it, unless before the evening of our death we send ahead everything that clings to us on the journey of this world, through love or through care, and hinders and slows us. Then through the whole night of this world we must wrestle to grasp and hold Christ with anxious effort in spiritual works and pursuits, and not be torn away from the love of Christ, as Jacob would not be torn from his embrace, until we wring out the blessing. Would that he might strike the sinew of our thigh with fear of his majesty, as a mark of this saving wrestling match, so that when it is numbed the strength of the flesh may grow weak and spiritual grace grow strong! In Jacob, however, the sinew of the stricken thigh withered as a type of Jewish barrenness and depravity. It pointed to that part of his descendants which fell away from the faith of the fathers and ceased to bear fruit for God. From this you learn that it was weakened in its fruitfulness in children and, straying from the commandments of its maker, limped along the paths of its own error.

Nonetheless we too must take care not to appear barren in the Lord's sight or to limp on a feeble foot along his way. Rather, being unfruitful in bodily offspring, let us turn that numbness of our father's thigh, struck by the divine hand, into the firmness of continence, so that, made strengthless toward the desires that hamstring the strength of faith, we may strengthen the soul with chastity. The apostle teaches this chastity, and even athletes of the flesh guard it carefully. All the more eagerly, then, must we keep it as we wrestle for that unfading crown, since even those who compete for a temporal and perishable crown cultivate it. Therefore, as we are about to fight before the Lord in the theater of this world, watched by men and angels, let us strip off works that oppose us, so that we may be clothed in healing [?] works. This is exactly what he who says "Follow me" wants us to prepare for, so that we may lay hold of him in whom we have been laid hold of by him. He calls us to the place where he sits at God's right hand in the glory of the Father, and says to all: "Come to me, you who are burdened and toil, and you will find rest for your souls." For he who made all people wants every human being, as far as it rests with him, to be saved. That is why he came down to us, so that we might go up to him. He was conformed to the body of our flesh, which was enslaved to sin, in order to conform us to the body of his flesh, which committed no sin, so that we may truly be restored to our original glory if we take on the divine likeness by imitating Christ. That only the image remained to us in Adam is shown by Genesis itself, which tells of the craftsmanship of the divine hand. There the likeness is named together with the image of God while the making of man is still being planned. But in the following chapter, where man, now made, is said to be only in the image of God, Genesis shows that the likeness was withdrawn from him as one who was going to sin. This was surely because God foreknew the future, and the likeness was to be kept in store for humanity in Christ, who through the obedience of his devotion reconciled to the Father the world that the disobedience of our first parent had estranged. And so the likeness of God, which the servant lost when he was puffed up with desire to be equal with his Lord, was recovered by the Lord himself when he emptied himself into the form of a servant. Man, who had fallen in his pride through the devil's deceit, rose again through faith in the humility of the Lord, when the devil was laid low by the humbling of the Most High Lord. So it was he who suffered for us and for our sake became obedient even to death on a cross, and he set before us the way of life and the perfection of virtue, not only in selling estates and giving away the proceeds, but in following him. And because he had said, "When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself," he therefore says: "Come, follow me." Blessed is the one who follows so close behind that he can say: "My soul has clung close behind you." Only that love can say this which is the end of the commandment and the fulfillment of the law, that is, the love which, from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith, so implants and fastens itself in God that, loving nothing outside God, it says: "And I am always with you." Therefore all our labor and our whole task lies in guarding our heart and stripping it bare. We cannot see its darkness, or the enemy's hidden lairs within it, unless the mind has been cleansed of the cares of external things and turned inward on itself. Not for nothing was it said: "Guard your heart with all vigilance."

I believe you have already learned by experience how laborious, constant and indeed daily our struggle with this enemy is, how many traps are laid in it, how strong the vices are there and how weak the virtues, how readily the heart slides back into wickedness and how sluggishly it strives toward God. Now the conflict of a different law, which was formerly shut up within me, lies open before me. Now I feel the force of the opposing law, which, as though laying hands on me, strives to drag me captive into the law of sin. And I recognize that the blessed apostle burns rather with my unhappiness and, grieving for me out of my own condition, cries: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" But the same teacher revives and refreshes me, showing me the way out to salvation, if only the will is there in me, so that I may be worthy to find perfection by the grace of God through Jesus [?] Christ our Lord. We must entreat him to prevail over our enemies and to overwhelm the darkness, to destroy in us whatever is foreign or merely our own, and to build up what is his. We know that the friends of God obtained this by prayer. They surely felt the trouble of their heart when they said: "Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit in my inmost being." Having obtained this by prayer, the psalmist now says with confidence: "Test me, Lord, and know my heart, and see if there is any way of iniquity in me." But so that he should not seem to have earned this confidence by his own strength rather than by God's grace, he also says: "For you, Lord, have possessed my inmost parts." For, as the Lord himself said, we can do nothing without him, because he is the true vine and we are his branches. If we remain in his love, we do not wither, for we live by the sap of the eternal root. We will not be cut off for the fire in his anger, but pruned for fruit by his discipline, as the blade of the gospel pruning knife cleanses us, so that with the overgrowth of our shoots cut back we may sprout more fruitfully.

So when he is about to begin his farming in us, he says: "I have come to cast fire upon the earth." With this fire he cleanses our heart, overgrown with sins like a field bristling with thorns, burning us in our vices and enlightening us in our senses. The devoted farmer goes after the stumps of our old deeds with his saving pruning hook, so that the fiery word may set alight the remaining stubble of the old harvest and prepare our soul like a field for new sowing. Then, once the thorns have been uprooted by the plowshare of the divine word driven deep, the soul may freely pour forth a rich crop of virtues and, with the roots of harmful weeds destroyed, multiply a harvest worthy of the heavenly granaries. But we are not only God's field but also God's building, cultivated and built up by his grace, his Spirit and his word. Intending to build us up along the road on which he calls us to follow him, he prepares us by this work, urging us first to free ourselves by selling our property. Since care for it or love of it blunts the very edge of the mind, and draws the soul away from its inner life and lures it toward external things, he says to us too through the prophet: "Be still, and see that I am the Lord." Does he not seem to be saying here as well: "You cannot serve two masters"? For by this word he does not urge idleness on us, he who warns us to pray and keep watch constantly so that we do not enter into temptation. He urges us rather to be free of the world so that we may be occupied with him, free of those affairs which, while we are entangled in them, leave us idle toward God.

So as we build newness of life within us, we must tear down the old. And since there can be no fellowship between darkness and light, or between mammon and Christ, we must exchange the old for the new. Reversing both what we were busy with and what we were free from, we must become engaged in what we used to neglect, so that in turn we may be free of what we were once entangled in. Let us die to what we lived for, and live in turn for those works and pursuits to which we were dead, when we were dead to the things of the living and, doing deadly things, lived among the dead. That is why the holy teacher asks something humane and fair: that just as we offered our members to serve iniquity, so now we should offer the same members as servants of righteousness, and with our masters changed, change our pursuits as well. For in changing masters we do not lay aside either servitude or freedom; we only gain happiness, since both our servitude and our freedom are changed for the better. We break the chain of iniquity, submit to the yoke of righteousness and are reined in by the fear of God, and with our path turned straight we begin to be free of sin, which we used to serve in a wretched freedom, rebelling against righteousness.

Now, then, having become in turn servants of God and rebels against this world, we enter the contest and, relying on the Lord, challenge the very enemy we used to serve. You surely recognize, my brother (for I am speaking as to a fellow soldier about things we have experienced together), how great the conflict is and how great the enemy within us. It is not of flesh and blood but, as the apostle says, of invisible powers and spiritual wickedness, with whom the agents of the vices of the flesh conspire. That is why they are also called rulers of darkness: according to the apostle, sinners are called darkness, and the demons rule over them as over their own kind. Moreover, the whole form of this world, which is passing away and entices hearts through the eyes, has the devil's nets spread over it, and whatever shape it takes it is a snare and a sword for the mind. Let us believe the prophet that we walk in the midst of traps, and that our life is spent among swords hidden by deadly tricks. This world welcomes us blossoming with all kinds of pleasures and poisoned with deceptive allurements. The serpent welcomes us with countless ambushes, he who has a thousand names and a thousand arts of doing harm. Often he attacks violently in open combat, and if he does not catch us with hidden snares, he aims at us with blazing darts. For "sharp are the arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals": they scorch our soul with the harmful fires of desire and leave it desolate of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. When this happens, various guests come in to occupy us, and "a man's enemies become the members of his own household." Now they puff us up with the wind of ambition, now they bring the torches of lust near us, now they bind us with the chains of avarice. Avarice is armed with every crime, and even if it alone captures us, it is enough both for the devil's malice and for a man's death.

What then are you doing, unhappy man, sent out among so many enemies? How will you fight the strong when you are weak, or the armed when you are unarmed? Blessed Job, wounded by many of the devil's darts though never wounded in his heart, cries out: "Naked I came out of my mother's womb." Who then will arm me against so many columns of the enemy of the air, so that I do not return to the earth naked, as I came? But see, I breathe again, I take heart, I rise up. "The Lord is my light, the Lord is the defender of my life; though armies encamp against me, my heart shall not fear." Even if I lack the weapons of my own strength, I shall not lose confidence. I have the armory of Christ, from which I may take up the armor of light, and with it overcome the princes of darkness and the ranks of night that oppose me in the heavenly places, that is, in the spiritual way of life, which they strive to overthrow with earthly allurements. Against them my armor-bearer and standard-bearer will be the one who is God's chosen vessel. He will bind my loins with the belt of chastity, he will fit the helmet of salvation to my head, and the breastplate of righteousness will enclose my chest. He will protect the whole of me with the shield of faith, and he will arm my right hand, or rather the whole of me, now made the right hand of Christ, with the sword of the Spirit and the word of truth, so that a thousand may fall at my side and ten thousand at my right hand. He will shod my feet with the preparation of the gospel, so that I may tread unharmed over the thorns and thistles of this earth and pass safely, my feet protected, through the rough places of the narrow road. Nor will I fear its bite, but will crush the head of the enemy serpent beneath me with the very heel it lies in wait for. I do not claim to say this arrogantly, out of the boldness of my own weakness; rather I claim the right to promise it to every believer [?] on the strength of Christ's power. For just as he calls the things that are not as though they were, so he is able, through his weak and lowly ones, as he always has done and still does, to destroy the strong and lofty things of this world. This is why he gave us a teacher, one who was his imitator, through whom we might come to imitate the Lord himself.

For this teacher himself teaches me to stand in the battle line, to run in the stadium, and to wrestle in the contest. He bruises his own body, forgets what lies behind and strains toward what lies ahead, and is so firmly founded on the rock that he glories even in his weaknesses; when he is weak, then he is strong, able to do all things, as he himself declares, in him who strengthens his own, Christ, who fights for us and conquers in us. This is why the apostle said: "So run that you may all obtain the prize." In earthly contests it is the opposite: there a match can end only with unequal fortunes for the contestants, so that one man's glory is the other's disgrace. But in Christ, since we who are many are one, we all run as one, and the race we all share leads to a single good. That is why we are told: "So run that you may all obtain the prize." For, as he also says, there can be no division in the body whose head is Christ, and the single framework of his members accompanies him as their common summit. Since the members cannot be at odds with one another, let us run together, so that we may all obtain the prize, without envious rivalry and with an equal share in the victory. Then, just as in the effort of the race we are Christ's labor, so at the finish we may be Christ's triumph, and he may bless us in the crown of the year of his goodness.

I see, however, that in this contest it profits us no more to conquer than to be conquered, because both an enemy and a friend dwell within us. Who is more my friend than the spirit that opposes the flesh, so that it may not drag me into the law of sin? And who is more our enemy than the flesh, which lusts against the spirit to bring about our ruin? Better for me, then, are the wounds of a friend, which Christ received in order to heal me, than the willing kisses of an enemy, with which the flesh, that evil counsellor, flatters me through the allurements of its pleasures, in order to betray me, as with that parricidal kiss of Judas, to enemies standing ready to take me captive. Yet the Lord did not accept that kiss to receive the traitor's peace, but to take back his own peace from the one who had become estranged. Even so, it is wholesome to keep that kiss in view as an example of perfect goodness: with the same love by which he commands us to love even our enemies, he gave the friendly kiss of peace to an enemy, returning love for hatred, he who was receiving hatred in return for his love.

It is easy, then, to discern: [?] the devil contend together with the flesh; for it is better to be conquered in goodness than to conquer by evil. So in this world the man whose tunic another has taken seems to be defeated; but in Christ the man triumphs who, when someone takes his tunic, lets him have his cloak as well. To repay injury in kind is human revenge; but to love even an enemy is heavenly vengeance. To sell one's estates and give to the poor is foolishness to this world but wisdom to God; while, on the other hand, to brood over riches, to increase money by usury and possessions by auctions, and to extend one's boundaries by violence counts in this world as industry and profit, but with God it is crime and punishment. So if you conquer by evil, you are a conquered conqueror, for although you have won through crime, you have been overcome by greed. But if you are conquered, you will conquer, provided you yield to what is just and the divine will prevails over your own. Let us then be emptied of our own strength, so that we may be filled with God's. Let us be conquered in body, but conquer in salvation. Let us remember that we are members of him who conquered when he was condemned, who overcame by yielding, and who by falling into death rose into glory, founding the dawn of our resurrection on the sunset of his passion.

Let us follow this Lord who calls us, so that he may teach us to conquer by yielding and to come to life by dying, killing in us that by which we are put to death and quickening that by which we may live. He is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him, who was seen on earth and lived among men. And because flesh and blood cannot reveal this to us, he says: "Be at leisure, and see that I am God." At this point I am roused to the boldness of asking: Who are you, then, O God, who made heaven and earth and appeared in the bush, who did great deeds in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, and terrible things at the Red Sea? To this day, Lord, there is no one who does not believe in you. Not only the Jews, a people formed in the law, who love you with their lips however far their heart may be from you, but even the Gentiles, who live without the law, confess by natural sense one Lord of supreme power. What difficulty is there, then, in seeing that you are God, when the heavens declare your glory and your invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made? What prevents a man from owning property? What harm is there in attending to other things as well, when even busy people can readily discern the plain truth of God and see the manifest light of supreme providence? "Day pours forth speech to day, and night shows knowledge to night"; and yet I am bidden to be at leisure in order to see that you are Lord, though even the nights know this light, that is, even the princes or workers of darkness.

But it is not without reason that the Truth, which has often revealed itself through many signs of divinity, declares that it cannot be perceived unless leisure is first secured. For to see merely that God is God is easy. This, as I said, every soul sees; to this no mind is blind; even the faith of unbelievers accepts it. But that God is in Christ, or Christ in God, the busy man, wrapped in a cloud of earthly cares, does not see. For the Word made flesh is foolishness to the wisdom of this world; and so it pleased God, to confound that wisdom, through whose pride this world did not know the wisdom of God, to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching.

And this is that treasure in the field, for whose sake even the field must be bought, since the price of our salvation lies in this: that we confess that God, the Son of God, came in the flesh to save the flesh. This is that pearl which must be bought by squandering our estates. But it is not bought the moment its price is made ready, for very many difficulties get in the way of the purchase itself. A sea may lie between, or a robber may intercept, or a greedier buyer may get there first, or a wealthier one may be preferred. So do not think that we have already bought the jewel because you see that we have got the price ready, nor that we have already built the house because we have cleared the site for building it. We have carted away visible riches, furnishings, money and estates like filthy heaps and troublesome rubble, so that we might lay the foundations of a more stable building more firmly in a cleansed heart, as in living ground. But just as, when the rubble has been cleared away and the soil beneath the filthy heaps laid bare, one often finds the knotted roots of tree stumps, or remnants of ruins, or many kinds of harmful creatures, and especially the young or the nests of vipers, so too, once the possession and care of temporal things has been removed from our breast, and we are free at last to examine our own heart, free of the things that used to draw us outward, we find in our inner faculties the knots of long-standing sins and the lurking places of spiritual enemies. Now the inner house begins to appear to us, and the creeping things there without number. Now the whole darkness of our wretched state lies open. Now at last we see how far we are from God, and how dead compared with the living.

Understand these things, and sigh with an anxious heart in your concern for us, bearing in mind that the praise of the same Lord is sung at the end, so that we may be perfected by grace in the spirit in which we began, and may obey to the very end of the precept the one whom we appear to have obeyed at the outset of the counsel. For he gives counsel, not a command, when he does not say, "Be perfect," but, "If you wish to be perfect"; because the freedom of the will, which when it is good stands above the law, is not compelled but persuaded, and is a law to itself. How great a thing it is to follow Christ you can gather from the apostle's saying: "He who says that he follows Christ ought himself to walk as he walked." How Christ walked another teacher shows us: "He committed no sin," he says, "nor was deceit found in his mouth; when he was reviled, he did not revile in return, but he gave himself up to death to one who judged unjustly." But from his own actions and precepts as well we can know how he walked. For he came for this very purpose, to set his life before us as a pattern and mirror of life. "I have not come," he says, "to abolish the law but to fulfil it"; and what this fulfilment is he himself teaches when he says: "Unless your righteousness exceeds the righteousness of the Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." For to fulfil is to add what is lacking. The law says, "You shall not kill"; but he says, "Nor shall you be angry with your brother without cause." The law forbids adultery; but the Truth himself condemns even a curious look at women. From this you see how much greater faith is than the law. The praise of faith comes not from men but from God, because the circumcision of the law is outward, while that of faith is hidden. The law breaks off the branches of sin; faith tears out its roots. Faith makes us spotless not in our works but in our inner senses, so that we may truly be restored to our original dignity, that is, to the likeness of God, cleansed not only in body but in heart. That is why the apostle testifies that, having put off the image of the earthly man, we put on the heavenly; and elsewhere he declares that the man who has already put on Christ is the glory of God.

See, then, how much we still have to do, if we, who are not perfected, as you say, but only beginners, as we know from experience, are to complete the length of the journey. We are commanded to exceed the righteousness of the law so that we may become the righteousness of God; our conduct is not to come from the law, but the law is to lie in our will: to follow Christ and to imitate God. And he who wishes us to be more righteous than the very law of his own righteousness, and perfect like his Father, demands not only that we flee human faults but also that we fulfil divine virtues. You can see that this is as difficult for those still engaged in the contest as it is glorious for the victors once the struggle is over. So meanwhile, while we are still in the arena, with fighting without and fears within, do not think or speak lofty things about us. Rather, fear; labor in spirit with those who labor, and help us with your prayers, so that through us too he may destroy the enemy and the avenger, he who chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong.

Ask him humbly to give us understanding on this road by which he calls us, so that we may see that he who was crucified out of our weakness, yet lives by the power of God, is himself God. Ask him to weaken in us the power of sin, so as to strengthen the spirit of his own power; to reverse both our poverty and our abundance, so that we may abound in the righteousness we lack and lack the iniquity in which we abound; that we may be stripped of sins and clothed with virtues; that he may bring us help against our own wills and not hand us over to the desires of our heart; and that against flesh and blood, against the devil and death, he may give us victory, as he gave it to Abraham against the four kings. That father of faith overcame them as a mystery signifying that our faith, if it is strengthened by the guiding Spirit, will subject the same number of elements of our body to the word of God. And just as he was victorious over kings on behalf of his kinsman, so faith, victorious on behalf of the soul, which thrives through the same number of senses, will triumph over the outer man, who is composed of the same number of elements and in whom the figure of the four kings is contained. Abraham overcame the hostile princes not by the numbers or strength of legions, but even then by the sacrament of the cross, whose figure is expressed by the Greek letter T, the number three hundred. By the power of this mystery the ark, built three hundred cubits long, rose above the flood, just as the church now sails over this world. So we too, relying not on our own resources or strength but solely on the knowledge of the Crucified, let us lift our eyes to him, so that he may show his wonderful mercies upon us, he who saves those who hope in him. For he is the Lord who crushes wars, mighty in battle, who has given us both the confidence to fight and the way to conquer, when, bearing in himself our human nature already triumphant, he said: "Be steadfast, for I have overcome the world."
XXV.

Though you do not know me by sight, I have already come to know you in my heart. My son Victor, very dear to me in the Lord, told me about your devout life, and so made me know you though you are absent, and begin to love you as one who will share with me in Christ. He told me how he had been your comrade and follower in your mess during your secular military service, in which you are still held. That is why I have ventured all the more boldly to write to you through him. For I hope that from the same road you will come to the true road, since you have sent this man ahead of you to us from among your comrades. The Church holds him as your pledge, so as to capture you after him. For there is nothing, blessed son, that can or ought to be preferred to him who is the true Lord, the true Father and the eternal Emperor. To whom could we more rightly devote our life than to him from whom we received it, and for whom we must keep it to the end, since we live by his kindness? If we serve as his soldiers in this world, we shall then deserve to pass over to him. But if we love this world more and choose to soldier for Caesar rather than for Christ, afterwards we shall be carried off not to Christ but to Gehenna, where the case of the princes of this world is decided.

So we must not prefer to God either family affection, or homeland, or honours, or riches, for it is written: The form of this world is passing away. And those who have loved this world will perish together with it. That is why the Lord himself solemnly declares in the Gospel: Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me cannot be my disciple. As for the riches of this world, which some embrace and love as the highest and indispensable good, he says: Treasures will not profit the wicked, but righteousness delivers from death. And again he says through the prophet: All who were exalted by gold and silver have been wiped out. In the Gospel too he cries out and condemns the rich of this world, saying: Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation; woe to you who are full, for you will be hungry! Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep!

Do not, then, go on loving this world and its military service any longer, for according to the authority of Scripture whoever is a friend of the world is an enemy of God. The man who soldiers with the sword is a servant of death. Whenever he sheds his own blood or another's, that is the reward he reaps for his pay: he will be held liable either to the outcome of death or to guilt. For a soldier in war, who fights not so much for himself as for another, must either, if he is afraid, meet his own death, or, if he is the victor, incur responsibility for a death, since he cannot be the victor unless he has first shed blood. That is why the Lord says: You cannot serve two masters, that is, God and mammon—in other words, Christ and Caesar—since Caesar himself now strives to be Christ's servant, so that he may deserve to be king over some nations. For no earthly king is king of the whole world; Christ, who is God, is that king, since all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. He is King of kings and Lord of lords; he does whatever he wills on earth, in the sea and in the depths.

Let us follow him, then, and soldier for him, in whose service the soldier who has once been belted is never unbelted, who bestows on those who serve him the glory of eternal life, the honour of the heavenly kingdom, the riches of his inheritance and an everlasting share in the knowledge of God. It is written: He who loves money will not be justified; and he who covets earthly possessions will, as it is written, be entangled in them. Hence the divine Wisdom speaks through Solomon in Ecclesiasticus: Many have been brought to ruin because of gold, and their destruction was before their eyes. Gold, it says, is a stumbling block, and it casts down those who pursue it; but none will perish by it except the foolish. Therefore flee from it, my son, as from the face of a serpent, trusting in Christ, who testifies to all people in the Gospel that a man's life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses.

But perhaps confidence in your youth, the pay of rank and the growth of your wealth are tempting you to say: “I am still young, and there is time for me to finish my service, marry a wife and have children, and serve God afterwards.” To this it is not I who answer you, but the Lord, who speaks in his prophets and apostles. The prophet says: Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day, lest his wrath come upon you suddenly. And in the Gospel he shows with what eagerness we must hasten to conversion when he says: From the days of John until today the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it. Such violence is pleasing to God; it strikes no one and is committed to no one's harm. Turn your hands to this kind of plunder, which carries no guilt and brings salvation. Why should you concern yourself with managing military pay and bear the odium of violence, when perhaps, being an honest man, you are even a moderate collector of debts? You could instead be violent without anyone's resentment and with God's favour, so as to seize the kingdom of heaven, which suffers violence. Christ rejoices to be invaded, for in the abundance of his love and power he is able both to bestow what he holds and to keep what he has given. For when he grants his saints to reign in his kingdom, he himself will reign in those whom he has taken up as sharers in the heavenly kingdom. It is written both that the kingdom of God will be with the saints and that the saints themselves are the kingdom of God. By God's grace, once you are converted, you will learn this by reading and understand it by believing.

As for the bloom of youth and the prime of life, who would dare to boast of it? For divine Scripture warns us: All flesh is grass, and all its splendour like the flower of the grass. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord abides for ever. Hence the prophet, longing rather for those dwellings in which the eternal glory of the body restored to life can abide after the resurrection, cries out: How lovely are your dwellings, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord.

As for the bonds of marriage and the other cares of temporal things, as thorny as they are empty, the apostle, in whom Christ speaks, warns us not to cast vain hopes into a long stretch of this world's time. He bids us recognise that the time has grown short, and says: From now on, let those who have wives be as though they had none, those who weep as though they were not weeping, those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, those who buy as though they had no possessions, and those who use this world as though they were not using it. In saying this he shows that those who are free ought not to become entangled, since he urges those who are bound to be set free. So if perhaps you are already bound to a wife, do not seek to be released; but if you are still free, do not seek to be entangled. For it is not to condemn marriage that the apostle compares the sanctity of this covenant with the great mystery of Christ and the Church; rather, because of the present necessity, he declares that it is good for a man to remain as he himself was. I want you, he says, to be free from anxiety—that is, to think of nothing but God and our salvation. For a wife and children, though they too are pledges given to us by God, are nevertheless burdens of the heaviest cares. That is why the same apostle says that such people will have trouble in the flesh, because our ties of flesh torment and wear us out all the more, the dearer they are to us. Once a man has taken a wife, he first longs for children; if none are born, he mourns his barrenness; if they are born, he fears to lose them. And so the mind never rests in fleshly affections without suffering torment: either it loves its kin when they are good and fears losing them, or it hates them when they are bad and wishes to be rid of them, and in either case it is always liable to bear miseries. Wretched is the man who loses a good wife, more wretched the one who has a bad one. Between these two misfortunes, the man who has known neither is far happier. Likewise with children, parents are very often utterly wretched, either because they are bereaved of good ones or because they have such children that they are driven to envy the childless.

Listen, then, my son, incline your ear to me, and break all the bonds that hold you entangled in this world. Exchange the world's service for a better one, so that you may begin to soldier for the eternal King. And now, since I hear that you are a helper and guardian of the citizens, become a companion of Christ. Again, in your service it is usual to set your hopes on this promotion in office, to be made Protectors. But if you prove yourself to God, you will begin to have God himself as your protector. See to what kind of service I invite you as a colleague: what you hope to be for a man, God will be for you. If you begin to follow him, you will begin to serve in the rank of his companions, and the end of your service will be a kingdom not of earth and time, but of eternity and heaven.
XXV*. TO HIS DEAREST SON CRISPINIANUS, PAULINUS SENDS GREETINGS IN CHRIST THE LORD.

When Victor, once your fellow soldier, returned to us from his homeland, I hoped to receive a letter from your honour, by which you would gladden me about your conduct, that is, about the progress of your faith. It was for this reason that I had earlier ventured to write to you through the same brother Victor, just as I write now, daring once again to press my counsel upon you, urged by God's command in which it is written: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. How else can I prove that I love you as myself, unless I desire for you the same thing I have judged best for myself? That is, that we renounce this world and all its pomps and the enticements of its vanity, flee from the wrath to come, and take refuge in the one salvation of the human race, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, our Lord and God, who was crucified and rose from the dead precisely in order to free us from everlasting death and lead us to everlasting life, and moreover to make us heirs, conformed to his image and sharers in his glory. Therefore, dearest brother and son, we must set aside everything that entangles us in this world and kills us as we follow the desires of our flesh; we must cast out of our hearts the vices of our pleasures and leave them behind us like dung. Thus, by accepting a profitable loss of worldly things, which harbour the material of sin and the cause of death, we may gain Christ, in whom are honour and treasure, in whom are the everlasting kingdom and the true light that enlightens the eyes of souls, so that we may understand that a little that the righteous man has is better than the great riches of sinners, and that it profits a man nothing if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul. So I felt bound to obey our blessed brother and good fellow citizen Victor, to write again to your charity, and to dare, in the grief of affection, to write to you even by way of rebuke. For when I was anxious to know how you were faring, he told me that, by God's mercy, you are even now a Christian in intention rather than in deed, forever thinking of the eternal and of setting out on the journey of life, that is, the way of Christ. But if you do not wish to become a private man, consider that your service should be changed, not laid aside, and exchanged for one that is as much better as God is a greater king than man.

Render to Caesar, then, the things that are Caesar's, so that you may begin to give to God the things that are God's. Tell me, I beg you, my brother, what are you waiting for? For what better prospect are you saving your resolve? To what days are you postponing your good? How long a life are you promising yourself?
