Even if you were certain that you would live as long again as you have already lived, you ought still to infer from the swiftness of time that the rest of your life will slip away just as fast, and that after the very short span and most laborious course of this life there will follow ages in which we must either live without end or die without end. Those who love this age must necessarily become exiles from that age. For just as it is written that no one can serve two masters and that Christ and mammon have nothing in common, so it is certain that the man who has loved the temporal and perishable things of this age cannot obtain the good things of the age to come. If you will not believe me, believe the Gospel, in which the Lord, speaking in the person of Abraham our father, shows that certain reversals are allotted to men, so ordered that those who have had tribulation in this world have refreshment prepared for them there, while those who have had a fruitless abundance here are repaid in hell with a rich poverty of punishments. That heartless rich man, who had been stingy to the poor and lavish to himself while he lived in this world, afterwards died, was snatched away to hell, and plunged there into Gehenna. Then he saw Lazarus the beggar far off. Now he no longer scorns him; instead, himself in need of life, he gazes in wonder at the man rich in joy whom in this world he had scorned as an outcast. He had not fed him when he was hungry nor tended him when he was covered in sores; while dogs licked his wounds, he, a man, had no pity for a fellow man, so that the rich man was shown to be worse than the dogs, since the madness of avarice had robbed him of human feeling. Proud of his feasts and royal clothing, the rich man had shuddered at this poor man, wretched and suppliant in this world. Afterwards, in the underworld, he sees him blessed while he himself is wretched—the one resting in light, himself burning in darkness; the one rejoicing in Abraham's bosom, himself roaring in the bosom of hell. Forgetting his pride and vanity, the wretch, deserving no pity, recognises the poor man as uselessly as he does belatedly, and mourns over his own pleasures in a place where he can no longer find the remedy of repentance. For, it says, in death there is no one who remembers you, Lord; and in hell who will confess you? Hence the prophet says elsewhere: They did not call upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear.

Here, then, while we dwell in the body, we must attend to our salvation and seek out remedies that will profit us, and as much as we have abounded in provoking the Lord by sinning, let us abound even more in making amends to him by worthy repentance. In hell, however, there is no longer any room for repentance for sinners, only for punishment. That is why, as I said above, with the situation of the two persons, the rich man and the poor, reversed, the dead man in the flames begs the very one whom, when he was alive and living in luxury, he had passed by with contempt and mockery as he begged and often lay half-dead in the pain of his sores. How justly does he who in the world above did not feed his needy neighbour now feed fires and worms in the world below! So begging has now been turned back upon him, and the man who was rich to his own harm, amid the abundance of his torments, begs the alms of a little dew from his beggar, who now abounds in the riches of life. But he receives a just requital: he is not to be refreshed by the mercy of the poor man whom he had never refreshed from his own plenty. And why is it that, though his whole body is burning, he asks only that his tongue be sprinkled by even the tip of the poor man's finger? Surely because he had sinned against the poor man most of all with that member, by which he had ordered him to be thrown out as he lay before his door, or had mocked the squalor of his afflictions. Both these crimes against him he had committed with his tongue, not considering that he and the poor man had one God and Creator, and that this same God is a more indulgent father to the poor, for he resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. He had not considered that it was written for him: He who gives to the poor lends to the Lord; and again: He who wrongs the poor man provokes God, who made him. So, handed over to hell as a son of Gehenna, he hears Abraham, the father of refreshment, say: Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are tormented. That is why the Gospel says again: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted; and on the other hand: Woe to those who laugh, for they shall mourn! Hence David also says: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. And Ecclesiastes declares with equal right that it is better to go to the house of mourning—that is, where past sins are washed away by healing grief in humility of a contrite heart—than to the house of feasting, that is, where through intemperance and luxury sins are piled up all the more, to be punished by eternal fire.

For this reason, blessed son, I long for you to come to your senses from the love of darkness and to be separated from the company of human error, for you know that it is written: Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly. If you are willing to share with those who now sow in tears, you will be their companion on the day of reward, for the saints will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves. Whatever a man has sown in this life, that he will reap in the next. That is why the apostle says: He who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but he who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit. Believe me, you will not be able to rejoice with Christ unless you stop rejoicing with this world. Unless you weep now, you will not laugh for ever; if you do not humble yourself of your own accord, you will not be exalted; if you do not despise the empty glory of the world, you will not attain the everlasting glory of Christ; if you prefer to be rich here for a time, you will endure poverty there for ever; if Christ finds you on the wide and spacious road, he will be compelled—God forbid!—to judge you on it.
XXVI. TO SEBASTIAN, HIS HOLY AND DESERVEDLY MOST BELOVED BROTHER, PAULINUS AND THERASIA SEND GREETINGS IN CHRIST THE LORD.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who chose you and took you up as a vessel of his election, set you apart from the womb of your ancient mother, and gave you the wings of a dove, so that, flying far away from the din of this world, you might say: “See, I have fled far off, and I have stayed in the wilderness.” Yet your solitude is not lonely, for it is not deserted but secluded: forsaken by the darkness of this world, it is thronged by the light of God; it is shunned by the grieving demons and tended by rejoicing angels. The Lord our God himself has granted us, though we are separated by a great distance, to draw near to you in love through the sweet fragrance of your reputation. We learned of it through our dearest brother in the Lord, Victor, who told us both of the work of your vocation and of your secluded dwelling: how, as a zealous imitator of the saints of old, you had set up a peaceful dwelling and a spiritual camp beside a torrent, just as the sons of the prophets once did beside the Jordan under Elisha’s leadership, and how a deacon, your blessed brother, ministers to you with the devoted service of the widow of Zarephath or the Shunammite woman. Blessed is he whom the Lord has commanded, as he once commanded one of the birds of the air, to feed you with the bread of devotion as you sit in seclusion like Elijah by the brook; and who, in this ministry, flies back again and again to your little cell, like the dove returning to Noah’s ark bearing a fruitful branch of holy growth.

Blessed are you both by the Lord, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house, and who has doubled in you the bond of brotherhood. He made you brothers in the womb of the Church, and under one faith he assigned you different offices, so that by different services each of you might feed the other: you, fasting and praying, help him with spiritual weapons, while he sows heavenly goods for himself as he supplies you with bodily food. Not that you need the outlay of perishable food, for your hunger hungers after righteousness and the kingdom of God. And yet, since the same Lord who made what is within also made what is without, and since the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak, he rewards your soul, though it lives on the word of God, which is Christ God, the living and true bread, with this kind of service: your brother serves your body, that is, the earthly frailty in you, with modest food, and he himself is fattened by the abundance of your fasts. For this is why he said, “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God”: because he took account of our weaker substance, and so the Creator himself showed that bread is necessary for the flesh as well.

But so that we should not place the care of the body before the soul, which is fed by the word of God, he showed that human life does not consist in bread alone. And so, when he said, “not by bread alone,” he also taught that human sustenance does consist in bread, which, even if the soul in its concern does not seek it, the nature of the body still demands. Blessed therefore is he whose soul is enriched by the needs of your condition, since you are still a man and must be fed with this visible bread, even though inwardly you are filled with that eternal bread. For spiritual virtue would not advance unless fleshly weakness lay beneath it; nor would the ministry of the faithful have any power unless a brother’s need often supplied the matter for ministering. Hence the apostle too speaks of a future recompense in favor of the saints, when he urges the Church of God to the comfort of this blessing and says: “Let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also supply your need.”

I dare say, moreover, that between the two of you the pattern of John and of the Lord is divided: John crying in the wilderness, and the Lord teaching in the temple. One of you has been called to the servitude of the ministry, the other to the freedom of the monk. But both of you have been called together into the one kingdom and glory of God; both are free, since both are under grace, and both are servants, since both are under the law of faith. Both are free from sin and both are servants of righteousness; both in your fasts observe the day to the Lord, and both at the feasts of sincerity give thanks to the Lord, who gives food to all flesh and gives living food to those who hunger for true life. One of you has heard, so that he may say: “I will go in to the altar of God, to God who gladdens my youth”; and the other has learned from the same prophet to say: “I am alone until I pass over.”

Therefore, since you have been so chosen and so loved by the Lord that you bear one another’s burdens, and with the perfect charity by which you feed one another you sustain, instruct and enrich each other, fulfilling the law of Christ, pray for us. Join your strong hands of prayer, so that you may overcome the multitude of our sins. For this is why the merciful and compassionate Lord himself procures and grants to his sinners the acquaintance and love of the saints: so that even the guilty who have no excuse may be absolved of the deserts of condemnation by a powerful advocacy. May you abide in the kingdom of the Lord, which he has caused to be within you through the pledge of the Holy Spirit dwelling in you, in whom you cry, “Abba, Father,” blessed sons of the Lord, sons of devotion, of peace and of light.
XXVII. Paulinus to Severus, his brother of one mind, venerable and ever most longed-for.

I will bless the Lord at all times and will not forget his rewards, for he has not repaid us according to our sins, he who satisfies our longing with constant and numerous consolations from you, my kindred soul. For within a few days the return to us of our holy brothers and common friends of one mind, Postumianus and Theridius, was followed by the arrival of other brothers, Virinus and Sorianus. Thus almost at one time a most abundant harvest of joys came to us, since all these whom we have mentioned as arriving together made the grace of their presence sweeter to us by bringing letters from you. And so our spirit rejoiced in the Lord, and our mouth was enlarged over our enemy, who was not allowed to say, “I have prevailed against them,” since it was rather the prayers of our longing that prevailed, so that we received the hoped-for judgments and words from you, who are the greatest concern of our soul.

So then, in order that we may owe one another nothing, as we are commanded, except mutual love, I will answer all your letters, and first the one I received first, in which you complain to me about the very men by whom you had written, asking why I either left you alone or drew them away from you. But you will recognize that I cannot be blamed on either count, for I have never set any limit to my longing for you, nor have I had any contest with you over laying claim to them. Otherwise I would gladly have yielded my right to you, had they been your possession first. For those who stayed with you would not be strangers to me, since you are wholly mine in Christ the Lord, through whom I in turn am yours; nor would I have gained as much grace in receiving them as I would have lost if I had snatched from you companions on the way of salvation, however desirable. Indeed, by my own judgment I would consider myself most deserving to be deprived of your love if I preferred any good for myself rather than for you. But when I found that these men, who had come to me by an unexpected gift of the Lord, were such as they soon afterward proved to be to you as well, I even envied myself, because I had been more fortunate than you in this respect, in that I rather than you had obtained, or had come to know first, men more worthy of your sight and company. Accordingly, so that I might as soon as possible rejoice in this grace, by which I counted myself blessed, with you as my partner, I both rebuked them in person for admitting that they had no friendship or acquaintance with you, and when they set out I charged them with nothing more earnestly than to hasten to see and embrace you, and to put knowing you before all their affairs and concerns at home, so as to make up, though late, for their long loss. And, thanks be to the Lord, we have received them on their return with rejoicing, bringing back a great joy of conscience at having believed us when we urged them to seek you above all others, like a blessed sheaf from a full field, loftier than the other fruits of their life. What thanks they gave, first to God, who had not only satisfied but surpassed their desire, so that they found more good things in you than they had anticipated; then to us, who had been the cause of so great a gain for them; and to themselves, for having obeyed us to their own profit!

I cannot express the delight with which they flooded me when they told of your deeds and words, and of your heart perfected in the knowledge of divine love. Through it you are humble and exalted, poor and rich, servant and free: a fellow servant to your servants, a servant to your brothers, rich toward the poor in the bowels of mercy, poor toward the rich in the spirit of meekness, humble in the virtue of devotion, lofty in the sublimity of virtue, a servant to God and free of mammon. They declared that Martin breathes wholly in you, that Clarus flourishes in you, that the gospel ripens in you. They thoroughly anointed our head with the oil of gladness; for this reason all that is within us blessed the Lord for a twofold cause of thanksgiving: because we understood that we had done you a very great service in your coming to know these most beloved brothers, as you have shown, and because we saw that they rejoiced in their acquaintance with you and your love as a divine gift. Moreover, among the works and gifts of God in you, how they admired your boys too, who flourish around you like young olive shoots, and to whom our God has made you what he himself is to all, so that they both revere you as a master and love you as a father! In hearing this account of theirs, however, we confess that we groaned over our own misfortune, since our heavier sins had made us barren of such sons. Yet we have been somewhat consoled, because we judge that the blessing of your happiness is close to us.

But so that our iniquity may not separate us from you by a longer distance, gird up that whole chosen band of holy youth with which you soothe God day and night, so that they may draw up a battle line of prayers on our behalf against our sins, and entreat the Lord to confirm what he has wrought for us: that is, that in your love, in which we now find rest and in which we glory, we may on that day be refreshed and rejoice.
XXVIII. Paulinus to Severus, his holy brother and fellow soldier of one mind.

Victor returns from me to you, so that he may return from you to me: Victor, our common pledge, our faithful companion and our customary comfort; Victor, mine in you and yours in me; Victor, the courier of our letters, a post-rider on foot or a two-legged post-horse; the victor over the longest roads, who may well be called at once both victor and vanquished, since he is vanquished by love, by which he vanquishes hard roads and great labors. In the sweat of his brow he eats his bread so as to refresh us with his yearly journeys back and forth between us, tirelessly carrying and bringing back the exchange of letters by which we pay one another, as a tax of due service, a mutual visit of our souls and hearts. May the lad Victor be blessed by the Lord, and may his land not bring forth thorns and thistles for him, since he is not lazy. For the ways of the lazy are strewn with thorns. But our Victor does not say, “There is a lion in the roads,” for he is so simple that he walks confident, faithful and chaste, so that he fears neither the terror of the night nor the arrow that flies by day. Therefore the Lord guards him in all his ways and commands his angelic sentries that he may nowhere strike his foot against a stone, and that the serpent lying in wait on the road may not bite his heel; rather, with feet shod for the course of the gospel, he will tread on it and crush it unharmed. I will therefore praise and bless in the Lord the feet of our Victor, and of these feet too I will dare to say: “How beautiful are the feet that bring me good news of peace” from you, when they announce your safety and the peace within you, when they announce your faith, through which Christ our peace abides in you, who also makes both one from us and in us, whether in that we two are of one heart, or in that we make the two substances of soul and body one, as Christ fuses us together by the fire of his Spirit, of which he says, “I came to cast fire upon the earth.” And what does the good Lord wish but that it be kindled in us, light up our darkness and consume our sins, since the Lord our God is a consuming fire? May the Lord grant me here that within me, too, there may be a fire consuming for my good. May my heart burn with this fire for eternal light for me, lest my soul burn with the same fire for everlasting punishment. For in this fire the day of the Lord will be revealed, and the fire will test what sort of work each of us has done.

Let us pray to this Lord to teach us to do his will, and may his good Spirit lead us into the right way, so that our labor may not be found to be wood, hay and stubble, but rather silver, gold and precious stones, and that we may be found living in the walls of that heavenly and free Jerusalem which is built as a city, whose sharing is in unity. For the dweller of this city is shown to be one in three; hence it is called the city of the great King, the city of our God, the city of the Lord of hosts, which the Lord himself, as it is written, has founded for ever. Of this city Christ has become not only the foundation but also the tower and the gate. For, it says, no one can lay any other foundation than him, who is our tower of strength against the face of the enemy, and who says: “I am the door of the sheep; no one can come to the Father except through me.” If, then, our house and our mind are founded on him, and a work worthy of so great a foundation is built upon it, he himself will be the gate for our entry into his city, he who will rule us for ever and will settle us in a place of pasture; for he has already begotten us for himself through the water of refreshment, and he nourishes us with saving food at the table which he has prepared for us against those who afflict us. Of this table he says: “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God,” for Christ is at once both the kingdom and the bread by which we are fattened and the serpent wastes away. For the serpent’s hunger and punishment is the food of our life, Christ Jesus, who became food for us, so that living by that bread and walking according to him we may say with the apostle: “But our citizenship is in heaven.” For when we savor and seek the things that are above, we cease to be earthly, so that we are no longer food for the serpent, who in turn has been given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia, so that he is eaten by those whom he eats. For us, on the contrary, this is saving: we eat Christ and are swallowed up by Christ, who, because he is life, swallows up our mortality, so as to clothe us with immortality and make us conformed to his image. He has given us power to trample unharmed upon all the strength of the enemy, through the same grace by which he gave those who believe in his name, which is above every name, power to become children of God. In him let us dwell, for he himself is also the city that cannot be hidden, since it is set on a mountain, and its foundations are on the holy mountains. This city the Most High himself founded, as it is written, for Wisdom has built herself a house. This is that house not made with hands; if we dwell in it with such works as make us worthy to become fellow citizens of the saints, our work will not burn. And that wise fire, as we pass through its testing, will not surround us with severe heat to punish us, but will receive us as ones commended to it and lick us with a gentle touch, so that we may say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment.”

But so that the letter may end with the same name with which it began, I will return to our Victor, on whose behalf I owe an apology. That he is returning to you later than agreed, do not blame his feet, which stayed with us longer not through the fault of laziness but out of eagerness to obey. Consider, however, not the time at which you said you released him, but the time at which you actually sent him, and you will see that I am in the right concerning our agreed arrangement for taking turns keeping Victor. For he did not come to spend the winter with us, as you had written; rather, as he declared, he was sent back to you from Narbonensis, where he had met brother Postumianus, and only then set out from you again, at a time when he could already have reached me had he been sent straight to me. So, since the winter was already ending when I received him, I was obliged to keep him through the spring months; and because that seemed a short period, since the Easter festival would soon close it, and since I had been very ill during that same time, so that I was not fit for the business of writing back, I added some delay from the summer days, to settle accounts with you, if I took as much of your time in him as you had taken up from the winter days. Therefore I will allow him, if he reaches you in autumn, to spend the winter with you again, since you see that it has been so arranged by the Lord’s good pleasure that the seasons of our common friend of one mind, which we had ceded to one another, have been changed, without breaking faith with our agreement, to his greater advantage. For now things have been fittingly turned about, so that what you wrote, indulging me beyond my merit and detracting from yourself, has become truer. For you, being truly fervent in spirit, will more healthfully warm him in the cold season with the fiery heat of your faith, while I, being cold, will be better suited to be his summer station.

But would that I were cold rather than lukewarm, so that I would not make my Lord vomit, and would relieve my neighbor’s heat! As it is, I rather cause disgust from a surfeit of myself in those who make use of the time of my sojourn, being of necessary use neither to those who are freezing nor to those who are sweltering; with the tepidness of my small faith I deserve to be spat out by those who have tried to taste the flavor of my company in the hope of spiritual sweetness. All the more do I marvel at your eagerness in desiring, or your patience in enduring, the tiresomeness of my follies. But would that as little sin from my much talking accrued to me as great is the reward heaped up for you from so tireless a love! For as though you were not wearied, but rather refreshed, by the great number and length of the volumes sent you before through our Victor, you have again asked through the same book-bearer that I burden you, if I can, with still more writings.

Besides this, flattering your poor friend far too lavishly, you have bidden me to instruct you, as one supposedly more expert, in whatever escapes you from the annals not of one nation but of the human race. But let the one who knocks at a poor friend’s door and searches an empty storeroom blame himself for his hunger. For I have never devoted strenuous study to investigating and collecting such things. Indeed, even in former days, when I seemed to read things that were not worth reading, I was a stranger to the historical writers. Nevertheless, now, taking an interest in your work, in which you have told me you are occupied with examining and comparing the reckonings of past times for the benefit of our faith, I have sought from the richer treasury of a brother of one mind what I did not have of my own. I sent the very memorandum you had enclosed in my letter by way of a reminder to the presbyter Rufinus, the companion of holy Melania on the spiritual way, a truly holy and devoutly learned man, and for that reason joined to me in close affection. If he, who is rich in both secular and saving literature, in Greek as well as Latin, does not set forth the causes of the gaps in history that rightly trouble you concerning the disagreeing calculation of years or reigns, I fear we shall seek them in vain from anyone else in these parts. But if he fulfills my confident expectation of him, at the first opportunity, God willing, I will send on to you whatever he writes back to me on this question.

Meanwhile, so as to carry out some part of your instructions, I have sent you some of those writings which I fear may be evidence of my sluggishness or imprudence rather than marks of heavenly assistance, or even proofs of human wisdom. Still, I have sent them to you; that is, I have entrusted my trifles to my own heart, not so that my darkness may defile your understanding, but so that it may be washed away by your understanding. I call them my trifles with respect to my words and ideas; the subject matter, however, is holy and more worthy of your talent and eloquence, and even if it is clothed by my language as if in a dark garment, it still preserves the appearance of divine light and of inner beauty, though in the cheapness of poor furnishings. You have, then, two little books from me. One is a birthday poem in verse, from my yearly song to my patron, to whom I pay daily with body and spirit, but yearly with my tongue, the sweetest tribute of voluntary servitude, offering to Christ a sacrifice of praise on his feast day of consecration and rendering my vows to the Most High. The other little book is one of those which I am thought to have written to my friend Endelechius, a blessed, that is, a Christian man, though I shall not be proven to have published it. For he was the instigator of this little work in the Lord, as his own letter, which is placed at the head of my little book as its theme, shows. I confess that I gladly accepted this task from my friend for this reason: so that in Theodosius I might proclaim not so much an emperor as a servant of Christ, powerful not through the pride of ruling but through the humility of serving, a prince not by his reign but by his faith.
XXIX. Paulinus to Severus, his brother of one mind.

Your letters speak of me in terms that weigh me down, and their love is, as I complain, beyond all measure. But you have tempered it with the fitting and measured grace of gifts that serve my good. For you sent sinners, who need both the prayer and the dress of lament, cloaks woven of camel's hair. As I lie prostrate in the sight of the Most High, they spur me on with useful goads: while the rough bristles prick me, they remind me to be pricked by horror at my sins and to be crushed in spirit within, while they chafe me outwardly as I wear them. Using them also brings many benefits for shaping my faith, through the memory of the saints of old. Elijah, who was taken up, comes to mind, and John, who was sent ahead: a belt bristling with hair girded the one, and the other, as it is written, was clothed in a shaggy covering of camel's hair. I remember too David and all his meekness, when he offered God a broken and humbled heart and put on sackcloth, and covered his soul with fasting so as to clothe it with spiritual fullness. From this we learn that the garment of the soul is the fast by which we abstain from everything that God's law forbids. We learn the same from the stripping of our first parents, who were left naked after they ceased to fast from the forbidden food. The prophet himself also teaches us with what kind of fast he protected his soul from the nakedness of shame, when he says to the Lord: "I have kept my foot from every evil way, that I may keep your word."

The wool of your gift also brings to mind the camel of the Gospel, which passes more easily through the eye of a needle than a rich man enters the kingdom of heaven. This makes me think of my own riches, which now consist only of sins. Since I cannot aspire to virtues like those of the godly men I have named, I long that at least the grace of that tax collector may come to me. With a crushed heart he accused himself before God. He beat his afflicted breast again and again, and he did not dare to lift to heaven eyes cast down by a guilty conscience. His load of iniquity and vice rivalled the camel's hump, yet he drew himself in to the humility that was due, and the self-levelling of a repentant soul made him straight. So he threaded himself through the eye of the needle, that is, through the way of the Word or of the cross, which leads by a narrow path to life, and he reached the ears of God. For, as Scripture says, "the prayer of one who humbles himself pierces the clouds." That rich Pharisee, on the other hand, was puffed up by his spirit of boasting. He reckoned up works that he owed, for the law made him a debtor bound to do them, yet he spoke as though he had done them of his own free will, beyond what was due. He was a herald of himself and an accuser of another, and he called God to account rather than asked anything of him. He could not enter, because narrow places do not admit the overstuffed. Broad boasting could not be received where narrow humility had drawn itself in, and, narrower than the narrow way, had passed through by the slenderness of a contrite heart.

May your prayers intercede for me, so that the needle of the Lord's cross, threaded with the saving word, may mend my soul, which is torn by much corruption and haphazardly pinned together with the thorns of my own senses. For I take faith and the word of Christ's cross to be this needle. By it the garment of our life is renewed and our mind is pricked, and we ourselves are sewn onto God through the intercession of the Mediator himself. In him too is that eye of the needle, because through him and in him lies that way to life, desired by many and passed by few, through which humbled iniquity enters more easily than proud righteousness. So I owe you all the greater thanks as spiritual physicians, for even your bodily gifts bring me spiritual benefit. You have sent me these cloaks as a goad to prayer and a garb of humility, like the basket of dung for that barren fig tree. In this, it seems to me, the eternal usefulness of devout humility is shown. Humility makes the barren soul fruitful, so that it does not, like that Pharisee, admire itself in an empty show of arrogance and run riot with useless leaves, like a tree that bears no fruit. How good and useful such dung is for cultivating salvation we learn from blessed Job, who ceased to be tempted once he had sat down on the dunghill. By perfect humility he had worn out the tempter's envy, for such humility can more easily rise than be cast down. One who sits in dung has nowhere to fall from, but he has the means to rise, through him who raises the needy from the earth, lifts the poor from the dunghill, and brings the proud down to dung. For, as it is written, everyone who is proud is unclean before God. That is why the man who accused himself of iniquity was more righteous before God than the man who proclaimed his own righteousness. The one accused himself by praising himself; the other defended himself by accusing himself.

So let us not flatter ourselves about our own works, but always commend our spirit into his hands, for with him is the fountain of life. Let us ask him for understanding of our way, for a man's steps are directed by the Lord. And even if, with his help, we are able to keep his commandments, we must still confess that we are unprofitable, because we cannot claim credit for service that we owe if we do no more than what is commanded. For that servant is unprofitable and worthless who adds nothing of his own willing devotion to the duty he is bound to perform. If he pays only the dues of his station, he will have no grounds to hope for a reward. Therefore even when we fulfil the commandments, let us always fear, as I often write to you, and say to the Lord: "Do not enter into judgement with your servant, for no one living shall be justified in your sight." The merit of vigorous service cannot commend us, sluggish as we are, but at least the humility of confession may win us acceptance with the Lord as modest servants. The Ninevites too prove how great a remedy it is, in the sight of God's mercy, for the sinner not to spare himself. Reconciled to God by the support of repentance, they were found worthy to escape the destruction that had been announced, because they tormented themselves with voluntary mourning and so forestalled God's sentence with their own.

I have nothing worthy to give you in return, either in words or in things. Yet I have one resource, love, and in that alone I am your equal. So I have sent you a tunic, and because I have worn it, please accept it as a rag picked up from the worthless dungheap. At least this much suits your innocence: it is woven from the tender fleece of lambs and is soft to the touch. I can add something more to its value and charm, which proves it all the more worthy of your use. It is a keepsake given to me as a blessing by Melania, a holy woman, illustrious among the saints of God. That is why it seemed more fitting for you, since your faith makes you closer kin to her than my blood makes me. I confess, though, that I was bold. Although I had meant it for you from the moment I received it, I took the lead and inaugurated it by wearing it myself. I knew that I would do you more service by this wrong than if I had honoured you with it untouched and new. At the same time I wanted to take a blessing for myself in advance, as if from a garment that was already yours, so that I could boast that I share your clothing, since, God willing, I had put on the tunic you would wear as though you had worn it already.

To your gifts and letters the Lord added this further grace: brother Victor reached me in the very days when I welcomed that holy woman herself, returning from Jerusalem after twenty-five years. What a woman she is, if she may be called a woman when she is so manfully Christian [?]! What am I to do at this point? Fear of boring you beyond endurance forbids me to add any more to my long letters. But the dignity of the person, or rather the grace of God, seems to demand that, having come to the mention of so great a soul, I should not pass over her in haste. Sailors who catch sight of some notable spot on the shore do not sail straight past it; they slacken their sails a little or rest their oars, and feast their eyes on the view. In the same way I should turn the course of my discourse aside for a little while to tell you about her. In this way I may also seem to make some return for that book of yours, so illustrious in its matter and its eloquence, if I celebrate a woman who, though of the weaker sex, fights for Christ with the virtues of Martin. Noble through her grandfathers who were consuls, she has made herself nobler still by despising noble birth according to the flesh.

I think it also adds to the abundance of God's grace that I begin my proclamation of her praiseworthy holiness with praise of her family. The most learned Luke is my witness that this order is taken not so much from the rules of the rhetoricians as from the examples of the Gospel. He revealed the merit of the blessed Baptist by starting from the distinction of his origin. And so that you will not think he mentioned the noble father of the Lord's forerunner merely for the sake of the story, he adds the venerable marks of ancient nobility and gives each parent a pedigree. He says that Zechariah was a priest of the course of Abijah, I believe in order to show by this very fact the dignity of his merit. He adds the name, no doubt a distinguished one among the Hebrews, of the priestly course to which Zechariah belonged and in which he had been allotted and exercised his honoured priesthood. Then he adds: "And his wife was of the daughters of Aaron." You see that the evangelist made the mention of their birth into a declaration of the saints' merits, putting ancestral names before the people whom he was about to praise for their own merits. "And his wife," he says, "was of the daughters of Aaron." By recalling the nobility of his marriage he increased the merit of the priest, and before praising his life he praised his family. So Zechariah would appear the more venerable, since with inborn holiness, as if by an inheritance of righteousness, he was worthy of holy ancestors, and as their successor he recalled Aaron, the foremost name among priests, both in the honour of his office and in the lineage of his wife. And she, who drew the yoke of truth in harmony with her husband along the way, was chosen through an angel to give birth to the one of whom it is written: "Behold, I will send my angel before your face." So she would appear more worthy both of her priestly husband and of a son to be ranked above the prophets, since not only a righteous life but also the privilege of her family had made her fit for divine gifts. Even the Lord himself had, besides the birth that flows from the divine source, this other birth by which he deigned to be the Son of Man, and two evangelists begin their account of it by listing his ancestors from the beginning. The two writers trace different lines of bodily descent, with equal faithfulness and dignity. For it was fitting that the only-begotten of God, the firstborn of all creation and the head of the whole body, should hold the first place even in the dignity of his bodily lineage. So the one Son of God in heaven, born before the ages from a beginning beyond words, also claimed on earth the highest of illustrious titles, renowned offspring of kings and priests alike, as the two authors testify. So I shall not seem to be following someone else's rule rather than our own if I proclaim the earthly nobility of this handmaid of God as well. For it is plain that the Lord made this too serve the glory of his work, so that this world, which glories in such titles, might be all the more put to shame. What human vanity uses to despise God, she used instead to despise the world. At the same time the authority of her saving example would be displayed all the more for humbling the eyes of the proud. A woman of the highest rank cast herself down, in a sublime way, to the practice of humility for love of Christ. Strong in the weaker sex, she would rebuke idle men; rich yet made poor, noble yet humbled, she would put to shame the arrogant of both sexes.

Her grandfather was the consul Marcellinus. To satisfy the ambitions of her family and the luxury of their wealth, she submitted to marriage while still of tender years, and soon became a mother. But she did not enjoy that mortal happiness for long, lest she love earthly things too long. Besides other bereavements, which she mourned with her husband while he still shared them, labouring in vain over children lost before birth, her sorrows grew until within the space of a year she lost two sons and her husband. Only one little child was left to her, more a reminder of her affections than a compensation for them. But the Lord provides us with the causes of heavenly goods out of the seeds of our ills, and through the losses of human love she conceived a love for God. She was made wretched so that she might be made blessed. She was struck so that she might be healed, for "I will strike, and I will heal," says the Lord. So great is the loving-kindness of the Father on high that even his anger comes from mercy, and he chastises in order to spare. So the blessed apostle was blinded in order to be enlightened. The persecutor fell so that the apostle might rise. On his journey he found the Way, and on the road of ungodliness he came to know the way of peace. In the same way the good Lord, at every time and to this very day, as he himself testified, works the works of the Father, spending the same loving-kindness even on us, the least of all. So too he corrected this holy woman with a father's love, not because he thought her unfaithful but to make her perfect. In mercy he struck her with trials so that he might crown her patience; for he scourges every son whom he receives. So, having followed the sorrowful procession of three funerals, widowed and bereaved alike, she came to Rome with her only son, who stirred up her tears rather than consoled them. Perhaps the infant felt their misfortunes before he was even aware of himself, and already knew how to mourn another's death when he did not yet know his own life. Or perhaps, wretchedly carefree in his ignorant infancy, he laughed at his pitiful games amid his mother's laments.

These lessons taught her not to let her life be bounded by this fragile world, and to place her hope in God alone, since he is the only one we cannot lose against our will. She put on a knowledge that brought salvation to herself and to her son: she loved her little one by neglecting him and kept him by letting him go. She would hold him more firmly absent, having commended him to the Lord, than she would embrace him present if she had trusted him to herself. As far as her circumstances allowed, she imitated the faithful vow of barren Hannah. Her own fruitfulness, so full of loss, had brought her close to barrenness. She feared becoming, after her fruitfulness had been emptied, what Hannah had been before she was granted fruitfulness, and so she dedicated a different gift to God with the same devotion. Hannah was anxious about conceiving a child, Melania about the child she had already borne. Hannah prayed that she might begin to be a mother, Melania that she might not cease to be one. Someone may judge the two cases unlike, because Melania's son was not placed in the temple to serve the Lord as Hannah's was, but enjoys the wealth and honours of the world. Yet see how, on the other side, the balance of devotion and faith is made equal: what glorious Hannah paid to the Lord in her son, Melania paid in her own person. Hannah was afterwards repaid for the vowed Samuel with more children. For Melania her only son was the sum of all her children and the end of her mourning. When Hannah had entrusted her firstborn to service in the temple, she was consoled by other children at home, by the fact that her son, though consecrated, was not far away, and by her regular visits back to the temple. Melania, once she had cut her only son from her breast and cast him into the bosom of Christ for the Lord himself to bring up, gave him nothing of her own care afterwards. She judged it a sin of distrust to look after one whom she had entrusted to Christ. How great was the faith with which she did this can be seen from the fact that, although she had a great many very powerful and dear relatives at Rome, she would not hand her little one over to any of them, even with a word, as the saying goes, to be raised, educated and protected. So certain was she that Christ had taken him up. And so she deserved to keep him, because she refused to enjoy him, and now she has deserved to see him again through the devotion of that faith by which, having once left him in God's hands, she did not long for him in this world. Therefore he who is mighty, and who gives believers more than they would dare to expect, has done great things for her. He granted her besides that she should see her son even in this life, just as he gave Solomon, because he chose to ask for wisdom, the other riches too, which he had not asked for, and gave them precisely because he had not desired them. Rewarding the good understanding by which Solomon had preferred the highest things to the lowest, he poured out the lesser gifts on top of the greater. So the man who chose to seek the highest things deserved to become the possessor of all riches. By this example we are all advised to be wise when we are taught to choose. For if we put lesser goods before greater ones and the lowest before the highest, that is, the earthly before the heavenly, then as the penalty of our foolish greed we shall lack every good, the highest and the lowest alike. We shall justly not receive the goods we did not desire, and we shall deservedly be cheated of the goods whose harmful love made us neglect the better ones. So too father Abraham received back the only son he offered to God, because he offered him readily when he was asked. The sacrifice of devotion completed in his heart was enough for the Lord. So, putting out an angel's hand, he caught the right hand of the father as it was already poised to strike, and set in place of the victim a sheep provided on the spot, so that God would not lack an offering nor the father his son. At the same time the mystery that was to be fulfilled in Christ, rehearsed in Isaac as far as an image could, was given shape in the ram. For the lamb that was later to be sacrificed in Egypt as a figure of the Saviour was already foreshadowed in an animal of its own kind, that is, in the ram that came forward as a victim in Isaac's place, so as to run ahead as a figure in Christ's place. So the ram was found for the one to whom the fullness of the mystery was not owed, but it was slain for the one for whom the perfecting of the sacrament was reserved.

Even at the first stages of this service she had many struggles against the envious dragon. The spite of the jealous enemy did not let her depart easily and in peace. He armed the whole power of her noble relatives to hold her back, and tried to thwart her purpose and block her way. But she had already been strengthened beyond the force of these temptations. While everyone wept, she joyfully cast off both the bonds of bodily affection and the moorings of her ship. She boldly took on the waves of the sea, so as not to have overcome only the waves of the world, and set sail. Leaving behind both the world and her homeland, she chose, by a spiritual gift, the city of Jerusalem as the place to live as a pilgrim away from the body, becoming an exile from her fellow citizens and a fellow citizen of the saints. Wisely and in holiness she chose to serve in the city that is in slavery, so that she might reign in the city that is free.

Of the many virtues of God in her I will proclaim at least one, and by it all her works can be judged. In the time of Valens, when the fury of the Arians was persecuting the Church of the living God with the emperor himself as the henchman of ungodliness, she was the leader or the companion of all who stood firm for the faith. She took in those who had been driven out, or went along with those who had been arrested. She had taken into hiding men who, because of their outstanding faith, were attacked by the heretics with special hatred, and who could be sheltered only at the cost of odium to those who hid them. Then a serious uproar, kindled by the devil's torches, broke out, and she was ordered, as one who defied the law of the state, to be dragged out and to suffer what awaited those men, unless she preferred to betray them. She came forward fearlessly, eager to suffer and exulting in the wrong of having her property confiscated. She did not even wait to be dragged, but flew ahead of those who were to drag her to the judge. He was so overcome by reverence at her presence that he did not carry out the wrath of unbelief, because he marvelled at the boldness of faith. In that same storm she fed five thousand monks in hiding with her own bread for three days, so that through her hand the Lord Jesus again fed the same number as he once had in the desert. It was all the more costly an act of mercy now, because those in hiding had less freedom to be cared for than the people long ago who had gathered to the Lord of their own will, in liberty and peace. She was not afraid of being caught, but confidently performed this forbidden service. She did not want to be known for the glory of the deed, yet its very greatness betrayed her, and she was as glorious among men for the number of her witnesses as she was known to God for the number of those she fed. Let us consider what merit she has. In the history of the Kings that man is celebrated who fed a hundred men of God hidden from the wrath of a king who was just as ungodly. Can anyone doubt, then, that she, who in a similar work surpassed this number a thousand times over, has borne fruit a hundredfold?

I will now pass over the rest of her deeds and years. To match her course, I will cross the very sea she sailed on her way back, so that I may sooner bring my discourse to an end by describing her arrival among us, in which I witnessed the great grace of God. She landed at the city of Naples, a short distance from the town of Nola where I live. There her children and grandchildren came to meet her, and she soon hurried on to Nola, to my humble lodging, arriving hedged about by an ostentatious retinue of her very wealthy family. In that procession of the mother and her children we saw the glory of the Lord. They were indeed in the procession, but in very different style. She sat on a lean little nag, worth less than a donkey, while senators escorted her with all the pomp of this world that men of rank and wealth could muster: swaying carriages, horses with ornamented harness, gilded coaches and many wagons, so that the Appian Way groaned and glittered. But the grace of Christian humility outshone the splendours of vanity. The rich marvelled at the poor saint, but our poverty laughed at them. We saw a confusion of this world worthy of God: purple, silk and gilded trappings in the service of old black rags. We blessed the Lord, who makes the humble lofty and wise, fills them with good things, and sends the rich away empty. Yet that same day we marvelled at the poverty of spirit that these rich people had gained from their mother's riches, for they gloried more in their mother's holy want than in their own visible abundance. The glory of the Lord seemed to be at work in this very thing, that we saw the riches of our dear poor woman in her children. So already in this life she was reaping the fruit of her faith, as she looked down on her own victory over the vanity of this world and saw close at hand all that she had left behind for Christ and had persisted in despising. Her children, dressed in silk and accustomed to shine in the toga or the stola according to their sex, were glad to touch with their hands her coarse tunic, which seemed woven of broom fibre, and her cheap little cloak. They longed to spread their own garments, precious with golden thread and fine workmanship, under her feet, and to have them rubbed against her rags. They believed that they would be cleansed of the contagion of their riches if they were found worthy to pick up some dirt from her shabby clothing or from her footprints.

Our little hut is raised off the ground as an upper storey and runs some length along a single portico, with guest cells set between. As if the Lord's grace had enlarged it, its cramped quarters proved big enough not only for the many saints who came with her but also for the crowds of those rich people. There the nearby roofs of our patron Felix echoed as choirs of boys and virgins sang. Nor did the guests on the other side of the same dwelling make a disturbing din, though their way of life was at odds with ours. Even in them a religious restraint imitated the silence of our discipline. Drowsy from sluggish bellies, they might pretend not to join in singing with those keeping vigil, yet they did not dare to strike a discordant note against the holy voices. They were kept in order by a faithful fear, and so, with the tumult of the worldly crowds hushed by the gentle voices of the psalm-singers, they too joined in the harmony, even in silence. But to return to the Lord's perfect dove: know now how great is this power of God in the weaker sex. For her, fasting is refreshment, prayer is rest, the word is bread, and rags are clothing. Her bed is a little cloak and a patchwork quilt, hard on the ground, but it becomes soft through reading, for the pleasure of reading eases the harshness of her rigid couch, and for a holy soul, to keep vigil in the Lord is to rest. So the daughter of Zion had her until now and longs for her; now the daughter of Babylon has her and marvels at her, for that city too is now in many respects more a daughter of Zion than a daughter of Babylon. And so it marvels at her as she lives in the obscurity of humility and in the light of truth, giving the rich incentives to faith and the poor consolation in their hardships. Yet she, burning with longing for her quiet and her retreat at Jerusalem, now cries out amid the crowds of Rome: "Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged! Was I held back so that I should now dwell with the inhabitants of Kedar?" For among the Hebrews, as I have learned, this name means darkness. So I think we should congratulate her on the virtues I have described, but also fear for her present abode. May so remarkable a soul give more to Rome than she takes from Rome. May she so sit by the rivers of Babylon as to remember Zion, and hang up the instrument of her body, out of reach of all the snares and allurements of hostile Babylon. Set firm in the steady course of her purpose, as on willows ever alive with their native moisture, may she never cease to flourish. Through abiding constancy of faith and the grace of virtue may her leaf not fall, so that, as her life is watched along the journey, her praise may also be sung at its end.

I could not bear, brother, that she should not know you. So that she might know God's grace in you more fully, I made you known to her through your own words rather than mine. For I myself read our Martin aloud to her, since she is most eager for such histories. In the same way I revealed you to the venerable and most learned bishop Niceta, who had come from Dacia and was deservedly admired by the Romans, and to very many of God's saints. In truth I was not so much proclaiming you as boasting of myself. For it is my glory that you are esteemed and loved, since your life, in harmony with your tongue, testifies that you are a servant of truth. On that day may the Lord grant us mercy from the Lord, through this grace of which he himself is the author. As we are now refreshed in the depths of your love, so may we be cooled from the flames we deserve by the finger of your lot. For I hope that, by the Lord's indulgence, we who love you so dearly shall have the support of your righteousness, even if, being unworthy, we dare not hope to share your crown.
XXX. Paulinus to his holy brother Severus, one with him in heart.

It was said to the blessed apostle: "Much learning has driven you mad." In this the real madness is that of the people to whom the wisdom of God that Paul spoke was foolishness. Empty of faith in the truth, they did not deserve to understand the wisdom of God, which is Christ. By Christ's favour I am not like those whose unbelief made that teacher of sound sense seem mad to them. Still, the freedom that comes from our oneness of heart, which our shared faith binds even more closely, lets me borrow their words, though not their attitude, and say: Severus, my Severus, your great love has made you almost delirious. Toward me, your little one in understanding though not in age, you are like a grandfather with a late-born grandson. Your excessive fondness has made you foolish, if your good sense will pardon my saying so.

How am I to answer the request in which you asked me to have our portraits painted and sent to you? By the depths of love, I beg you: what comfort for true love do you look for in empty shapes? What sort of image do you want us to send you, that of the earthly man or that of the heavenly? I know you long for that incorruptible beauty which the heavenly King has loved in you. No other form of ours can be of any use to you except the one in whose likeness you yourself were formed. It is by that form that you love your neighbour as yourself and wish to stand above us in nothing, so that nothing between us may seem unequal. But I am poor and sorrowful. I am still caked with the grime of the earthly image, and in my fleshly senses and earthly deeds I resemble the first Adam more than the second. How shall I dare to paint myself for you, when my earthly corruption shows that I deny the image of the heavenly? Shame hems me in on both sides. I blush to paint what I am, and I dare not paint what I am not. I hate what I am, and I am not what I love. But what good will it do me, wretch that I am, to hate wickedness and love virtue, when I keep doing what I hate and am too lazy to work at doing what I love? At odds with myself, I am torn apart by civil war, for the spirit fights against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit, and the law of the body, by the law of sin, attacks the law of the mind. Unhappy man that I am, for not even the wood of the cross has let me digest the poisoned taste of the hostile tree! That venom inherited from Adam still lives in me, the venom with which our father, when he transgressed, infected his whole race. By natural goodness I had the eyes of my mind open to innocence and closed to wickedness. Yet when I chose evil by eating the ill-fated food of the forbidden grove, I drank in a deadly knowledge of good and evil, and I was blinded and wrongly enlightened at the same time.

If only I had at least washed away the crime of unlawful desire by this remedy: having gained the knowledge of good and evil through that harmful taste, I could have chosen the good! This is all the more true because I had heard the saving counsel of God urging me, when water and fire, life and death were set before me, to stretch out my hand to the water and choose the gift of life. But my crime of folly grew into the guilt of presumption. Although I had been given the choice of the good as well, I preferred to go after what did me harm. What pardon for sin is left to me, wretch that I am, when I no longer have the excuse of ignorance? I recognized the good and did evil, though I was just as free to do good. I could have done it if I had not, through a fault of the will, despised what was good for my soul. By that fault I did what was not to my advantage, because I did not keep myself within what was permitted. So I rightly lost those eyes of innocence with which I did not see evil, and in exchange I received these eyes of wickedness, with which sin is recognized and conscience is punished.

Scripture declares that the first parents of the human race both saw and did not see. "The woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes to look at." It says she saw, so she had eyes. And what does it add next? "When they had eaten, their eyes were opened." So they had been blind. From this we notice that blindness and sight of the eyes cannot exist together in the same body. Yet there is certainly something blind in us even when we see, and something seeing even in the blind. I think this is why the Lord said: "For judgement I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind." He came into this world to seek what was lost and to give light again to what had been blinded. And so man, needing this physician, cries out in the prophet: "Light up my darkness, O Lord." The Lord is merciful and compassionate. In the darkness of human blindness he rose as a light, to raise up the crushed, to free those in chains, to give light to the blind. How then could he have come to blind those who see? Indeed, the gospel teaches us that he gave sight back to many blind people and took it away from no one. But it is written in the law, "I will kill and I will make alive," and also in the gospel that "he is set for the fall and the rising of many." The saying "For judgement I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind" is meant in the same way. The Lord came so that the old things might pass away and new things arise. And what he had said was fulfilled: "I will kill and I will make alive." By taking on our old man he put it to death, nailing it to the cross. Stripping himself of the flesh, he made a public show of the principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself. And he brought the new man to life from the resurrection of the dead, ascending on high and setting him in the heavenly places.

So he came to give light to the blind and to blind those who see. The eyes that had been opened to transgression were to be blinded, and in turn the eyes that had been blinded were to be opened. I am blind in a good way if I do not see sin, and sharp-sighted in a good way if I discern righteousness. Pray, then, my brother, that the Lord may do both in me. May he blind my seeing part, so that I do not see vanity, and give light to my unseeing part, so that I may see what is right. May he put to death in me the old man with his deeds, so that my flesh may bloom again in Christ and my youth may be renewed like the eagle's. For this is "the change of the right hand of the Most High," when we are changed from ourselves into the man who has been created according to God and whose image is heavenly, and put off the man who is corrupted according to the desires of error. I pray that God may crush that man's image in me. May he bring to nothing our image, the earthly one, in the beleaguered city, and restore and complete in us his own image. We are not ashamed to be painted in that image, and if we bear it we may truly say: "My heart and my flesh have failed; God of my heart, and God my portion for ever." By the good change that comes to man from the right hand of the Most High, my heart and my flesh will fail, that is, the acts of my will and the fruits of my flesh. Then at last, freed from bodily bonds and cleansed of my own heart, may I dare to say: "God of my heart, and God my portion for ever." May the word of Simeon in the gospel be fulfilled in me, so that Christ may become for me a fall and a rising: a fall for my outer man and a rising for my inner man. May sin fall in me, sin that stands when the soul falls, and may the immortal man rise, who fell when sin rose. The standing of the outer man is the fall of the inner man. That is why, when the outer man grows weak, the inner man is renewed day by day. In this sense the perfect teacher says: "When I am weak, then I am strong."

But thanks be to the Lord, who has painted our likenesses with a more lasting and living art. He has not painted them on panels that rot or in wax that melts, but on the fleshly tablets of your heart. There you keep us imprinted and shaped to your soul by the unity of faith and grace, and you will look on us in an undivided and ever-present gaze, not only here but also in the eternal age. Even here, if your love is so great that you want to catch hold of visible comforts too, you can use the lines your mind draws as a guide and describe us even to painters who lack skill or do not know us. You can set your memory before them, the memory in which you hold us painted, as though offering them the faces of sitters to copy. But the hand may be too unskilled in its art to follow your words and so go astray. Then it will paint us looking unlike ourselves to others. Yet you always contemplate us and embrace us in your mind, so whatever faces its inexperience paints under our name, in your heart we shall still be ourselves.
XXXI. Paulinus to his holy brother Severus, one with him in heart.

Among his other accounts of your works and vows, brother Victor told us that you want a blessing from the holy relics of the saints for the basilica you have just built at our Primuliacum, which is larger than the earlier one. With it your household church would be adorned, as befits your faith and grace. The Lord is witness that if we had had even a scruple of holy ashes beyond what we shall need to dedicate the basilica that will shortly be completed in the Lord's name, we would have sent it to you, who are one with us in heart. But we did not have a supply of this gift. Victor also told us that you have high hopes of the same grace from the holy Silvia, who had promised him relics of many martyrs from the East. So we have found something worthy to send you, both to sanctify the basilica and to crown the blessing of the holy ashes: part of a fragment of the wood of the divine cross. This treasure was brought to us from Jerusalem by the blessed Melania, a gift from John, the holy bishop there. Our common fellow servant has sent it especially to our venerable sister Bassula. But what is given to one of you belongs to both of you, because the same principle remains in each of you, and faith does away with the difference of sex as you both hasten together to the perfect man. So receive it from your brothers, who are one with you in heart and long to share with you in every good thing. Receive a great gift in a small one. In a sliver of a tiny splinter, almost an atom, take a safeguard of present salvation and a pledge of eternal salvation. Do not let your faith be narrowed by fleshly eyes that see only small things. Let it see with its inward vision the whole power of the cross in this tiniest piece. When you think that you are looking at that wood on which our salvation, the Lord of majesty, hung nailed while the world trembled, rejoice with trembling. Let us remember too that the rocks split at the sight of this cross, and let us at least imitate the stones and split our hearts with the fear of God. Let us also consider that the veil of the temple was torn by the same mystery of the cross. Let us understand that the tearing of that veil was held out before us so that, when we hear the voice of the Lord and the mystery of his boundless love, we may not harden our hearts. Instead we should separate ourselves from fleshly things and tear the veil of unbelief, so that with the face of our heart unveiled we may see the mysteries of God's saving gifts.

We do not write this so that you will copy the way we have presented it, enclosing an object of such blessing in a little golden tube. Rather, in this adornment we have imitated your faith, sending you your own likeness in the form of gold. For we know that, like gold tried in the fire, you have within you the kingdom of God, that is, faith in the cross, by which the kingdom of heaven is taken by storm. "For if," he says, "we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him." So we have sent you, in the Lord, the gift of the saving wood. It is not meant to strengthen your faith, since by faith you have gone beyond the need for sight. It is because of the merit of your faith, which you received by hearing and prove by your deeds. We sent it so that you might possess in the body also the cross that you hold in the spirit and carry by the strength of your resolve.

Faith itself seems to call for it, so I think it not out of place to tell the particular history of how the cross was uncovered and found after the time of the passion, for it deserves to be known. If that history is unknown, it is easy to see how hard it would be to prove that this wood comes from the Lord's cross. It is certain that if it had fallen into the hands of the Jews, who took every precaution against faith in Christ, it would have been broken up and burned. The men who sealed the tomb would not have been careless about getting rid of the cross. They could not have allowed the passion of one to be honoured through a surviving cross when they cannot bear to see honour paid to his resurrection, which was proven when their seals were broken and the tomb emptied. Why then ask now where it had been hidden? Plainly, unless it had lain hidden, it would have been destroyed, especially in the times of persecution that followed the hostility of the Jews and almost surpassed it in savagery. We can easily guess how violently those who persecuted even the place of the cross would have cut the cross to pieces if they had seen that it still existed. For the emperor Hadrian thought he would destroy the Christian faith by desecrating the place. On the site of the passion he consecrated a statue of Jupiter, and Bethlehem was profaned by a shrine of Adonis. He thought that the root and foundation of the Church would be torn up if idols were worshipped in the places where Christ was born in order to suffer, suffered in order to rise again, and rose again in order to reign as judge, or rather to judge as king. Woe is me! The almighty Lord did not refuse to endure even these things for our sake. Where he had hung crucified for the salvation of the human race, there he was scorned by the sacrilege of men. At his cross the world had been shaken, the sun had fled, the tombs had burst open as the dead were raised, and the whole of nature had tottered. Yet above that cross stood the statue of a demon, and the altar of the statue smoked with the burnt flesh of cattle. The name of god was bestowed on statues of the dead, while he who is the God of the living, and himself the resurrection of the dead, was blasphemed with the reproach of a man who had not only died but been crucified. In Bethlehem too, where the ox had known its owner and the ass its master's manger, the rulers of men denied God the Saviour and worshipped the shameful loves and deaths of men. A new star had revealed the cradle of the eternal King, and there the Chaldeans had knelt and worshipped with their treasures. In that same place the Romans consecrated barbarous lusts. Where the shepherds, on that night lit up with light, had greeted the newborn Saviour with heavenly joy as they sang along with the army of angels, there harlots mixed with eunuchs lamented the lover of Venus. What sorrow! What devotion of men could make up for such impiety? Where the holy infancy of the newborn Saviour had cried, there an infamous rite howled with the wanton wailing of those who act out the lament of Venus. Where the Virgin had given birth, adulterers were worshipped.

This outrage of the former age lasted until the times of Constantine, which are close to our own. He earned his place as first among Christian emperors as much by the faith of his mother Helena as by his own. She was inspired by divine counsel, as the outcome showed. When she came to know Jerusalem, she, who shared the throne with him under the title of Augusta, asked him to give her the means to cleanse all the places there that bore the imprint of the Lord's footsteps and were marked by the memorials of his divine works for us. She wanted to destroy the temples and idols, purify those places from every taint of profane impiety, and restore them to her religion, so that the Church might at last be honoured in the land of its origin. Her son the emperor readily agreed. Once the treasuries had been thrown open for holy works, the mother and Augusta made full use of the whole imperial purse. With all the expense and splendour a queen could command and religion could urge, she built basilicas that covered and adorned every place where the Lord our Redeemer had accomplished for us the saving mysteries of his love, through the sacraments of his incarnation, passion, resurrection and ascension. One thing among these is marvellous. In the basilica of the Ascension there is the spot from which he was taken up in a cloud and ascended, leading our captivity captive in his flesh. That spot alone is said to have been so hallowed by the divine footprints that it has never allowed itself to be covered with marble or paved. The ground always rejects and throws off whatever human hands, eager to adorn it, have tried to lay on it. So in the whole extent of the basilica this spot alone stays green, looking like its own turf. Its sand, plain to see and within reach of those who venerate it, preserves the reverence imprinted by the divine feet on the dust that God trod, so that it can truly be said: "We have worshipped where his feet stood."

But hear a great and truly divine miracle in the history of the cross. When that venerable queen came to Jerusalem, she went over all the places there and round about with diligence and devotion. She was eager to see the signs of divine works and longed to take in with her eyes the faith she had received with devout ears and from writings. Then she set out to search most earnestly for the Lord's cross. But what way or method was there of finding it, when no reliable informant could be found? The great age of the place and the long reign of impious superstition had wiped out the memory and care that a religious conscience or observance would have kept. Yet the Lord, who knows and witnesses everything hidden in the earth and in hearts, was there, and the faithful woman earned the Holy Spirit through her devoted love. Under his inspiration, after she had diligently but vainly sought something that God had removed from human knowledge, she set herself to learn at least the place of the passion. So she sought out not only Christians full of learning and holiness but also the most knowledgeable of the Jews, as informants about their own impiety, in which the wretches even glory. She summoned them and gathered them in Jerusalem. Then all of them agreed in a single testimony about the place. At once, no doubt driven by the impulse of the revelation she had received, she ordered the work of digging to begin on that very spot. A workforce of citizens and soldiers alike was soon got ready and quickly finished the labour of this undertaking. Against everyone's hopes, but in keeping with the faith of the queen alone, the hollows of the earth were opened by deep excavation and the secret of the hidden cross came to light. But three crosses were found together, just as they had once stood fixed for the Lord and the robbers. Then the joy at their discovery began to be confused by anxious doubt, from the rightful fear of the devout that they might choose a robber's gibbet in place of the Lord's cross, or dishonour the saving wood by throwing it away as a robber's stake. The Lord looked on the devout cares of these people burning with faith. On her above all, who led them in this devout concern, he poured the light of a plan: she ordered that someone recently dead be sought out and brought there. There was no delay. The order was given, and the corpse was brought in. It was laid down, and one of the crosses was brought close to the lying body, and then another. But death scorned the wood of the guilty. At last resurrection revealed the Lord's cross. At the touch of the saving wood death fled, the corpse was shaken out of its funeral, and the body rose up. The living trembled as the dead man stood. Freed from his grave-bands, like Lazarus of old, he immediately walked about among those who watched, restored to life.

So the Lord's cross was covered over for so many ages. It was hidden from the Jews at the time of the passion, and it was not revealed to the pagans when they built their shrine, though they were no doubt digging up earth for that very building. Was it not kept hidden by the hand of God so that it might be found now, when it was being sought with devotion? In this way, as befitted the cross of Christ, the cross of Christ was found and proven by the test of resurrection. Soon it was consecrated with a fitting setting, a basilica built on the place of the passion. The basilica gleams with gilded ceilings and is rich with golden altars, and it keeps the cross laid up in a secret shrine. Every year, when the Lord's Pasch is celebrated, the bishop of that city brings it out for the people to adore, and he himself leads those who venerate it. Apart from this day, when the mystery of the cross is celebrated, the cross itself, which is the cause of the sacraments, is not brought out as an emblem of the sacred festival, except now and then at the request of very devout people. These have travelled there for this sole purpose, and its unveiling is granted to them as a kind of reward for their long pilgrimage. They say this can be obtained only by favour of the bishop, and it is only by his gift too that these tiny pieces of the holy wood from that same cross may be had, for a great grace of faith and blessing. This cross, though made of senseless matter, holds a living power. Ever since that time it has lent its wood to the prayers of almost countless people every day, yet it suffers no loss and stays as if untouched. Each day it is divided for those who take pieces of it, and it is always whole for those who venerate it. Surely it drew this power of not decaying and this solidity that does not wear away from the blood of that flesh which suffered death but did not see corruption. We hope that for you too it will be not only a memorial of blessing but also a seedbed of incorruption. May the sight of it kindle your faith also by reminding you of that blessed robber. He turned his robbery to good.
