By a moment's faith and a moment's confession he outran the long paths that the saints travel through great labours, and he deservedly took possession of the kingdom ahead of the apostles and martyrs themselves, the kingdom prepared for them, as He says, from the beginning. He was the first to seize it, a holy robber plundering heaven. For he saw Christ crucified, suffering a punishment like his own, in a state that had made even the disciples' faith waver in confusion. Yet he confessed him as the Lord of majesty, which he was. He asked to be remembered in the kingdom of God, and so he believed in the glory of the resurrection before the resurrection itself. The apostles believed in it only after it had happened, and not only by seeing it but by putting it to the test. Even they doubted less about whether the flesh would rise than about what the resurrection would be like. Clearly, since they were to be sent into the whole world to teach all nations, they had to grasp the faith they would preach not only with their ears but also with their eyes, so that they might teach all the more steadfastly what they had learned all the more firmly.
XXXII.

When these little verses had been put in, the page lying open tempted my tongue and my hand to fill the empty space, and it came to mind that I had something to write. For I am exceedingly glad that we have shown a single likeness of heart and body, and of works and vows as well, by adding basilicas to the Lord's sheepfolds at the same time. But you, at that same time, also built a baptistery set between two basilicas, so as to outdo me even in raising these works that are built for the eye to see. But thanks be to the Lord, who has given us something in which we may count even defeat a victory. For I win in my wish, in that I am outdone in grace by one whom in my judgment I place above myself, and in love count my equal. You are the one I am speaking of; you, I say, the greater and better part of me, you my rest, you my joy. In you my head reclines and my mind has its dwelling, and this, not only in the present time but, as I hope and trust in the Lord, will remain mine forever by his gift and in his body and Spirit. So if by the Lord's grace you accomplish anything more, you surely do it with me, and certainly for me.

But in this I fear that into your works, by which you straighten the crooked paths of worldly ways and level the steep ones, you are mixing a stumbling block of offence, out of that affection of yours for me of which I am always complaining. You darken the splendid inscriptions of your devotion in Christ with my name, and you work this injustice into righteous labours, so that you pollute a holy place even with the faces of the wicked. It is right that Martin should be painted in the place where human beings are refreshed, for he bore the image of the heavenly man by his perfect imitation of Christ, so that those who lay aside in the bath the oldness of the earthly image may meet the likeness of a heavenly soul to imitate. But what place is there for me there, who match neither infants in innocence nor men in wisdom, and am set apart from the spotless by my wickedness and from the perfect by my weakness? What fellowship, then, has light with darkness? Wolves with lambs? Serpents with doves, that is, I with Martin? Have you not mixed a cup of milk and gall? Yet it is well that with people placed together in one spot it is not as with liquids blended in one cup: if they differ in merit, the sweetness of the good is not poisoned by the bitterness of the bad. On the contrary, it turns out that the sinner set beside the righteous looks all the dirtier, and the righteous man shines out all the more when compared with the sinner. So I am the less troubled by the error of your love, since you have done that blessed man no wrong but have rather added to his glory, painting the venerable face opposite a despicable one, so that his splendour might flash out more clearly by comparison with darkness, he who shines with conspicuous brightness even among the splendours of the saints. And indeed, if I did not know that you had designed this picture out of the eager zeal of your excessive love for me, I would accuse you of malice and cunning, for setting beside that holy head my lowly person, darkened by the night of the soul and painted on the facing wall opposite. Then you would have painted him alone and rather disfigured me, exposing me, who once Martin's face has been seen deserve to be spat upon, to the shame of a ridiculous comparison.

But because of me, since your great love for me deceives you into making something false, this design of yours, slipping out of love, might be laughed at, as indeed it can and should be. So that this might not happen, I have obeyed you only so far as to send you some verses about this picture of yours, in order to bring out the reasoning behind your plan: that, wholesomely concerned with the formation of the newly baptized, you set before them images far unlike each other, so that those emerging from the sacred font might see at once what to avoid and what to follow. So here it is; use it if you like:

You who wash your souls and limbs in the bath,
see the ways set before you toward good deeds.
Martin stands here, the rule of a perfect life;
Paulinus teaches how you may earn pardon.
Sinners, look at this one; blessed, look at that one;
let that one be a model for the saints, this one for the guilty.

Also on the same:

Rich in wealth for Christ, poor for himself, Severus
set up a beautiful building for the sacred font.
And since he was founding a hall for heavenly acts,
where people would be renewed by the font and by God,
he had a twofold image painted, worthy of the sacraments,
so that the reborn might learn the gifts of life.
The venerable image of one man bears witness to Martin;
the other figure shows the lowly Paulinus.
The one arms faith with examples and bold words,
so that it may carry off undefiled the palms of merit;
the other, redeeming his sins by pouring out his money,
teaches that wealth should be worth less to each than his own salvation.

Surely it is now proved that you are not to be laughed at but rather approved, if you are seen to have painted side by side two so utterly unlike for this reason alone: that in Martin might be seen the form of righteousness and the sum of virtues, and in me the contrition and confession of a conscience aware of its iniquity. So an example would lie open both to the blessed and to the wretched; in him courage would have a mirror, in me sloth a consolation. Those able to fulfil the commandment by their virtues would gaze at him, while those wishing to bring a remedy to their sins would take comfort in me, since for those stripped of the confidence of innocence and bound by the chain of iniquity, only redemption can help, as for captives. Yet I beg you not to make my obedience a crime by removing, as you threatened, those verses of yours of light and honeycomb [?]. I beg that your threat was made more out of modesty than in earnest; and if you think these of mine should be added, let those of yours remain, so that they may be like little gems among these, lending value to cheap things and setting off the dark with the bright. Indeed, having received permission, I told my tongue, not, as the prophet says, to stay at rest and guard my ways, but rather to break the reins of the guard set over it, so long as it was serving you. I love you so much that I would fear the sin of disobeying you more than the sin of much speaking.

For this reason I have also intended some verses for your basilicas, as votive inscriptions, so to speak, for the sacred font. If anything in them seems aptly said, this too is thanks to brother Victor, through whose eyes and words I have seen all that you have done and are doing in Christ the Lord. So you will regard him as the author of the verses I have included about the basilicas as well, since he dictated the material by recounting your deeds. These, then, will be about the baptistery itself; the ones above are only about its painting:

Here the font that begets souls to be renewed
drives a living river with divine light.
The Holy Spirit comes down from heaven into this stream
and weds the sacred waters with a heavenly source;
the wave conceives God, and from its nourishing waters
brings forth holy offspring from eternal seed.
Wondrous is God's kindness: the sinner is plunged in the waves,
and soon emerges from that same water justified.
So a person, passing through a happy setting and rising,
dies to earthly things and rises to things eternal.
Guilt perishes, but life returns; the old Adam dies,
and a new one is born for an eternal kingdom.
Most chaste in body, mind and faith, a dweller in Christ,
Severus joyfully founded this building for God.
He himself flourishes wholly as God's temple, with Christ as his guest,
and carries in his humble heart a rejoicing Lord.
See: as he worships one Mind under a threefold name,
so he has consecrated a threefold work in a holy structure.
He gave the people ample roofs in twin buildings,
so that their number might accord with the sacred Laws.
For as one faith joins in Christ to God
the two testaments made through one lawgiver,
so he set the font under a towered roof
between two halls of different heights,
so that Mother Church may joyfully receive in her twin bosoms
the new offspring the water has brought forth.
The hall is double in its roofs, as the Church is in its testaments,
but one grace of the font is present to both.
The ancient law confirms the new, the new fulfils the old;
in the old is hope, in the new is faith.
But the grace of Christ joins the old and the new;
that is why the font is set in the space between.
From there the priest, as a parent, leads from the sacred font
infants white as snow in body, heart and dress,
and gathering the untried lambs around the festal altars
fills their unaccustomed mouths with saving food.
Here the older throng rejoices with its fellow flock;
the fold bleats Alleluia in new choirs.

Having given these verses to the handmade works of your Unanimity, I could not keep silent about that grace of God not made by hands in your household church, by which he has granted you Clarus to be your guest there forever. So I have ventured to compose verses for his holy memory and to send them to your Unanimity, not because I could say anything worthy of his divine merits, but to express the zeal of my great love for his soul. When you recite them before the Lord to his holy soul, which always shares your dwelling in the Lord, you will excuse my boldness and commend my service.

Bright in the title of his name, and as bright in the light of his mind,
Clarus the priest is covered here; yet only his perishable limbs are in the tomb,
while his mind, freed from the prison of the body, rejoices among the stars,
pure, having gained the seat of the proven and the devout.
His holy bones rest beneath the eternal altar,
so that while chaste offerings are made to the kind Christ,
the fragrance of his soul may be joined to the divine rites.

Also on the same, so that you may choose whichever you prefer. But I know that in this matter what you ought to hesitate over is not which to choose for an inscription, but how to avoid doing an injury to God's saint with any of them.

Here lies the priest Clarus, bright in merit and in name,
Martin's companion in his pursuits and now a sharer in his reward.
The altar is a worthy house for this devout man; beneath it his limbs
are laid, lifeless, for his spirit rejoices in the heavens
and above the stars joins the disciple as an equal to his master.

Clarus, bright in faith, brighter in deed, brightest in fruit,
you who match the title of your name with your merits,
the chaste altar fittingly veils your body,
so that God's altar covers Christ's temple.
But since you are not held in this seat where your body is,
you who, a spirit, fly among the heavenly ones by your merits,
whether you recline in the bosom of the fathers, or are laid beneath the Lord's altar,
or are fed in the sacred grove,
in whatever region of the sky or of paradise you dwell,
Clarus, you live blessed in eternal peace.
Kindly accept these prayers of sinners who ask
that you remember Paulinus and Therasia.
Love those commended to you through the intercession of Severus,
whom you did not know in the body, yet who have thus earned it [?].
Let a common love be the kindling for both of one mind
of an everlasting covenant in the Lord most high.
You cannot tear apart those who are entwined; if you draw one,
the one who is snatched up will snatch up those who cling to him.
So embrace together these inseparable brothers,
and as we are, so love us, sharing yourself between us.
So God called us, so Martin loved us;
so you too, Clarus, protect us equally as equals,
equals not in merits but in love. You, holy one, will be able
by your prayers to make us equals in merit too,
if you labour together with Martin in kindred devotion,
so that your prayers may overcome our sins,
and we may be led together in the lot of your Severus,
and your wing may always shelter us in its fold.

Now suppose the Lord fulfils your soul's desire according to your faith, adding to the adornment and sanctification of your works by letting you obtain sacred ashes from the blessed relics of the glorious apostles or martyrs. I have learned that, in anticipation of this wish, you have prepared another basilica at our Primuliacum, larger than the first. I think it worthy of the work of your faith and of what will no doubt be a most celebrated dedication of a work faithfully carried out, and fitting also for the relics of the saints, that you should venerate this piece of the cross which I sent as well, laid down and consecrated together with them. If this pleases you, these little verses, if you see fit, will announce your decision:

The venerable altar covers a divine covenant:
martyrs laid together with the sacred cross.
All the witnesses of the saving Christ meet here:
the cross, the body, the martyr's blood, God himself.
For God always keeps his gifts for you,
and where Christ is, there are the Spirit and the Father.
So where the cross is, there too is the martyr, since the cross belongs to the martyr,
having been for the saints the holy cause of their martyrdom.
The cross brought forth the food of life for mortals, and the crowns
that make servants sharers with their Lord.
On the cross was fixed the flesh on which I feed; from the cross
flowed that blood by which I drink life and wash my heart.
Christ, let these gifts of yours come together for your Severus;
let him be the bearer and witness of your cross.
Let him live by your flesh, let your blood give him
drink, let him live and act in your word.
And by the way he saw your Martin ascend with his companion Clarus,
let him too go, carried by your gift.

But if you would rather keep this blessing from the cross at hand for daily protection and healing, lest once enclosed in the altar it should not always be ready to hand when need requires, the other grace will also suffice for consecrating the basilica, if we give it to the apostles and martyrs. If their venerable ashes are placed beneath the altar without the company of the cross, this inscription will point out those covered there:

The glory of the divine table veils the pledges of the saints
taken from the bodies of apostles,
and the Spirit of the Lord, present with healing powers,
proves by clear signs that the sacred ashes are alive.
So a twofold grace breathes upon devout prayers,
from the martyrs below and from the sacred rites performed above.
The precious death of the saints, in a little dust,
aids the prayers of the priest and the welfare of the living.

Here you have verses that are indeed unworthy of your holy and magnificent works, but suited to the opinion you hold of me, which you believe more than I do. If you are not ashamed to inscribe them on the walls of your household church for all to see, I shall be avenged. For I believe that then at least you will blush at my follies and regret your desire and your demand, when you look in confusion at buildings that still shine with the unblemished grace of your work, now darkened by the dirges of my foolishness and, to use a word worthy of my verses, smeared with soot, while many laugh or feel sick. Nor will you need to work at deceiving the reader into thinking you the author and charging my song, that is, my crime, to you, since the folly, which no one knows to be in you, will itself inform the reader. Yet you are still to blame, whether you are called the betrayer or the writer. But lest anyone judge me unjust by that rule which prescribes, "What you would not have done to you, do not do to another," you will prove to him by the evidence at hand that I first inflicted the same on my own basilicas. So you will show our unanimity in this too: that, comparing myself to you whether by favour or by injury, I have sinned with the same rashness against your buildings as against my own. But whether this is a favour, as your mind, most patient toward me, will take it, or an injury, as my most unworthy gift deserves, hold our Victor to be its author or its culprit. That most holy interpreter of our love presumed that the more weighed down he came back to you under the unjust burden of my follies, the more welcome he would return to you from me. For he wanted this too added to his bundles: to bring you both the verses and the pictures of my basilicas. And he will be quite right if he comes before you fainting and bent double with this complaint, crying out, "Behold, because of the words of your lips I have walked hard ways," and crying, "Sinners have built upon my back, who have prolonged their iniquity into so many letters."

So I took on this too as an addition to the heap of my sins, granting a brother who was most eager for such a load, by which his soul was lightened as his body was burdened, the injury he desired. For this request of his truly seemed to suit our unanimity, since he insisted that it was right for my buildings in the Lord to become known to you just as you had wished to show me yours in inscriptions and pictures. Persuaded by this reasoning, then, I have taken care to bind my basilicas to yours in writing too, just as they are joined in the time of their building and the kind of vow behind them, so that our union, which is joined in spirit though apart in place, might be pictured in this as well. Thus these buildings also, which we have laboured to construct in the name of the Lord by the same Spirit, though separated in different regions, will be seen as if sealed together in the course of the same letter. That basilica, then, which has now been dedicated and is thronged in the name of the Lord Christ God at the shrine of our lord and common patron, and has been added to his four basilicas, is venerable not only through the honour of blessed Felix but also through relics of apostles and martyrs consecrated beneath the altar within the three-lobed apse. The apse, its floor and walls faced with marble, is made bright by a vault decorated with mosaic, and these are the verses for its picture:

The Trinity shines in its full mystery:
Christ stands as a lamb, the Father's voice thunders from heaven,
and through the dove the Holy Spirit flows down.
A wreath surrounds the cross with a shining circle,
and to this wreath the apostles are a wreath,
represented by a choir of doves.
The holy unity of the Trinity meets in Christ,
though the Trinity also has its own emblems:
the Father's voice and the Spirit reveal him as God,
the cross and the lamb proclaim him the holy victim,
the purple and the palm show his kingship and triumph.
He himself, the rock of the Church, stands upon a rock,
from which four sounding springs flow:
the evangelists, the living rivers of Christ.

On the lower band, where a ledge of plaster set between them joins or divides the boundary of wall and vault, this inscription points out the holy of holies laid beneath the altar:

Here is piety, here kindly faith, here the glory of Christ,
here the cross is joined to its martyrs.
For a little splinter from the wood of the cross is a great pledge,
and the whole power of the cross is in that tiny fragment.
Brought to Nola by the gift of holy Melania,
this supreme good came from the city of Jerusalem.
The holy altar veils a twofold honour for God,
uniting the cross with the ashes of apostles.
How fitly the bones of the devout are joined to the wood of the cross,
so that those slain for the cross may find rest upon the cross!

The whole space of the basilica outside the apse is widened under a high, coffered roof by twin colonnades on either side, along which a double row of columns runs, arch by arch. Chambers, four in each colonnade, set into the long sides of the basilica, provide places suited to the private prayer of those praying or meditating on the law of the Lord, and also places fitted for the memorials of religious persons and family members, for the repose of eternal peace. Each chamber is marked over the front of its threshold with two verses, which I did not wish to include in this letter. But I have written out those at the entrances of the basilica itself, since, if you wish to borrow them, they could suit the doors of your basilicas too, such as this one:

Peace be with you, whoever you are who enter, pure,
with a peaceful heart, the inner sanctuary of Christ our God.

Or this, about the Lord's sign painted over the entrance in the form the verse describes:

See the crowned cross of the Lord standing above the courts of Christ,
promising lofty rewards to hard toil;
take up the cross, you who would carry off the crown.

Where an entrance opens into the other basilica, a private one as it were, from a little garden or orchard, these little verses open that more secluded door:

Enter the heavenly ways through pleasant green lawns,
Christians; fitting is the way in here from joyful gardens,
from which the deserving are granted a holy way out into paradise.

This same door is marked on its inner face with other verses:

Whoever you are who leave the house of the Lord, your prayers duly completed,
go back in body, but remain in heart.

The front of the basilica does not face east, as is the more usual custom, but faces the basilica of my lord, blessed Felix, looking toward his tomb. The apse, however, curves out into two small conches on the right and left and so is widened within its spacious circuit. One of these lies open to the bishop as he offers sacrifices of jubilation; the other, behind the priest, receives those at prayer in its roomy recess. With a most joyful view, this whole basilica opens at once into the basilica of the confessor I have mentioned, through a screen with three equal arches that lets the light through, by which the roofs and spaces of the two basilicas are joined to each other. For a wall, blocked by the apse of a certain tomb set in the way, shut the new basilica off from the old. It has been opened on the confessor's side by as many doors as the new basilica's front was opened by at its entrance, and so it offers a see-through appearance to those looking from either into the other, as the inscriptions placed between the two sets of doors indicate. So at the very entrances of the new basilica are these little verses:

The kindly house lies open to those entering by a triple arch,
and the threefold door bears witness to a devout faith.

Likewise, on the right and left, with crosses painted over them in red, are these epigrams:

The lofty cross is encircled by the ring of a flowering wreath,
and it is red, stained with the Lord's shed blood.
And the doves that rest above the heavenly sign
show that God's kingdom lies open to the simple.

[Also on the same:]

By this cross put us to death to the world, and the world to us,
giving life to our souls by the death of guilt.
You will make us too doves pleasing to you, Christ,
if your peace flourishes in pure hearts.

Within the screen itself, by which the short gap that used rather to separate the neighbouring basilicas is now made continuous, on the side facing the new basilica, above the middle arch, are these verses:

As Jesus, our peace, broke down the dividing wall
and, destroying division by the cross, made the two into one,
so, now that the barrier of the old building is destroyed,
we see the new roofs joined by a covenant of doorways.
A gleaming basin runs through the holy courts with water for the servants
and washes the hands of those entering with its serving stream.
A twin people worships Christ in the hall of Felix,
which Paul, its bishop, governs with apostolic speech.
These epigrams, each marked with two little verses, are over the other arches on the right and left.

A new light opens to astonished eyes, and standing on a single
threshold one sees both halls at once.

On another:

The twin halls have opened through three pairs of arches,
and each admires the other's worship through the shared thresholds.

Likewise on the same arches, on the face that opens toward the basilica of lord Felix, over the middle one, are these:

You whom devoted faith urges from every quarter
to celebrate blessed Felix in crowded throngs,
pour in your gatherings freely through the threefold entrance;
the courts will lie open, spacious however countless you are,
which, joined to each other by arches open face to face,
Paul the bishop dedicates for everlasting use.

On the others, these two:

You who have come out of the ancient hall of holy Felix,
pass over into the new building of Felix.

[Also:]

One faith, which worships one God under a threefold name,
receives those of one mind through a threefold entrance.

In the two side chambers which I said earlier stand on either side of the apse, these verses state what each is for. On the right of the apse:
Here is the place where the holy store is kept, and from which
The kindly procession of the sacred ministry goes forth.

On the left of the same:
If anyone is held by a holy wish to meditate on the law,
He may sit here and give his mind to the sacred books.

Let us now leave this basilica at Nola and pass on to the one at Fundi. Fundi is the name of a town which was just as familiar to me while I still held the estate there, which I used to visit more often. So it was my wish to give a basilica in that very town, whether as a pledge of a kind of civic affection or in memory of my former patrimony, since the town needed one, having only a small and ruinous church. For this reason I thought I should also add these little verses, which we are preparing for the dedication of the basilica in that town. It is still under construction, but by God's favour it is close to its dedication. What chiefly persuaded me to include them, however, was this: my Victor took a great liking to the picture designed for its apse and wanted to bring it to you, in case you should choose to paint one of the two in your newer basilica, in which, he told me, an apse has likewise been built. But whether I ought rather to say absida or abside, you must judge; I confess I do not know, since I do not recall ever having read this sort of word. In any case, this little basilica too will be consecrated with sacred ashes from the blessed relics of apostles and martyrs, in the name of Christ, the Saint of saints, the Martyr of martyrs and the Lord of lords. For he himself has testified that he will in turn confess those who confess him. That is why, besides the inscription for the picture, the inscription for this church has been doubled on account of this grace. On the picture:
The labour of the saints and their reward are fittingly joined:
The steep cross, and the cross's lofty prize, the crown.
God himself, Christ, our leader to the cross and to the crown,
Stands amid the heavenly grove of flowering paradise
As a snow-white lamb beneath a blood-red cross,
The Lamb given as an innocent victim to an unjust death.
The Holy Spirit, in the form of a gentle bird, pours himself upon him as he opens his mouth,
And the Father crowns him from a glowing cloud.
And because he stands above on a lofty rock like a judge,
The twofold flock surrounds his throne, the kids a breed at odds with the lambs;
The Shepherd turns away from the goats on his left
And embraces with his right hand the lambs that have earned their reward.
See, beneath the lighted altars a royal slab of purple marble
Covers the bones of the holy.
Here grace presents apostolic powers as well,
Great pledges in a little dust.
Here is father Andrew, and Luke of great name,
And Nazarius the martyr, renowned for his blood;
And those whom God revealed to his Ambrose after long ages,
Protasius with his peer Gervase.
Here one little casket embraces a holy company together
And holds such great names in its tiny bosom.

These, my brother, and other visible works of this kind I had laboured to build out of earthly things on earth. But blessed be the Lord day by day, who alone does wonders: just as he turned the rock into a pool of water, so he changes earthly things into heavenly ones, and deigns to make this exchange with us, though both here and there it is made out of what is his own, so that what I laboured to build bodily on earth is secretly built through him in heaven, to be revealed to us then, when we shall see with our very eyes what we now foresee by faith. So here we sow and there we reap; here we scatter and there we gather; here we live and there we have our citizenship; here we gird ourselves and there we serve as soldiers; here we fight and there we conquer, or, if we conquer here, there we are crowned. Thus what we build here with our hands we establish there by faith. And if the construction of these buildings of ours, earthly though they are, is carried out with spiritual intent and zeal, it is a blessed preparation of heavenly dwellings. For while we build these in the Lord by the attainment of faith, we ourselves are built by the Lord through progress in that same faith. Indeed, that centurion in the Gospel is an example to us, giving sure hope that an eternal reward will be received especially for this kind of work: in earning his son's healing and in having the Lord himself [?] as the herald of his faith, his merit prevailed chiefly because the Lord's people, who at that time were still found only among the Jews, supported him by testifying that he had built their synagogue.

Why then, wretches that we are, do we now sit idle and yawning, and stand empty-handed in the noisy marketplace of this world as though we were hirelings no one had taken on? Or, if we do reckon that we owe the householder his denarius for having been hired to do some work in his vineyard, why do we perform that very work as though it were not owed but a favour, and even think of charging it to the Lord's account, as if what we do were to benefit him rather than ourselves? O wretched men! We believe we are giving something away; we are doing business. We are thought generous, when we are proved to be utterly greedy, and indeed more greedy than the most grasping moneylenders on earth, by as much as it is a greater thing to buy heavenly goods with earthly ones, and blessed goods with poor and needy things, than to trade earthly for earthly and perishable for things that will perish, and to lend at interest to the Lord rather than to a man. The law condemns the one who has lent his money at interest and taken bribes against the innocent. See, the grace of the Gospel shows us how these same crimes are changed into innocence and holiness, and bring a recompense not of punishment but of reward, provided only that they are turned toward the divine commandments by the saving desire of faith. Lend your money at interest, but to Christ, and the interest brings salvation.

Likewise, in the world judges who have been corrupted by the bribes of defendants are condemned. But whoever you are, caught in some sin and distrusting your own innocence, if you bring the price of your salvation to our Judge, do not fear that you are wronging God's justice by corrupting it. Christ gladly accepts from you the price of your salvation, because he desires mercy rather than sacrifice. But perhaps you ask where you may find him, and how you may corrupt one whom you cannot see. "Rise," it says, "you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and you will reach Christ." That is, shake off the sleep of fleshly sluggishness, and lift up your mind, weighed down by earthly thoughts, from dead concerns, that is, from fleshly ways of living, raising and directing your soul to the Lord, and you will reach Christ. By carrying out his commandments you will see him in every poor man, touch him in every needy one, receive him in every guest, since he himself testifies that whatever is done to the least of his in his name is done to him. See, now you know in turn how you may see the invisible and grasp the incomprehensible. So let us be poor here now, that we may be rich there then. Let us weep now, that we may rejoice then. Let us hunger now, that we may be filled then. "The poor," he says, "you have with you always." You see that we never have any excuse for putting off doing good, since, if only our will is not lacking, a poor man is always at hand.

Let us therefore lend now without anxiety to the needy, and to Christ in his poor, so that we may share in the glory that will abound to him in them. For this is why the Lord himself warns us beforehand, saying: "Make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous mammon." You see how the Almighty makes light out of night and righteousness out of unrighteousness, "so that when you fail," he says, "they may receive you into the eternal dwellings." For the human race is held in balance by a kind of alternation of plenty and want, as the Gospel revealed in the rich man below in hell and the poor man above in the kingdom. So we are to understand the plan of our common Creator, by which he has provided the rich man for the poor and the poor man for the rich, so that the wealth of the one who has plenty may be sustenance for the needy, and the poor man may be the occasion of righteousness for the wealthy, so that, as the apostle said, there may be equality: in that age, when their present want is to be repaid to them with eternal riches, their abundance may overflow to supply our need, if our abundance here has been lent to supply their want. Let us therefore sow fleshly things there, that we may also reap spiritual things from them. Let the hand labour now with earthly things, that the soul may then be refreshed with heavenly ones. Let present hope build the reality to come. Let us make roofs here that will shelter us there. Let the poor man be fed here, where he is in need while I am rich, so that he may feed me there, where he will be filled while I am in need. Behold this spiritual commerce, and deny if you can that we are greedy, we who sell land and tribute in order to buy up exemption in the kingdom, together with eternity.

We lay down crumbling sand in order to found an eternal house, and to reach the stars with cheap rubble. From it we do not contrive, in futile labour, that tower of confusion and pride which was doomed to be destroyed; rather, we are founded on the cornerstone itself, so that through him we may rise up to the fullness of him who is the tower of strength against the face of the enemy. He himself commands us to build this tower after first counting the cost, lest, failing with the building broken off, we bear the brand of improvident rashness and the ridicule we deserve for our vainly bold sloth. Our cost, however, is firm faith. So whoever believes in accordance with God's truth, and holds the Lord [?] as his hope, his wealth and his strength, all his building, fitly joined together, grows and rises, and is an ascent into the fullness of God. So, unless the Lord builds the house, we shall toil in vain as builders. But lest, even when the building has been completed with the Lord's help, we lean back and relax our hands as though secure, holy Scripture adds that, even when the house is built, unless the same God guards it, the watchmen keep watch in vain.

Let us pray to the Lord, then, that while we build for him outwardly dwellings that are seen, he may build within us those that are not seen, namely that house, as the Teacher says, not made with hands, which we shall understand at the last when we have entered it, seeing then face to face what we now see in a riddle and know in part. But now, while we are still placed in the tent of this body, living as it were under the hides and tents of that ancient tabernacle in the desert, with the word of God going before us across the dry land of this world, either in the pillar of cloud, to overshadow our head in the day of battle, or in the pillar of fire, so that we may know his heavenly way on earth, let us pray that through these tabernacles of the Church we may now enter all the way to the house of God, where the Lord himself stands as that supreme stone, made for us by the Lord, cut from the mountain and grown into a mountain, which is marvellous in our eyes. May he now offer himself to our building both as its foundation and as its summit, for he is the beginning and the end. Upon that same rock (for the rock is Christ), apart from which no one can lay the foundation of a stable house, let our hands not heap up stubble or hay and straw, like those who served in Egypt with the basket, lest in muddy buildings of sordid labour we "wash the brick," as the saying goes, and, bent under the burdens of servile toil, turn our back away from the Lord; for just as he refreshes with light those who turn to him, so he strikes with blindness those who turn away.

As we build, let us consider what we can build, out of our frail and earthly substance, that is worthy of the divine foundation, so that, made living stones by that chief stone itself, we may be fitted into the structure of the heavenly temple. Let us melt down the gold of our understanding and the silver of our speech in Christ, so that, purified in the furnace of this world, he who tests the souls pleasing to him may make us gold refined by fire and coin worthy of his image, and that we may bring ourselves to him as precious stones from the works of light. Let us not be stolid in heart with the hardness of wood, nor dry in our works with the dryness of hay, nor shifting and weak in faith or love with the frailty of light straw. Rather, so that the work of our will may be made ready not to be burned, and may rise unshaken through peaceful labour, let us pray to the Most High for that peace in our building by which that wall was once made into the wall of the temple, so that hammer and axe and any iron tool may not be heard in it; nor, as later when that same temple was being repaired through the hostile envy of the Persians, may an enemy attack hinder and interrupt the rising structure. For we shall be completed as a house of prayer and peace only if no anxiety of fleshly thoughts cuts us down, and no tumult of the world drowns out our quiet. For our hammer is the worry about food and the worry about clothing; our axe and iron are the desire for temporal things, the nightly fear of death, hostile envy, and the affairs of this world, through anxious care for which or fond love of which the soul is devoured and the mind fettered. Then the peace of good will, which is strengthened when the senses are composed in religious silence, and the intensity of prayer, which is directed unhindered from a free and pure heart, are torn apart by the barking of fleshly cares, as if by the din of a hammer or the blow of an axe. But because he who is in us is greater than he who is in this world, the Lord is able to crush Satan under our feet, so that the prophecy may be fulfilled for us as well: "The hammer of the whole earth has been broken."

It is good for us, however, that even when the temple of our heart has been built, the Lord Jesus should often visit it again, coming with the whip of his fear, to drive out of us the tables of the moneychangers and the sellers of oxen and doves, so that our mind may not practise any trade of greed, nor the sluggishness of oxen be stabled in our senses, for "where there are no oxen, the mangers are clean"; and that we may not be sellers of our innocence or of divine grace, lest we make the house of prayer a den of robbers. For when our senses have been purged of all the leaven of malice, our Lord Jesus Christ will gladly walk about in them, and Wisdom, the power of God, who heals all our infirmities, will stroll as if in those five porticoes. For in our soul too, as in that portico by the pool that once brought healing, many lie sick and weak. If the soul hears the word of God, he will drive out by his healing command the leprosy of greed, the rust of envy, the blindness of intemperance, the frenzy of anger and the paralysis of lust; and, having restored us not only to the health of innocence but also to the strength of patience, he will bid us at once not only to rise from our sickbed but also to take up the bed itself, so that, made strong, we may carry what carried us when we were weak. This is surely fulfilled also in the spiritual kind of sickness or health that is ours. Our flesh, to which we were given over and on which we lay as on a bed, in the chains of vices and the weakness of virtues, we afterwards take up like that pallet once we are healed, when the inner man has been renewed by the word of God, through the grace of Jesus Christ, to a good and incorruptible mind; and with the spirit now prevailing we carry it, taking it along behind us wherever we wish. In it we used to lie weak, waiting for someone else's help and always beaten by the speed of those who reached the pool first, because there was no one to stretch out a hand or to save, until he himself came, greater than envoys and angels, since he is the Lord of prophets and angels, and in his mercy took up all our weakness, cleansed it by taking it on himself, filled the hungry soul with good things, and bade us go away to that house of ours which, as I said above, is not made with hands, in which there is the voice of joy and salvation, and in which Christ himself will be dwelling, kingdom and king to all his own, as the apostle testifies, for we shall be with the Lord for ever; to him be honour and glory and power for ever.
33. PAULINUS TO ALETHIUS, HIS BLESSED, DESERVEDLY VENERABLE AND DEAREST BROTHER.

Thanks be to God, who has made known to me the fragrance of his grace in you through the eloquence of your letter. For through my brother Victor, most dear in God, who serves as God's soldier in this duty of ministering to brotherly love, providing us, separated by long distances, with a tireless letter-carrier on his yearly journeys, and spending his bodily labour with spiritual affection on the devout duties of those who visit one another; through this brother, then, my fellow servant in the Lord and the common friend of us both, one in heart with us (for he boasts that he is most welcome to you too by the same grace by which he is grafted into us); through him, I say, my holy and venerable brother, I have received a gift as sweet as it was unexpected: your letter, in which the good treasure of your heart appeared to us. So I rightly rejoiced at the blessing of your kindness, for, having seen the face of your inner self in your most chaste eloquence, I recognized how great a help the Lord is granting me in you.

But in the tasks you thought fit to lay upon me, you who are rich and yet set such a value on a poor man, you showed indeed the holy confidence of the purest love. Yet, as far as I can tell, you were led on by the persuasion of reports about the Lord's work, so that you supposed that, along with the work of the Lord, who has deigned to inspire in us concern for our redemption, I also had the resources of talent and eloquence at my command. But your hope, misled by empty opinions, has disappointed a good desire held with great faith. For where would I get as much water as you thirst for, or a cup that you could worthily drink? Where would I get as many loaves as you ask for? You will yourself be to blame for the injury of going hungry longer, since, longing for the Gospel's food of light and life in the deep night of this world, you knock at the bare pantry of a sleepy and poor friend; since, thirsting for rivers of living water, you scratch at a dried-up little vein and try to squeeze moisture out of pumice. For either there is no spring within me, owing to the dryness of my lack of inspiration [?], or else a bitter one from the gall of malice. I wish that your prayers and letters, sent to me more often, might make it overflow and grow sweet through the wood of your faith and the sweetness of your eloquence, so that, when [the rock?] of my heart has been struck by the word of God, which you as a good minister will have brought forth with your devout lips, as by the rod of the prophet [?]
34. ON THE TREASURY.

It is not for nothing, my dearly beloved, that a manger is set up for beasts. It does not lie there merely to be looked at. It is a kind of table, belonging to irrational creatures, yet built by human reason so that four-footed animals may take their food from it. But if those who have taken the trouble to build mangers neglect to put fodder in them, the beasts will soon waste away and fail in the empty stall, and hunger devours the animals that are not fed. Those owners will then suffer the loss their negligence or greed deserves, since they took the trouble only to prepare the manger and lacked the care to fill it. Along with the dead animals they will also lose the use of the manger, justly bearing two heavy losses because they spared the one necessary outlay of a useful expense. By this example, then, dearly beloved, we must take care not to incur harm to the soul and the loss of salvation by neglecting the table which the Lord has set up in the church for the needy, and which we look on with contemptuous eyes or pass by with dry hands. Far be such a contagion from your minds, I beg you. For the cancer of avarice creeps easily into hearts not fortified by any feelings of mercy. It binds the captured soul with viperish chains, if the enemy serpent finds it bare of good works and overflowing with the stuff of captivity, that is, with unfruitful wealth. So let us not allow the Lord's table to be left empty for us and bare for the needy, standing there only to be seen and not to be used, lest the groans wrung from the hungry by our negligence be turned back against us. For, as it is written, he who despises the poor man provokes the one who made him, that is, the common Creator of all, who rejoices when the needy are refreshed and grieves when they fail.

Let us therefore rouse ourselves from the sleep of sloth. To shake off the torpor of negligence and break the chains of avarice, let us look carefully into all the words, precepts, promises, works and counsels of God our Saviour. Let us consider within ourselves why this table is set out in the courts of the Lord's house, in the sight of all his people, and on whose authority. Above all, let us consider for whose good, for what grace and for what fruit it is placed there to shine and stand open. Consult the very oracles of truth, and the prophet will answer you: He who has pity on the poor lends to the Lord. This table, then, belongs to the heavenly banker. It builds up a treasure of life and plies God's lending in order to trade for the pearl. For he who lends to the Lord's poor awaits from the Lord the repayment of an eternal reward. The blessed apostle Paul too, in his teaching, testifies that among his anxieties for all the churches his care for the poor was not the least. He says: Only that we should remember the poor, which very thing I was eager to do. Elsewhere the same apostle cries: We brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything out; and again: What do you have that you did not receive? And so, dearly beloved, we should not be tight-fisted with what is our own; rather we should lend out of what has been entrusted to us. For a stewardship, he says, has been entrusted to us. The use of money is temporary and shared, not the eternal possession of a private estate. If you recognize that it is yours only for a time on earth, you will be able to make it yours forever in heaven. Remember those in the Gospel who received the Lord's talents, and what the householder paid back to each on his return. Then you will know how much more profitable it is to place your money at the Lord's table to be multiplied than to keep it idle with barren faithfulness. You will also know that a sum kept back, yielding no return to the creditor and costing the useless servant dearly, was kept only to increase his punishments.

Hasten, then, to deserve to hear the voice that says: Well done, good servant, enter into the joy of your lord, rather than the one that says: Wicked and lazy servant, out of your own mouth I judge you, and the rest, which is well known. The useless servant was cast into the outer darkness, and his talent was given to the one who abounded in the sums entrusted to him and multiplied: For to everyone who has, he says, more will be given, but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Let us remember also that widow who, careless of herself out of care for the poor and mindful only of the future, emptied out the whole substance of her livelihood, with the Judge himself as witness. For others, he says, gave out of their overflowing abundance. She was perhaps needier than many even of the poor, since her whole fortune was two small coins, but in spirit she was richer than all the rich. Looking only to the wealth of eternal reward and greedy for heavenly treasure, she gave up all at once the whole of that substance which is taken from the earth and returns to the earth. She put in what she had, so as to possess what she had not seen. She put in perishable things, so as to purchase immortal ones. That poor little woman did not despise the plan that God has arranged and ordained for receiving what is to come. Therefore the one who arranged it did not forget her: the Judge of the world himself ran ahead of his own sentence and proclaimed in the Gospel the woman whom he will crown at the judgment.

Let us therefore lend to the Lord out of the Lord's gifts. We possess nothing except by his gift; without his will we would not even exist. And what should we in particular think our own? By a greater and special debt we are not our own, not only because we were made by God but also because we were bought. Yet let us rejoice that we were bought at a great price, namely the blood of the Lord himself. By that price we cease to be cheap and for sale, for to be free of righteousness is a freedom baser than slavery. Such a free man is the slave of sin and the captive of death. Let us then give back to the Lord his own gifts. Let us give to him who receives in every poor person. Let us give, I say, with joy, so that, as he says, we may receive from him with exultation. For he is pleased by this kind of assault, when we do violence to his kingdom and break open the bars of heaven by good works. For our Lord, who alone is good, as the one God, desires to receive not out of greed but out of generosity. What could he lack who gave all things? Or what could he fail to possess who possesses the possessors themselves, since all men of wealth are in his hands? But his boundless justice and goodness alike wish that we make gifts to him in return out of his own gifts. In this way, because he is good, he creates an occasion for his kindness toward you; and because he is just, he makes for you a merit, so that you may deservedly receive a reward.

So the treasuries of his good things lie open and the riches of his goodness are at hand. No one need wait to receive; each may freely seize for himself as much as he wishes. For the good Lord and holy Father made us so that we might be good for our own good. What good from outside could he need, who is himself, in all his greatness, wholly goodness and blessedness? For this reason, dearest ones, as far as it lies with him, he wishes every man to be saved, because in every man he loves his own work. He is lavishly generous to you from his own riches, provided that you are not grudging and miserly toward yourself with the things God has made yours. He gave them to you not to be a cause of death but a road back to life. O the abundance of God's goodness! He wishes to borrow from what he himself has bestowed. He longs to become a debtor for his own gifts, so that he may pay you your interest at a lavish rate.

Hurry, then, brother, to bind so rich a debtor to yourself. Then he will call you his friend instead of his servant, and, having found you faithful with your earthly coins, he will make you rich from his heavenly treasures. Do not tremble, do not delay, do not hold back. Use force on God; seize the kingdom of heaven. He who forbids us to touch what belongs to others rejoices when his own property is invaded, and he who condemns the rapacity of greed praises the plunder of faith. Your guests have long been standing at your doors, waiting for the hour and for the master of the table. You are keeping your guests waiting. Run in haste, so that they do not go on fasting any longer, and so that he who made them is not provoked by the wrong done to them, for it was he who made them poor for your good. The almighty Lord, dearly beloved, could have made everyone equally rich, so that no one would need anyone else. But by the counsel of his infinite goodness the merciful and compassionate Lord arranged things this way, in order to test your heart through them. He made the wretched so that he might recognize the merciful. He made the needy so that he might exercise the wealthy. Your brother's poverty is the material of your riches, if you take thought for the needy and the poor and do not keep for yourself alone what you have received. For God has given you that man's share in this world as well, precisely so that he might owe you whatever of his gifts you freely offered to the needy, and in turn might enrich you on the eternal day out of that man's share. For through the poor Christ receives now, and then he will repay on their behalf. The rich man in the Gospel teaches us this from Tartarus, and so does Lazarus, no longer a beggar, in Abraham's bosom, who overflowed with the refreshment of life while the burning rich man suffered his penal destitution. This example teaches, I say, that the human race has been allotted a reversal of fortunes between here and there. There the poor will be repaid what seems to be denied them here. The rich, on the other hand, who here were poor toward the poor, will have no share in the happiness of the poor; instead, perpetual beggary with an abundance of punishments will be paid back to them as fitting vengeance for the wrong done to the poor.

Therefore, as it is written, walk as children of light in the light, while you have the light. Act in this way, Christian, while there is still a day for repenting and providing, so that you may deserve to hear from the Lord: Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful in a few things, I will set you over many. Look, then, and pay heed to this word, brother, and do not neglect the grace that has been offered to you. Do not go down empty-handed into the house of Christ, which is the Church of the living God. If you give even a little out of your much, you have prepared for yourself a great increase of what remains to you. Very many are waiting for you and hang on your coming, looking about to see when they may catch sight of you. The prayers of all the needy and the vows of the sick are spent on you. Take care that they are not forced to change such devout feelings and turn their prayers into complaints. They are worn out, and if you show no mercy, their distress will wring groans from them against you. Take care that those groans do not strike home and summon God, the father of orphans, the avenger of widows and the fellow-sufferer of the poor.

If you love yourself, beware of loving yourself alone, for that love belongs to iniquity, and, as it is written, he who loves iniquity hates his own soul. The fullness of the law is love of neighbour, since every human being is a brother to every other by kinship of nature. Take equal care, then, for yourself and for the poor man, and so imitate the imitator of Christ by seeking what is useful not to yourself but to others, so that God may care for you all the more. See how great a crime it is when pride or avarice separates you from the one to whom God joined you by his work. Refresh the hungry soul, and you will not fear the wrath that will come in the evil day. For blessed, it says, is he who takes thought for the needy and the poor; in the evil day the Lord will deliver him. Work, then, brother, and cultivate this tract of your land, so that it may sprout a fertile crop for you, full of the fat of wheat, and bring you at great interest a hundredfold yield of multiplied seed. In the desire for this kind of possession or business, and in the pursuit of it, avarice is holy and saving. Such covetousness, which earns the heavenly kingdom and desires everlasting good, is the root of good things. So covet riches of this kind, as was said above, and possess this kind of inheritance, which your creditor will pay out to you at a hundredfold yield, so that you may enrich your heirs along with yourselves with everlasting goods. For this possession is truly great and precious. It does not weigh its owner down with a worldly heap but enriches him with an eternal revenue. It flows with milk and honey, and it offers its farmers a nectar of sweet liquids not pressed from hives or flocks but poured out through joyful rivers.

But, dearly beloved, you should make provision by present care and diligent practice of righteousness, not only so that you may seek eternal goods but also so that you may deserve to escape countless evils. For you need great help and protection, and we stand in need of the patronage of many unfailing prayers. Our adversary does not rest. The enemy, ever watchful for our destruction, besieges all our ways and diligently spies out everyone's goings out and comings in. He fastens himself to each one's footsteps as an inseparable companion. He throws hedges across our paths and sets them between our feet, so that if you are careless you trip over a hidden rough patch even on level ground. Hence it is written: There are ways that seem level to men, but their end leads down to hell. And if you fall, careless on level ground and incautious on slippery ground, he rushes upon you at once and presses down on you as you lie; nor will he let go until he has broken and devoured you. Beware, then, in everything; as you set down your foot, look all around. For the devil threatens from every side like a lion ready for its prey. Do not trust even your own ground. It must be trodden with a cautious step, or rather a guarded one, for it recognizes the sin of the first father in all human flesh, and, fertile in thorns and thistles, serpents and beasts, it carries out the Creator's sentence. Besides, many crosses beset us in this world, and countless dangers. Plagues of disease, the fires of fever and the darts of pain rage against our souls. The torches of desire are kindled. Everywhere snares lie hidden in our path; on every side drawn swords bristle. Life is spent amid ambushes and battles, and we walk through fires hidden under treacherous ash.

Therefore, before you fall into the ruin of some one of these great sicknesses, whether by chance or by your own deserving, hasten to be taken into the Physician's care and to become dear to him, so that in the time of need you may have the remedy of salvation ready. It is one thing when you pray for yourself alone, and another when a multitude is anxious before God on your behalf. You are silent, and while you are silent, they cry out for you. They see you and smile at you. They meet you and greet you, and, forgetting their want and infirmity, their bodies are invigorated by your health and their souls grow strong at the sight of you. You are a fertile field for them, a fruitful estate; and they in turn are a rich and precious possession for you. They put you before their own children. Each is anxious for you before himself, and prays for your welfare either together with his own or before it. They do not neglect themselves; rather, each has transferred his love to you and loves himself in you, and he prays for your life as for his own, because your life is his fruit and your riches are his wealth, the riches of his poverty. In all the churches they pray for you; in all the streets they rejoice over you; and wherever they are, when your name is mentioned, they rise up blessing the Lord and kiss you in their hands, though you are absent. They always see you and never fail to see you, because they embrace you with the mind, by which we behold those who are absent. For you are written and imprinted on their hearts through your great kindness toward them. They do not fear hunger, since they are sure of your food, nor do they dread winter, because you forestall it and shut it out by providing clothes. Blessed is the man whom the Lord, when he comes, will find doing this!
Letter 35. Paulinus to Delphinus, his most blessed and venerable father, ever most longed for by us.

We received the brief letter of your holy affection with our whole heart, which had longed for it; through the great affection in it, it was rich to us. But since there is a time for everything, it seemed that now, in a time of sorrow, it was also time to keep our words short. We confess that we are deeply saddened, not so much by our brother's bodily death as by his spiritual negligence. He was more mindful of the cares to be left behind here than of the remedies to be provided there, and so he put first what should have come after, and put after what should have come first. He ought to have cared for those weightier things for his own sake without overlooking these temporal things for his children's sake. Hence we ask you, sharing our grief with fatherly affection, to be so kind as to remember that by the grace of God he was once born to you as a spiritual son. This cause is therefore especially your concern. Do not let us bring shame on your fatherly love, which used to glory in us as sons, by squandering the substance of our inherited portion. Rather, may it be granted to you through your prayers that a drop of refreshment, trickling even from the smallest finger of your holiness, may sprinkle his soul. And may divine mercy, through your intercession, come to our aid for the confession of our sin, while there is still time, as we run back to you and cry: Father, we have sinned against heaven and against you; we are no longer worthy to be called your sons. Otherwise we may consume the whole substance of our eternal Father, which our sins squander daily, and be overwhelmed with shame at the thought of returning; and, lingering in a far country, we may be led off, God forbid, to tend swine and eat their unworthy food.
Letter 36. Paulinus to Amandus, holy, deservedly venerable and most beloved.

In the short discourse of your holiness we have tasted the sweetest savour of your mouth. Just as a drop of honey tastes the same as the whole honeycomb, so the dripping of your tongue, even in a single word, conveys the whole savour of your holy soul, for whatever is brought out of a good treasure is good and precious. A pearl is not cheap because it is small. It is all the more precious because even in its small size it holds great value, so much so that, as the authority of the Gospel also testifies, people seek to buy it even at the cost of squandering their whole estates. The grain of mustard seed too, which seems the smallest of seeds, nevertheless stands out as the greatest of herbs. The word of this seed has been sown in you and flourishes in your heart, so that your heart burns within you on the way of the Lord. Therefore even your brief discourse holds the sweetness and vigour of the heavenly word together and ministers them to us, so that we too may be seasoned with the salt of your wisdom.

And so we too shall imitate the economy of your speech in this letter, even if we cannot imitate the fullness of your thought. We reply only this: as we wrote, our chief concern came from the fresh grief of being torn from our brother. We know that he has been taken from this world only for a time, and that we must soon follow him into the next. Yet we mourn his death more truly for this reason: from what he did or arranged toward his end, we have seen that he acted more in keeping with our sins than with our prayers, so that he chose to pass to the Lord a debtor rather than a free man. For this reason we earnestly ask you, as a brother, which you are so kind as to be to us in the Lord, to help your brothers who are of one mind with you. Add this further reward to the merits of your faith: share our weakness on his behalf and join us in the labour of prayer, so that through your prayers the merciful and compassionate God, who does all things in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the depths, may refresh his soul with the drops of his mercy. For just as the fire kindled by him will burn down to the lowest hell, so without doubt the dew of his forgiveness will also penetrate the underworld, so that we who swelter in the burning darkness may be refreshed by the dewy light of his loving-kindness.

Pray for us too, that we may not die in our sins. May the Lord make our end known to us, so that we may know what we lack and hasten to fill up what remains. May we not be carried off in the midst of empty days, weaving a spider's web of hollow works, but may our days be found full, so that we may die as children a hundred years old, that is, little ones in malice and mature in understanding. So may it come about that in our death we leave to those who survive us the example of a wholesome repentance, and that our mourning may not last more than seven days, if on the way of this life we come to terms with our adversary, that is, with the Spirit and the word of God, which opposes us when we sin. For the Spirit convicts the world of sin, and the word of God, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel, will be our accuser if we do not obey it, and will hand us over to the judge, the Word. He will demand an account of his talent to the last penny, and unless he receives double interest on his money through the practice of godliness, which is profitable for all things, he will assign idle faith its place among the unbelievers. For whoever bears a faith that is dead, without works, under the empty name of Christian is next door to an unbeliever. This is the fool, whose mourning lasts all his days, because he had no fear of the Lord and so did not hold to the beginning of wisdom. He has become the tail, because he who loves iniquity and hates his own soul does not dwell in the midst of the house. He is handed over to the officer of the prison of hell and cast into the outer darkness, because he lived according to the outer man. That is why he must be mourned here without end: condemned to eternal fire, he will die without end.

Let us therefore have peace with the Lord: not the peace of this world, which is friendly to sins and at odds with God, but the peace of Christ, which joins us to God and conforms us to Christ. This comes about if our soul cleaves to the word of God, so that we become one with God through the intervention of the Mediator, who is our peace. He made both one, uniting in himself the discordant natures of God and man, and he makes the two one in us, that is, he brings the flesh into agreement with the spiritual soul. And then the fire [?] will remain in our midst, whether the agreement of these two in us invites him, or the agreement of three, with the Spirit, to make in our heart a dwelling pleasing to himself, together with the Father and the Spirit, and in turn to lead us where he himself is, saying: Enter into the joy of your Lord.
Letter 37. Paulinus to Victricius, his brother of one mind.

Like cold water to a thirsty man, and like good news from a distant land, so were the words of Your Holiness a refreshment and restoration to us. We received them in a letter, brief in words but generous in love, from the hand of a very dear bearer, our son Candidianus. We rejoiced at the grace given him: for the sake of the words of holy lips, with a willing spirit, he pressed the tireless beast of his weak flesh into service on hard roads, relying not on strength but on faith. Without doubt your prayers strengthened him, and he received, as it were, the wings of a dove or the feet of a deer to fulfil this ministry of love. So, though small in body, he became like a giant and rejoiced to run his course, and he filled our soul with the blessing of sweetness, bringing us letters more desirable than gold and very precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Our mind was bitter with its sins; but just as the bitter water of Marah was changed in the hand of Moses by the wood of the mystery, so the holy and sweet breath of Your Blessedness turned it, by spiritual gentleness, into the sweetness of joy. For we had also been saddened and had felt bitterness because you had not come to us from Rome, as we had hoped, by a short journey, you who had come to Rome across such vast distances of land. I confess that the loss of this blessing left me not only saddened but also ashamed. Never had my sins been more plainly shown to me, not to speak of others, than when they begrudged me the light of your face from so close at hand. Could the hand of God, which had brought you so far, not have been able to bring you the short distance further? But our sins, set like a great wall against our desires, have separated us from you. Woe is me, a wretched sinner of unclean lips, who dare to say that you were near us or we near you, when, even if you had come all the way to us, we would still have been just as far from Your Holiness. For so great a distance in virtues and so vast a remoteness in merits could not have been made equal or joined together by place.

Nevertheless, this work of kindness would have been added to the fruits of your holiness, and your reward in heaven would have grown through so devout a labour, if you had also fulfilled that saving word of the Lord by visiting our weakness at close hand, with your face and your hand: for it is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick. For I do not want you, man blessed by the Lord, to feel so sure about us as to think that all the ailments of our soul, by which we have sinned and still sin against the Lord, are already healed. And this is so, even though the supreme Perfumer himself, who compounds for the remedies of our salvation the various sweet fragrances of healing ointments and powers, has prepared the medicine of our life not only from the outpouring of his Spirit but also from his taking on of our body. As it is written, he was made sin for us through the likeness of sinful flesh, in the reality of our flesh, so that by sin he might condemn sin: that is, so that he who was himself free from sin might condemn the root of our sin out of the very material that had previously been sinful. He blotted out by the blood of his passion the bond of the deadly decree that stood against us; he slew in himself the enmity by which our sins had come between us and God and separated us from him; and in his flesh he triumphed over the hostile powers, giving us an example of how to live and how to conquer, within ourselves, our spiritual and invisible enemies in that spiritual and invisible battle which is waged between the law of the mind and the law of the flesh, which strives to take us captive to the law of sin.

But pray to the Lord and entreat him to take up arms and shield and rise up to help us, and to say to our soul: I am your salvation; so that our way may not become darkness and a slippery place, and the shadow of death may not cover us, and the enemy may not say: I have prevailed against them. While you bend the bow of prayer on our behalf, we shall not be turned into a crooked bow. Let God arise in us, so that our enemies may be scattered; for because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, whose lot we share, the Lord has arisen to turn our evils back upon our enemies and to save sinners, of whom we are the foremost, as we are the lowest of the servants of Christ. We cannot even do what we ought, though we ought to add of our own will some voluntary service beyond what the law requires, as the Teacher himself did, whom you imitate. He had the right to live by the gospel, yet would not use his right; and by forgoing what was permitted he found in this an opportunity to heap up reward for himself with Christ, by offering the gospel free of charge.

Your Holiness, however, holds the rich glory of Christian poverty not only by forgoing what is permitted and abstaining from visible comforts, but also, as I have learned, by the multitude of your opponents and your endurance of trials; for unjust witnesses have risen up against you, and iniquity has lied to itself. But no knot could be found in the bulrush, no blemish in the light. For your lamp did not lie hidden under a bushel; it stands high and shines brightly on the holy lampstand, to give light to all who are in the house and to be the kindling from which many lights are lit for the Lord. And so your lampstand remained unshaken and steady, because it was human hands that pushed at it to make it fall. You did not deserve to have it moved to its ruin by the hand of him who holds the seven stars and walks among the seven golden lampstands, who has in his mouth the two-edged sword. With it he has armed the right hand of your mind, so that with the torch of both Testaments you may victoriously quench the burning darts of the enemy, and a thousand may fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but they shall not come near you, for the truth of God will cover you with an impregnable shield, so that the bows of those who are said to have sharpened the swords of their tongues against you may be broken. Their blows have become as weak as the arrows of little children, and they could find no place to wound a body fenced about by the mighty armour of God. For the Lord is your protection, and the Lord is the light of your heart; he has instructed you in the spirit of truth, so that, after the teaching of Paul, you may be a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, proclaiming the mystery of Christ not with puffed-up knowledge nor with lofty speech, but professing to know nothing among men except Christ [?] and him crucified.

Your faith and confession, then, as we believe and trust, bear witness that the Trinity is coeternal, of one Godhead and substance, one work and one kingdom. It holds the Father to be God, the Son to be God, and the Holy Spirit to be God, who is and who was and who is to come, who sent you, like Moses and the apostles, to proclaim the good things of the Lord to the nations. And this you teach just as you yourself were taught by God: you join the unity of the Trinity without confusion, and you distinguish the trinity of that same unity without separation, so that no person is merged with another, and in each of the three persons the one God shines forth. The Son is as great as the Father and as great as the Holy Spirit, yet each, always distinguished by the property of his own name, keeps an undivided harmony in equality of power and glory.

We are sure, too, that you so proclaim the Son of God that you are not ashamed to confess him also as the Son of Man, as truly man in our nature as he is truly God in his own; but Son of God before the ages, for he is himself the Word of God, God, who was in the beginning with God, equally God, co-almighty with the Father and his fellow-worker. For through him all things were made, and without him nothing was made. And by a mystery of boundless love this Word was made flesh and dwelt among us: not merely the flesh of our body, but the whole man, by taking on both our body and our soul, and a rational soul, which by God's natural workmanship has a mind implanted in it. Otherwise we shall wander in the darkness of Apollinaris, if we say that the man assumed by God had a soul empty of human mind, such as cattle and beasts of burden have, and that the man whom the Son of God took up was such; whereas he must have taken up the whole man, with that truth by which he is the Truth and by which he created man, in order to renew his own work with full salvation. And our salvation is no salvation unless it is full; for the Son of God would have taken up not a man but some other kind of animal, a creature without reason, if the soul of the man he assumed had no mind of its own, and if, against the nature of the human race, that man above all, the firstborn of all creation, assumed into the form of human perfection, so lacked a mind of his own that he is said to have had his mind not from a human spirit but from the divine Spirit. This is said by the mouths of those in whose hearts this poison is conceived, so that they make even the Truth a liar. But the word of truth and the truth of God are near you and within you. Nor are you lacking in the Holy Spirit, you who confess, believe and proclaim that the Lord Jesus, the Son of God, abides as God in the glory of God the Father and as King of kings at the right hand of power, and that at the resurrection of the dead he will come as judge of the living and the dead.

Remember us, and glory, as the Apostle says, because this brief trial has worked for you an eternal weight of glory and has laid up for you a crown of righteousness, which you will receive from the hand of the Lord. This war was allowed to be stirred up against you to provide material for victory, so that you too, following blessed Paul your teacher, may glory in your sufferings and, with your mouth opened wide over your enemies, tell how you have laboured in patience, in the Holy Spirit, in love unfeigned, in the word of truth, in the power of God, with the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, through glory and dishonour, through ill repute and good repute, as a deceiver and yet true, as unknown and yet well known, as chastened and yet not killed, as sorrowful yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich. For this very trial of Your Holiness has turned out for many to the advancement of the gospel, since no one has been put to shame in you, as the grace of Christ and the truth of your faith shine out not only in the soundness of your teaching but also in the power of your way of life, which is in heaven. For the kingdom of God, it says, is not in word but in power. What more, then, is to be sought, when in you that which surpasses even the word stands out? For who could doubt that the faith of truth dwells in the spirit of a man in whose life he sees the power of faith displayed?
38. Paulinus to his holy, deservedly venerable and dearly beloved brother Aper.

I rejoiced at what you wrote to me, and at the faith which you conceived in your heart and have now testified with your mouth.
