If the grace of the Lord makes me a sharer in so great a spirit, I hope that we shall go into the house of the Lord. There, gazing together face to face on the truth at what we have now grasped in a common hope and faith, we shall sing a hymn in harmonious exultation, and say to the Lord our God: "We believed that we were ashes and earth." We shall say it if in this present time our feet are so firmly set in the courts of Jerusalem that we cease to be earth and ashes in act and deed. Then in a spirit of humility we will remember that we are earth and confess it to the Lord, so that, because by the condemnation of sin we are earth, through the reconciliation of grace we may deserve to be earth no longer. Blessed are you, brother, and it will go well with you, for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you; you learned it by the revelation of the Spirit of the heavenly Father. At the most holy close of your letter to me you affirmed what you hold with unshaken faith and profess with a free voice: Christ Jesus crucified, the Son of God, God, to whom every knee bends in heaven, on earth and under the earth, and whom every tongue confesses to be at the right hand of power and in the glory of God the Father. Him you embrace with the whole mystery of hidden devotion as our Lord and God, since no other shall be reckoned beside him: Lord and God, Son of God before the ages, made of the seed of David in this age, and now, through the resurrection of the dead, living for ever as the hope of human eternity. You believe in him as he is, and as you believe, so you preach. And will you call yourself unskilled and an infant before God? I do indeed believe that in one respect you have become a little child, but in malice; in understanding, the profession of your faith teaches me that you are mature. For the knowledge of the truth which you have grasped in a shortened word is the fullness of wisdom. And so the teacher of the Gentiles himself, the chosen vessel and vessel of God, who declares that Christ speaks in him and that he has the Spirit of God, does not glory in loftiness of speech or in knowledge of the law. Instead he declares that he has cast away and counted as dung all the glory with which the wisdom of either Jews or philosophers is puffed up, so that he may gain Christ, and by the loss of that knowledge win the profit of this ignorance. So he says: "I know nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified." Since in Christ is contained the whole fullness and perfection of wisdom and knowledge, the apostle mocks this world, and with a loftier spirit looks down on its letters and all its wisdom as vanity, saying: "Where is the scribe? Where is the wise man? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" He also shows the cause of this error, for which the wisdom of this age deserved to be struck so hard that it is folly to God. Through the arrogance of a wisdom they took to be their own, though no one has anything unless he has received it, the wisdom of God seemed to them folly. Rightly, then, by the justice of God, folly and wisdom change places, and these people are condemned to be fools precisely because they seem wise to themselves. They do not think their wisdom comes from God's gift, but from their own good, as if it belonged to them.

All the more, then, do I congratulate you, my kindred spirit, because you have spurned that wisdom which God has rejected, and have chosen fellowship with the little ones of Christ rather than with the wise of the world. From this you already merit from the Lord a further grace: as you were good enough to tell me, glorying in a godly way, everyone hates you. That would not happen unless you had begun to be a true imitator of Christ, for this world would not hate anything except what it saw to be already estranged from it and set against it. Rejoice and exult; even in your first beginnings the power of perfection is at work. It is plain how firmly you have believed in Christ, since it has already been granted to you to suffer for Christ. See what the Lord himself says, and understand how blessed you are: "Do not be surprised if the world hates you, for it hated me first. If you were of the world, the world would surely love what was its own." And again: "The servant is not greater than his master. If they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more those of his household?" See now whether it is right for us servants to refuse to suffer for our Lord what the Lord first endured for us, his servants. O blessed injury, to be displeasing along with Christ! We have more to fear from the love of those whom one pleases without Christ. "Did I not hate those who hated you?" says the psalmist. And he added: "I hated them with a perfect hatred." What dealings can we have in fellowship with those whose lot is separate from ours?

You rightly glory, most venerable brother, and say with exultation that this is how you yourself believe you are a Christian: those who used to love you have begun to hate you, and those who used to fear you have begun to despise you. And you know in your own heart that if you were still only yourself, they would love and revere you just as they used to. Rejoice, then, and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven. It is not you they hate, but him who has begun to dwell in you. His work in you is both the humility they scorn and the chastity they loathe. Recognize with joy that in this good you share the lot of the prophets and apostles: of the prophet when he says, "They slandered me because I followed justice," and of the apostle when he says, "We have become the offscouring of all," and again when he testifies that "we have been made a spectacle in this world to all, to angels and to men." From the beginning of the ages Christ suffers in all his own. For he is the beginning and the end, veiled in the law and revealed in the gospel. He is the Lord, ever wonderful, both suffering and triumphing in his saints. In Abel he was slain by his brother; in Noah he was mocked by his son; in Abraham he wandered as a stranger; in Isaac he was offered up; in Jacob he served as a slave; in Joseph he was sold; in Moses he was cast out and put to flight; in the prophets he was stoned and sawn asunder; in the apostles he was tossed about on land and sea; and in the many and various crosses of the blessed martyrs he was slain again and again. He still bears our infirmities and our sickness, for he is the man who is ever stricken for our sake and knows how to bear the weakness which without him we neither can bear nor know how to. He himself, I say, still endures the world for us and in us, so that by enduring it he may destroy it and perfect his strength in weakness. It is he who suffers reproaches in you too, and it is he whom this world hates in you. But thanks be to him, for he conquers when he is judged. As you know from Scripture, the Lord triumphs in us through the form of a servant, winning the grace of freedom for his servants. He does this by that mystery of his love by which he put on the form of a servant and deigned to humble himself for us even to death on a cross, so that by a visible humility he might work within us that invisible exaltation in the heavens. Look at where we fell from in the beginning, and you will understand that it is by the counsel of God's wisdom and love that we are being refashioned for life. In Adam we fell through pride, and so we are humbled in Christ, so that we may wash away the sin of that ancient crime by obedience in the opposite virtue, and may please by serving, after giving offence by our pride.

Let us therefore exult and glory in him who has made us both his battle and his victory, saying: "Be steadfast, for I have overcome the world." Likewise, in the Book of Kings I hear the prophet speaking to King Jehoshaphat when he was terrified by the vast scale of the war and the great multitude of his enemies: "Thus says the Lord: Do not fear or be dismayed before this multitude, for this battle is not yours but the Lord's." Moses too had said much the same long before: "You shall keep silent, and the Lord will fight for you." So let those who trust in their own strength or wisdom, and who glory in the abundance of their riches, sharpen against us as they please the weapons of their teeth and the arrows of their words; let them spew the poisons of their evil treasury from their vipers' tongues. In our place they have the Lord to answer them: "I have kept silent; shall I always keep silent?" As Scripture says, let us hedge our ears with thorns, that is, with the word of God and with faith in the word. With the strong hedge of innocence and patience these protect the crop of our life. They resist the devil like thorns against thieves when he tries by his tricks to find a way into our hearts. And they pierce the hearts of the king's enemies, that is, of those who love the enemies of Christ, these detractors of Christians, as they behold our life and our steadfastness. So let us keep silent before these people while we speak to the Lord in the silence of humility and the voice of patience. Then he who is unconquered will himself fight for us and conquer in us. Then the prince of this darkness will be cast out. He is cast out not from this world but from man, when he is shut out of us as faith enters in. He gives place to Christ, whose dwelling casts out sin and banishes the serpent he has driven away.

What we ought to do in this kind of suffering the prophet teaches us, saying: "But as for me, when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting." This means we should overthrow our detractors by the very appearance of humility that provokes them. Then the more we glory in the thing for which they are put to shame in us, the more they will be confounded before the Lord as they persist in the guilt of their old pride. For God loves a workman who has no cause for shame, just as he loves a cheerful giver. So, standing firm in the faith of truth and in the practice of justice, we answer the hatred or abuse of such people better by our lives than by our words. For, as you have it written, he who hates discipline will cast your words behind him, and he who rebukes a fool brings insult on himself.

Let the orators keep their letters, the philosophers their wisdom, the rich their riches, the kings their kingdoms. For us, Christ is glory and possession and kingdom. For us, wisdom lies in the foolishness of preaching, strength in the weakness of the flesh, and glory in the scandal of the cross, by which the world is crucified to me and I to the world, so that I may live to God. Yet it is no longer I, but Christ in me, with whom we have been buried. In him we are now hidden from the eyes of this world, so that we may be revealed with him to the world's confusion, when it remembers what it now throws in our faces and says: "These are the ones whose life we thought madness; how have they been counted among the children of God?" Meanwhile, dearest brother, let them enjoy their glory and their life and take possession of their fruits, for like green herbs they will quickly wither, and their days pass like a shadow. Their hope is shut up within the span of this age, because they have neither faith in the truth nor the will to believe. Intent only on present things, they give themselves over to greed and lust so as not to believe in God, since the fear of the Lord puts an end to both desires. That fear is strengthened by faith in Christ, through whom we learn to recognize the truth, whether in despising temporal goods or in longing for eternal ones. Since Christ is also the truth, those who are estranged from him must remain in this blindness of unhappy errors. So they think the fragile solid and the solid empty; they laugh at true things as vain and marvel at vain things as true. If they were willing to understand so as to act well, they would lift up to the salvation of justice the eyes they have set on bending to the earth, and raise themselves a little from the ground. Then they would easily be enlightened by the very conversions of men which they disparage as empty and foolish. For, as Scripture says, the Lord sets free those in fetters and the Lord gives light to the blind; and again: "The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones." Changing a man is the work of God, for only he can restore what he has made. Christ, the wisdom of God, has long been doing this throughout the whole world. He carries himself everywhere among the nations by his flying word and sends himself into chosen souls, so that, as he said through the prophet, he may hold the first place in every nation.

The day of reckoning draws nearer every day, and every hour brings us closer to judgment. So the good Lord hastens and makes every effort to snatch us from the wrath to come and to lead us out of the embrace of this harmful generation of vipers, as Scripture calls it. That is why in every place signs and wonders grow more frequent than usual every day, so that, as far as lies with him, he may save every man. In a few cases he shows what would benefit all, if they were willing. The pattern of a few is enough to instruct everyone. It is set before people for either result: as an example to those who believe and as a witness against those who harden their hearts. So if those who deny in their minds the humanity they display in their outward form have any human sense at all, let them marvel at what is done in you and praise God. Let them not think this most blessed change of your mind and life an error of folly on your part, but let them understand it as the power of the wisdom of God. The more they remember that you were wiser and more learned than others, the more evident to them the working of God's power should be. For nothing can turn a wise man from the course or position of his own judgment except the highest Wisdom itself, that is, God in Christ, the Power of powers and the Mind of minds, the Lord of majesty, the exalted arm. By that arm, as Scripture says, the proud are scattered in the imagination of their hearts, the mighty are put down from their seat, and the humble are exalted. By this arm, that is, by Christ, the hungry are filled with good things and the rich are sent away empty. We see this being done in you as well. Look into yourself, and you will find both things that God casts down or raises up in your one person.

You have been brought down from pride and raised up to humility. You have been put down from the seat of unjust power, so that you might be set on the throne of peace and justice. You have been emptied of riches so as to be enriched in poverty. You have been emptied of that bloated surfeit of superfluity, so that, hungering for justice, you might be filled with the true goods of holy poverty. Where now are you, who were once so formidable, whether as an advocate before the tribunals or as a judge upon them? Where is that neck of yours, which was then more truly what you now falsely call it, the neck of a fat bull? How has it become docile and slender under the yoke of Christ since you turned and groaned, and God was pleased with you as with a young calf? You have laid aside the bull's neck and taken on the meekness of that ox which knew its owner. Blessed are the eyes of those who behold these wonders of God in you, and so wretched are those who see and do not see.

Who will give me wings like a dove, so that I might fly to you and rest in your presence and your conversation, and feast with the voice of exultation and praise? I would see you no longer yourself; I would see a calf where there was a lion, and see Christ in the boar. You are now a boar to the world and a lamb to God, your ferocity and your strength having changed places. For you are no longer a boar of the forest but of the cornfield, since you grow fat on the good fruits of discipline, and your fodder is the harvest of the virtues. You are armed with the tusks of the two Testaments to tear the nets of Nimrod the hunter. All the weapons you once bore in pride on behalf of the world, you now humbly turn against the world. Now you are truly wise, truly eloquent and truly powerful, you who are foolish and dumb to this world. So you may serve God, the author of your tongue and mind, with eloquence and wisdom drawn from his own gifts.

Now, better instructed in divine law, you may plead your own case as an advocate, and as a more just judge you may judge yourself and pass sentence on yourself and concerning yourself. In this way you will deserve all the more to be acquitted and will make yourself worthy not only of pardon but of glory, since you present yourself by accusing yourself and sanctify yourself by condemning yourself. You understand that to be holy and innocent is to please not men but God. That is why, as you write, you rarely go into the cities, and have come to love the familiar seclusion of the quiet countryside. You do not prefer leisure to work, nor withdraw yourself from serving the Church, but you avoid the tumults of the churches and their restless councils, which now almost rival the crowds of the forum. I believe, though, that this very thing is preparing greater benefits for the Church: by a wholesome decision you devote yourself to holy instruction, and, intent on spiritual studies, to which solitude is a friend, you form and strengthen Christ within you day by day. So, as a more useful servant and a more learned teacher, you may make yourself more worthy of the see in which you have been placed by the will of God, powerful alike in deed and word. With tongue and mind in harmony, you may offer in yourself a true pattern of apostolic discipline, both doing and teaching the Lord's commandment. Only then will it be clear that you are a priest not by human vote but by divine judgment.

I believe this is already being proved by both your faith and your life. So I ask and earnestly beg you always to include us in your prayers and to take care to visit us by letter whenever there is opportunity. I demand this gift from you not so much because I am eager to receive a courtesy as because I long to refresh my spirit. I want to receive both the comfort of love and joy together when, reading your letters, I see that you remember me in holy matters and are devoted to your progress in spiritual knowledge and in understanding of a heart burning toward God. Then I will weigh you no longer by your word about power, that is, by your preaching of Christ, but by the power of that word itself. That is, I want you to confirm by your speech and by your life alike that you believe Christ [?] crucified to be Lord and God. For we ought to bear the image of the heavenly man with the same devotion with which we formerly bore the image of the earthly man. Otherwise, who will give us what is our own, if we have not been as faithful in what is ours as we were in what belonged to another? We were made for this, to be good and to serve our Creator. If we live against his commandments, then by [?] our own fault we shall act not only against our life but also against our nature, and so such people are compared to beasts, which have no understanding. Yet God's goodness makes this bargain with us: forgiving our past ungodliness, he is content if we are servants to him for our own good, just as we were servants to the devil against ourselves. As the apostle says, just as we offered our members to serve iniquity, so we should offer the same members to serve justice. That is, we should delight in the Lord with the same affection with which we delighted in sin. So let us seek the kingdom of God as eagerly as we sought the honors of the world, and, finally, let us care for heavenly goods as diligently as we cared for earthly ones.
39. TO APER AND AMANDA, THEIR HOLY, DESERVEDLY VENERABLE AND MOST BELOVED BRETHREN, PAULINUS AND THERASIA, SINNERS.

Let others receive income from their estates as rents are paid each year. For us, whose estate is your love in Christ, the income comes from the services of your affection and is counted out in the kindness of your letters. Thanks be to the Lord our God, who repays living goods in place of dead and perishable ones, and has also granted you to us as a most fertile estate. In earthly matters the dearer field is the one that answers the greedy hopes of its farmer with an overflowing harvest, or charms the eyes of a fastidious owner with its beauty. In the same way, among our spiritual estates, that is, among the holy brothers whom the love of Christ has joined to us and given us as an everlasting possession, we reckon that person a richer field who has been more attentive to us and more fruitful to us in providing the blessings of salvation. That being so, see how great a holding of this kind we possess in you. Besides the affection you pour out on us in return for ours, you also bestow other gifts, which we cannot match, from the abundance of your tongue and the riches of your mind. For the services and the eloquence of your letters, which you pay us so generously by your yearly messenger, show how broad an estate you are to us and how fertile a soil you are to God. Already you bring forth thirtyfold fruit from your continence with each other; with the daily growth of the faith you share you are coming near to sixtyfold; and from your virgin offspring you promise a hundredfold.

You write that your property and the care of your children are obstacles to your purpose, since they are the cause of the necessity that makes you look after earthly things when you long for heavenly ones. We judge, rather, that these things have been set before you by divine design as material of many kinds for exercising your faith and perfecting your virtue. Since the whole property of this world was evidently established for the sake of man and made subject to man, who can doubt that in every place in the world and in every part of nature benefits have been prepared for the human race? From them we may not only take bodily profit but, much more, gather spiritual lessons. That is why Wisdom herself, the maker of all things, who orders all things sweetly, says through Solomon that husbandry was created by the Most High, so that you may cultivate it not only with bodily effort but also with spiritual zeal. She shows how much can be drawn from the countryside for the instruction of the soul when she sends her followers to the ant and the bee, both of them creatures of the countryside: the one provides for life from the crops, the other works honey from the flowers. And how many things the Lord taught in the Gospel by examples from country life! He pointed out the signs of the last times from the fig tree and from the fields turning golden as the harvest drew near. He warned that we must learn in the field what to guard against in the spirit: that the enemy may sow deceit, the rival of our faith, among us as he sows tares among the wheat. So he called us his field and showed that he himself is the sower of our life within us. He expressed the differences between souls by the different natures of soils. Let us take care, then, that our soil is not barren, and let us also cultivate ourselves with zealous devotion to the law of the Lord, to bear the fruitfulness we owe to God, which is also profitable to ourselves.

So when you are in the field and look at your land, think that you too are Christ's field, and look at yourself as you look at your field. Whatever appearance you demand that your steward give your field, give the same cultivation of your heart to God the Lord. And understand that whatever displeases or pleases you in your field likewise pleases or displeases Christ in your soul. If the soul lies waste and foul with sins as with brambles, and is not watered by the clouds of the prophets and apostles, grace will abandon it and it will be condemned to a dry wilderness. But if it takes care of itself, cultivates itself with frequent prayers, grows rich on the sacred Scriptures, presses the plough of the cross deep into the heart, roots out its thorns with the rake of the fear of God, and is burned in its faults and enlightened in its senses by the fiery word of God, then the master of the house will surely delight to walk about in your heart and to go through every region of your soul. Rejoicing over you as over his own, if you prove a diligent cultivator of yourself, he will say to you: Well done, good servant, enter into the joy of your Lord; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many.

But what shall we say for ourselves, who in perverse order give advice to the strong though we are weak ourselves? We are in fact as poor in spiritual things as you suppose us to be in earthly things, and we are humble not by strength of mind but by lack of strength. That cramped little garden which you describe so grandly, with your rich gift of speech, barely large enough to hold and produce a single cabbage, is ourselves; and we are more insipid than half-cooked beet, as the prophet said. Let us grant that that cabbage is not the only tasteless thing in our house. Yet the cabbage has a better excuse for lacking salt, for it did not receive any because of our poverty or our stinginess. It is we rather who are boiled, we who are more culpably unsalted. In us foolishness overflows from sins we chose to commit, so that the apostolic salt has lost its savour and the spiritual seasonings have fled from the sight of our sins. Unless we are refreshed by your prayers, not even that single cabbage will flourish in us, and in our utter desolation we shall lack even an unsalted vegetable.

Pray, then, that the harmful caterpillar may not lay waste the shoots of our soul, that the greedy locust may not devour the crop of our mind, that the sluggish cankerworm may not settle in our heart, and that blight, the last companion of these little beasts, may not eat away the inmost fibres of our vital parts. For evil beasts press hard upon our inner self, and troublesome birds often attack us, to snatch the seed of the word from us if they can. But thanks be to God that we did not fall from the sower's hand beside the way; rather we were sown in the Way itself, that is, placed in the bosom of our Catholic mother. That we may not be cast out from it like stillborn children, we need his mercy, so that he may give us understanding in this way which he has commanded and enabled us to walk, and fix his eyes upon us, so that we may not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.

But let us return to our talk of farming. For God our Father is himself the farmer, God our Saviour is the true vine, and the Holy Spirit is the one who waters our souls. May it come about, then, through your prayers, that the supreme Master of the house, the heavenly Farmer and diligent Gardener, may visit the garden of our soul, come to it often, and set his seal on it, as he did that garden in which he taught, prayed and rose again. May he strengthen in us the bond of his love, so that we may live as branches abiding in him. May he command his clouds to rain upon us, and remove from our heart the wicked passions of fleshly thoughts, as he removes those creatures that are enemies of good crops, so that the prophet's word may not be fulfilled in us: What the caterpillar left, the locust has eaten; what the locust left, the cankerworm has eaten; and what the cankerworm left, the blight has eaten. For in our body there are just as many chief incitements to vice, by which the human race is most troubled: hope, fear, joy and grief. Two concern the present and two the future: in the present, distress of mind or joy; in the future, fear or hope. So we must take care that, while we flee one of these vices, we do not run into its opposite.

So the caterpillar, the locust, the cankerworm and the blight are to be understood as the passions of our affections. Some of them cling to the heart only briefly; others grow little by little and, if they are not cast out, reach to the very marrow and drink up all the sap of the soul. See how these monstrous vices in our hearts correspond to the damage that such monsters do to crops. For example, if I desire something forbidden and at once reject the thought, that is the caterpillar sitting on the leaf and shaken off. If I do reject it, but the thought returns, and the rejecting and returning begin to happen more and more often, that is the locust flying off and coming back. If it begins to linger and spends more time eating than flying away, it is called the cankerworm. And if this cankerworm, which no longer flies away much but mostly sits, is not cast out, it turns into blight. Once that has fixed itself deep within, it is never driven out of the soul, or only with difficulty, just as blight is never, or hardly ever, driven out of the stalk.

I fear that by wearying you with my chatter I have settled on you more troublesomely than a locust or a cankerworm. Shake off this little letter, then, like a caterpillar, and throw it far away, so that longer contact with our words may not make you catch the blight of our foolishness, which would dull the brightness of your heart and blunt the vigour of your mind. Yet forgive us for this sin of wearying you so heavily, if only because we are abusing your patience by the licence that love allows. We trust that your heart is so full of love for us that it will take no offence at us even if we do you a wrong for which we deserve to give offence, if indeed you could ever be offended by us, even when we deserve it.
LETTER 40. MEROPIUS PAULINUS AND THERASIA TO SANCTUS AND AMANDUS, BROTHERS IN CHRIST OUR GOD, GREETINGS.

For everything there is a time, and a time for every matter under heaven. Above heaven there is no time, because eternity has no time. The Creator has given eternity even to the creatures in heaven, though he alone has eternity as his own and dwells in unapproachable light. True eternity exists only in him who alone is what he is, as he himself says: I am who I am. All other things exist only in him. So there is a time for every matter under heaven: a time for leisure and a time for business, a time for silence and a time for speaking, a time to go hungry and a time to feast. Until now it has been our time to fast from your words, and now the time has come to be fed on them. You have fed us with your letter, sweet with the word of God and anointed with the oil of gladness, with which we gladly anoint our head, because in you the work of the olive does not fail; in you dwells love from a pure heart, a good conscience and faith unfeigned. But since no one who is very hungry can be satisfied with a single loaf, we confess that we are not yet filled. Rather, this one letter of yours has spurred on our longing for your letters. We count it as just one, because so far we have received only one such letter from you, one that fills our soul as with marrow and fatness.

Yet even if there have been changes of season in our duties toward each other, such as a time to keep silent and a time to speak, there has never been a time for loving and a time for neglecting. As you surely remember, holy brother, I began to love you long ago, and I have loved you constantly. That love, however, was not the love that belongs to Christ. It was the friendship of human familiarity, which has flattery on its lips but no root in the heart, because it is not founded on the rock, for it is not built in Christ. So it is sometimes shaken and broken up by any passing breeze of fickleness. Holding a brief flower of passing favour, it withers quickly like grass and soon falls like the flower of the field. But the love of the Lord, by which we are bound to one another both to live together and to die together, endures for ever, because the love of Christ is strong as death. The law of death cannot be broken, and neither can the chain of love, and this shows that love and death have equal strength. For as the prophet says, Who is the man that shall live and not see death? So too the apostle cries out, Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Therefore, blessed one, a richer fruit of this love will come to you, since you were the first to be wounded by its darts. You went ahead of us with blessings of sweetness through the chaste and faithful words of your letter, in which your tongue dripped honey and milk from the word of the Lord.

In fact I had written to your loving self before, and when I received your short letter in reply to the one I had sent, I sank back again into my long silence, as if I had paid what I owed. But Christ was keeping sharper watch in your mind, and you were the first to blossom again in wisdom so as to rouse in us the observance of love, so that it would not fall asleep in the death of forgetfulness. Where my unkindness had abounded, your kindness abounded all the more toward me. You have enriched me many times over with the affection and service of your love: you took as a companion in visiting us the Lord's blessed servant, brother Amandus, and set him beside us as a strong patron. We trust that, just as he has become your partner in writing to us, he will also be your colleague in praying for us. Spiritual brotherhood indeed demands this: as you have one spirit in faith and in confessing Christ, so you should have one love and one labour in claiming your neighbours for him. So you will reap from the supreme Rewarder an abundant reward in common, raised high in his towers, because a brother who helps a brother will be exalted. Only remember always to pray and sigh for us, and from now on take care not to burden us with words of praise, lest you lay a stumbling block for yourselves too by calling sweet what is bitter. For you have read that praise befits the upright, those who are truly holy, not sinners [?] lying in the gall of bitterness and still bound by no slender cord of wickedness, so that ruin and misery cannot help but be present in our ways.

Yet in this way too there ought to be contrition in our minds, because God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Who will give us a heart of flesh, so that the hardness of our senses may be softened, and we may feel the Lord's arrows piercing our flesh with holy fear, and, with the pain of our wounds awakened, weep before the Lord who made us? Let Jeremiah lend us that fountain of tears with which he lamented his day and his people. Let David also pour over us the rivers of his eyes, with which he watered his bed, bathing not only the cheeks of his face but his whole couch with overflowing tears. For our iniquities have gone over our head and are multiplied beyond the hairs of our head, since more works of wickedness than of righteousness can be counted in us. Therefore our scars have festered and grown worse because of our folly, and our bones have grown old because we kept silent before God. Adding iniquity to iniquity, after we had set our eyes on bending down to the earth, we raised them slowly and with difficulty to the mountains of God, from where our help comes from the Lord, who alone is able to heal all our diseases and rescue us from the body of this death. For we were bound through Adam and are set free through Christ, provided that we bear the image of the heavenly man as we have borne the image of the earthly; that is, provided that we serve righteousness and truth for our salvation as faithfully as we diligently served unrighteousness and cruelty for our death. The apostle asks something within human reach: just as we yielded our members to serve iniquity unto destruction and shame, so let us yield those same members to serve righteousness unto life and glory. For we still have with us the fruit of those works of which we are now ashamed.

But thanks be to the Wisdom of God, to Christ our God, who, remaining in himself, makes all things new and orders all things sweetly, so that there is a time for every matter: a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to laugh and a time to weep, a time to build and a time to tear down. Let the time for killing, tearing down and laughing now have passed for us, I pray, and let the time for healing, building and weeping come at last. For behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. The night is far gone, and the day is at hand. Let us cast off the works of darkness and take up the weapons of light. Let us walk in the light as children of the day, for behold, our enemies have made ready their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark. They cannot shoot those who stand in the light, since such people see them before they strike and, being on their guard, easily avoid them. Yet the two kinds of season can be joined in one and the same work, so that the seasons distinguished above work together in us. For in that by which we are given life we are killed, and in that by which we are killed we are given life, through him who said, I will kill and I will make alive. Unless Christ kills us, we shall not live. Of him it is written, The Lord puts to death and brings to life, because unless he destroys our sins he will not bring our souls to life. That is why the prophet says to him, I rose up, and I am still with you. O that you would slay the sinner, O God! We shall rise, emerging from the mire of the dregs and from the shadow of death, and we shall remain with him, if he kills the sinner in us and creates the righteous man, because the cup of our frailty is in the hand of the Lord; with it he humbles one and exalts another. For unless the outer man is humbled, the inner man is not exalted. Thus the times for killing and healing, and for tearing down and building, come together in one work, when the life of sin is torn down in us so that the life of righteousness may be built up. Newness cannot be built unless oldness is torn down, nor can we love Christ unless we begin to hate mammon. Nor shall we be able to rejoice in that world unless we mourn in this one, because those who sow in tears will reap in joy.

So the prayer in the Psalms of the poor man, troubled and mourning, now suits us, for our days have almost vanished like smoke, and still our wickedness has not vanished. Behold, he has made our days old, drawn out by the course of the years. Old age no longer merely sprinkles our head with grey; it drenches it. Yet we are still living the infancy of spiritual life, crawling with first efforts and with childish understanding. Barely beginning to speak the word of God, our soul is like an infant crying its first sounds as we loosen a tongue that is mute and untrained in the sacred Scriptures. Once we were fluent in the literature of human fables; now we stammer in the words of truth. We are wise in folly and fools in wisdom, strong in vices and still tender in virtues, raw recruits whose will toward righteousness is barely born, and veterans whose life has been spent in sins. For a long time, as you know, holy and blessed brother, we wallowed in this world and grew old among our enemies. Would that we had grown old to our enemies, so that the life of the broad road might now have failed in us who have withdrawn into leisure, and our youth be renewed in Christ like the eagle's, so that we may put off the old age of the old man and put on the new man, who is created according to God. But since we cannot yet be like the pelican of the wilderness, when shall we become like the night raven in the house? When shall we be roused to that vigour of a lofty mind, so that, winged with spiritual eagerness and made perfect at the steep summit of the heights of virtue, we can say, I have watched, and have become like a sparrow alone upon the housetop? Let us consider here, if you please, on what principle and in what order the prophetic word arranges these kinds of birds in the person of the poor and troubled man, that is, the penitent, brought to poverty of hope by some fall. You will bear, I think, the chatter of my foolishness, since you have provoked it by despising yourselves. I have learned from a certain holy and very learned man, very dear to me, who has come to know many things not only by reading but also by travelling, that the pelican is a bird common in Egypt and the regions near it. It roams the deserts close to the river Nile and feeds on serpents, which it strikes down in combat. So it fights in order to conquer; if defeated it dies, but if victorious it both escapes death and gains its food. He also maintained that where nycticorax is written, nycticora is more accurate, and he seemed to demonstrate this with plausible reasoning. He said that the bird meant in this passage is the one we call the owl, because it practises its song and its flight secretly at night and is given light in the darkness, by which almost all animals are blinded. Hence it is more fittingly called nycticora than nycticorax, because nycticorax means 'night raven', whereas nycticora means 'seeing by night', since the pupil of the eye is called [?] by the Greeks. It is plain that the owl has nothing in common with the raven. Moreover, it is clear, as I said, that like certain other night birds it sees better in darkness and is blinded in daylight; it endures night during the day and makes use of light during the night.

Now then, my blessed ones, see how well this bird fits the sorrowing poor man, that is, the penitent. He has been impoverished of the riches of grace; with a mind conscious of wretched falls he mourns the loss of his glory; he toils in pitiable affliction in his groaning; he strives to regain the life of his soul through the death of his own flesh; and he seeks remedies for his wounded salvation through the outlay of prayers, the support of groans and the earnest pleading of tears. How aptly is such a poor sinner called an Egyptian or a nocturnal bird! For he shuts himself away in sorrow from the common assembly of the Church, within the prison of his little cell, to weep over and confess his sins. He flees far from this world to remain in the solitude of lamentation, and there he wars against the desires of his flesh and fights in spiritual combat to crush his sins. Surely, both in his dwelling and in his battle, he becomes like the pelican of the wilderness, and he imitates that bird, the enemy of serpents, as he fights against the devil himself and the princes of darkness to overcome sins and the thoughts of the flesh. If he wins in that contest, he will live on, surviving his enemies. He seeks food for himself from his victory, because as conqueror of sin and of the devil he gains the merit of life. We experience daily, in the dangers of our inner man, how the devil with his whole army of spiritual wickedness creeps in with various arts to destroy us. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through [?] Christ our Lord, so that we may tread on the asp and the basilisk and trample the lion and the dragon. It is against such arts, then, that we wage this rival struggle for our salvation, against those who are the princes of darkness, that is, men powerful in sins, whom the apostle calls darkness. Pray that, while we live in the desert of this world, we may destroy these serpents after the example of that solitary bird. When they have been crushed and devoured through victory, our inner man will be enlightened, as though a cloud of darkness had been scattered. Then he will become like the night-seeing owl in the house, that is, in the house of the Lord, so that amid the darkness of this world he may direct the sharp gaze of a mind once failing, and, with eyes so enlightened, may say with the prophet, For darkness shall not be dark to me, and the night shall be as bright as the day. This certainly happens when the two substances in man agree with each other, so that the flesh too, renouncing its earthly nature, passes over with spiritual affection into harmony with the soul. And then the night will be as bright as the day, when the flesh too becomes spiritual like the soul.

If it is granted through your prayers that we imitate the pelican of the wilderness in crushing the viperous enemy, and see with the eyes of the night owl amid the darkness of this world, then at the end, with our feet set upon the heights of perfect virtue, watching in prayer and meditating on the law of the Lord, we shall become like the sparrow alone upon the housetop. With body and spirit in agreement in the will of God, we shall rightly say, I am alone until I pass over. And who is this sparrow, in whom the pattern of the perfect man is found, if not that sparrow which has found itself a house, and which, with the turtledove, has made your altars its nest, O Lord of hosts? Perhaps this sparrow is one of those two, of which one does not fall to the ground without the Father's will. For this highest sparrow did fall in the body, but he also rose again. He fell by consent of his will, becoming obedient to the Father even to the death of the cross. This sparrow is that Wisdom who shows herself gladly to those who seek her in the ways. Now she meets them at the gates, now she encounters them in the streets, now from the walls or the lofty towers she calls her lovers to herself and invites them to the heights of her dwellings, to fulfil her word that, once lifted up, she draws all things to herself. Who will give us wings like a dove's, covered with silver, so that, winged by the words of the Lord, which are chaste like silver tried in the fire, we may fly to the prize of the heavenly calling, following this solitary sparrow as he soars above us? He is the only Son of God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly. He who descended into the lower parts of the earth is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, leading captivity captive, so that he might fill all things. If we can follow this sparrow in direct imitation, walking in the same footsteps in which the beautiful feet of those who preach the gospel have trod, then, set on high, we shall be able to say, I have watched, and have become like a sparrow alone upon the housetop.

Yet even when raised on high, let us remember the Lord's word that whoever is on the housetop must not go back into his house to take his goods; that is, we must not run back into ourselves and seek again the works of the flesh, like goods left behind below. For no one, he says, who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God. Even if we are on the housetop, that is, even if we have flown up above our earthly nature and do not yield to the flesh, let us fear, after the example of birds, to fly down to low places. For it is written that not without cause are nets spread for birds. And we know that fowlers, lying in wait for the simplicity of birds, set snares on the ground. Often they bring the birds down by deception with scattered bait or hidden lures, and entangle the trusting creatures in nooses covered with treacherous turf. But when the fowlers of spiritual wickedness tempt us with a similar art, through the enticements of this world spread out before us, let us, armed with faith and enlightened by truth, say: In the Lord I put my trust; how can you say to my soul, Flee to the mountain like a sparrow? Depart from me, all you who work iniquity. Therefore let us pray to the Lord, who enlightens every man coming into this world. I think 'every man' is said because no one is a man unless he acknowledges God, and rather has been found worthy to be acknowledged by God. Those who do not acknowledge him are compared to the beasts and have become like them. Let us, then, who by his great mercy have been justified from ungodliness through faith and not by works, run after the fragrance of his ointments, so that from his name we may draw the fragrance of life and become the good fragrance of Christ to God. Let us be given to drink, as it is written, of the wine of ointments from the cup of salvation, in which he himself, like a perfumer, as is written in Ecclesiasticus, mixes ointments of sweetness, dividing his gifts to each as he wills, so that all things may be filled in all, and he may make manifest in us the fragrance of the knowledge of him, because his name is ointment poured out. So that this name may always be invoked over us and named in us, let our citizenship be in heaven. For we shall become like the sparrow alone upon the housetop if we do not set our minds on or seek the things that are on earth, but the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of the Father. With countless eyes he watches our deeds and looks on at this contest, in which, though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh.

For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood but against invisible enemies and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. This is not because evil spirits act in the heavenly places, but because they oppose those who live a heavenly life. So let us put on the weapons of light. In our God let us leap over that wall which separates us from God, and let us not, because of the weakness of our flesh, fear an adversary who is violent by his spiritual nature. For strength is made perfect in weakness, and a man is not mighty by his own strength; rather the Lord makes his adversary weak. The Lord of hosts himself, the King of glory, confounded that adversary for us through such a manner of combat that in the cross of Christ it was not divine strength but human weakness that overcame him. Let us therefore follow Jesus in his triumph, and may his truth surround us with the shield of faith, so that we may not fear the terror of the night or the arrow that flies by day. A thousand shall fall at our side and ten thousand at our right hand, not by our strength but by Christ's. His is the battle in which we fight and his the crown by which we conquer, because we are members of his body, provided that we put to death our members on earth so that they become weapons of righteousness. Girded with these, let us offer Christ, his angels and ourselves a joyful spectacle in our contest, and, flying out of the hunters' snare, let us sing with chattering thanksgiving: Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare is broken, and we are set free, for our help is in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. For there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved. Triumphing in this name, let us confess to the Lord his mercies and glory in his praise, not in our own. For, as the prophet says, if we have anything good, it is from him, and if anything excellent, it is his; for he made us, and not we ourselves. And so the apostle says, What do you have, O man, that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? In this he warns that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord. So our distress becomes light when we seem to be praised. We are conscious of no good of our own, such that the one praising us should press hard on our modesty as though we recognized the good as ours, because we know that it is not we ourselves but the gifts and works of divine goodness that are being proclaimed. If anything good is seen or believed to be in us, it belongs to him who alone is good, from whose fullness we all receive, and with which we are sprinkled according to the capacity of our merit or faith. For the dew that comes from him is health to us, and we rejoice in its drops. So this error of yours in praising us will do you no harm. More than that, such devout faith heaps up an abundant reward for you, since in judging that we, whom in our own minds we know to be wicked and depraved, members of the perverse generation of this world, have been made good, you put your trust in the almighty Lord, who is able to justify the ungodly, to give life to the dead, to enlighten darkness and to make the scarlet white.

So pray earnestly that we may receive a heart worthy of so great a work, or rather gift, of God, and that we who have received contempt for our inheritance may receive contempt for ourselves as well. For we tread a narrow way and walk unsteadily, as if on a tightrope, and unless we plant our steps with a sure balance of mind, so as not to turn aside to the right or to the left, the enemy will easily push us into a fall on one side or the other. That is why Wisdom sings to us in Solomon: “Do not turn away from the Lord, lest you fall.” For the Lord Jesus himself is the way, the truth and the life, and he says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance,” because we can slip into vices along the very paths of the virtues. Unless, as I said, we keep the movements of the soul balanced and steady, we will draw pride out of humility itself, and the semblance of devotion will vanish if conceit creeps in through the praise of poverty. And what good will it do to be without riches if we remain rich in vices? So we beg you not to flatter us on the strength of that word of the Lord, as though we had already done it: “Sell what you possess.” For what remains is greater: “and come, follow me.” And it is easy to see how great a thing it is to follow Christ, for it means that a human being imitates God. But you also know that “God has spoken once; these two things I have heard.” For this saying, like almost all of divine Scripture, opens onto two paths: “Go and sell all that is yours.” We possess not only money and estates, which are goods outside us, but also the inner wealth of our soul, which is truly our substance. To sell this, that is, to part ourselves from it, is a victory as much greater as it is harder to separate what is inborn than what has been added, and to tear out what is fixed within than to throw off what is attached from outside. For whoever renounces his own ways and disowns himself changes and overcomes his very self, and so fulfills that mightiest word of God: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.” Remembering these words of the Lord, let us pour out our soul to him, and he will nourish us; he will cherish our life, hidden in himself, and will reveal himself in glory, provided that we pray for this same soul at the acceptable time, that is, now, in this world. For in hell who will give him praise? Here we die to our sins, so that there we may not live in punishments. For the death that is called the second death is nothing other than a life of punishments.

Let us beware, then, of the lowest hell, where Gehenna will torment body and soul forever: the sinner’s soul dies without end, while feeling remains and the stuff of corruption endures. For the dead too, as it is written, will rise incorruptible, not into the immortality of glory but into that of punishment. “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle, who has shattered the bars of iron and humbled the slanderer, so that he might raise me up from the gates of death and I might tell of his wonders in the gates of the daughter of Zion. May the Lord bless you out of Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem, and pray for us all the days of your life, so that our portion may be shared together in the land of the living.
XLI.

On the back of your letter we have read the note listing the letters which you indicated are mine. Truly, I had so completely forgotten almost all of them that I would not have recognized them as mine had I not trusted your letter. From this I have received a greater proof of your love, since I saw that I am better known to you than to myself. I am glad to have received the hymns I was longing for. By this gift, holy brother, you have reminded me to make my little torch ready with care while there is time, so that I may not be shut out with the foolish if I do not go out to meet him with the wise. Pray, then, that our souls may be both virgin and fruitful: virgins without barrenness, fruitful without corruption. For it is in this mystery that the law calls cursed the man who has not raised up seed in Israel, and that the gospel speaks of the wise virgin who, having procured oil, waits with watchful care for the bridegroom's coming with her torch well oiled, and as he arrives kindles a light which its rich fuel will not let go out.

Therefore let our mind be fertile for God and bring forth the fruits of life by good works. Let the spirit be a virgin, so that no enticement of the world may corrupt it and it may remain untouched by every stain of vice. For those foolish virgins seem to me to be the souls that are barren of virtues, and the wise ones those that are uncorrupted by vices. Then too, five are set down in each kind of virgin, so that we may understand this to refer to the integrity or corruption of a person's senses; for we are all endowed with five senses, through which we receive either life or death. Grieving over them the prophet says: Death has come in through your windows. Let us block these windows with the fear of God, so that we may be deaf and blind to all the shapes and voices of this world. Let us hedge our ears with thorns against a wicked tongue and enticing melodies; let us turn our eyes away, so that they may not see vanity; let us block our nostrils too, so that we may not draw the smell of death from the corruption of this world. Let not the disease of gluttony creep in through the alluring sense of taste and sap the strength of continence with the foods of desire; nor let us flatter the body with soft clothing, lest limbs wrongly caressed by delicate garments stir us toward fleshly touches and unlawful embraces. So it will come about that in each one of us, with all the senses chaste and steeped in the oil of faithful teaching, all five virgins will remain wise, and with oil stored in their vessels will rest in untroubled expectation, ready to go out soon to meet him with torches easily trimmed, once they are roused by the first stir of the bridegroom's arrival. For in the great congregations of the church there are to be seen not only virgins, countless though their number is, but also married women and widows, differing both in conduct and in fruits. I do not think, then, that only five foolish virgins and as many wise were set down for any other reason than this: the two figures differ across the whole body of the people, but the number, for the reason given above, is contained in each person individually, so that each one has within himself either foolish or prudent virgins according to the quality of his senses; where these are watchful, the virginity is wise, where they are sluggish, it is foolish. For the foolish, though so unlike the wise, are nonetheless called virgins just as the wise are, because virgins according to the flesh have a barrenness that bears nothing, while according to the spirit they have a fruitful chastity. Therefore the wise do not have a barren virginity, because they are wise, nor do the foolish have a fruitful one, because they are foolish. Their type seems to me to be the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness with God, and the wisdom of the flesh, which is truly a foolish virgin, because it is not joined to the law and is not subject to the law and wisdom of God. And its lamp is easily put out, because, empty of the Holy Spirit, it lacks the oil of truth, by which the inner eye is enlightened and the head of the soul is anointed—that head being our faith, whose oil is the pouring in of heavenly teaching.

So let not the oil of the sinner anoint our head, nor let dying flies spoil the oil of sweetness, so that Christ may always be our head and oil may never be lacking to our head, since his name is ointment poured out. And then, perfected in all our senses, we shall be wise virgins, if the wisdom of God remains in us, through which virginity was made fruitful even in the body. I am wearying you too much, and presuming too much on the patience of your love. But I ought to listen to Solomon speaking in the wisdom of God, and set my foot of words more sparingly, even among those who love me most, lest they grow sated and hate me. Yet I know that just as no one can hate his own flesh, so you cannot hate my lowliness, which you have mingled with your own inmost being. May the peace and love and grace and humility of Christ the Lord Most High abound in you, blessed brothers, deservedly venerable and most beloved.
XLII. Paulinus to Florentius, most blessed and deservedly venerable father.

We rejoice in the Lord that we have been visited by a letter from your Holiness and invited to correspond. We had not previously enjoyed the favor of your acquaintance, but now, by a sudden gift of God, we have gained the full confidence of a friendship as if it were an old one. "Wine," Scripture says, "and a friend will grow old, and you will drink it with pleasure." See, your Holiness has surpassed this saying of the prophet. You have begun to love us with such perfect affection that at the very outset of this bond you have given us the sweetness of a long-matured love, so that we need not wish for any growth in a love whose full maturity we experience in its abundant beginnings. We can compare the richness of your soul to great springs, which burst from their source with a wide mouth and are rivers at the very moment they rise. Blessed therefore be the Lord, who has so abounded over our sins with such grace that he has enriched us, unworthy even of your acquaintance, with your love as well. We lacked until now a lesser good, since we had no bodily acquaintance with you, and he has granted us a gift of you as much greater as the spirit is a more excellent substance in man than the flesh. Therefore our heart exults, and with our mouth full of joy we say: The Lord has done great things for us. For you have gone before us with blessings of sweetness through holy words, tested like refined silver, visiting us, as I said, and rousing us from the stagnation of our sloth to the practice of love for you. In that love we were not asleep through ignorance; rather, we were silent because we did not know you. So blessed be the name of the Lord, and may he rejoice in this work of his goodness too: to us who do not know your face in the flesh he has shown instead this appearance of your mind, in which you are more beautifully formed in Christ. For "a man's speech," Scripture says, "reveals him," and "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks."

So your words, seasoned with apostolic salt, conveyed to us the savor of the grace given to you, and from what dropped from your lips we have tasted how sweet the Lord is in you. You have been made and set at the head of the people, chosen from the sheep to be the ram of the flock, to rule the sheep of the pasture of him who laid down his life for his sheep. That same Lamb and Shepherd will rule us forever, who made us sheep out of wolves, and is now the Shepherd who guards those sheep for whom he was a lamb offered in sacrifice. This, then, our Lord and God, who was seen on earth and lived among men for our sake, is both sheep and shepherd within us, for he rules us inwardly with an invisible staff and a saving rod, so that even if we walk in the shadow of death we fear no evil, because God is with us—that Emmanuel, Lord of majesty and son of a handmaid, the one by birth, the other by becoming. He is at once creator and redeemer of man, God from God, man for man's sake, Son of God before the ages, Son of Man for the world's sake, taking the form of a servant for the freedom of servants, and made poor so that he might enrich the poor by his poverty. For he is rich toward all in every good, who is filled all in all, the fullness of divinity, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far off on the sea, God our Savior, the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who is in the glory of God the Father, God over all, blessed forever.

He has deigned to take you into the lot of his apostles, so that by their craft you might be a fisher of men and, with the hook of the saving word, draw out of the bitter and deep waves of this world a catch for God that is to be given life rather than killed, as indeed you do every day. He is the God who has made you a helper in his building and his husbandry, and who has deigned to instill love for our lowliness into your soul, which is lofty through humility of heart; for without doubt it is through the gentleness of a sheep and the innocence of a lamb that you have earned the right to be a shepherd. This God, I say, deigns to make you love us, not dealing with us as our sins deserve but according to the riches of his goodness, so that help may accrue to us from the protection of your prayers, and to you a reward heaped up from your great love even for your lesser neighbors. May he make you mindful of us always, and mingle concern for our salvation with all your prayers and offerings. Otherwise this great outpouring of your love, in which we glory in the Lord, may become a stumbling block to us, if we cover the ravenous beasts of our untamed senses with sheep's clothing. So pray until you prevail, that our heart may be made spotless in the sight of the Lord, so that we may not be put to shame or dragged away together with those who speak peace with their neighbor while evil is in their hearts. Rather, in harmony of tongue and mind, may we believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto life. Only then will the devotion with which you love us return to you with fruit, if your prayer for us is so effective that we are changed from our earthly form and carried over into your likeness, so that we bear the image of the heavenly man with equal truth.

Then we shall truly be made happy by your love, if you obtain for us that we are not unlike you in love. Yet in this we do not stretch our wish so proudly as to hope to reach the summit of your merit. We wish only that, enclosed within the bounds of salvation, we may follow the footprints of truth along a straight road after the pattern of your faith, and that our end may be he who is also the beginning, the head and foundation of his body, the rock that is Christ. That rock follows us with a spring that goes along with us as we thirst for righteousness in the deserts of this world, and refreshes us with sweet drink, so that we may not be scorched by the heat of fleshly desires. On that rock a house built firmly does not fall. And from that rock, when its side was pierced by the lance, water and blood flowed, pouring out for us two saving streams together, the water of grace and the blood of the sacrament, so that he is both the fountain and the price of our salvation.

But woe is me, a sinner! How far have I gone on, or rather slipped? While I plead with you at length that I may deserve your prayers for my sins, or rather against my sins, when you pray, I am piling up through my talkativeness the very burden I ask your prayers to lighten, as though I had forgotten what is written: In much speaking you will not escape sin. What then shall I do? With what face shall I ask to be cleansed? Or on what grounds can I be defended before you, when I have knowingly and deliberately acted against the prophet's word, so as to wound myself with the sin of much speaking and weary your Holiness? I shall be held fast in this charge, and not even your prayer will be able to cover me, unless you yourself first forgive me this fault of wronging you, and offer a sacrifice of atonement to God for me, as blessed Job was commanded to do for his talkative friends. For I claim so large a share in your heart that I presume your indulgence will let this verbosity of mine go unpunished, not doubting that you have as much patience as you have love.
XLIII. To his holy and deservedly venerable brother Desiderius, most desired, the desire of my desires, Paulinus and Therasia, sinners, send greetings in Christ the Lord.

Long ago we had given our brother Victor a short letter for you, and I wanted that too to be delivered to your Holiness, so that it might testify for its bearer that his delay with us was not of his own choosing. The reason it was so short was this: soon after he arrived, Victor was in a hurry to get back from us to you, and had set himself so stubbornly on retracing his journey that he scarcely gave us time for even a short letter to you. Meanwhile sudden obstacles held him back as he was setting out, since winter closed off sailing and fear closed off the roads. Hindered and called back by these, the man who had refused a postponement when love asked for it granted necessity a long delay. During these delays he also fell ill, and indeed suffered so severely that, after being brought back from the gates of death, he spent more time recovering his health than he had spent enduring the illness. Afterwards, with the feast of the apostles already near, we thought it would be inhumane to send him away. So to the longer delays which the necessities mentioned had forced on him, we added this short delay of our own choosing, so that, after he had celebrated the apostles' feast with us as the companion of our vow and of our annual journey, he might return to you as the messenger of this business of ours as well.

The letters he is carrying to the blessed man of God, our brother Severus, we wrote at different times, as the pressure of haste allowed, as reading them will show by their variety. Victor demanded the shorter ones when he was hurrying and, so to speak, standing at the door ready to leave; the longer ones we wrote when we had become sure of his long stay, with our mind relaxed and, as it were, at leisure. Our brother Severus had written asking us to send him back, and had set the time so that he would be back by the days of the grape harvest. Since we could not obey him in this, we have tried at least to show obedience in this way: he will receive Victor back, if not in the year he had hoped, then at the time of year he had ordered. And if he is unwilling to blame Victor's lateness on the necessities I have explained, let him count his staying on as my fault. Yet let him credit even this late return to his own prayers. For when Victor was ill and had been entirely given up, I hoped for his recovery from the faith of Severus, though I despaired of it from my own merits. I saw Victor's innocence being scourged because of my sins, so that my iniquity was punished in him, since divine justice was avenging in him what went astray in his love for a sinner. For love brought a penalty on me too, so that, suffering with him in anguish of heart and mind, I bore the affliction which a man one in heart with me was suffering in his body.

As for the question you wrote to me about through him, seeking sweet and abundant water in a bitter and dry stream, I hand it back rather to your grace to explain; for I confess I have not dared to touch the weight of such great names and mysteries even with a finger. For I have read that wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, and so, conscious of my own malice, I could not be confident of divine revelation, since with a darkened heart I could not grasp the light of understanding. But you, blessed one, a vessel clean and fit for God: if you have received understanding of that blessing in which the patriarch, blind in body but enlightened, addresses his sons in the prophetic spirit, explain to me in your reply the mysteries of the kingdom and the sacraments hidden from the ages and revealed for the ages in Christ Jesus. In him the different figures of all the saints come together; he is prefigured in the patriarchs, speaks in the prophets, works in the apostles, and is filled all in all, for in him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and he is the beginning and end of all things. But if you have not yet received it—perhaps because, believing it had been given to me your neighbor, as though it were already laid up in your own storeroom, you put off asking the Lord for it for yourself—ask, and you will receive according to your faith and your soul. The more chaste your soul is in its members, the more lively it is in its senses; and the purer it is in heart, the more room it has for Christ, who is possessed by the humble and seen by the pure in heart.

As for you, so that you may take it less hard that my poverty has disappointed your expectation, think of it as though you have suffered from me what the Lord himself suffered from that fig tree. He came to it hungry, and finding it without fruit he struck it with the word of his mouth, so that the tree which had been barren under the Lord's blessing became withered under his curse. But I beg you, brother, though you have found me like that unhappy tree, not to strike me with a like word, lest I wither completely and, empty of the fruit I owe, be stripped even of my covering of leaves, that is, the foliage of grace. But thinking again that the Lord, merciful and compassionate, does not wish anyone to die, and that in that tree it was not his own creature that he condemned with his curse but the tree's defect, which was hostile to his planting, I beg you rather to curse my barrenness, so that no fruit may ever spring from it, and so that fruit for God may spring from my very self. For the destruction of my barrenness is to my profit, so that the fruitfulness of the Lord's planting may revive in me. When the vice that makes me fruitless dies, may I grow green again for my husbandman with the yield of good will, so that the Lord himself, hungering for my life, may find me offering him the fruits owed to him on fruit-bearing branches.

But about this same tree Mark has added material for no small question. While he agrees with the other evangelists about the cursed and withered fig tree, he said something more profound: having said that the Lord found no fruit on that tree, he added something that seems to excuse the tree, saying: For it was not the season for it to have fruit. If so, the tree seems to have been cursed without cause, since it was free of blame for its barrenness if it did not yet have fruit ready at an unsuitable time of year; it was not unfruitful through any fault, but unripe because of the season. But what the apostle says about cattle we can apply to the tree too, and say: Is it for a tree that God is concerned? Surely it was written for our sake, in whom God always wishes to find his food. For he has both a field and a vineyard in us. He winnows us on his threshing floor; in us he cleans the wheat, scatters the chaff and burns the tares. So in that tree he was hungering for man's salvation and seeking from man the fruit owed to him. But when he came to his own, his own did not receive him, and the barren synagogue of the unbelieving Jews did not yield the harvest of faith owed to him, which he had sown in them through the law and the prophets. He came to their tree seeking from the sons of his planting the sweet food of the growth he had looked for; but the tree withheld the fruits of devotion and gave him gall for food. When he asked for grapes it offered him thorns, and it gave the very planter of the good vineyard, the true vine himself and the cluster of sweetness, burning vinegar to drink. Hence their table was turned into a snare for them, their grapes became grapes of bitterness, and their wine the incurable rage of dragons.

But you, my brother, pray the Lord that our vine may not come from the vineyard of such men, for their stock has degenerated from the vineyard of the Lord of hosts into the vineyard of Sodom. And unless the Lord, in the branches of the apostles, had left us a seedbed of life from the roots of the patriarchs, from which the salvation of the gentiles might sprout and in which the line of the blessed seed might endure, we would have been like Sodom and Gomorrah in the full measure of wickedness. But since it is the last hour, and the axe is already laid to the roots of the trees, threatening a just felling to dry and unhappy wood, I beg you to pray for pardon and a respite for me. Then, with death put off, I may perhaps receive the sap of fruitfulness from the diligence of your love and the tending of my own care, so that divine fear may dig around my heart and needful repentance may enrich my stock with the dung of humility. Roused then to watchful care, may I stand ready at every hour, and be anxious while the Lord is away so that I may be secure when he comes, so that at every time and on every day Christ may find me fruitful for him. That is, may I never appear unripe for any work of his will. If perhaps at a time of anger he should ask me for his peace, may my mind not be unripe for concord through the bitterness of anger; nor may I wait for the sun to go down on my anger, lest my life go down if evening closes the day before peace has put out my rage.

What I have said about anger, take as said of every kind of vice. For I think this is the meaning of the Lord's seeking fruit on that tree before its season. He who knows the secrets of the heart and saw through people's thoughts did not fail to see what lay before human eyes. Nor was he inferior even to human understanding, so as not to know the season of the year, which even little children know, and demand autumn's fruit in spring. Rather, the craftsman of our salvation, the creator, whose whole life and action on earth was a pattern of conduct and character for us, set out his invisible counsels in visible form, and in creatures without reason expressed for the rational soul a likeness of the form he would give it, so that he might teach us everything for our salvation by the written signs of his deeds and words. And this is what he wanted us to understand through the evangelist, when he showed us that he had sought fruit from the tree out of its season: that man should know he owes fruit to God at all times. For the good Lord, who is preparing mortal man for immortality, wishes him already in this world to put on the likeness of eternity, so that he may bear fruit not according to the season, but may at every season be ripe for him with whom, or in whom, he is to abide beyond time.
XLIV. Paulinus and Therasia, sinners, to their holy, deservedly venerable and most beloved brother and sister, Aper and Amanda.

Who would give me the fountain of your letter, so that I might reply to it? Your letter is woven with varied flowers of spiritual graces, eloquent now with divine rather than scholarly speech, and flowing, as if from the land of divine promise, with the milk of devotion and the honey of wisdom. You have sucked that honey and oil from the firm rock, that is, Christ the Lord, who is the foundation of the eternal house. On this foundation you have begun to raise the building of salvation with living works, and you are striving to build on it not wood, hay and stubble, but gold, silver and precious stones. For, laying aside with the old man the hardness, dryness and fickleness of your former heart, you have become a well-watered tree which, flourishing beside the running streams, will yield its fruit in its season and will never be stripped of the glory of its leaves. Your mind is gold tried in the fire, and your speech is silver refined seven times; shining with spiritual grace, it brings forth the pure words of the Lord from a pure heart and from a tongue that shows forth the heart.
