You keep a good and firm treasure in an earthen vessel by an unbreakable faith, for the vessel of the grace entrusted to you is your mind, which, strengthened within the frailty of the body by the guiding Spirit, keeps a sure guard over the divine gift. Poor and sorrowing as I am, how shall I obey Wisdom, which has bidden me put my hand to the table of the mighty on this condition, that I know I am becoming a debtor for a like spread? For see, you have become for me the table of the mighty. You have set rich food before me, which in my hunger easily carried me off into all your words as into delicacies of varied, choice dishes, delightful to taste and sight, so that, mindful of my gluttony rather than my poverty, I dared to take what I cannot match. What, then, shall I do? From whom shall I ask to be given or lent either furnishings with which I might rival the rich man's dining room with fitting display, or the means by which, poor as I am, I might feast the rich man in return? Who will help me under the bond of this debt but you, Lord Jesus, who always make yourself the debtor of every poor one of yours who lends, and who promise to repay on behalf of those who now have no means to repay? Stand by me now, and on behalf of my poverty pay my debt to your Aper out of your own riches. Water his furrows abundantly and multiply your generations in him, that he may stand in your house like a fruitful olive tree, flourish like the palm, and grow like the cedar of Lebanon.

But I shall return to your letter, in which I rejoice as one who has found great spoil. And though I can give back nothing like it in words of my own, I shall do as starving people do. When the dishes of a rich banquet have been digested and they begin to hunger again from their own want, they console their hunger by remembering their past fullness and feed their empty souls by thinking now of the absent feast. So I shall weave this letter by going back over your words and shall recount my own delight, bestowing nothing on you, and speaking not so much of my wishes for you as of what I have found in you. For your letter has portrayed to me the face of your heart: that letter of good hope, letter of unfeigned faith, letter of pure love. What holiest love it breathes! How sweet and how great is the fragrance of Christ that rises from it! What wealth of a sincere heart wells up in it! How it breathes out to us your thirst, and the longing and fainting of your soul for the courts of the Lord! What thanks it gives to God, what it obtains from God! What sights it offers me as I read: the graces of God flowering in you and the virtues already at work!

There the little ones, or even the half-grown children, of Babylon are dashed against the rock: that is, the vices of worldly confusion and pride. Faith will overcome them more readily in combat if it forestalls their growing strength by dashing them against Christ at their very beginnings. There too the cedars of Lebanon, laid low to the ground and raised up into the building of the ark by the joinery of love, cut through the waves of this world with timber that does not rot. There likewise Christ, awakened, is seen calming the winds and seas for you, to bring the course you are steering to his own steadfastness; for he now sails in the ship of your body and has his pillow in your heart, because the sparrow has found a house for itself there, and he has in you a place to lay his head. There too your wife, who does not lead her husband toward softness or greed but has been brought back into her husband's bones to continence and strength, is wonderful in imitating that great marriage of God with the Church. The love of Christ, into whose body you have both passed from your own, joins this unity of yours, brought back and restored to you, with spiritual bonds that are the firmer for being the chaster.

Blessed are you by the Lord, who has made both one, forming the two in himself, who alone does wonders, who converts not only souls but also affections, turning temporal things into eternal. See, you remain husband and wife as you were, yet not husband and wife as you were; you are yourselves and not yourselves; and as with Christ, so you no longer know even yourselves according to the flesh. This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, which, remaining unchanged in itself, makes all things new and turns the sea into dry land, drawing the floods of vice into the dryness of continence. Blessed is she among women, faithful and most acceptable to the Lord for this devotion too: she has set herself against the demands of the world on your behalf, like a tower set firm on an immovable rock against the storms. Truly, founded with the solid footing of a strong mind on that very rock on which a house that is built will not fall, she has become for you a tower of protection from the face of the enemy. She breaks the waves and whirlwinds of the world by the barrier of her devoted service, so that you, withdrawn from the open sea, may safely ply the ship of an unshaken mind in the harbor of the Church, in constant meditation on heavenly studies and works, as though with the oars of salvation. For bodily exercise, he says, profits little, but godliness is profitable for all things. It is godliness that has made you subject to Christ, so that you prefer to lie low in the house of the Lord rather than stand high in the tents of sinners; and godliness has pledged your fellow servant to bodily labors out of spiritual love for your soul, so that she made her servitude the price of your freedom, serving in worldly business not the world but Christ, for whose sake she endures the world so that you need not endure it. Truly, in accordance with the divine work and word, she was made a helper for you; turned toward you, she hangs on your nod and stands in your standing, walks in your footsteps, lives in your soul, spends herself for your life so as to be restored in your life. She takes care of the cares of the world so that you need not care for them; she takes care that you may care for heaven. She seems to possess, so that you may not be possessed by the world but may be possessed by Christ. No discordant will separates her from your resolve; rather, and this is more wonderful, a concordant faith divides by task one who is joined to you in will. For, managing a thing of bondage in freedom of spirit without bondage of mind, she has strengthened her hands for works of virtue. She has stretched out her arms to useful tasks, girding her loins with strength, and, not eating the bread of idleness, she has become for you like a ship that brings its goods from afar. By a necessary division she renders through herself to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, so that through you she may minister to God the things that are God's. For when, as it is written, she has paid tribute to whom tribute is due, then, opening her hands to the poor and holding out the fruit of her labor to the needy, she pays a spiritual tax and supplies the income of the estate as wages for your service, greedier for a saving loss than for a deadly gain. When she is such a woman, the heart of her husband trusts in her. For, as it is written, she does her husband good and not evil all the days of her life; and so you are not anxious about what goes on in your earthly house, but you pursue vigorously and freely what goes on in the heavenly house. Nor will you be put to shame when you speak with your enemies in the gate, because a wise woman such as has been given to you, more precious than precious stones, makes you careful and watchful at the doors of the Church. And she has made double cloaks, it says, for her husband. Does it not seem to you that she is weaving these double cloaks for you, and for herself garments of purple or fine linen? For her faith doubles your grace, since a good woman is a crown to her husband; and in turn your honor is purple to her, because, by the tempering grace of the Lord, clothed simply in the unity of faith, you clothe each other further by the working of spiritual virtues. You are her head in Christ, and she is your foundation; by her labor your foot stands firm in the way of the Lord, and the bond of faith, making you members together in the Lord's body, will make her a sharer of her head. For even in the difference of your concerns, while the agreement of one mind is kept, she is joined to the purpose of your resolve. While you, as a faithful and skillful multiplier of the master's talents, carry out the stewardship entrusted to you, she does not hoard on earth what she earns from earthly produce, but lends it at interest to your works rather than to the ruinous profits of greed. Therefore she will be given the fruit of her hands, and her husband will be praised in the Lord in the gates of the daughter of Zion. The Lord prepares for you a common harvest from the crop you have sown by labor in the same work, different in task but equal in zeal, so that on that day you may come together with rejoicing, bringing your sheaves, she the servant of the seed and you the sower of the ministry. For she will not be cheated of a share in your reward, through the merit of this exchange. In it she obeys not her own will but your salvation, and by the evidence of this very work she proves the judgment of her faith. She shows plainly how much better she too judges it to despise the world than to use it, since she chose spiritual things for you, preferring not this world to Christ, but you to herself.

May the Lord add blessings upon you and upon your children. For, as it is written, the mercy of the Lord will raise up their children because of the merits of the parents, and they shall be enriched with the good things of the Lord. I hope that, just as your wife, like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house, overflows for you with the fruits of devotion, so that a thousand may fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, so your children too will be found worthy to stand around the Lord's table with you like young olive shoots. I think they are now being fed like eaglets on the food of divine wisdom and of your good way of life, so that they may even now learn to eat the flesh stripped by their parents' hunting, that is, the fleshly enmities that oppose the spirit, and to devour them with spiritual hunger, and to fly up to the heights of the virtues on the strengthened oars of their wings. Let them be brought up like the sons of the prophets, who, turning away from the tumult of life in the city to settle their souls in the peace of silence, marked out secluded dwellings for themselves beside the bed of the Jordan. Let them be consecrated like the sons of Aaron, yet not like those who kindled strange fire before the Lord and were burned up by the divine fire which they themselves lacked, but like Eleazar and Ithamar, who were rightly the lasting successors to their father's dignity, because they were heirs of his holiness who did not fall away from it.

Now it seems to me that anyone kindles strange fire who, having lit in the sanctuary of his heart the fire of some bodily or worldly desire, dares to approach the altars of the Lord. These receive the kindling of no fire but that of which he says: I came to cast fire on the earth, and what do I wish, if it is already kindled? With this fire, Lord Jesus, kindle us always, that we may be enlightened in our minds and burn away in our vices; for only this fire that comes from you will withstand the eternal fire. Having a heart that burns on the way of the Lord, we kindle for the Lord not strange fire but his own; and, protected by this fire amid the fires of the world, we shall be bedewed in the flames like those youths in the furnace, with a breeze whistling through, and amid the cooling fires we shall sing a hymn to the Lord, the Son of God singing with us. For he himself said that he would always be present even where two or three are in concord. Hence we trust that he also dwells in the midst of your house, where in you and your children a single assembly of many souls is gathered. Into this assembly we pray that you will join us too, absent only in body, by a spiritual presence, and water the thirsty little garden of our soul not only with your words but also with your prayers. We can tend it neither with our own hands, since we are weak, nor with hired hands, since we are poor, and we cannot find the way by which to seek your way, because we are not able to dig and are ashamed to beg. So we stand all the more in need of the help of your prayers; for who will hire useless laborers, or give to those who do not ask? Yet sometimes those who have poor and untilled fields, despairing of a harvest from their own means or hands, turn all their hopes to divine help; and often, when the outcome is granted according to their faith and devotion makes up for want of diligence, devout prayers [?] have helped those whom skillful cultivation failed.

Pray, then, that the almighty Lord, who turned rivers into a desert, may turn our dry ground into springs of water, and may strike and break open the hardness of our heart, so that he may turn this rock too into a pool of water. And would that he might sprinkle us with that dew with which he soaked the mystic fleece on the threshing floor! For the dew that comes from him is healing for us. Pray, I say, that he may deign to enter our little garden and bid the north wind arise and the south wind come, so that our shoots may come to life as they breathe their life-giving breezes. And if, entering his vineyard, he finds our tree without fruit, may he refrain from cutting it down, and, with mercy granting delay, trust the gardener who intercedes and promises by his diligence to wring fruit from the barren fig tree. For the Lord himself, who intercedes for our sins and who calls the things that are not as though they were, is able to make even of us, needy and dry as we are, a fruitful tree, and to fatten our empty soul with the richness of his word as with a basket of dung; for it is written: By his grace the borders of the desert shall grow fat. This basket of dung, which makes a barren tree fertile, seems to me to be above all spiritual humility. Through it, crushing our heart with repentance for past vanity, we empty out what is empty and take in the sap of virtue, so that we who were barren of works of righteousness are made fruitful. It is good for us, then, to enter our inner recesses and to humble our soul in fasting, the fast by which we abstain from the works of darkness, so that from the dung of this humility, which is vile to the world but dear to God, our soul may be raised up by him who raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dunghill. The grace of God be with you.
XLV. To Augustine the bishop, holy one of the Lord, most blessed, uniquely one in heart with us, our venerable and longed-for father, brother and teacher: Paulinus and Therasia, sinners.

Your word is always a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths. So whenever I receive a letter from your most blessed Holiness, I feel the darkness of my folly dispelled; and as if the eye-salve of your explanation had been poured on the eyes of my mind, I see more clearly, now that the night of ignorance has been driven away and the mist of doubt wiped off. I have often felt this gift bestowed on me at other times through your letters, but especially through this little book that is your latest letter. Its bearer, as welcome as he was worthy, was a man blessed by the Lord, our brother Quintus the deacon. He gave us the blessing of your lips a long time after he had come to the City, when I had come there, as is my custom every year, after the Lord's Easter, to venerate the apostles and martyrs. Yet, once the time he had spent in Rome without my knowing was forgotten, he seemed to me to have come fresh from your presence, so that I believed he had come to me from you at the very moment I first saw him, when he offered me the full fragrance of your sweetness in your words, fragrant with the purity of heavenly ointment. I confess, however, to your venerable Unanimity that I could not read the volume itself in Rome as soon as I received it. There were such crowds there that I could not study your gift carefully and enjoy it as I wished, that is, read it straight through once I had begun. And so, as usually happens, secure in the expectation of a banquet already prepared, I reined in the hunger of my mind, eager though it was. With sure hope of being filled, since I held in my hand the bread of my desire in a volume waiting to be devoured (and afterwards, as I devoured it, it was most sweet both in my mouth and in my stomach), I easily held back my appetite, gaping for the honeycombs of your letter, until I had left the City. Then I could give wholly to this task the day that had to be set aside as a halt on the journey, which we spent in the town of Formiae, so that I might feast on the spiritual delights of your letter, free from all the dregs of cares and the stifling press of crowds.

What then shall I, lowly and earthly as I am, reply to this wisdom given you from above, which this world does not grasp and which no one savors except one who is wise with the wisdom of God and eloquent with the Word of God? Therefore, since I have proof of Christ speaking in you, I will praise your words in God, and I will not be afraid of the terror of the night. For you have taught me, in the spirit of truth, the healthy balance with which the mind should be tempered amid the deaths of mortals. By this balance, as you saw, that blessed mother and grandmother Melanium wept for the bodily death of her only son with a grief that was silent indeed, yet not dry of a mother's tears. As a spirit nearer and more equal to her soul, you understood her restrained and dignified tears more deeply. From an equal standing, through the likeness of your own heart, you better perceived the mother's heart of a woman perfect in Christ, without loss to the strength of her manly spirit. So you saw that she wept, first
17] (2 Corinthians 13:3). 18] Psalm 55:11. Psalm 90:5.

moved by natural affection, and then pierced by a weightier cause. She wept not so much for that human loss, that she had lost in this present life her only son, who had paid the debt of our mortal condition, as because she believed he had been taken away almost while still caught in worldly vanity, since the ambition for senatorial rank had not yet left him. He had been taken, she thought, not in accordance with the holy greed of her prayers, which longed that he should pass from the glory of a converted life to the glory of the resurrection. He would then have received rest and a crown together with his mother, if in this worldly life he had followed her example and preferred sackcloth to the toga and the monastery to the senate.

Yet this same man, as I think I have told your holiness before, left this life so rich in these works that, though he may not have worn his mother's noble humility in his dress, he displayed it in his mind. For, as the Lord says, he was so gentle in his ways and humble of heart that it is not without reason we believe he has entered into the Lord's rest, since there is a remnant for the peaceful man, and the meek shall possess the land, pleasing God in the land of the living. He certainly fulfilled that saying of the Apostle too, not only in the quiet disposition of a gentle man but also in the visible duties of a devout one. Though he was a colleague in rank and honour of the great ones of this world, he did not, like the proud of the earth, set his mind on high things; rather, as a perfect imitator of Christ, he associated with the humble, and persisted all day long in showing mercy and lending. So his seed too became mighty in the land, among those mighty ones of God who are greatly exalted over the earth, so that the man's holy merit is revealed also in the most blessed visitation of his family and house. "The generation of the upright," it says, "shall be blessed": glory that does not fade and riches that do not slip away are in his house, the house that is built in heaven not by the labour of hands but by holiness of works. But I will stop recounting more in memory of a man so dear to me and so devoted to Christ, since I recall that in my earlier letters I said a good deal about him. Nor could I say anything better or holier about this son's blessed mother Melania, the root of these holy branches alike, than what your holiness has deigned to say and discuss concerning her. For since I, a sinner with unclean lips, could say nothing worthy of her, being far removed from the merits of her faith and the virtues of her soul, you, that man of Christ, a teacher of Israel in the Church of truth, were prepared by the grace of God, which arranges things for the better, as a worthier herald of a soul so manly in Christ. You could see with a spirit closer to hers her mind strengthened, as I said, by divine power, and praise in worthier eloquence the piety mingled with virtue in her.

You have deigned to ask me what activity there will be in that world of the blessed after the resurrection of the flesh. But I consult you, as my teacher and spiritual physician, about the present state of my own life: I ask you to teach me to do the will of God, to walk after Christ in your footsteps, and first to die that death of the Gospel by which we forestall the dissolution of the flesh by a voluntary departure, withdrawing from the life of this world not by death but by choice. For this life is wholly made up of temptations, or rather, as you once said to me, it is wholly temptation. Would that my ways might be so directed after your footsteps that, following your example, I may loose the old shoe from my feet, burst my bonds, and rejoice in freedom to run my course, so that I may attain that death by which you have died to this world, that you may live to God, with Christ living in you. His death and his life are both recognized in your body, your heart and your mouth, for your heart has no taste for earthly things and your mouth does not speak of the works of men; rather the word of Christ abounds in your breast, and the Spirit of truth is poured out upon your tongue, gladdening the city of God with the rush of the river from on high.

What virtue brings about this death in us but love, which is strong as death? For it so blots out and destroys this world for us that it achieves the effect of death through love of Christ. Turned toward him, we are turned away from this world; living for him, we die to the elements of this world. Nor do we make our decisions as though we were living in their sight and making use of them, for our portion is the death of Christ. We do not attain in glory to his resurrection from the dead unless we imitate his death on the cross by putting to death the members and senses of the flesh, so that we no longer live by our own will but by his, whose will is our sanctification. He died and rose again for us precisely so that we might live no longer for ourselves but for him who died and rose again for us, and who gave us the pledge of his promise in his Spirit, just as he placed the pledge of our life in heaven in his own body, which is of our body. Therefore the Lord is now our expectation, and our substance, which was made by him, is with him and in him and through him. He was conformed to the body of our lowliness in order to conform us to the body of his glory and place us with him in the heavenly places. For this reason those who are found worthy of eternal life will one day, in the glory of his kingdom, be with him, as the Apostle says, and remain with him, as the Lord himself said to the Father: "I will [?] that where I am, they too may be with me." Without doubt they will have what you find in the Psalms: "Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you for ever and ever."

Now I think this praise must be uttered by the voices of those singing together, even though the bodies of the saints will be changed when they rise, so as to be like the Lord's body as it appeared after the resurrection. In that resurrection the living image of human resurrection shone forth, so that the Lord himself, in the very body in which he had suffered and risen, was like a mirror for all to contemplate. Since he rose in the same flesh in which he had died and been buried, he often met with people and showed to their eyes and ears all the functions of all his members. If even the angels, whose nature is purely spiritual, are said to have tongues with which to sing praises to the Lord their Creator and never cease to give him thanks, how much more will human beings have tongues in their mouths and utter voices with speaking tongues? Their bodies will indeed be spiritual after the resurrection, yet all the members of the glorified flesh will remain, and through all those members their own forms and proportions. With these voices they will express in words the divine praises, or the feelings of their senses and joys. Perhaps the Lord will even add this to the grace and glory of his saints in the ages of his kingdom: that they will sing with tongues and voices as much more excellent as they have advanced, by a blessed transformation, to a more blessed bodily nature. Established in bodies that are now spiritual, might they perhaps speak no longer in human words but in those angelic and heavenly ones such as the Apostle heard in paradise? And perhaps that is why he testified that those words were unspeakable for a human being: because new tongues are being prepared for the saints, among the other kinds of rewards. Men of this world are not yet allowed to use them, so that they may be spoken, fitting their glory, by those who are already immortal, of whom it is said: "For they will shout and sing a hymn." They will do so without doubt in the heavenly places, where they will be with the Lord and delight in abundance of peace, rejoicing before the throne, casting bowls and crowns before the feet of the Lamb and singing him a new song. Joined to the choirs of angels, powers, dominions and thrones, they themselves, together with the Cherubim and Seraphim and those four living creatures, will sing in unceasing voice: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts," and the rest, which you know.

This, then, is what I ask, I who am needy and poor, that foolish little one of yours whom you, as one truly wise, are accustomed to bear with: teach me your knowledge or opinion on this matter. For I know that you have been enlightened by the Spirit of revelation from the very leader and fountain of the wise, so that, just as you have learned the past and see the present, you can also judge about the future. Tell me what you think about these eternal voices of the heavenly creatures, and of those who act above the heavens in the sight of the Most High: by what organs, after all, are they produced? When the Apostle says, "If I speak with the tongues of angels," he may indeed have shown that the angels have a language proper to their nature, or, so to speak, to their race, as far above human understanding and speech as the nature and station of the angels surpasses mortal inhabitants and earthly dwellings. And yet perhaps he spoke of the tongues of angels to mean kinds of voices and languages, just as, when discussing the variety of charisms, he counts kinds of tongues among the gifts of grace, signifying that it was given as a sign that individuals could speak in the languages of many nations. Again, the voice of God, often sent forth to the saints from a cloud, shows that there can be speech without a tongue, since the tongue is a bodily member, small yet great. But perhaps precisely because God placed the function of the voice in this member, the Apostle called even the words and voices of the incorporeal angelic creation a tongue, just as Scripture is accustomed to assign to God too the names of bodily members according to the kinds of his operations. Pray for us and teach us.

Our dearest and sweetest brother Quintus is as slow to return to us from you as he is quick to hurry back from us to you. His insistence in demanding a letter is shown by this very letter, which has more erasures than lines: this sheet reflects the excessive haste of the taskmaster I have mentioned. He came to us on 14 May to ask for a reply, and secured his dismissal on the 15th, before noon. Judge, then, whether by such testimony I have commended him or accused him. Perhaps, or rather without doubt, he will be judged more praiseworthy than blameworthy, since he has most rightly hurried back from darkness, which is what we are compared with your light, to his own light.
46. PAULINUS TO HIS BROTHER RUFINUS, GREETINGS.

Even a short letter from you, my kindred soul, is a great refreshment to us, as a thirsty field is revived by dew when rain is scarce. So we confess that we have been refreshed by your letter, brief though it was, yet still yours, brought by the servant of our common children. Yet we were also troubled again, since you told us that you are even now suffering at Rome in the heat of anxiety and the uncertainty of delays. May the Lord grant that we may soon be gladdened in the Lord by news of your affairs, so that, as we share your suffering in your anxiety, we may also share your joy when you are cheered, and may at least begin to hope for the fruit of your presence, once you have become sure of your decision, or of the Lord's good pleasure concerning you.

Indeed, with the affection by which you love us as yourself, you are good enough to urge me to apply myself more attentively to the study of Greek. I accept this gladly, but I cannot carry it out unless perhaps the Lord grants my wish to enjoy your company for longer. For how can I make progress in a language I do not know if there is no one from whom to learn what I do not know? I believe that in my translation of Saint Clement you noticed, among the other shortcomings of my ability, above all this poverty of my inexperience: in some places where I could not understand or render the words, I translated what I grasped of the sense, or, to put it more truly, what I guessed it to be. So I am all the more in need of God's mercy, that he may grant me fuller access to you, since for a poor man it will be riches to gather even the crumbs falling from the rich man's table with the eager mouth of a hungry heart.

While this letter was being written, in the course of the appointed reading there happened to fall under my eyes that chapter of Genesis in which Judah is blessed by Jacob. And since the Lord had given me this most opportune occasion, I decided to knock once more at the door of your heart after some time. So if you love me, or rather because you love me greatly, I ask you to write to me how you understand those blessings of the patriarchs, and if you know anything in them that is difficult in meaning and worth knowing, please let me know it. Especially, though, I ask about the passage where it says: "Binding his foal to the vine and the foal of his ass to the sackcloth." Whose is "his foal," what is the ass, and what is the ass's foal? And why is his foal tied to the vine, but the ass's foal to the sackcloth?
47. PAULINUS TO HIS BROTHER RUFINUS, GREETINGS.

Our son Cerealis has left me uncertain whether he will go on to you at the time he returns to Saint Peter's. Still, we judged that not to write to you by him, who is as much yours as ours, would be as blameworthy on our part as it would be saddening for you. So, preferring to risk the loss of a sheet of paper if he should not see you, rather than a lapse in duty, as we believe it would be, if he should visit you, we have entrusted this letter not to chance but to faith. For we believe in the Lord that the way of both our words and our son will be directed to you, since for those who desire good all things will turn out for good; and he desires you as much as you ought to be desired by one who understands what he gains from your company. Therefore I am confident that, according to his faith and devotion, his desire will be satisfied with good things: he will reach you and remain with you, and our saving protection before the Lord will be doubled in you both. You will gain so good a son, companion, disciple and helper, and you, granted him by the Lord as a father and teacher of every good, will add the strength of spiritual grace to the effective power of his prayers. As for us, though in view of your love we may presume that when you return to the East you will not bring yourself to leave without visiting us, we fear because of our sins that the daughter of Babylon may turn you aside, even though she is so near to us. So we commit our desires and prayers to the Lord, that he may deal with us not according to our merit but according to our desire, and direct your way to us in the way of his peace; for those who do not walk in that way have been condemned to a reprobate mind, so that they do not deserve to long for you.

With the persistence with which I have been accustomed to knock at your door even at midnight, never driven by fear of refusal to shame or moderation in asking, I now hand over to you this task concerning me. You have already set out for me, in written pages, the beginning of the blessings of the twelve patriarchs, the prophecy concerning the person of Judah, in a threefold interpretation as requested. I ask you to be good enough to expound the rest of it, as distributed among Jacob's other sons, so that through you I may come to know the truth, and may have you as the author of great favour and praise for me, if I answer those who, thinking more of me than I deserve, have judged that I should be consulted for the sake of this necessary work, with divine things that come from your spirit rather than foolish ones from my own understanding. May the grace of God remain with you for ever, as it does now, brother of one mind with me in Christ.

* * * * For if you look today at the bishops worthy of the Lord, whether Exsuperius at Toulouse, Simplicius at Vienne, Amandus at Bordeaux, Diogenianus at Albi, Dynamius at Angoulême, Venerandus at Clermont, Alethius at Cahors, or now Pegasius at Périgueux, you will see that, however the evils of the age may stand, they are guardians of the whole faith and religion most worthy of advancing it. * * * *
49. PAULINUS TO MACARIUS.

It is an honourable thing to proclaim the works of the Lord, and that is the reason for this letter. The affair of this householder Secundinianus, whom I am commending to your Unanimity, cannot be told, as you will find, without the glory and praise of the Lord. For just as he said in the Gospel, "My Father is working still, and I am working," so he does now too: the good Lord does not cease to rouse and truly to challenge our faith with clear proofs of his truth. And so God our Saviour, appearing to us, as it is written, in diverse signs, works on our behalf on land and sea, and what he does in individuals he provides for the faith and salvation of many. See, then, how wonderful and how worthy of proclamation is the work that the Lord Jesus wrought with his holy angels in one old man. This is the story of our friend and brother named above, a man faithful in Christ. Last winter in Sardinia he was compelled, along with the other shipowners, to take on grain in his own ship for transport to the state granaries. Under pressure from the public authorities he sent off his laden vessel without waiting for the usual sailing season of the convoy, before the mild weather of summer. At once, as he told me, a storm arose in the nearest strait, drove back the fleet of many ships that had rashly put out from port, turned them from their intended courses and wrecked them on the shore. At a certain place on that island which they call Ad Pulvinos, the crew tried to secure his ship with anchors so that it would not be dashed against the shore like the others. But the violence of the same storm prevailed and the cables snapped, and the terrified sailors let down the skiff, either to save the ship by holding it more firmly with fresh anchors set deeper, or to rescue themselves, if they could, from the ship's danger. But the gale, it is said, immediately swept them away, with the fragile refuge of their little boat, onto the rocks and overwhelmed them with the breaking waves. One man out of the whole crew, an old man assigned to bailing the bilge, they left behind, either forgetting him in their fear or despising him as a worthless life. Meanwhile the ship, bereft of sailors and anchors, was carried off into the open sea.

The old man, who had not known he was left behind, felt himself tossed and rolled about and came up from the depths of the ship. He saw everything empty: sea on every side and sky on every side. As his solitude heaped fear and danger on the wretched man [?], he spent six days and nights without food, for his tears were his bread day and night. Then, when he was by now more eager for death than for life and longed for an end to his torments through the departure of his soul, the merciful and compassionate Lord deigned to come to him face to face and to revive him with the food of the word. He himself, still weeping, tells of the happiness of his peril, and no one can hear him without tears of the heart and joy of the spirit: how Christ came and spoke to him, how he was strengthened by his encouragement, how he was ordered to cut down the mast, since felling it was at that moment the ship's only remedy. What many very strong men can scarcely do without danger to themselves and to the ship, he, alone and feeble, dared at the word of God, though he would not have dared to attempt it on his own. The mast was struck with the axe only twice and lightly, touched rather than hit, as by an old man's hand, yet it sprang away from the cut so violently that it was hurled far out of the ship into the waves and fell without doing harm. Then, in the various tasks that tossing on the sea and the ship's rigging demand, whenever the foresail had to be rigged or the bilge had to be emptied, the Lord called him by the name of Victor and bade him merely stretch out his hand to any task, as if to make a show of doing it. Among the many and varied graces of divine wonders shown to this old man, this gift of God too should not be passed over: he also received the name under which he is now registered in his regeneration and written down by men and angels. By his family name he was called Valgius, he who is now called Victor by the Lord; and he is a victor in the Lord, who gave him a name suited to the works he did in him. For at sea he triumphed over storms and shipwreck through the help of Christ, and recently on land, through the same grace, over sins and the devil, so that, being wholly renewed in Christ, he should remain old neither in his name nor in his person.

Wondrous is the faithfulness and unspeakable the kindness of the saving Lord! If the old man, sluggish with sleep, was perhaps slow to get up for his tasks, the Lord would first touch him lightly with a gentle hand, so that he would not wake in alarm, and then rouse him by softly tweaking his ear. And when the old man set to work with only slight effort, he would see the job done by angelic hands from his very first attempt. He had scarcely touched a rope as if to haul on it, and already the topsail stood spread out on its spars, or the ship was under sail. Water coming in through the ship's seams had threatened to sink it, yet after one or two scoops of his little bailer the ship was drained of water and dry, and he had nothing left to do. He was astonished that the labour was taken from him without labour and that his task was forestalled by a hidden hand, if a hand can rightly be called hidden that gave such evident help. Nor were the workers themselves concealed from the simple eyes of this most innocent old man; for he often saw armed men, plainly soldiers of the army of heaven, keeping watch over the vessel and performing all the duties of seamanship. And indeed no sailors but angels befitted that ship, whose helm was the Governor of the world. For the Lord himself, now flashing in his own countenance, as he is described in the Apocalypse, and shining in his hair, now in the venerable features of his confessor and friend, my lord Felix, our common patron, sat at the stern, as sailors say, at the steering oars, or rather in place of the steering oars, which the ship had lost along with its anchors and sailors on that shore of shipwreck. Unfortunate, yet fortunately so: in place of all its lost men and gear it gained either the Lord's martyr or the martyr's Lord. The old man, weeping with joy, tells how he used to lie prostrate at the feet of the one steering for him, now the Lord, now the martyr; and how, as He drew him into even closer intimacy, he had the holy knees and lap as a blessed pillow for his head, amid divine breaths of fragrance.

Shall we now doubt that the bosom of the patriarchs lies open to faithful servants in Christ, when his boundless goodness cherished this man, then still a catechumen, in his own lap or in that of his saint? For he himself was present in his saint, he who said to the Father, as you know: "The glory which you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one, even as we are one: I in them, and you in me." And again he said to the apostles, and in them to his whole body: "Behold, I am with you all the days of my life, until the end of the age." This he proves to us daily by his power, working with conspicuous miracles through the hands of his apostles and martyrs, so that we may believe that the Son of God, our Lord Jesus, reigning in heaven at the right hand of the Father since his resurrection from the dead, is the Lord of the living and not of the dead. So when he cherished the old sailor in the likeness of his holy confessor, he himself was present in his saint. He soothed the weary, exhausted man with gentle words and refreshed him with the word no less than with food, because he himself is the true bread which came down from heaven to give food to all flesh. For in every man he loves his own handiwork, and he wills every man to be saved, as far as it lies with him; for he, the giver of life and wholly life himself, did not make death. Nor does he who prefers mercy to sacrifice rejoice in the destruction of the living; nor does he who made all show partiality, but he judges according to merits, because God is judge.

In short, this sailor was not worth less to him because of the disaster of shipwreck, or because of his old age and poverty. Rather, by all the very things for which even his shipmates had despised him, he moved Christ and stirred his heart to its depths. For his eyes always look upon the poor. Truly this poor man too cried out, and the Lord heard him. Perhaps the Lord, and the very occasion of his danger, even put prophetic words into his mouth for his prayer, so that he cried out: "Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul. I have come into the depths of the sea; let not the storm of waters drown me, nor the deep swallow me up. Let your mercy come quickly to meet me, before I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep and the pit closes its mouth over me. Look upon me, for I am alone and poor; I have become like a pelican of the wilderness, like a night raven in the house," and so in my ship "like a lone sparrow on the housetop." The Lord heard and had pity on him, sent his angels round about him, and became his salvation. He commanded the gale, and it fell to a breeze. He rebuked the sea, and its waves were silent, and he led him through many waters, seeing the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. He fed him with the finest of the wheat, and as Christ spoke with him he was filled as with honey from the rock. He who blessed the poor in spirit looked upon the lowly man. He who promised comfort to those who mourn spoke to the weeping man. And he who gives their fill to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, he who is himself bread and righteousness and the fountain of life, fed this fainting man by watering him from his own self. He pitied him with no other compassion than that with which, devoted to the Father even to death on the cross, he pitied every man tossed about on the sea of this world; for one man is a part of the whole, and the whole is the pattern and the cause of each man.

In short, he steered not only the ship but also the man himself, for whose sake he was protecting the ship, and assigned to him the distinct duties of flesh and spirit. He bade him rest securely at night and keep anxious watch by day, promising that he would watch for him while he slept and work with him while he was awake. In these words of the Lord you will surely recognize that disposition by which he always cherishes our hope without relaxing our vigilance, and provides for the weak flesh in such a way that the spirit does not cease to be willing. So he allowed the weary old man to sleep, yet without releasing him, old and tired as he was, from the duty of watching, lest he sink into sluggish slumber and begin to sleep not only in body but also in mind. Fearing this, a certain holy man said: "Enlighten my eyes, O Lord, lest I ever sleep in death." For torpor of soul is a fall close to death; and then the enemy will say, "I have prevailed against him," if sleep has weighed down the eyes of the mind as well. We recognize, then, that the one present with the old man was the very one who said to his drowsy disciples, "Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation," and who said again to them when they were awake, now confident in the vigour of those he had roused, "Sleep now and take your rest." That this was said not so much of bodily sleep as of firmness of faith he teaches elsewhere, saying: "Be steadfast, for I have overcome the world." For this is man's true rest: steadfast in faith and secure from every enemy through Christ's victory, to enjoy peace in unity of heart. He himself is our rest, he who is our peace, who keeps watch for us so that he may rest in us, and who now bids us keep watch for the sake of everlasting rest.

The Lord himself deigned to perform in this one old man the same gifts of his kindness that he wills to be performed throughout the whole world. Severe yet tender, indulgent yet not without the curb of fear, he tweaked his ear to shake off the sleep of torpor, and offered his lap to grant him everlasting rest. For twenty-three days this man was shut off not only from land but from men: the plaything of every wind, an exile from every land, a guest of various seas and cut off from the human race, amid the waves and monsters of the sea, sheltered in a drifting ship, worn out by hunger, old age and fear. Tell me, I ask you, did he survive by his own nature? To whom, then, could it be unclear that God was within him? And what God do I mean? Is it not he who alone does wonders, who calls the things that are not as though they were? By his power the ship swam on, alone on the whole expanse of the sea, moving forward under an invisible helmsman as though it were empty, yet with all its heavy bulk, with the man shut up in its cabins along with the grain. It floated like the ark in the Flood, pregnant with the seeds of the world; and tossed on more than one sea, it changed its course as the storms changed.

First it was driven toward the City and sighted the lighthouse of the port of Rome; then it coasted along Campania over long stretches; then, when the whirlwinds shifted, it flew across to the shores of Africa, and, snatched away from them again, it ran past Sicily. Around that island the straits are made turbulent and full of whirlpools, they say, by the many islands, and courses among the windings and obstacles of the islands are dangerous for ships even with a helmsman. Yet the old man passed by them at his ease, on so straight and unharmed a voyage that the ship seemed divine and, made wise by a spirit sent from God, of its own accord avoided what was to be avoided, made for what was to be followed, and turned usefully and skilfully through the necessary detours, until at last, on the twenty-third day, God now taking pity, it was to bring its wanderings and dangers to an end on the shores of Lucania. As it approached them, the eternal Lord, so that his untiring goodness might work its wonders to the very end of the voyage he had taken in hand, by the silent prompting of his inspiration sent fishermen out from the shore in two small boats to meet it. When they caught sight of this ship from afar, they fled in terror at the first glimpse; for, as they themselves later reported, it seemed to them full of armed men, like a warship. Then, called back at length by the loud and oft-repeated shouts of our old man, they reasoned among themselves, and, with the Lord at work in them, understood that they had nothing to fear from the ship to which they were being called. They came up to the vessel, and only with difficulty, though the old man assured them of it, did they believe that what they had seen from afar packed with soldiers was empty of them; they finally believed their own eyes once they had boarded the ship. There the old man welcomed them with a meal which he had prepared the day before at the Lord's command, and rewarded them generously, filling them with the plentiful loaves of the lost sailors and giving them these as gifts. Delighted with this pay, with their little boats at its service, they towed the ship ahead of them into their harbour, like a veteran discharged from a hard war and crowned from the contest, as indeed it was: a survivor of shipwreck, victorious over winds and waves. What would they have made of this ship, those vain people who, in the error by which they worship everything they invent, enshrined in their fabulous literature the stern of the ill-starred Argonauts, and even now believe they see it in the sky and count it among the choirs of the stars? With no less madness they venerate the ship that carried the Epidaurian serpent, while the serpent itself, whose embodied phantom they carried, mocks them.

But let us flee from fictions and foreign tales, and not mingle the lies and poisons of those who are perishing with the light of our truth. We have ships of our own, so that we may more fittingly use true examples from our own household. We have the ark of Noah. We have also the ship of Tarshish and the ship of the man from Tarsus. But the ship from which the whale, at once avenger and guardian, received the prophet fleeing from God can be compared with this ship only insofar as it was in danger before the lots were cast. The third ship, however, matches my example in this: it carried the apostle and martyr, and because of him and in him it received Christ, above all when He granted him the whole crowd aboard the ship that was about to perish.

Let us, then, set before ourselves and contemplate in our minds this most beautiful spectacle of a divine work: one ship snatched from the wreck of many ships and of all its own sailors, crossing different seas with a single old man, alone on the deep, and he alone in it. Now the ark of the Flood, the image of the Church, will pass before our eyes, floating firm over the whole world above the drowned earth, on the single face of a sea spread everywhere, between the outpoured waters of heaven and of the abyss. This ship bore its image in many ways on a smaller scale. For as the ark was full of seeds of every kind, so this ship was full of various kinds of grain, since besides the public cargo it also carried a good deal from the sailors' wages and private stores. The ark carried one family to restore the human race; this ship carried one man to bring many to faith. To the ark a dove brought the branch of peace; to this ship the Lamb displayed peace. Into the ark entered a bird, an image of the Holy Spirit; to this ship Christ came in the image of his confessor. Let us look also at Jonah's ship: we shall see that this one was saved by a more generous gift of the same power and by a greater miracle. For that ship was saved with all aboard safe except one; this one with all lost but one who remained. Yet this ship also seems to have imitated that whale, the harmless devourer of the living prophet, since it likewise carried a man shut up in its belly through the depths of the sea and set him safe and sound on the shore. So too that beast, fasting from the prey it had not digested, cast him out with heavings at God's command from the prison of its spacious belly and gave him back to God, at whose command it had received him; and, the mystery of the saving passion fulfilled, it vomited him forth on the third day in hope of the resurrection.

More fortunate, indeed, was the crowd on that ship which was granted to the apostle, though not by their own merits; for they deserved shipwreck, having sailed in contempt of the apostle's advice. But we can glory no less among the works of God in this vessel. Although its men lacked such an advocate, yet in its one sailor the apostle's God himself was present as helmsman; and it deserved to be delivered for the sake of the safety of one innocent man, which that first ship, which had received the chosen vessel in chains, did not deserve, condemned as it was for its contempt of the apostle and for the crime of holding him prisoner. But that ship's company seems to me to have been set free also for the sake of a mystery of grace, so that they escaped naked from the wreck of the doomed ship. Thus, freed from the former ship, that is, from the sin of Adam's flesh, cleansed by the very waves through which they had escaped, lightened of all the burdens they had thrown into the sea, that is, of worldly baggage, and stripped of the garment of the old man, heavy and soaked with waves as with sins, they might be received by a sound and solid ship, which, displaying the full form of the Church of faith, carried them safely into harbour and on to Rome. In these events, too, mystical signs are formed. For the change of ship is life renewed in Christ, and the Church's harbour of salvation bears a name which, as the Greek tongue attests, means strength: Rome. Let us therefore bless God and exult in our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly, who takes no pleasure in the strength of the horse or in the tents of a man, but is well pleased with the humble and with those who fear him, and who, as he showed in this old man too, heals all the broken-hearted and binds up their wounds.

I am chattering too much, brother. I know it, but please bear with me a little longer. For I should like to ask you: would you rather be honoured with any dignity of this world than with this favour of God which this old man enjoyed? Do they seem more blessed to you who gleam in purple, who drink from jewelled cups, who are stuffed into the toga and decked out in the palm-embroidered robe, and who, while lording it over their fellow mortals, most of them better than themselves, are slaves of their desires and possessions: insolent toward God over God's gifts, destitute of Christ, rich in sin, barren of life, fruitful in death? What harm, I ask you, did it do this old man that his role was bilge-bailer, the lowest among sailors, that his dress was a pauper's, and that he wore the sheepskin of the Sardinians? For he was clothed in stitched hides when the Lord of hosts, the King of glory, blessed him with his conversation, enlightened him with his countenance and lulled him to sleep in his lap. Surely he loved in him this very thing, that he imitated Elijah's sheepskin mantle and the bristly garment of John the forerunner. To see the king of this world at close quarters and to be sprinkled with his words, however disdainful, a great part of the world thinks such bliss that, if they cannot obtain it otherwise, they will even buy it at a loss, and once they have obtained it they forget not only other men but themselves. Than how many is this man happier in dignity, whom the King of kings has honoured? Than how many is he nobler in nobility, whom Christ has acknowledged? Than how many is he richer in wealth, on whom so many blessings of so many saints have been conferred together: that he should see Christ as Israel did; that he should speak with the King of heaven face to face, as Moses did; that he should rest in Christ's bosom with almost the same intimacy with which John reclined on his breast; and finally that he should receive a new name, like the friends of God whom you know well among the patriarchs and apostles. A little while ago I asked you whether you would prefer to be granted this man's grace rather than all the glory of this world. For my part, I believe that the very rulers of this darkness, if they were found worthy to see it, would prefer the most blessed calamity of our poor old man to their own wretched good fortune and joys, which must be mourned forever.

Perhaps you will ask by what merits this old sailor, who had always lingered in the darkness of ignorance and was a stranger both to the works of righteousness and to the knowledge of the truth, seems to have obtained what is not readily granted even to the very few labourers who have borne the burden and heat of the whole day, from the morning watch until night. The apostle will surely answer you that the graces and gifts of God are without repentance, and that no flesh will be justified by works. This is the time of grace, and faith is reckoned as righteousness, for children of Abraham are raised up daily from stones. For now is the acceptable time, now is the day of salvation, in which we offer sacrifices of peace and praise; and the sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit, and the temple of God is in man, saving things are in the believing heart, and the holy of holies is in purified breasts. Therefore he who does not despise the contrite and humbled has himself accepted our old man, pleasing to him by his natural goodness, as a sacrifice for an odour of sweetness. For he is said always to have been so pure of mind through his inborn simplicity that he did not know how to sin. Now, in the old age of his last years, a child in body and an infant in malice, he bears the infancy not only of grace but also of mind. For recently, as I said above, he was reborn in Christ and dedicated to the Lord, through whom he escaped the [waves] of life and through whom he escaped the waters of death.

So receive him joyfully in the Lord, as the good fragrance of Christ, as a lamb of the month of new fruits. I, the shepherd of a small flock but the giver of a great pledge, have sent him to you, my dear friend of one mind with me, as a spiritual gift: a spotless lamb with gleaming fleece, newly born of mother Church. I thought no one more worthy of such a gift than you, who would know how to look upon him and receive him in keeping with God's grace and working. I seem to see already with what joy, what wonder and what faith you will hear about him and see him, when you consider that angels sailed with him, that a martyr steered for him, that he slept in Christ's bosom, that Christ tweaked his ear and gave him a name. I confess to you that my affection, in my excessive wonder at and love for such remarkable works of God in a man of our own time, was almost cruel to the old man himself. I pulled at his ear so constantly that I nearly wore it away. I would even have liked to cut off a piece of at least one ear, had it not been that what would have been a keepsake for me would have been a wound for him. No other feeling draws people to Jerusalem than the wish to see and touch the places where Christ was bodily present, and to be able to say of their own experience: "We have entered his tabernacles, and we have worshipped where his feet stood." Even though a higher meaning may be taken here, the simple, literal sense should not be set aside when the matter calls for it. If, then, it is a devout longing to see the places where Christ walked and suffered, rose again and ascended, and if it is a blessing to take and keep a little dust from those places, or even a splinter of the wood of the cross, consider how much greater and fuller a grace it is to look upon a living old man, a witness to divine truth! The manger of his birth, the river of his baptism, the garden of the Master at prayer, the court where he was judged, the pillar where he was scourged, the thorns with which he was crowned, the wood on which he hung, the rock in which he was buried, the place where he rose and was taken up: all these are honored as memorials of a divine presence once there, and in lifeless things living proofs confirm the ancient truth to present faith. How reverently, then, should we look upon this man! God's word deigned to speak with him, the divine face did not hide itself from him, and Christ showed him now his martyr, now himself. In his living clay we see the imprinted traces of the Lord's body, if with faithful eyes and spiritual sight we read in him what Christ's bosom and hand have touched, as we often stroke with our own hand the white hair that so often lay on the Lord's knee and grew warm in the Lord's bosom, and often feel the little ear that heavenly fingers pulled when the Lord was jesting.

There you have my gift, my brother. Eat it in the spirit of charity, and if the bitterness of my long-windedness turns your stomach, you will relieve the nausea with the grace of the Lord and the sweetness of this heavenly story. But I know for certain that you will look and long for some way to show this man the love with which you love Christ. An occasion is at hand. Apply the zeal of your loving devotion, and stand by his master Secundinianus with all the affection of your faith. Almighty Christ preserved his ship for the sake of this man's safety and restored it to him when he had already given up hope. In helping him you will be upholding Christ's gift. Do not allow what God gave back to Secundinianus out of the shipwreck to be snatched from him through the devil's envy by a wicked man, or, now that it has been snatched, to be withheld from him. The man is said to be the steward of a Christian, our brother Postumianus. Greedier than the sea, and playing the pirate on land without a pirate skiff, he seized that ship when it drifted ashore on the coast of Bruttium, where the senator's estate runs down to the sea, and having captured it, he emptied it. Even now it lies empty on that very shore, bearing witness to the loss of a cargo saved in vain at sea only to be lost on land. Complaints about this robbery have often been lodged with the provincial governor, but our Pharaoh has hardened his heart, perhaps so that wonders may be worked on him. When he was summoned through the officials, he first resisted by force and then fled to Rome. This necessity has forced my Secundinianus to travel to the City, and by land at that, with his only sailor. I have no doubt that our brother Postumianus will be moved both by your intercession and by his own faith and sense of justice. So we must intervene with this restraint, as you will surely do even without my urging: with equal effort you should defend and excuse his culprit to that excellent senator, a Christian man, so that the robber himself may be satisfied with the gain of going unpunished, while we are content to recover God's gifts from him.
L. Paulinus to Augustine.

Concerning a few matters which have come to mind just now, as the letter-carrier is already running to his ship and I am hurrying along in his haste, I shall put forward some questions, so that you may not write back to me without a little something extra. If perhaps these things are clear and only seem obscure to me, let none of our wise sons who may happen to be standing around you at the hour when this little letter is read laugh at my foolishness; rather, let them support me with the goodwill of brotherly love by instructing me, so that I may become a sharer with those who see, and with those who, their minds enlightened by your teaching, consider the wonderful things of the law of the Lord.

Tell me, then, blessed teacher of Israel, what is meant by what he says in the fifteenth psalm: "To the saints who are in his land he has made all his wishes wonderful among them. For their infirmities were multiplied; afterward they made haste." Whom does he call saints, who are saints in the land? Surely not those Jews who, as children of Abraham's flesh and not children of the promise, are excluded from the seed that is called in Isaac? Are they called saints in the land because they are holy by fleshly descent but earthly in life and understanding: people who set their minds on earthly things and grow old in the oldness of the letter through carnal observance, not being born again into a new creation, because they did not receive him through whom the old things have passed away and all things have been made new? For perhaps he calls them saints in this psalm in the same way as in the Gospel he calls them righteous, where he says: "I came not to call the righteous but sinners". That is, he means those righteous people who glory in the holiness of their descent and in the letter of the law, to whom it is said: "Do not boast of Abraham as your father, for God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham." A figure of them is set before us in that Pharisee who recounted his righteous deeds in the temple as though to a Lord who did not know them. He did not pray to be heard, but demanded payment as if it were a debt owed to merit, for works that were good indeed but displeasing to God, because what righteousness had built, pride was tearing down. Nor did he do this in silence; he cried it aloud, so that it was plain he was not speaking for God's ears, since he wished to be heard by men as well. And so he did not please God, because he pleased himself; for the Lord has scattered the bones of men who please themselves. "They were put to shame," it says, "because he despised them": he who does not despise a humble and contrite heart.

Then, too, in that very parable of the Gospel in which the Pharisee and the tax collector are compared, the Lord himself clearly shows what he accepts in a man and what he rejects, as it is written: "God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble." That is why he declares that the tax collector, by confessing his sins, went away from the temple more justified than the Pharisee who reckoned up his righteous deeds. And rightly did that self-praiser go away rejected from the face of God. Though he displayed his expertise in the law by his very name, he had forgotten the Lord who says in the prophet: "Upon whom shall I dwell but upon the humble and quiet man who trembles at my words?" The other, however, accusing himself with a contrite heart, is accepted and obtains pardon for the sins he confessed, through the grace of humility. Meanwhile that holy Pharisee, holy in the way the Jews are holy, carries home the burden of his sins because of his boasting of holiness. Of him, surely, those Jews are an image of whom the Apostle says that, desiring to establish their own righteousness, which is from the law, they did not submit to the righteousness of God, which is from faith. This was the faith reckoned to our father Abraham as righteousness, not works, because he believed God according to God's omnipotence. With God that man is truly righteous who lives by faith. He is holy not on earth but in heaven, because he walks not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. His citizenship is in heaven, and he glories not in the circumcision of the flesh but in the circumcision of the heart, which is performed invisibly, not by the letter but by the Spirit; and so his praise is not from men but from God.

Next, as to what he adds in the same verse, "He has made his wishes wonderful among them", I believe he says this because he first lit the lamp of the law for them and gave them precepts for living. For it says: "He made his ways known to Moses, his wishes to the children of Israel." Then he worked the very mystery of his loving-kindness among them: God was born in the flesh from a virgin in their nation and was made man from their flesh, of the seed of David. Then came the mighty works of healing which he accomplished among them and before their eyes. Yet through these works he was not only not believed but even blasphemed by them, when they said: "If this man were from God, he would not heal on the sabbath," and "He casts out demons only by Beelzebub, the prince of demons." Because of this mind, blinded by hardened impiety, their infirmities and their darkness were multiplied.

But what does he mean by "afterward they made haste"? Was it to repentance, like those in the Acts of the Apostles who, cut to the heart by the preaching of blessed Peter, believed in him whom they had crucified and, eager to be cleansed of so great a sin, ran to the gift of grace? Or rather, since the powers of the soul are strengthened by faith in God and love of God, were the infirmities of the soul multiplied in those wicked men who were empty of both, so that their souls were seized by the deadly sicknesses that come from impious crimes? For Christ is the light and life of believers, and healing is under his wings. So it is no wonder that the darkness and the infirmities of those who did not receive the life and the light, and would not remain under his wings, were multiplied to their destruction. As he himself testifies, weeping, in his Gospel, he often wished to gather them under his wings as a hen gathers her chicks, and they would not. With their infirmities multiplied, then, where did they hasten? Perhaps they hastened to clamor for the Lord's cross and to wring it with wicked shouts from an unwilling Pilate, so as to fill up the measure of their fathers. Their fathers had killed the very prophets by whom it was announced that this Savior of the world would come, and now they would kill the Lord of the prophets: "afterward they made haste." For "their feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known": that is, Christ, who says, "I am the way."

In the following psalm I wish to have explained to me what is meant by: "With your hidden things their belly is filled. They were sated with pork" (or, as I hear is written in some psalters, "they were sated with children") "and they left what remained to their little ones."

Again, I often marvel at another psalm, the fifty-eighth, which I understand to be the Son speaking to the Father. Speaking of the Jews his enemies, of whom he had said above, "Behold, they will speak with their mouth, and a sword is on their lips," he says a little further on: "Do not slay them, lest at some time they forget your law. Scatter them by your power and bring them down, O Lord." We see this fulfilled in them to this very day. For they have been brought down from their ancient glory and live scattered among all the nations, without temple, without sacrifices and without prophets. But why should we marvel that he was already asking through the prophet that they not be slain, when even at the very time of his passion he prayed for them as they were leading him to the cross, saying, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do"? But what he added, "lest they ever forget your law", I confess is obscure to me, for it suggests that their life was necessary for this reason, even without faith in the Gospel. For what does it profit them toward salvation, which is sought by faith alone, to busy themselves with remembering and meditating on the law? Perhaps it is for the honor of the law itself or of the race of Abraham, so that the letter of the ancient law might endure even in the earthly part of his fleshly seed, which seems to be reckoned like the sand of the sea, in case some, by reading the law, may be enlightened to faith in Christ. For Christ is the end of the law and the prophets, and he shines forth, prefigured and prophesied, in all their books. Or perhaps it is because from these very wicked ones there will come a generation of the elect, who will be chosen from each tribe and sealed, twelve thousand from each. To them the Revelation of blessed John bears witness through the voice of an angel who foretells it: wholly undefiled and strangers to human union, they will cling more closely to the retinue of the eternal King. Of them it says specifically: "They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, because they have not defiled themselves with women; for they are virgins."

In the sixty-sixth psalm, among other things, this is most obscure to me: "But God will shatter the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk about in their sins." What does it mean to walk about in sins as to the crown of the hair? For it did not say "the crown of the head" but "the crown of the hair", which has no feeling. Does it mean to show a man filled with sins? It is written: "Every heart is in pain, from the feet to the head." And a little further on it says: "the tongue of your dogs, from the enemies, by him himself". By whom himself? And can the Gentiles be called God's dogs, since he himself calls them dogs in the Gospel? Or does he perhaps mean by God's dogs those who might be reckoned such: any who bear the Christian name but live like Gentiles, whose portion is set with the unbelievers, because they deny by their deeds the God whom they worship with words?

So much for the psalms for now; now let me put forward something from the Apostle as well. To the Ephesians he says what he had said in another epistle about the grades or orders in God's arrangements, where the Holy Spirit works the distribution of graces: "And he gave some to be apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, and others pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints," and so on. I would like you to make distinctions for me in this variety of names [?]: what is the particular character of the office or grace belonging to each name, what is proper to apostles, what to prophets, what to evangelists, what to pastors and what to teachers. For under all these different names I see that a similar and almost single office of teaching was carried out. The prophets he placed after the apostles, however, I do not think are those who came before the apostles in time. I think they are those to whom, already in the time of the apostles, grace granted either the interpretation of the scriptures and insight into minds, or the foretelling of time to come. So Agabus saw ahead: he foretold the coming famine, and he declared by word and showed by the sign of Paul's belt what blessed Paul was to suffer in Jerusalem. I also want to learn what difference there is specifically between pastors and teachers, since both names are commonly given to those set over the church.

Likewise, regarding what he says to Timothy, "I exhort, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made for all men", please explain to me what distinction there is in this variety of words. For everything he said should be done seems to me to belong to the office of prayer.

Likewise, I ask and beg you to explain fully to me what he says to the Romans. For I confess that I am quite blind about this saying of the Apostle concerning the Jews: "As regards the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers." How are these same people enemies for our sake, we who have believed from among the Gentiles? Is it as though the Gentiles could not have believed if the Jews had believed? Or was the one God, creator of all, who wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, unable to gain both unless he took possession of one in place of the other? Next, "beloved for the sake of the fathers": how or why are they beloved, if they do not believe and persist in being enemies of God? Does it not say: "Did I not hate those who hated you, O God, and pine away over your enemies? I hated them with a perfect hatred"? Surely, I think, this is the Father's voice speaking to the Son through the prophet, in the same psalm where he had said above of the believers: "But to me your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their dominion is exceedingly strengthened." And what does it profit them toward salvation, which is gained only through faith and the grace of Christ, if they are beloved by God for the sake of the fathers? What good is it that they are loved, when they must be condemned precisely because they are enemies of the Gospel of Christ, having departed through their unbelief from the faith of their forebears, the prophets and patriarchs? If, then, they are beloved by God, how will they perish? And if they do not believe, how will they not perish? If they are loved for the sake of the fathers without any merit of their own, how will they not also be saved for the sake of the fathers? But "even if Noah, Daniel and Job were in their midst, they would not save wicked sons; they alone would be saved."

Draw up for me yet another, more obscure passage from the depths and bring it into the shallows. In the Epistle to the Colossians I cannot work out at all what he means when he says: "Let no one lead you astray, wishing to do so in humility and the worship of angels, walking in things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh, and not holding the head." Which angels does he speak of? If he means hostile and evil ones, what is their worship, or what humility? And who is the master of this seduction, who under the pretext of some angelic religion or other teaches things he has not seen as though he had seen and verified them? Undoubtedly the heretics, who both follow and spread doctrines of demons, using inventions conceived by their spirit. They fabricate phantoms they have not seen as if they had seen them, and sow them with pestilent disputations in hearts all too ready to believe. These are those who do not hold the head, that is, Christ, the fount of truth, and whatever opposes his teaching is madness. And these are the blind guides of the blind, of whom I think it is said: "They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water."

Then in the following chapter he added: "Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle—things that all perish in the very use—according to the precepts and teachings of men; which have indeed a rationale of wisdom in superstition and humility, for not sparing the body, not in any honor, for the satisfying of the flesh." What are these things, in which the teacher of truth testifies that there is a rationale of wisdom, yet denies that the very truth of religion is in them? Perhaps he is speaking of people like those of whom he says to Timothy: "having the appearance of godliness but denying its power"? I ask you, therefore, especially to unravel for me word by word these two passages from the Epistle to the Colossians, because he has mixed things to be abhorred with things to be praised. For what is so praiseworthy as the rationale of wisdom? And what so abhorrent as the superstition of error?
