Humility, too, which is pleasing to God and most praiseworthy in true religion, is attributed, together with the rationale of wisdom, to the very people about whose teachings and deeds we are told: "Do not touch, do not taste" things that lead to destruction. These things are not from God, and "whatever is not from faith is sin." But God has scattered the counsels of the wise, who are foolish before God through the prudence of the flesh, which cannot be subject to the law of God. For he knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain. I ask what kind of humility and what kind of rationale of wisdom he says is present in a superstition that comes from the teachings of men. And as for what he says, "for not sparing the body, not in any honor, for the satisfying of the flesh", I understand it hardly at all, because within this one sentence there seems to me to be a great inconsistency. I think he says "for not sparing the body" of some feigned or useless abstinence, such as heretics like to put on. He added "not in any honor" because those who practice the appearance of a holy work outside the faith of truth act for no honor of glory and no fruit; and in this they expose their perverse error to great reproach, disguising themselves as ministers of righteousness. But what he added, "for the satisfying of the flesh", seems to me contrary to what he says, "for not sparing the body". For it seems to me that the man who does not spare the body is the one who tames his flesh with fasting, as the Apostle says: "I bruise my body and bring it into subjection." And the satisfying of the flesh is foreign to such work. Unless perhaps by "not sparing the body" he meant that very concern for satisfying the flesh, which is especially shameful in those who make a show of religious observance. This would accord with the precept of decency he gives elsewhere: that each should know how to possess his own vessel in honor, so as to present his body as a living sacrifice pleasing to God, and not for the satisfying of the flesh, because a bloated body kills the soul's sobriety and is an enemy of chastity.

It remains for me to put before your Beatitude something from the Gospel passages as well. These will not be as many as usually occur to someone reading at leisure, for I had no time now to search out things scattered through the books or to ransack my memory in recalling them. I will ask about just a few that come to mind at the hour of this dictation. First, there is the letter on the form of the resurrection with which you replied to my second inquiry while I was spending the winter at Carthage. It was not long, but it was full of instruction in the faith. If you have it recorded among your papers, I ask you to send it, or at least to compose it again for me, which is easy for you. For even if the text does not survive, since perhaps you did not think it worth keeping among your books because it was a short letter written in haste, renew it for me, drawing out the same meaning from the treasury of your heart. Send it to me among the other answers you will give me, as I hope, if Christ grants you and me a span of days. Then I may receive these answers, so that your labor may bear fruit in me, concerning these passages of scripture about which I have questioned you, who see as it were through God, so that I may hear what God says to me in you or through you.

This, however, I ask you to make clear to me: how, or for what reason, after the resurrection the Lord was both not recognized and recognized, first by the women who came to the tomb, later by those two on the road, and then by his disciples. For he rose in the same body in which he had suffered. How, then, was the appearance of that same body not the same as it had been? Or if it was the same, how was he not recognized by those who had known it? That he who had not been recognized by those walking on the road was revealed in the breaking of bread I believe belongs to a sacred mystery. Yet even this I want to hold according to your understanding, not mine.

And regarding what he says to Mary, "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father": if she was not allowed to touch him while he stood close by, how would she touch him once he had ascended to the Father? Could it be by progress in faith and the ascent of the mind, by which God becomes far from or near to a person? She, too, had been in doubt about Christ, for she had thought he was the gardener. That is perhaps why she deserved to hear, "Do not touch me." For she was judged unworthy to touch with her hand the Christ whom she had not yet grasped by faith and had not understood to be God, since she had taken him for the gardener. Yet shortly before she had heard about him from the angels: "Why do you seek the living among the dead?" So the sense would be: "Do not touch me, because for you I have not yet ascended to the Father, since to you I still seem only a man. Afterward you will touch me, when by believing you have climbed up to recognize me."

Explain to me also what you think about the words of the most blessed Simeon, so that I may follow your understanding. He had come into the temple, moved by the Spirit, to see Christ as God's oracle had promised, and when he had taken the infant Lord into his arms and blessed him, he said to Mary: "Behold, this child is set for the fall and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against; and a sword will pierce through your own soul too, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed." Are we to believe that he was prophesying about a passion of Mary, which is recorded nowhere? Or was he speaking of her love as a mother? Later, at the time of the Passion, she stood by the cross on which the child she had borne was fastened, and she was pierced through with a mother's anguish. The sword of the cross, which before her very eyes had run through the one who was her son according to the flesh, also pierced her soul. For I see that in the Psalms too it is said of Joseph: "They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul," just as Simeon said in the Gospel: "and a sword will pierce through your own soul too." He does not say "flesh" but "soul." The soul is where loving devotion resides, and there the sting of grief works like a sword. This happens either when someone suffers some injury to his flesh, like Joseph, who endured the sufferings not of death but of mistreatment when he was sold as a slave, chained as a criminal and thrown into prison, or when someone is tormented by sorrow or pain within. So it was with Mary. Her mother's heart had certainly led her to the Lord's cross, and at that moment she thought of him only as the son of her own body. So when she had seen him dead, she mourned him in human weakness and gathered him up for burial. She expected nothing for herself from his resurrection, because the torment of the Passion before her eyes blinded her to faith in the marvel that was to follow. Yet as she stood by his cross, the Lord consoled her. He did not tremble with the weakness of a dying man. He held in his power the very death by which he was willingly departing, and from the cross he spoke to her with the full strength of one who lives and the steadfastness of one about to rise again. He said of the blessed apostle John: "Woman, behold your son," and likewise to John, who was standing there: "Behold your mother." For now that he was passing, through the death of the cross, out of the human frailty in which he had been born of a woman and into the eternity of God, so as to be in the glory of God the Father, he handed over to a man the duties of human devotion. Being young himself, he chose the youngest of his disciples, so that he might fittingly entrust a virgin mother to a virgin apostle. In one and the same saying he teaches two things at once. First, he leaves us a pattern of devotion in his concern for his mother: the one he was leaving in body he would not leave without care. And in fact he was not going to leave her in body either, since she would soon see alive again the one she now saw dying. Second, by the hidden plan of divine counsel he signifies in these words the saving mystery of his love, which concerns the faith of all. He was entrusting his mother to another, to be held as a mother and comforted in his place. In turn he was giving her a new son in place of his own body, or rather, if I may put it so, begetting one. In this way he showed that apart from himself, who had been born of her as a virgin, she neither had nor has any son. For the Saviour would not have cared so much about her being left alone had he not been her only son.

But let us return to the words of Simeon. At their close, I confess, my understanding grows dim. "And a blade," or sword, he says, "will pierce your soul, that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed." Taken literally, this is completely obscure to me, since nowhere do we read that the most blessed Mary was killed, which would let us think that the holy man had prophesied a future passion for her by a bodily sword. But consider what he added: "that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed" (for, as it says, "God searches hearts and minds"). And the apostle says of the judgment to come that "then God will make manifest the hidden things of hearts and the secrets of darkness." Likewise the apostle, describing in spiritual terms the heavenly armour with which we ought to be armed in our inner self, calls the word of God the sword of the Spirit. Of this he says to the Hebrews: "The word of God is living and effective and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing," he says, "even to the division of soul and spirit," and the rest, which you know. What wonder, then, if the fiery force of this word, whose edge is keener than a two-edged sword, pierced the soul of holy Joseph long ago and later that of blessed Mary? For we know of no iron passing through the body of either of them. And to make it clearer that the prophet there put "iron" for the sword of the word, in the very next verse he says: "The word of the Lord set him on fire." For the word of God is both fire and sword, and the Word who is God himself says each of himself: "I came," he says, "to cast fire on the earth, and what do I want but that it be kindled already?" And elsewhere he says: "I came not to send peace but a sword." You see that he called the single power of his teaching by two different names, fire and sword. Otherwise, how would a passion or affliction inflicted on Mary by a sword bring this about? So this is what I long to know: what did it have to do with Mary that the thoughts of many hearts should be revealed? Or where has it ever been shown that the thoughts of many hearts were revealed because a sword passed through her soul, whether a fleshly sword of iron or the spiritual sword of the word of God? Explain to me, then, above all this closing phrase of Simeon's words. I do not doubt that it is clear to your holy soul, which through the purity of its inner eye has earned the light of the Holy Spirit, through whom it can search and look into even the depths of God. May God have mercy on me through your prayers and make his face shine upon me through the lamp of your word, holy lord, most blessed brother, one in heart with me in the Lord Christ, my teacher in the faith of truth and my protector in the deep love of Christ.
LI. Bishop Paulinus to his holy children Eucherius and Galla, rightly to be praised and revered, and most dearly beloved.

Blessed be the Lord our God, who grants their wish to those who desire it, always surpasses our wishes and answers our prayers. I did not expect it, but he has deigned to give me an opportunity as timely as it was longed for, through the devout young men Gelasius, Augendus and Tigridius, my sons and indeed our fellow servants in the Lord. They come from the holy and most chaste company of his community, and our brother and my fellow presbyter Honoratus, a man worthy of praise and distinguished in Christ, sent them to me at the Lord's prompting, to refresh my lowliness with the example of your love. Out of the love I owe your merits, I asked them anxiously how you were living and whether you were well, for I could have no doubt that your way of life was devout and heavenly. They gave me an answer that revived my soul: by God's grace they had left you in good health, caring for the works of your venerable calling, carrying on its pursuits, and seeking heaven with the one heart with which you left earthly things behind.

I remembered that my sons, whom you sent a year ago to visit my lowliness out of kindness to me, had told me where you live, and also where the venerable lord Honoratus lives. They said that you were staying on nearby islands, separated by a short stretch of sea and rock, which even bear related names, Lero and Lerinum. So when these sons of ours said that they had come from the one called Lerinum, I recognized it and easily called to mind the island with the similar name, where I already knew that your holiness lived as a refugee from the din of this world. Knowing, then, that a letter from me would be a welcome service to your love, and since I owe it to you as a lasting favor, I gladly seized this opportunity offered by my spiritual sons, so that they might carry my letter to your blessed unity of heart in Christ the Lord. As sons and as ministers of obedience, taught as they have been by God and in God's way, they accepted the task most readily. So receive in these few words of my littleness the tokens of no little love, and keep this letter of mine as a kind of pledge of your own soul and a witness to my heart and my love for you.

I hope, through the mercy of Christ the Lord, that you will receive these words of mine in good health, and that if he later grants a timely opportunity through couriers of this kind, you will be quick to write back. Your affection would no doubt have done so by these sons of mine as well, if you had known that their journey was directed to me. When I asked them about this, since I knew you were their neighbors, they said that they had sailed from their monastery without your knowledge. Still, as the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power, so too love, in whose perfection and fullness the kingdom of God is contained and gained, rests in the treasury of the heart and in the power of faith. I desire your letters, then, for the sake of the familiar affection of your united hearts. For the rest, trusting in the most devout affection of your souls, I have no doubt that I cling to your minds even when you are silent. For it was not human friendship but divine grace that made us known to one another, and we are bound together through the heart of Christ's love. And so the harmony that was joined with Christ as its author must remain forever between our hearts. For what force or forgetfulness could separate what God has joined?

May the Lord bless you out of Zion with the blessing with which the man who fears the Lord is blessed, you who are spouses and parents forever, together with the offspring of your most noble holiness, who are blessed to God along with you. May you see the good things of Jerusalem and together be found worthy to dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days, holy children, rightly revered, loved by me with the deepest love and always longed for.
THE PASSION OF SAINT GENESIUS OF ARLES.

The most blessed martyr Genesius belongs to the city of Arles as its own native son: its nursling by right of birth, its patron by the power of his death. From the very beginning all the zeal of the faithful and all the writings of devout men ought to have celebrated and exalted him, so that the glorious proofs of such great merit, set down in trustworthy writing and entrusted to living records, might come down to later generations unimpaired and whole, where admiration would always make them new and veneration would prove them ancient. But since the generations that succeeded one another through the uncertain span of life preferred to hand these things on to one another's memory rather than commit them to writing, they must now at least be passed on in faithful writing to the ages to come. Otherwise what is still told from living memory just as it happened might, as the trustworthiness of those who hand it on or receive it fades with time, come to be believed a fable.

In the flower of his early youth, then, Saint Genesius began his training in the provincial service. He took up with zeal and skill that part of the office which catches with the hand the words of advocates or judges, noted down in the abbreviations of short signs, and matches the sound of the voice with the speed of the signs and of the right hand. In this he prefigured a spiritual image of his future glory, as one who would swiftly hear the divine commands and take them down in the faithful notes of a devout mind. Now it happened that while he was performing this duty, impious and sacrilegious orders were read out, commanding persecution. His hearing, devoted to God, rejected them, and his holy hand shrank from impressing them on the wax. He threw his tablets down at the judge's feet, and his mind, already consecrated to the Lord, fled from that grim service. And so that the martyr's conduct might in no way stray from the precepts of the Gospel, by which we are permitted, or rather commanded, to avoid the onslaught of persecution, he moved from one hiding place to another and even from city to city, since it is also written elsewhere: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." So for a little while he hid himself from the wrath of the raging judge. The judge ordered him to be seized at once and brought before him, but since the search could not easily find the hiding place he had arranged, he commanded the most cruel agents of punishment to kill him with the sword wherever he was found. When blessed Genesius learned of this, whether from secret messengers or from rumor, he changed his hiding places again and again, as the outcome shows, not from weakness of spirit but from the trembling of the flesh.

Meanwhile, though he need not have been anxious about the confirmation of the faith he had already embraced, he was not yet reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, and so he asked the bishop of the catholic religion, through trusted go-betweens, for the gift of baptism. But the bishop, whether hindered by the pressure of the times or distrustful of his youth, put off his ardent wish, and faithfully told him that the ready shedding of his blood for Christ would give him the full completion of this gift as well. And this delay on the bishop's part, as one may readily suppose, was brought about and arranged by God's will and judgment, so that human ministrations should cease around his solemn consecration, since there was being prepared for him the twofold grace of a single baptism, namely both the water and the blood from Christ's side.

But now the Lord, who through the Holy Spirit was to guard the secrets of the future martyr, had either created or foresaw in him the steadfastness to undergo his passion, and he would not allow the crown to be delayed when he saw that the victory was ready. So he put him in the way of his killers and showed him to those whose greedy cruelty gaped for him. When Genesius saw that he had been found, he made for the Rhône at the Lord's prompting and committed his holy body to the river, so that there, as in the waters of a second Jordan, a hidden Baptist might cleanse him of his mortal crust, and in a mutual and reciprocal mystery might consecrate his body by the waters and the waters by his body. And surely this was the reason that he got across with the help of swimming, though, stretching toward Christ after the example of most blessed Peter, he could have walked over the surface of the waters. He crossed to the far side of the river, secure, with Christ as his guarantor, of the rewards of the passion he was to undergo. In the place that the Lord had chosen for the shedding of his glorious blood, which is now visited with constant prayer and with vows never made in vain, the executioner overtook him. With the longed-for stroke of the sword he released from the bonds of the body that held it a soul hastening to God. And as each substance sought again the elements of its own origin, he committed the earthly limbs to the earth for the time being, but sent the heavenly spirit up to heaven.

The faithful servants of God of that time, however, made provision that the protection of a single martyr should guard both banks of the river, which were to be encircled by twin cities. For they left the traces of the consecrated blood at the very place of his blessed passion and carried his honored relics across to the other side of the river, so that Genesius, present everywhere, might be possessed there in his blood and here in his body.

All these things have been told faithfully and just as they were done, said or learned. Those of you who knew them, recall them with willing and devout hearts; those who did not, come to know them. And as you behold with the eyes of the mind the glory of so great a martyr, growing year by year and destined to live on through the eternal ages, let each of you, as far as your strength allows, prepare your hearts for the like, should faith require it. And pray that blessed Genesius, who stands before the throne of the Lord until the time of his vindication, may be a patron to the bishops, ministers and clergy, to all of us, and to him who composed this for your instruction, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in the perfect Trinity lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
LETTER I. TO MARCELLA.

The love of Christ has given my lowliness great confidence in writing to your reverence, for it is that love which has made you humble in heart through devotion and rich in works of blessing. Such a report of the holy riches of your faith has gone out that it has reached even us who live far away, and the news of God's grace has, like an oil of gladness, made our bones fat. For your goodness has become known to us, since the Lord has made his face shine upon you. He has set you apart from the womb of your kindred and your land, not in place but in the spirit of good will, so that, having made you faithful with earthly wealth, he might make you a sharer in heavenly riches, of which it is written: "Wise women have built themselves houses." When we heard this of your heavenly happiness, we poured out our hearts before God, and feasting with the voice of rejoicing we said: "The Lord puts to death and gives life; he brings down to the grave and brings back again. The Lord makes the rich poor and the lowly exalted, for the cup is in the Lord's hand: he humbles one and exalts another." And though this seems to apply to the whole mystery of the kingdom, it can still be applied in a special way to the grace given to you. By the great design of the merciful Lord you were exalted so that you might be humbled, and you were humbled so that you might be exalted.

For we are not unaware, venerable sister and blessed daughter, of the glory you once had in this world. Indeed, we saw you ourselves at the time when a royal marriage alliance was courting your house, standing out among those honours that pass away. For even though these too are granted by the Lord Most High, since all power comes from God, all things carried on under this world, whose form passes like a shadow, are frail and fleeting. So we marvel all the more at the grace that has been given to you, and we magnify in you the Lord, who placed you among the troubles of men and visited you with the saving rod of a father's love, so that, having afflicted you in a few things, he might set you rightly in order in many. The apostle bears witness: "We are disciplined in this world so that we may not be condemned with this world." So too David says: "Let the righteous one rebuke me in mercy and reprove me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head." And since you have given yourself to spiritual studies, you have no doubt learned that it is likewise written in Solomon that "the Lord disciplines the one he loves." He scourges every son whom he deigns to receive, to make him ready for eternal life. Nor is the apostle put to shame or crushed by this; rather he glories in it and becomes strong in his weaknesses. To strengthen us by his example, he confesses and declares about himself (though the way had been opened for him to ascend even to the third heaven, and not even that fiery sword could bar him from entering paradise, where he had heard the speech of angels that no tongue can utter) that nevertheless, so that he should not be exalted by the greatness of his revelations, he was governed by the guidance of that same Lord who glorified him so greatly. An angel of Satan was set upon him as a thorn in his flesh, that is, as a bodily affliction, so that he might be pressed down for his health rather than puffed up to his punishment. "For this reason," he says, "I asked the Lord three times to take it away from me, and he said to me: My grace is enough for you, for power is made perfect in weakness."

Therefore, daughter, since you have been trained in the virtue of patience and in the hope of eternal glory by so great a teacher and guide, be confident, as you have already begun to be, and glory in your past sufferings, calling to mind also these words of the same teacher. For as one who knew the secrets of heaven, he faithfully testifies that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us. "For affliction," he says, "produces patience, patience produces proof, and proof produces hope; and hope does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts." Rooted in this love, we endure all things. That is why David says: "I will love you, O Lord, my strength." For love of the Lord is the strength of salvation, since God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God. And because the prophet also knew that a moment of affliction in this world produces, as the apostle says, an immense weight of everlasting glory, that holy king says in the psalm, so that he may be counted worthy to be tried in the fire of temptations: "Prove me, O Lord, and try me." So again the same psalmist of ours, as if repenting of the glory he once had, confesses when he says: "Before I was humbled, I went astray." And because he was healed by being humbled, he immediately says: "Therefore I have kept your word." For this reason the prophet says again: "Give us help in affliction," and: "Vain is the salvation of man." For the salvation of men is vain when it is thought to lie in this mortal life alone, of whose vanity it is said to man: "As for man, his days are like grass." And you, holy daughter, have been taught by your own experience to prove the truth of the saying: "All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord," and whoever has done it, "abides for ever," just as the Lord himself, who is before the ages, abides for ever. This is why it is truly said, "Vain is the salvation of man," since all things under heaven are vanity. Hence you also have in the psalms: "Every living man is altogether vanity."

But in what follows he shows what kind of men he means: those who are troubled in vain by love of their riches. Like blind beasts they gape after these riches with endless desire for getting and heaping up, storing up treasure on earth without knowing for whom they gather it. "They will leave their riches to strangers," he says. And when their days have ended in vanity, they will all be snatched away to hell, not as masters of their riches but as their slaves, and there they will find nothing in their hands, because they have sent nothing ahead except what earns eternal punishment. But the salvation of man is not vain when it is the salvation of which he says: "Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people." And again: "The salvation of the righteous is from God." Therefore hope placed in God will not put us to shame as man's vain salvation does, since the salvation hoped for in Christ and bestowed by Christ is not vain.

So since you have received help in affliction, so that you would not desire the day of man or rejoice in man's vain salvation, glory in the Lord and bless him who gave you understanding, so that you would not persist in standing in the way of sinners or remain among the children of this generation. For them there is no salvation, since they grow strong in their vanities and forget the truth; trusting in the abundance of their riches, they do not make God their helper. But your lot has fallen in the inheritance of Jacob, and your eyes have been opened to the knowledge of the truth, so that you understand that a little for the righteous is better than the great riches of sinners. The Lord is merciful and compassionate, and he prepares his own ways for such as these to further the life of men. That is why he allowed you to be tossed by the waves and winds of this world, so that, having suffered shipwreck, you might take care not to run into such danger again. And so everything you have suffered, as you understand, was indeed a wound to your body but a remedy for your soul.

Do your works in circumcision of heart, so that your glory may come not from men but from God, who brings down the mighty from their seat and exalts the lowly, fills the hungry with good things and sends the rich away empty. See with how great a recompense the Lord, the God of knowledge, has exchanged your glory! He chose to make you a sharer in heavenly things rather than let you remain bound to earthly ones to the end, and to bring you from human rank into the kingdom of God. Indeed, God deigns to offer similar help toward gaining eternal salvation to many people held captive by the vanity of this world. But most of them, as the pleasures of wealth or of the body overpower sound counsel, refuse to understand so as to do good, and prefer to stroll down the broad road of destruction with the many rather than find the narrow path with the few. So you too, most blessed one, are one to whom it has been given not to be hardened by loving discipline but corrected by it; not to glory in riches but to place your hope and your wealth in God; and to pass from the lot of the sinful rich, whose heart is like ashes because they sink their hearts, like their treasure, into the earth, to the lot of the blessed poor, whose form Christ took when he became a refuge for the poor. For it is not the rich but the poor who are blessed, and to them, he declares, belongs the kingdom of heaven.

It is now your part, then, to give thanks greatly, to confess and sing praise to the Lord, with whose dress, as we have heard, and with whose humility of heart you have adorned yourself, so that David's words may fit your tongue and mind: "It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your statutes." You may rightly add what follows immediately: "The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces." For you have chosen to place your treasures in the commandment of the Most High. And so we too, rejoicing with you, say in the words of the prophet: "Rejoice, daughter of Zion; be glad, daughter of Jerusalem," and forget the evils that came to you from the goods of this world, you who have chosen for yourself the good part, which will not be taken from you. For no one can take away treasures laid up in the bosom of Christ or overthrow a house founded on the cornerstone himself. You have not set your building on weak sand, with rotting wood, brittle straw or withering hay, but on the immovable foundation that is Christ, other than which no one can lay any foundation; and on it you have begun to raise in Christ a building of silver, gold and precious stones that will never be brought to an end. And because you are completing this building (for it is God's building), that wise architect stands over your work, to teach you to run the good race, to forget what lies behind and to strain forward to the prize of the upward call, so that you may lay hold of that for which you were laid hold of, and receive the crown of righteousness and the diadem of glory from the Lord's hand. Then, when that great day begins to be revealed in fire, your work will not be burned up by the testing of that wise fire but proved; and your light will not be put out but will shine among the brighter stars, among those who will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God and like the moon made perfect for ever, those whom the sun will no longer strike by day nor the moon by night. For they will dwell for ever in Jerusalem, that heavenly city, for which the Lord himself, as it is written, will be both name and light.

Seeing, then, and foreseeing in the spirit of revelation a great harvest of everlasting joys blossoming for you, we rejoice in the Lord, and sharing your joy in your fruits we sing the psalm with the voice of exultation: "Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills." For where his afflictions abounded greatly, his goodness abounded all the more, since he has called you into the lot of those who have everlasting joy, a heavenly inheritance, royal honour and a seat among those who sit in judgment. The sufferings of humiliation must be endured in this world, and these he has weighed out to you [?]. And you, blessed one, take comfort in these words too, so that you may forget your old sorrows and, made firm in your present purpose, for which you have raised your hands with a perfect heart to works of salvation, may confidently promise yourself, in joyful meditation, the lasting happiness of the good things to come. Run ahead of yourself into heaven with an eager spirit, and while your body still lingers on earth, reach Christ already in your mind. And while you strive to imitate Christ and fix yourself in his footsteps, lay down the burdens, hindrances and fetters that hold the rich of this world, who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, so that, already set free and unencumbered, you may follow the crucified Lord of majesty. No one can bear his image except one who has made himself naked and dead in this world, so as to say with the Lord himself: "The prince of this world comes and finds nothing in me," or in the words of David's prophecy: "I have become among the living as one dead," so as to be free among the dead and able to say with the apostle: "I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me." For you have become like glorious Judith, mighty among the virtues of chastity through the merit of an unblemished widowhood, and like the venerable Anna, persevering night and day in chaste fasting and constant prayer.
LETTER II. TO CELANTIA.

There is an old and well-known saying of Scripture that there is a shame which brings glory and grace, and again a shame which commonly gives birth to sin. The truth of this saying is plain enough to everyone by its own clarity, yet somehow it has come home to me more closely in the present case. Your letter called on me to write, pleading with me in remarkable terms to do so, and I confess I hesitated a long time over a reply, because modesty bade me keep silent. Against this, however, the faithful eagerness of your requests resisted strongly and pressed me hard. The humility of your pleading fought fiercely with my hesitation, and with a great force of faith it beat upon the bars of my lips. And as conflicting thoughts weighed my mind, wavering this way and that, shame almost shut out duty. But the wise man's saying I quoted above armed me to drive off a useless modesty and to break a harmful silence, especially since I saw that the very reason for writing was so honourable and so holy that I believed I would sin if I kept quiet. For I kept in mind those words of Scripture: “A time to keep silence and a time to speak,” and again: “Do not hold back a word in the time of salvation,” and that saying of blessed Peter: “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason.”

For you ask, and ask earnestly and urgently, that I lay down for you from the holy Scriptures a fixed rule by which to order the course of your life, so that, knowing the Lord's will, you may prefer the furnishings of good character to the honours of the world and the allurements of wealth, and so that, being set in marriage, you may please not only your husband but also him who granted marriage itself. Not to satisfy so holy a request and so devout a desire—what is that but failing to love another's progress? I will therefore comply with your prayers, and since you are ready to fulfil God's will, I will try to spur you on with his own words. For he is the true Lord and Master of all, who both commands us to please him and teaches us how we can please him. So let him shape you, let him teach you. When a young man in the Gospel asked him what he should do to merit eternal life, he at once set before him the divine commandments, showing us that we must do the will of him from whom we also hope for our reward. That is why he testifies in another place: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he will enter the kingdom of heaven.” This shows clearly that we do not earn so great a reward by confessing God alone, unless works of faith and righteousness are joined to it.

For what kind of confession is it that believes in God in such a way as to count his command as nothing? Or how can we say from the heart and truly, “Lord, Lord,” if we despise the precepts of the one we confess as Lord? Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” And again: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” And once more he speaks through the prophet: “A son honours his father, and a servant will fear his master. If then I am a father, where is my honour? And if I am a master, where is my fear?” From this it is plain that those who do not keep his precepts neither honour the Lord nor fear him. Hence it is said more pointedly to David, who had committed sin: “And you counted the Lord as nothing”; and the word of the Lord comes to Eli: “Whoever honours me, I will honour; but those who count me as nothing will be brought to nothing.”

And are we to feel secure and at ease, we who by every single sin dishonour God and provoke our most merciful Lord to anger, and who in our utter pride despise his commands and so insult so great a majesty? What could ever seem so proud, or indeed so ungrateful, as to live against the will of him from whom you received life itself? As to scorn the precepts of him who commands anything only so that he may have grounds for rewarding? For God does not need our obedience; it is we who need his command. His commandments are more to be desired than gold and very precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, for in keeping them there is great reward. And this is why he is angry with us, why that boundless goodness of God is all the more offended: because we despise him even at the cost of so great a reward, and count as nothing not only his commands but his promises too. So we must turn over often—no, always—this saying of the Lord: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” This is what the whole Law urges upon us; this the prophets, this the apostles teach; this the voice and the blood of Christ demand of us, for he died for all so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them. And to live for him is nothing other than to keep his precepts, which he commanded us to keep as a sure pledge, as it were, of our love for him. “If you love me,” he says, “keep my commandments,” and “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me,” and again: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.” True love holds great power. One who is perfectly loved claims the lover's whole will for himself, and nothing is more commanding than love. If we truly love Christ, if we remember that we were redeemed by his blood, we ought to want nothing more, and to do nothing at all, but what we know he wants.

There are two kinds of commandment in which the whole of righteousness is contained: one forbids, the other commands. For just as evil things are forbidden, so good things are enjoined. The one requires us to refrain, the other to strive; the one restrains the soul, the other spurs it on; under the one, doing is blameworthy, under the other, not doing. Hence the prophet says: “Who is the man who desires life and longs to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and let your lips speak no deceit. Turn away from evil and do good.” And the blessed Apostle says: “Hating what is evil, holding fast to what is good.” This twofold and distinct precept, then—of forbidding and of commanding—is laid on all alike with equal right. No virgin, no widow, no married woman is free from this command. In whatever way of life, in whatever rank, it is equally a sin to do what is forbidden or not to do what is commanded. And do not let the error of those people lead you astray who choose at their own discretion which of God's commandments they will most readily despise, or which they will scorn as cheap and small, and who are not afraid that, according to the divine saying, by despising the least things they will fall little by little.

It is indeed the way of the Stoics to remove all difference between sins, to judge all offences equal, and to make no distinction between crime and mistake. We, though we believe there is a great difference between sins, because we read so, nevertheless say that it greatly helps our caution to fear even the least sins as if they were the greatest. For the more we fear any offence, the more easily we abstain from it, and one who dreads even small things does not quickly advance to greater ones. And indeed I do not know whether we can call any sin light which is committed in contempt of God. The wisest person is the one who considers not so much what has been commanded as who commanded it, and who weighs not the size of the command but the dignity of the one commanding.

So as you build a spiritual house, not on the shifting sand but on the solid rock, let innocence first of all be laid as the foundation, so that on it you may more easily raise the lofty summit of righteousness. For whoever has harmed no one has fulfilled the greatest part of justice, and blessed is the one who can say with holy Job: “I have harmed no man; I have lived justly with all.” That is why he spoke boldly and simply to the Lord: “Who is there who will contend with me in judgment?”—that is, who can appeal to your judgment against me and prove that he was wronged by me? It belongs to a most pure conscience to sing confidently with the prophet: “I walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of my house.” Hence he says elsewhere: “God has not withheld good things from those who walk in innocence.” Let the Christian soul, then, drive away from itself malice, hatred and envy, which are the chief, or rather the only, seeds of harming; and let it guard its innocence not only in hand and tongue but in heart as well, and dread doing harm not only in deed but even in wish. For as far as the reckoning of sin is concerned, the one who has planned to harm has already harmed. Many of our writers define as innocent, absolutely and fully, only the person who does not harm anyone even by ceasing to do them good. If that is true, then rejoice in a clear conscience of innocence only if you never cease to help when you can. But if these are separate and distinct things—if not harming, which you can always do, is one thing, and doing good when you can is another; if not doing evil is one thing and doing good another—then remember in turn that it is not enough for a Christian to fulfil one part when both are commanded of him.

For we must not look to the example of the multitude, which follows no discipline of conduct and keeps to no order of life, and is not so much led by reason as carried along by a kind of impulse. Nor should we imitate those who live a pagan life under the Christian name, who testify one thing by their profession and another by their conduct, and, as the Apostle says, “profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds.” Between a Christian and a pagan, life as well as faith ought to make the distinction, and show a different religion by different works. “Do not,” says the Apostle, “be yoked together with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? What accord has the temple of God with idols?”

Let there be, then, the widest separation between us and them. Let error and truth be distinguished by a clear line. Let those set their minds on earthly things who have no heavenly promises; let those entangle themselves wholly in this short life who know nothing of eternal things; let those not fear to sin who think sins go unpunished; let those be slaves to vices who do not hope for the future rewards of virtue. But we, who confess with the purest faith that every person must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil, ought to stay far from vices; for those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. Let those who profess themselves disciples of the truth not follow the straying crowd.

In the Gospel the Saviour certainly shows two ways of conduct, two paths of life leading in opposite directions. “How broad,” he says, “is the way that leads to death, and many are those who enter by it”; and again: “How narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.” See how great the separation is between these ways, how great the difference. The one leads to life, the other to death; the one is thronged and trodden by many, the other is scarcely found by a few. For the broad way, made gentler and smoother, as it were, by habitual vices, and pleasant as if with the flowers of pleasure, easily draws to itself the crowds that pass along it; but the narrow way, with its unaccustomed track of virtues, gloomier and rougher, is chosen only by those who care less for the delight of the journey than for the benefit of the destination. For an excessive habit of vice has made the way of virtue harsh and unpleasant to us; if that habit is turned in the other direction, it will find, as Scripture says, the paths of righteousness smooth. Let us now, then, take account of our life and learn, with conscience as our witness, which way we are chiefly walking. For everything we do, everything we say, belongs either to the broad way or to the narrow. If we find the narrow road and a fine sort of path along with the few, we are heading for life; but if we keep company on the way of many companions, then according to the Lord's saying we are going to death.

If, then, we are possessed by hatred and envy, if we yield to greed and avarice, if we prefer present advantages to future ones, we are walking along the broad way, for in these things we have the multitude as our companion and are hemmed in on every side by throngs of people like ourselves. If we wish to satisfy the craving of anger, if we wish to avenge an injury, if we curse the one who curses us and bear a hostile spirit toward an enemy, we are likewise carried along with the majority. If we flatter, or gladly listen to a flatterer, if we curry favour and fear offending people's feelings more than speaking insincerely, again we are on the way of the many. We have as many companions as there are strangers to the truth. But on the contrary, if we are strangers to these vices, if we present a pure and free soul and, trampling on every desire, strive to be rich in virtues alone, we are struggling along the narrow way; for that manner of life belongs to the few, and it is very rare and hard to find fit companions for the journey. Indeed, many pretend to walk this way and then, by various byways of error, return to the road of the multitude. So much must we fear that those whom we believe we have as guides on this right road may turn out to be our companions in error.

If, then, examples can be found that lead us along this way to life and keep to the straight path of the Gospel, they are to be followed; but if they are lacking, or thought to be lacking, the pattern of the apostles has been set before everyone. The chosen vessel cries out and summons us, as it were, to this narrow road, saying: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” And certainly—what surpasses all—the example of the Lord himself shines out, who says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart.” If it is dangerous to imitate those about whom you are unsure whether they should be imitated, it is surely the safest course to imitate him and follow in the footsteps of him who said: “I am the way, the truth and the life.” For one who follows the truth never goes astray by imitating. Hence John too says: “Whoever says he abides in Christ ought himself to walk just as he walked.” Blessed Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you should follow in his steps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but handed himself over to the one who judged him unjustly. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that, dead to sins, we might live for righteousness.”

Let every excuse for error cease; let the shameful consolations of sinning be removed. We achieve nothing at all when we defend ourselves by the example of the multitude, and, often counting up other people's vices to console ourselves, say that we lack anyone we ought to follow. We are directed to the example of him whom we all admit must be imitated. And so let it be your chief care to know the divine law, through which you can see the examples of the saints as if they were before your eyes, and learn by its counsel what is to be done and what avoided. For the greatest help toward righteousness is to fill the mind with the divine words and always to meditate in the heart on what you desire to carry out in action. When the people were still untaught and unused to obedience, the Lord commanded through Moses that, as a reminder by which they might recall the Lord's precepts, they should have tassels on the borders of their garments and mark them with scarlet of a hyacinth colour, so that even when their eyes happened to glance here or there, the memory of the heavenly commandments might be awakened. Concerning these tassels the Pharisees are rebuked by the Lord, because by a perverse use they began to wear them not as a reminder of God's precepts but for self-display, namely so that the people would judge them holy for their supposedly greater diligence in observance.

But you, who keep not the letter of the precepts but the spirit, must cultivate the memory of the divine commandments spiritually; for you, God's precepts are not so much to be recalled frequently as to be pondered always. Let the divine Scriptures, then, always be in your hands and continually turned over in your mind. And do not think it enough for you to hold God's commandments in memory and forget them in your works; rather, learn them so that you may do whatever you have learned must be done. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. The field of the divine law stretches wide and boundless; blooming with the various testimonies of truth as with heavenly flowers, it feeds and refreshes the reader's mind with wonderful delight. To know all these and always ponder them is an immense benefit for preserving righteousness. But as a kind of reminder in a compact form, you should choose that saying of the Gospel and write it upon your heart, which was uttered by the Lord's mouth as a summary of all righteousness: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.” Expressing the force of this precept, he adds: “For this is the Law and the Prophets.” For the kinds and parts of righteousness are countless, and it is very hard not only to pursue them with the pen but even to grasp them in thought; yet he has included them all in this one brief saying, which, by a secret judgment of the mind, either acquits or condemns the hidden conscience of each person.

So let this saying be brought to bear on every act, every word, and even every thought, so that, like a mirror kept ready and always at hand, it may show you the quality of your will and either convict you of an unjust deed or gladden you over a just one. For whenever you hold toward another the same attitude you wish another to keep toward you, you are on the path of justice; but whenever you are toward another such as you want no one to be toward you, you have left the road of righteousness. There you have the whole of what is so arduous in the divine law, the whole of what is so difficult! These are the harsh commands for which we protest against the Lord and say that we are weighed down by the difficulty, or even the impossibility, of the commandments. And it is not enough for us to leave his commands undone; we must even pronounce the one who commands unjust, complaining that the very author of justice has commanded things not only hard and arduous but even impossible. “Whatever you wish,” he says, “people to do to you, do the same to them.” He wants love to be joined and bound together among us by mutual kindnesses, and all people to be united by a reciprocal love, so that, as each person gives another what he would wish all to give him, the whole of righteousness and this commandment of God may become the common good of humankind. O wondrous mercy! O unspeakable kindness of God! He promises us a reward if we love one another, that is, if we give each other the things we each need in turn; and we, with a spirit at once proud and ungrateful, resist the will of him whose very command is a kindness.

Never disparage anyone at all, or wish to appear praiseworthy by finding fault with others; learn rather to adorn your own life than to pick at someone else's. And always remember the Scripture that says: “Do not love to disparage, lest you be uprooted.” Very few people renounce this vice, and you will rarely find anyone who wishes so to present his own life as blameless that he does not gladly find fault with another's. So great a craving for this evil has invaded people's minds that even those who have withdrawn far from other vices still fall into this one, as into the devil's last snare. But you must flee this evil so thoroughly that not only do you not disparage others yourself, but you never believe another who does so, nor lend any weight to a slanderer by your agreement and nourish his vice by nodding along. “Do not,” says Scripture, “agree with those who speak ill against your neighbour, and do not take sin upon yourself on his account”; and elsewhere: “Hedge your ears with thorns and do not listen to a wicked tongue.” Hence blessed David too, listing the various kinds of innocence and righteousness, did not pass over this virtue either, saying: “And he took up no reproach against his neighbours.” For this reason he not only opposes the one who disparages but even pursues him, for he says: “The one who secretly disparages his neighbour, him I pursued.” This is truly a vice that ought to be stamped out first of all and utterly shut out by those who wish to order their lives in holiness. For nothing so disturbs the soul, nothing makes the mind so fickle and unsteady, as readily believing everything and following the words of slanderers with rash assent. From this arise frequent quarrels, from this unjust hatreds. This is what often turns even the closest friends into enemies, when an evil-speaking tongue separates souls that were in harmony but too ready to believe. On the other hand, it shows great peace of mind and great seriousness of character not to listen rashly to anything bad about anyone. Blessed is the one who has so armed himself against this vice that no one dares to disparage others in his presence. If we took such care not to believe slanderers indiscriminately, everyone would by now be afraid to disparage, lest by disparaging they make not so much others as themselves contemptible. But this evil is widespread, and this vice rages in many, precisely because nearly everyone listens to it gladly.

Shun also the fawning of flatterers and the harmful blandishments of deceit as you would a plague of the soul. Nothing corrupts human minds so easily, nothing strikes the spirit with so sweet and soft a wound. So the wise man says: “The words of flatterers are soft, but they strike the inmost parts of the belly,” and the Lord says through the prophet: “My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and confuse the paths of your feet.” This vice reigns in many people, especially in our own time, and, worst of all, it passes for humility and goodwill. As a result, anyone who does not know how to flatter is now thought either envious or proud. It is certainly a great and very subtle art to praise another while commending oneself, and by deceiving him to bind the deceived man's heart to oneself; and this vice is commonly put to the further use of selling counterfeit praise at a fixed price. What great fickleness of mind, what great vanity it is to abandon one's own conscience and follow the opinion of another, and an invented and feigned one at that; to be carried off by the wind of false praise, to rejoice in being cheated, and to take mockery for a kindness! So if you truly wish to be worthy of praise, do not seek the praise of men. Prepare your conscience for him who will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and reveal the purposes of hearts; and then your praise will come from God.

Let your mind, then, be intent and watchful and always armed against sin; let your speech be measured and sparing in everything, showing that you speak from need rather than from desire. Let modesty adorn your good sense, and, as has always been the chief thing in women, let modesty surpass all your other virtues. Consider long beforehand what you should say, and while still silent take care that you will not regret anything you have said. Let thought weigh your words, and let the scales of the mind measure out the tongue's service. So Scripture says: “Melt down your silver and gold, make a balance for your words and a straight bridle for your mouth, and take care that you do not slip with your tongue.” Never let a curse come from your mouth, for you are commanded, as the crown of kindness, to bless even those who curse you. “Be merciful,” it says, “humble, not repaying evil for evil or curse for curse, but on the contrary blessing.”

Let your tongue know nothing at all of lying or swearing, and let your love of truth be so great that you regard whatever you say as said under oath. Of this the Savior says to his disciples: “But I say to you, do not swear at all,” and a little later: “Let your word be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; anything more than this comes from evil.” In every action, then, and every word, keep your mind quiet and calm, and let the presence of God always come to your thoughts. Let your spirit be humble and gentle, and roused only against vices. Let pride never lift it up, avarice never bend it, anger never hurl it headlong. For nothing ought to be more tranquil, nothing purer, nothing in short more beautiful than the mind that is to be prepared as a dwelling for God, who takes no delight in temples gleaming with gold or altars studded with gems, but in a soul adorned with virtues. That is why the hearts of the saints are called the temple of God, as the apostle affirms when he says: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him; for God's temple is holy, and that temple you are.”

Hold nothing more excellent or more lovable than humility. It is the chief preserver and, as it were, the guardian of all the virtues, and nothing makes us so pleasing both to men and to God as being great in the merit of our lives and lowest in humility. For this reason Scripture says: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor before God,” and God says through the prophet: “On whom shall I rest, if not on the one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?” But pursue the humility that is expressed by the pure affection of the heart, not the kind that is put on show and feigned by the bearing of the body or a broken tone of voice. For it is one thing to have a virtue and another to have its likeness; one thing to pursue the shadow of things and another to pursue their truth. Far uglier is the pride that hides beneath certain signs of humility, for somehow vices are more shameful when they are concealed under the appearance of virtues.

Never set yourself above anyone on account of noble birth, and do not think that women of more obscure family and humbler station are beneath you. Our religion knows nothing of persons or of human ranks; it looks at souls, and pronounces a person slave or noble according to character. With God the only freedom is not to be a slave to sin; with God the highest nobility is to be distinguished in virtue. Among men, who is nobler in God's sight than Peter, who was a fisherman? Among women, who is more illustrious than blessed Mary, who is described as the betrothed of a carpenter? Yet to that poor fisherman Christ entrusted the keys of the heavenly kingdom, and this carpenter's betrothed was found worthy to be the mother of him who gave those very keys. For God chose the lowborn and despised things of this world in order more easily to bring the powerful and noble to humility. Besides, it is futile for anyone to pride himself on noble birth, since all who have been redeemed by the one blood of Christ are of equal honor and equal worth before God; nor does it matter in what condition anyone was born, since we are all reborn equally in Christ. For even if we forget that we were all begotten from one man, we ought at least always to remember that we are all regenerated through one.

If you begin to fast and abstain, be careful not to think yourself already holy. This virtue is an aid to holiness, not its perfection; and you must take particular care that your contempt for permitted things does not give you a kind of license for forbidden ones. Whatever is offered to God beyond what justice requires ought not to hinder justice but to help it. What good is it to make the body thin by abstinence if the mind swells with pride? What praise shall we earn for the pallor of fasting if we are livid with envy? What virtue is there in not drinking wine while getting drunk on anger and hatred? Abstinence is splendid, I say, and the chastening of the body is fine and noble, only when the soul fasts from vices. Indeed, those who practice the virtue of abstinence rightly and with understanding afflict their flesh in order to break the pride of the soul, so that it may come down, as it were, from the heights of disdain and arrogance to fulfill the will of God, which is perfected above all in humility. They withdraw the mind from its various cravings for food so that they may devote its whole strength to the desire for virtue; and the flesh feels the toil of fasting and abstinence less when the soul hungers for righteousness. For when the chosen vessel chastens his body and brings it into subjection, lest after preaching to others he himself should be found reprobate, he does this not for chastity alone, as some ignorant people think. Abstinence assists not only chastity but every virtue whatever, and the apostle's glory does not consist chiefly or entirely in not committing fornication. His aim is that the soul may be trained by the chastening of the body, and that the less it desires of pleasures, the more it may think about virtues; so that the teacher of perfection may not show anything imperfect in himself, the imitator of Christ may do nothing outside the command and will of Christ, he may not teach less by example than by word, and after preaching to others he may not himself be rejected and hear along with the Pharisees: “For they say, and do not do.”

It is the apostle's precept and example alike that we should care not only for our conscience but also for our reputation. The teacher of the Gentiles does not teach this needlessly or to no purpose: he wants even those outside to be advanced toward the faith through the works of the faithful, so that the discipline of religion may commend religion itself. That is why he bids us shine like lights in the world in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, so that the unbelieving minds of those who are astray may recognize the darkness of their own ignorance by the light of our actions. So he says to the Romans: “Providing good things not only before God but also before men,” and elsewhere: “Give no offense to Jews or to Gentiles or to the church of God, just as I please everyone in everything, not seeking what is useful to myself but what is useful to many.” Blessed is the one who has ordered his life so holily and so gravely that nothing evil can even be invented about him, since the greatness of his merit fights against the lust of slanderers, and no one dares to invent what he thinks no one will believe. If that is difficult and too hard to attain, let us at least take such care with our lives that evil minds find no occasion for slander, and that no spark comes from us that might kindle evil rumors against us. Otherwise we are angry with our slanderers in vain, if we ourselves supply them with material for slander. But if, while we diligently and carefully provide for honorable conduct in everything and put the fear of God before all our actions, they rage against us nonetheless, let our conscience console us. It is safest and most secure precisely when it has not given even an occasion for thinking ill of it. For woe is pronounced through the prophet on those who call good evil, who call light darkness and call what is sweet bitter. To us, then, the Savior's word will apply: “Blessed are you when men curse you falsely.” Let us only see to it that no one can speak ill of us without lying.

Look after your household in such a way that you still grant your soul some leisure. Choose a suitable place, somewhat removed from the noise of the household, where you can withdraw as into a harbor out of a great storm of cares, and calm the waves of thought stirred up outside in the tranquility of solitude. Let your zeal for divine reading be so great, your prayers so frequent, your thought about the things to come so firm and concentrated, that this leisure easily makes up for all the occupations of the rest of your time. We do not say this in order to draw you away from your family; on the contrary, our aim is that there you may learn and meditate on how you ought to conduct yourself toward them.

Govern and cherish your household in such a way that you wish to be seen as the mother of your people rather than their mistress, and win their respect by kindness rather than severity. Service that springs from love is always more faithful and more welcome than service that springs from fear. Above all, in a marriage that is honorable and undefiled, keep to the order of the apostolic rule.

First of all, let your husband keep his authority, and let the whole household learn from you how much honor it owes him. Show by your obedience that he is master, show by your humility that he is great; you yourself will be honored all the more, the more you honor him. For, as the apostle says, the head of the woman is the man, and nothing adorns the rest of the body more than the dignity of the head. So he says elsewhere: “Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.” And the blessed apostle Peter too says: “Likewise let wives be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives.” If, then, honor is owed by the law of marriage even to pagan husbands, how much more must it be paid to Christian ones?

And to show with what ornaments women joined to husbands ought to adorn themselves, he says: “Let theirs not be the outward braiding of hair or the putting on of gold or fine clothing, but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich in the sight of God. For so once the holy women too, who hoped in the Lord, adorned themselves, being subject to their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him her lord.” In giving these instructions he does not order them to be squalid and dirty and covered in shabby patched rags; rather, he forbids excessive finery and overly elaborate adornment and commends simple dress and appearance. Of this the chosen vessel also says: “Likewise also let women adorn themselves in seemly dress with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or costly clothing, but, as is fitting for women who profess chastity, with good works.”

I have learned that, burning with the ardor of a wonderful faith, you resolved on continence some years ago and consecrated the rest of your life to chastity. It is the sign of a great soul and the mark of perfect virtue to renounce suddenly a pleasure one has known, to flee the familiar allurements of the flesh, and to quench the flames of an age still warm with the love of faith. But at the same time I learned something that troubles and pricks me not a little: that you began to keep this great good without the consent and agreement of your husband, although apostolic authority altogether forbids this. In this matter alone it has made not only the wife subject to the husband's authority but also the husband to the wife's. “The wife,” it says, “does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body.” But you, as if you had forgotten the marriage covenant and were unmindful of this agreement and law, vowed chastity to the Lord without consulting your husband. Yet it is dangerous to promise what is still in another's power, and I do not know how welcome a gift is when one person offers what belongs to two. We have already heard of and seen many marriages broken through ignorance of this kind, and—it is painful to recall—adultery made ready under the pretext of chastity: while one party abstains even from what is permitted, the other has slipped into what is forbidden. And in such a case I do not know who ought to be accused more, who ought to be blamed the more: the husband who, rebuffed by his wife, commits fornication, or the wife who by rebuffing her husband in a sense throws him into fornication. So that you may know what the truth is on this matter, I must set out a few things from divine authority. The rule of apostolic teaching neither puts the works of marriage on a level with continence, as Jovinian does, nor condemns marriage, as the Manichee does. The chosen vessel and teacher of the Gentiles steers a moderate middle course between the two, allowing a remedy for incontinence while summoning continence to its reward. His whole meaning in this matter is that chastity should be undertaken by the decision of both, or else that the common debt should be paid by both.

But let us now set down the apostle's own words and go over this whole question again from its beginning. He says to the Corinthians: “Now concerning the things you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman.” And although he has praised chastity here, nevertheless, lest anyone think he forbids marriage, he adds: “But because of fornication let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Let the husband render to the wife what is due, and likewise the wife to the husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another.” And again, lest by saying so much on behalf of marriage he seem to exclude chastity, he goes on: “unless perhaps by consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer.” And at once he as it were retracts what he said about “for a time,” lest he seem to be teaching a temporary and brief continence rather than a perpetual one; for he says: “because of your incontinence. But I say this by way of concession, not of command.” Hence by saying “for a time” he teaches that chastity ought to be practiced, so that, having tested the strength of their continence over set intervals of time, both may promise without danger what both must keep forever. What he wants without qualification he states plainly: “I wish all men to be as I myself am,” that is, to live in constant and perpetual chastity.

Do you see how cautiously, how providently, how without giving occasion for any scandal the teacher established his teaching on chastity, not wishing so great a good to waver through the rashness of one person, when it ought to be bound and confirmed by the consent of both? And indeed, what chastity is firmer or safer than one begun by the decision of two and kept by both, or in common? Neither party is anxious for itself alone; each encourages the other to persevere in virtue. For with this, as with other good things, what deserves praise is not merely to have begun but to have completed. As you see, my discourse has for some time been moving over rocky and difficult ground, and does not dare to lean to either side, since it fears both equally; but recognize your own peril from our difficulty. We have preferred to grieve you, perhaps, by telling the truth rather than deceive you with false flattery. The evil, as you see, is twofold, and the danger is equal on both sides; you are hemmed in and constrained from either direction. To scorn and despise your husband altogether is plainly contrary to the apostle's teaching. But to lose the chastity of so long a time and not to pay God what you had promised is a thing to be feared and dreaded—as the common saying goes: you will easily make an enemy of a friend if you do not keep your promises to him. For Scripture says: “If you make a vow to the Lord God, do not delay to pay it, for the Lord God will surely require it of you, and it will be a sin for you.” It says, therefore [?]: show your husband the honor due to him, so that with the consent of both you may be able to pay the Lord the debt you vowed. We do not doubt his conscience, had you waited a little—not that we would draw you back from the good of chastity, but that we would urge his mind with all our strength toward the oracle [?] of chastity, so that he might offer God a voluntary sacrifice for a sweet savor, so that the mind, stripped of all worldly ties, might be free from bodily pleasures, and you might both cling more fully to the Lord's commandments. And lest you think we have said anything carelessly, we have demonstrated it by testimonies of the divine Scriptures, as the apostle also says: “And the two shall be in one flesh”; now not one flesh, but one spirit.

This is a great mystery, and the road of chastity is hard; but great are the rewards, and the Lord calls us in the Gospel, saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” The same Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is sweet and my burden light.” And the same Lord says to those who will be on his left: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels; I do not know you, workers of iniquity. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” All those will certainly wail and mourn who so entangle themselves in the cares of the present life that they forget the life to come, whom the coming of the Lord will overtake [?] while they are weighed down by a kind of sleep of ignorance and false security. So he himself says in the Gospel: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly; for it will come like a snare upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth,” and again: “Watch and pray, for you do not know when the time will be.”

Blessed are those who so await and watch for that day that they prepare themselves for it daily, who do not flatter themselves on their past righteousness but, as the apostle says, are renewed in virtue day by day. For righteousness will not profit a man from the day he ceases to be righteous, just as his iniquity will not harm the wicked man from the day he turns from his iniquity. So neither should the saint feel secure as long as he is engaged in the contest of this life, nor should the sinner despair, since according to the prophet's words quoted above he can make himself righteous in a single day. The whole span of your life is the course you are running, so that you may carry righteousness through to the end and not grow slacker by trusting in your past righteousness. Rather, as the apostle says: “Forgetting what lies behind and straining toward what lies ahead, I press on toward the appointed prize of the heavenly calling,” knowing that it is written that God searches the heart. That is why he strives to keep his soul pure from sin. For this reason it is written: “Keep your heart with all vigilance,” and again: “The Lord loves pure hearts; all the blameless are acceptable to him.” Therefore make it your aim to order the rest of your life without offense, so that you may sing in safety with the prophet: “I walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of my house,” and again: “I will go in to the altar of God, to God who gives joy to my [?],” for it is not enough to have begun: righteousness lies in having completed.
BOBBIO EXCERPTS.

The Lord commanded the ravens to feed Elijah as he sat by the brook Cherith. It is truly a wonderful thing that an unclean bird should supply a holy man with what he needed to live. So if we too imitate Elijah's poverty, even despising what is our own, believe me when I say that unclean animals, that is, sinful men, will serve us with devoted obedience.

Why do we read that Elisha, who was gentle and mild, handed little children over to wild beasts? The prophet Elisha bore the figure of Christ. Indeed, his name is interpreted as [?] of God. And what is the salvation of God but his Son, who is also the Savior of the world?
