The little children who mocked the salvation of God in Elisha represented the Jews, who cried out, saying: "Go up, baldhead, go up!" For Christ was to go up onto the cross at the place of Calvary. And he turned, Scripture says, and cursed them in the name of the Lord. And two bears came out of the wood and killed forty-two children. So too Christ, after his passion and his ascension to heaven, just as Elisha went up to Bethel, that is, to the house of God, turned and cursed the Jews forty-two years after his ascension, and sent two bears, that is, two dreadful kings, Vespasian and Titus, who came out of the forests of the Gentiles and struck them down in cruel slaughter.

"The righteous man falls seven times a day, and rises again." How can someone who falls once and then again be called righteous? He is called righteous because when he falls he gets up again. The number seven signifies rest. Whoever has fallen the seventh time must take care not to fall any further. He ought already to have been on his guard for the future after a single lapse; but God, who is merciful, patiently bears with lapses of this kind, so that a person may come to his senses at least by the seventh. But if someone grows more careless and goes beyond the number of risings, he cannot be called righteous; because of the multitude of his offenses he is counted among the sinners. A person offends in two ways, by intention and by mishap: one wants to sin, while another is overtaken by sin. Mishap, in turn, is divided in two ways, into ignorance and weakness. Judas sinned by intention, saying: "What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?" He willingly carried out what he had intended, and therefore received the just wages of his most wicked will. Peter, on the other hand, denied the Lord out of weakness, fearing death, though he had promised that he would suffer death for Christ. But because he had been overcome suddenly, he therefore earned swift pardon for his lapse. Paul, too, who became a persecutor in ignorance, was healed by speedy pardon, as he himself testifies: "I persecuted the church of God, but I obtained mercy, because I did it in ignorance." So you see that some fall against their will, while others are struck down by their own will. There are also two things in a person, forgetfulness and ignorance. A person forgets God when he purposes to sin; but he is ignorant when he offends by being overtaken. For instance, one man has committed fornication unwillingly [?], while another, though resisting fornication, was overcome by weakness. The sin of both is indeed one and the same, but the penance will not be equal, because the one [fell] unwillingly [?], whereas the other, unwilling, was overcome in the struggle and gave way. Do you see how great the difference between sins is? See how the righteous man falls and is saved when the Lord puts his hand beneath him.

Let us assist God's will with our own power, so that he by his strength may favor our will, for it is written: "It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy." To will and to run is ours; but to show mercy is God's, as the Truth itself testifies to the apostles: "Without me you can do nothing." Likewise John says: "No one can receive anything on earth unless it has been given him from heaven"; and Paul says: "What do you have that you did not receive? If you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" And so on.

So if anyone has now provoked God, let him imitate the example of Moses, who wiped out the guilt of his doubting by the satisfaction of penitence and humility. If anyone has incurred the crime of sacrilege, let him imitate Aaron, who, cleansed of the crime of his transgression through the remedy of confession and humility, was found worthy of the chief priesthood. If anyone has committed adultery and murder, let him consider David and do penance, and, once made whole by this medicine, let him remain in the fear of God. If anyone has been overcome during his confession of faith and, yielding to torture, has become a betrayer of the faith, let him become an imitator of Peter, who denied. Going outside, that is, going out from his faithlessness, let him weep bitterly and run back to the faith. The offenses of great men are displayed in great sins, so that if anyone weak or lowly has gone astray in a similar way, he may look to the example of great men, find easy access to life, and return to faith and penance. And so on.
